#5494. Exaforce’s ExaU lets security staff spin up a personal team of AI agents

Agentic security operations startup Exaforce Inc. today announced the launch of ExaU, a service that lets any security staff member spin up a personal team of artificial intelligence agents.

The new service seeks to move past the first wave of AI agents in security, which Exaforce says were built to offload a single task such as alert triage, risk assessment or penetration testing.

Exaforce argues that as AI absorbs more of the routine work, security staff are now responsible for outcomes that cannot be handed off one task at a time. Added to the mix is that staff are also facing a backlog of tasks, such as checks they mean to run, questions they plan to chase down and briefings owed to senior management.

Leading the list of ExaU features is the ability to create an agent by describing the job in plain language, down to the way a practitioner wants it done. Templates are also available. Each agent is designed to retain decisions, exceptions and past instructions.

To use, a security staff member begins by telling an agent what they are responsible for. The agent then works out what needs doing next and when. The response includes discoveries, questions and recommendations.

The new service also supports sharing agents across a security organization. A chief information security officer’s briefing agent can gather status from the agents used by every team. Exaforce’s own example has a finding setting off a threat hunt, an activity audit and outreach to an employee at the same time. A single assessment then pulls the results of all three together.

Everything runs inside Exaforce on the customer’s own data. With connections to identity providers, cloud services and security telemetry already part of the platform, there are no tokens to mint for ExaU agents. The company’s real-time security knowledge graph is claimed to give each agent an understanding of how systems relate from its first task.

Investigations are carried out by the agents on their own. Under the controls built into ExaU, any action affecting employees, systems or communications requires approval first. Recorded in the Exaforce audit log, every step an agent takes can be reviewed later.

Exabots, the agents Exaforce manages itself, already handle threat detection, alert triage and investigation for every customer on the platform. ExaU is pitched as a complement to that standing workforce. Available now as part of the Exaforce platform, the release follows the September launch of Exaforce AI Security, a kill switch for AI agents that go rogue.

HarbourVest Partners, Peak XV Partners, Mayfield Fund, Khosla Ventures and Seligman Ventures were among the investors in Exaforce’s $125 million Series B round in May. Including that round, total funding since the company’s 2023 founding comes to $200 million.

#5491. What music sells a house? Agents say it’s not about genre

Taylor Swift, classical or silence? Agents explain how they pick open house music, the one rule most follow and why none can prove it works.

Ask real estate agents what soundtrack sells a house, and you’ll get two answers. One is a carefully curated playlist, while the other is silence.

Inman asked agents and brokers from Manhattan to Breckenridge, Colorado, and they described the music they play at showings and open houses and how they match it to the property.

None could point to hard numbers showing a playlist moved a home faster or for more money. What they did offer was a clear set of rules from the agents who use music, and an equally firm argument from those who won’t touch it.

Ben Jacobs, co-founder of the Chestler Jacobs Team at Douglas Elliman in New York City, thinks music raises more questions than it answers. He said he’s not a fan of playing music during showings.

“Buyers may wonder if the agent is trying to mask something, whether it’s street noise, construction nearby, sounds within the building or even a noisy appliance,” Jacobs told Inman. “You want buyers to experience the home as it actually is, without anything distracting from their ability to evaluate the space.”

His co-founder, Jessica Chestler, said music has its place. That place is just not a private showing.

“Music can be wonderful for setting a mood at a cocktail party, listing launch or special event, but during a showing, I think there’s something to be said for letting the property speak for itself,” Chestler said.

Megan Sullivan works at the same brokerage, and she uses music for the very reason Jacobs avoids it. Sullivan sells large estate homes across Fairfield and Westchester counties out of Douglas Elliman’s Greenwich, Connecticut, office. Some of those homes sit within earshot of things a seller can’t fix.

“I actually do like incorporating music into certain showings, particularly when a property is impacted by outside noise from planes, trains or automobiles,” Sullivan said. “Thoughtfully selected background music can help create a more welcoming atmosphere and soften those distractions, allowing buyers to focus on the overall experience of the home. I think it’s very property-specific.”

Jeffrey Hensel is a broker associate with North Coast Financial, a California hard money lender that funds fix-and-flip and probate deals. He looks at it from the investor side.

“Dead silence can amplify every creak, clank, and drip in an otherwise quiet home,” he said. “Background music masks these sounds and provides some white noise to help set a calm mood.”

Agents in the pro-music camp mostly aren’t trying to cover anything up. They simply want buyers to stay longer.

Sandra Daniels of Harry Norman, Realtors | Forbes Global Properties serves the East Cobb and Marietta area outside Atlanta. She’s currently listing a $3.9 million estate in The River Club in Suwanee, Georgia.

For those showings, she rotates light classical piano, The Macarons Project and a Spotify playlist called “Nora Ephron + Nancy Meyers Dinner Party.”

“Put a buyer in a home with a glass of Champagne or a cup of coffee and the right music playing, and that cozy, inviting atmosphere encourages people to stay, relax and feel at home,” Daniels told Inman.

Daniels also has a low-tech trick for vacant listings she expects to sell in the first week. She bought an old-school CD player and a few classical CDs. She leaves it on repeat through the first weekend of showings and stops by each evening to turn off the lights and music and lock up.

Natalia Bassova, founder and CEO of Resort Real Estate in Breckenridge, Colorado, saw the same effect at a luxury mountain listing. The home looked great, she said, but it showed cold.

“By adding some background instrumental music, it gave the buyers more time to spend in the home. They spent more time in the kitchen and great room areas,” Bassova said. “The property didn’t change, but the atmosphere did.”

For mountain and luxury homes, Bassova plays acoustic and piano music, including Ludovico Einaudi and The Piano Guys. For condos and new construction, she switches to soft contemporary instrumentals.

Agents who play music disagree on genre, but almost all agree on one thing: avoid lyrics.

“If the buyer begins to think about the music, then it is having a negative impact,” Bassova said. Her never-play list covers anything with strong lyrics, politics, swearing or heavy bass.

Andrea Seeney is a global real estate advisor with Atlanta Fine Homes Sotheby’s International Realty and a trained opera singer and classical pianist. She compared lyrics to a seller’s personal effects.

“Acoustic performances are best because they set a tone and allow the buyer to fill in the blanks with their own thoughts,” Seeney said.

She leans toward jazz and usually plays Spotify’s Coffee House radio or its Ella Fitzgerald playlist. She says music works on buyers through memory: a song can take someone back to a time and place they enjoyed, “and that memory then reflects positively on the home.”

Hensel takes the lyrics rule a step further, to genre itself. If an agent plays hip-hop or country for a buyer who doesn’t listen to it, he says, that signals an assumption about who the buyer is. That can create friction neither side notices. His pick is quiet cocktail-lounge jazz like Miles Davis or Bill Evans, at a steady tempo and volume.

He also cited retail research by psychological scientists Adrian North and Lorraine Sheridan of Curtin University and Charles Areni of Macquarie University. It found that shoppers who heard classical music rated merchandise as higher quality and were willing to spend more.

Some agents ignore the rulebook completely.

Rachel Kilmer, an agent with ReeceNichols Real Estate in Kansas City, Missouri, plays Taylor Swift at nearly every open house. She swaps in country for more rural listings.

“In Kansas City, she’s a conversation starter,” Kilmer said. “People come in, and it’s, ‘Are you a Swiftie?’ ‘No, but I love the Chiefs!’ It really helps loosen up the conversation.”

She added, “I’m the one sitting there listening to it for two hours!”

Monica Shea, a broker with KW Aspire in Colorado Springs, Colorado, builds whole open houses around a theme, and the music follows.

She played the Eras Tour set list at a Taylor Swift–themed open house and the Frozen soundtrack at a hot cocoa bar event. A Halloween open house got not-too-spooky Halloween music. For regular showings, she has sellers put on a YouTube channel with seasonal background music and scenery.

Shea’s never-play list puts her directly at odds with a few other agents: smooth jazz. Shea says she never plays “anything that sounds like the Weather Channel.”

Marcel Finkelstein of Team BlackStar at eXp Realty hosts open houses every Sunday across Monmouth County, New Jersey. He sees music as more of an icebreaker than a staging tool.

His Apple Music rotation includes lounge instrumentals, vocal-free dance-pop and Bon Entendeur. It also has Afro house from DJ Alex Niyazov and the warm trumpet and sax of Fausto Papetti and Paul Mauriat.

He uses the same approach whether the listing is a $600,000 two-bedroom condo in Manalapan or a $2 million six-bedroom in Colts Neck.

“I want the atmosphere to feel calm, comfortable and welcoming, rather than like a sales presentation,” Finkelstein said.

Finkelstein added that his Instagram followers also know how much he loves music.

“Every week, I share new songs and incorporate music into my stories and posts about homes,” he said. “It’s a personal interest that carries through into how I present properties.”

On setup, agents who play music give similar advice. Keep the volume low enough that buyers can ask questions and the agent can hear their feedback. Use one good speaker rather than several.

Bassova puts hers in the middle of the home, and Seeney puts a small Bluetooth speaker in the kitchen. When sellers have a Sonos system, Daniels connects to it from her MacBook or iPad. Otherwise, she brings her own Bose speaker.

Kilmer runs her music from an iPad instead of her phone. “That way, incoming calls and texts don’t interrupt the music,” she said.

As for proof, none of the agents Inman spoke with track music as a performance metric. Bassova said she gets buyer feedback that certain homes feel relaxing, but nothing tied to days on market or offers.

So the evidence is anecdotal, and the playlists don’t agree. Agents can’t even settle on jazz. Both camps share one goal: the buyer should notice the home, not the soundtrack.

As Bassova said, “If the buyer begins to think about the music, then it is having a negative impact.”

#5490. Palo Alto Networks report finds organizations struggle to track and secure AI agents in the cloud

A new report out today from cybersecurity company Palo Alto Networks Inc. finds that artificial intelligence agents have quickly become a fixture in software development, but many organizations can’t properly track or secure what those agents are doing in the cloud.

Now in its sixth year, the State of Cloud Security Report 2026 is based on a survey of 2,800 security executives and practitioners in 10 countries. Along with how AI is being used to build and deploy software, the report looks at how quickly organizations are able to respond when something goes wrong.

The use of AI agents was found to be close to universal, with 99% of respondents saying they use agents for autonomous or semiautonomous actions in their development pipelines. Some 73% said the agents are allowed to modify code, pipeline configurations or production environments, and agents are even doing security testing at 44% of organizations.

The amount of change is going up as a result. Some 82% said AI-driven development has increased the volume of infrastructure updates reaching their cloud, yet organizations on average enforce fewer than three of the eight predeployment security checks measured in the survey. AI is also being used to generate infrastructure-as-code templates at 42% of organizations, but only 34% scan that code before production.

Not surprisingly, problems are getting through. Respondents said that on average, 19% of high and critical application security issues reached production over a 90-day period. It takes an average of 18.4 days to get a fix for a security issue found in code into production.

When respondents were asked what was stopping them from fixing issues before deployment, the most common answer was business pressure to release quickly at 39%. Unclear risk acceptance policies came second at 30%.

Accountability is also an issue when it comes to agents. Two in five organizations said they are unable to reconstruct what an AI agent did, a share that rises to 46% in financial services, while 53% said agent activity is logged under a developer’s identity or personal access token. That means when something goes wrong, investigators first have to figure out which actions were taken by a person and which were taken by an agent before they can work out what was affected.

Removing access once something does go wrong is also slow. Some 60% of organizations still need manual intervention to revoke access for nonhuman identities, and it takes an average of 2.5 days to revoke or rotate compromised developer credentials, API keys or pipeline secrets.

Data governance has its own issues. Nearly all organizations, 99%, said they had found ungoverned AI in their environment in the past year, yet only 9% are able to automatically discover and classify it. Some 40% said governed data had been copied into ungoverned AI tools, and 39% had seen sensitive or regulated data used to train or fine-tune models without authorization.

Despite the gaps, confidence is high. Almost every respondent, 97%, said they are at least somewhat confident they can secure their AI supply chain and applications, though only 36% can monitor AI behavior in production and just 30% can detect prompt injection.

The final section of the report looks at the threat from frontier AI models that can find and exploit software vulnerabilities on their own. Nearly all respondents, 98%, said they are concerned about it, and 65% said it poses a significant or severe threat to global critical infrastructure and financial systems over the next 12 to 18 months. Utilities were the most likely of any sector to rate the threat as significant or severe at 79%, compared with 48% in telecommunications.

Interestingly, though the report refers to “frontier AI-powered capabilities,” the survey questions at the back of it call them “Mythos-grade” threats, a reference to Anthropic PBC’s Claude Mythos models. Palo Alto Networks was one of the launch partners in Anthropic’s Project Glasswing, which gave defenders early access to Claude Mythos Preview in April.

The report argues that against attackers working at machine speed, an 18.4-day fix cycle leaves organizations exposed for more than 17 days after a vulnerability can be discovered. Part of the problem, according to the report, is fragmented tooling, with only 19% of organizations saying they operate with unified telemetry and workflows across code, cloud, identity and runtime. Nearly half of organizations, 47%, still do the work of correlating application vulnerabilities with runtime threats by hand, a number that’s even higher in the U.S. at 55%.

The report ends with a series of recommendations for organizations to secure their cloud environments as AI agents take on more work. Agents should be given their own identities with a clear owner and only the permissions they need to do their job. Security teams are also advised to automate the fixing of recurring issues, though only after rollback procedures have been put in place.

#5488. Goodbye, manual work: AI-native CRM platform Dreamteam raises $53M to automate enterprise sales

Intelligent sales software startup Dreamteam AI Inc. said today it has raised $53 million in early-stage funding to try to flip the narrative around customer relationship management platforms, which often seem like more of a hindrance than a help, by actually getting work done for sales teams.

The funds come by way of a seed and Series A round led by Accel Partners with participation from Together Fund and Premji Invest.

CRM platforms such as Salesforce and Hubspot have served as vital cogs in the wheel sales-focused enterprises for more than a quarter of a century. But these days they often create just as much work as they save, says Dreamteam co-founder and Chief Executive Anand Venkatraman (pictured, center, alongside co-founders Ramesh Parthasarathy and Senthil Kanthaswamy). While organizations are striving to use artificial intelligence to automate more of their business processes, CRMs are holding them back, he believes.

The problem with legacy CRM platforms is that they’re totally reliant on manual data entry, Venkatraman explained. Because their architectures are built around structured data fields and rigid, hand-coded workflows, they create a tight bottleneck that makes it almost impossible for autonomous AI agents that feed primarily on semantic data to get anything done.

“When a sales prospect expresses price hesitation or mentions a competitor, a salesperson registers it immediately,” he said. “But a legacy CRM, starving for unstructured nuance, misses it entirely, leaving AI agents without the vital context needed to reason effectively.”

To provide this context, Dreamteam has rebuilt the CRM from the ground up around the idea of a “company brain,” or a living memory of the business that constantly updates itself by ingesting new information from meetings with clients, prospects and team members, emails and other connected tools. As with all AI-native platforms, there’s also a generous dose of automation in the shape of four AI agents, or teammates, which specialize in different tasks.

The agents include Rachel, which handles account research; Sally for meeting preparations and follow-ups; Raj, which monitors for pipeline risks; and Alex, which serves as the CRM administrator, keeping the platform ticking over without any human intervention.

Venkatraman said he and his co-founders designed Dreamteam’s architecture specifically to address the historic shortcomings of legacy CRM platforms, which struggle to dig up the most vital business intelligence, leaving teams flying blind. “When a CEO asks why the quarter’s three biggest deals were lost, RevOps spends two weeks building a partial answer from whatever the reps happened to type,” he said. “The richest signals from meetings, emails, and calls were never captured, so the answer is always incomplete and always late.”

Legacy CRMs also fail to capture institutional knowledge, which means that everything a senior sales representative knows about the clients they work with leaves when they depart the company. There’s also a heavy administrative tax, with users forced to waste valuable time entering data to keep the platform up to date.

“CRMs don’t have a shortage of features,” Venkatraman said. “But they have a shortage of context and trust, and they lack the ability to get actual work done.”

Dreamteam does things differently. By capturing the unspoken context around each deal an organization does, it says, its platform can help to prevent new leads from going stale. Monitoring everything that’s said and agreed to in meetings, via chats and emails and other tools, the platform can pick out the most important signals, such as pricing sensitivities, objections and stakeholder dynamics.

It remembers all of the fine details of each specific deal. That way, even if the main sales rep involved suddenly leaves, it will retain all of the context so whoever takes over the account knows what needs to be done next.

The platform also employs humanlike reasoning. “When a prospect says, ‘The board is pushing hard on costs,’ it knows the proposal should lead with ROI, not features,” Venkatraman explained. “The CRM was supposed to give companies a complete picture of their customers, yet the richest parts of that picture have always lived outside the CRM.”

The startup has already witnessed significant traction with its agentic, contextual approach: It’s used by hundreds of organizations across the AI, healthcare, manufacturing, consulting and online media sectors. Dreamteam has enabled those early adopters to transform the way they handle sales.

Because the CRM continuously self-updates its records following daily customer interactions, it means sales people have much more time to focus on actually selling rather than data entry. Senior leaders have more visibility into deal pipelines, and can immediately find out why deals are stalling or how their customer’s sentiments are shifting.

Scott Olechowski, chief product officer at the video streaming service Plex Inc., said he was especially taken with the tight level of integration with Dreamteam and the company’s existing information technology stack. “The combination of simplicity and power hits the sweet spot for us,” he said. “The ability to integrate with the AI tools we are using across our organization is a game-changer.”

Venkatraman believes Dreamteam can have an even greater impact in future by expanding its shared intelligence layer beyond sales operations. His ambition is to build a platform that spans the entire customer lifecycle, from onboarding to customer success, renewals and upselling, to ensure that organizations can squeeze the most value out of the deal context it captures.

“Much of what’s learned during sales is lost or fragmented when a customer moves into implementation or customer success,” he pointed out. “But the same company brain that knows why a customer bought should also help teams onboard them, spot risks and find ways to grow the relationship.”

One way Dreamteam intends to pursue this vision is through what it calls “Magic Apps,” which is a capability that lets users build custom dashboards and tailored CRM workflows using natural language prompts. “The apps live inside Dreamteam, inherit its data permissions and action-level authorizations, and stay connected to customer records, workflows and the Company Brain, so you can customize without rebuilding the foundation,” Venkatraman said.

Premji Invest’s Saravanan Nattanmai has already bought into this vision, stressing the need for CRM systems to become more than just a system of record. He characterizes what Dreamteam is building as a “system of intelligence.”

“Dreamteam sets out to intuitively understand user intent, build deep contextual intelligence and execute workflows seamlessly through autonomous AI teammates,” he said. “We believe the future of enterprise software lies in AI-native systems that don’t just augment existing workflows but fundamentally reimagine how work gets done.”

#5487. NAR’s latest data, must-have AI tools, Compass’ 15 new lawsuits

Congratulations, you’ve made it to Friday again this week. But before you head out for the weekend, we’re bringing you a quick catch-up on the biggest headlines and the most helpful how-tos for your business. So, Take 5 and peruse our top editor picks for this week and why they matter to your business.

P.S. Don’t miss The Download, our weekly column that breaks down one of the week’s top stories and equips you with what you’ll need to meet next Monday head-on.

Homeownership is slipping further out of reach for young Americans, according to the National Association of Realtors’ 2026 Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers. The report, released on Thursday, revealed that the share of first-time homebuyers rose 1 percent year over year to 22 percent. Despite the small gain, first-time buyer activity remains near historic lows (21 percent) and 18 percentage points below pre-2008 trends (40 percent). Same as last year, the median age of a first-time homebuyer was 40 — roughly a decade older than the typical median age in the 1980s.

Why it matters: This annual report gives you a pulse on national real estate trends and how you might want to pivot your strategies. For example, as noted above, the median age of the first-time homebuyer is 40, and the share of single women homeowners has risen to 20 percent. A longer nurture campaign might be in order (ahem, see below), and if you’re not already marketing toward single women, perhaps you should. Read the full report for more.

EXTRA: The buyer who can’t close for a year is your best asset in 2026

AI has been the topic of conversation for the past couple of years. And there’s a lot of talk. So how do you suss through the noise and find what works for your business? Jimmy Burgess has created a no-nonsense list of seven AI tools that are actually worth your time.

Why it matters: Burgess shares not only his top tools but also how to use them. These tools will help you turn prompts into better questions, find the questions your future clients are asking, remember the details that matter, evaluate your AI search visibility, turn one video into multiple pieces of content, make video editing easier and use AI as a strategist rather than a writing assistant. Don’t feel overwhelmed. You don’t have to use all of them at once.

Krystopher Benyamein recently sold a property in San Pedro where his team hosted nine open houses, mailed 500 postcards, ran digital advertising and created a video that generated more than 1.5 million organic views. They found a buyer and opened escrow, but shortly before closing, that buyer backed out, and they had to start again.

They eventually found another buyer and successfully closed, but when they shared the case study on Instagram, they didn’t lead with the sale price or how much marketing they’d done. They opened with, “Imagine finally selling your house. Then the buyer backs out right before closing.”

That opening puts the reader in the seller’s position. Most homeowners can imagine how frustrating that experience would be, and it naturally creates curiosity about what happened next. From there, they explained how they responded, got the property back in front of buyers and ultimately closed.

Why it matters: In today’s market, there are many stories of buyers backing out of deals. This approach allows you to create content that keeps you top of mind, show sellers exactly how you work and reach a wider audience. Benyamein shows you how to do it and shares a FREE Canva template to help get the job done.

VA loans often get passed over for conventional loans. Inman’s Nick Pipitone spoke with Fathom Realty’s Lindsey Schmidt, an Army veteran who served in Iraq, about why VA financing still carries a stigma among sellers and listing agents, how she gets around it and why VA assumptions remain one of the most misunderstood tools in the market.

Why it matters: Military members often have to move. Understanding and busting myths about VA loans can help you get ahead of objections before making an offer, which will help you get more deals across the finish line and get more service members into homes.

Compass has been busy, creating and formalizing policy around employees in association leadership positions and how Compass brokerage agents cooperate on private listings.

The company announced Thursday that it is filing 15 federal antitrust lawsuits against MLSs across eight states, accusing the organizations of illegally restricting how agents can publicly market homes outside their systems. Compass alleges that the MLSs unlawfully fine agents for publicly marketing listings outside the MLS, with penalties it says can reach $15,000.

Why it matters: Compass International Holdings is currently in litigation with 16 total MLSs across 18 federal lawsuits. Not only is this big news that’s making waves throughout the industry, but its ripple effects could impact your MLS’s rules, if they haven’t already.

EXTRA: What Compass’ leadership ban signals for agents and associations

#5485. Anthropic's IPO filing shows Amazon and Google will own about 28% of its stock

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Amazon is set to hold nearly 15% and Google about 14% after the IPO and a roughly $26 billion private placement

Amazon $AMZN and Alphabet $GOOGL's Google are set to own about 28% of Anthropic stock in aggregate after the company's IPO and a concurrent private placement, according to Bloomberg.

Amazon would hold nearly 15% of Anthropic's outstanding capital stock and Google about 14%, according to Bloomberg. Google's stake takes in non-voting stock worth around $10 billion, which it committed to purchase in a private placement worth about $26 billion that is running in tandem with the IPO.

Google will hold 32% of Anthropic’s non-voting Class N stock, and Amazon will hold 34%, according to Bloomberg. Amazon’s holdings would climb to 24% of all outstanding stock if the company lifted its ownership cap and converted every one of its notes. The agreement allows Amazon to convert notes only if doing so wouldn’t push its overall stake above 12%, and Amazon has committed to leaving the cap in place.

Anthropic and its co-founders could raise as much as $64.4 billion through the IPO at the top of the range, according to Bloomberg. Counting the private placement as well, the sale would be the largest initial share offering on record, topping SpaceX's base offering of $75 billion in June.

The IPO is scheduled to be priced Wednesday, Nov. 18, with shares starting to trade a day later, according to Bloomberg. Goldman Sachs $GS and Morgan Stanley $MS are leading the offering alongside 20 other banks, and Anthropic shares are expected to list with the ticker ANT on the Nasdaq $NDAQ Global Select Market.

Anthropic launched the roadshow for its IPO on Nov. 10 with an expected price range of $70 to $78 a share. At the top of that range, the company could carry a fully diluted valuation as high as $1.405 trillion. Microsoft $MSFT and Google are among seven companies that agreed to buy $26 billion of Class N common stock in the private placement at the IPO price, a purchase that depends on the IPO being completed.

The filing says Amazon, Google and Microsoft each wear several hats for Anthropic, backing it financially, buying its services, helping distribute its products and competing against it, according to Bloomberg. Customers who buy access to Claude through accounts with the three cloud providers generated about 44% of Anthropic's revenue over the opening nine months of 2026.

Anthropic also disclosed lock-up agreements that restrict certain holders from selling or otherwise transferring stock in connection with the offering without written consent from the underwriters' representatives, with listed exceptions.

#5484. Google says an AI framework turned security patches into exploits with no human in the loop

A new report out today from Google LLC’s Google Threat Intelligence Group finds that for the first time, attackers have used an artificial intelligence framework running with no human in the loop to turn security patches into exploits.

Called exploit_agent, the framework turned up on an exposed staging server, where it was wired into several frontier and locally hosted large language models. Its job, according to GTIG, is continuous comparison of popular web application code before and after each patch announcement. Once a likely flaw is identified, the exploit it drafts is executed automatically.

Data taken from victims was sitting on the same server, alongside scripts for brute-forcing, installing webshells and even removing webshells left by rival attackers. Victim telemetry suggests the operator was most interested in French websites tied to media, entertainment and education. Written in Russian, one comment in the framework’s configuration file tells whoever set it up to enter the keys “right here, not in the chat.”

In the previous edition of the quarterly tracker two months ago, GTIG said it had not observed fully autonomous attack pipelines deployed against targets in the wild. That changed over the past quarter, according to the new report, titled “Agentic Threat Activity Crosses a Significant Threshold.” Because the source material for a patched flaw is finite, GTIG believes attackers may find it more efficient to point LLMs at n-day vulnerabilities than to hunt for zero-days.

How quickly the gap between disclosure and a working exploit can close shows in the case of two flaws in print management servers from PaperCut Software Pty Ltd., chained together and exploited as zero-days in late August. Security researchers and Huntress Labs Inc. used large language models to generate working exploits within a day of disclosure.

A campaign tracked by GreyNoise Intelligence Inc. four days after disclosure is believed to have relied on LLMs to build its exploits before it hit hundreds of organizations. One foothold in that campaign reached domain administrator within minutes, GreyNoise found.

Elsewhere, open-source agentic penetration testing frameworks are being used to automate discrete steps of live intrusions. During one intrusion against the U.S. aerospace sector, a threat actor was observed using the multi-agent framework CAIRN.

Another actor ran a customized platform built on PentAGI between late August and early October to scan a wide range of organizations in Asia for vulnerabilities. For now, the noisy forensic trail left by unrestricted autonomous execution is said to make the frameworks easier to detect.

According to GTIG, influence operations now use models for far more than writing posts. Using cloud phone farms, a turnkey platform that one commercial contractor was building with help from the Gemini API is designed to run more than 100,000 social media accounts. To make generated photos pass as smartphone shots, prompts behind a separate platform, which targeted political sentiment across Europe and the Middle East, are said to have called for deliberate camera flaws.

Among government-backed actors, photos on the fake recruiter profiles that a suspected North Korean group tracked as UNC6836 used to approach cryptocurrency organizations in North America and Europe were found to carry Google’s SynthID watermarks. By way of altered .claude/settings.json files in internal code repositories, the group later rigged each launch of Anthropic PBC’s Claude Code to download its SOMBERMEME backdoor.

Google said it disabled the accounts and assets tied to the Gemini misuse it found. Google DeepMind has also used the findings to strengthen its classifiers.

#5482. White House formed multi-agency team to prevent repeat of nationwide flight shutdown

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Officials from the FAA, Defense Department, Transportation Department and intelligence office are working on preventing a repeat of the Nov. 13 ground stop

The White House organized a "tiger team" that draws on officials from the Federal Aviation Administration, the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, the Defense Department and the Transportation Department, with the aim of keeping another nationwide ground stop from happening, according to CBS News. The group has held its first meeting at the White House.

A tiger team, according to CBS News, brings together a handful of specialists to tackle one particular problem that routine operations are poorly equipped to handle.

The FAA issued the nationwide ground stop at about 3:30 p.m. ET on Nov. 13 after a technical problem, and air traffic resumed at 8:15 p.m. that day. About 3,500 aircraft were in the air and all landed safely. Operators canceled about 12,462 flights, though the agency said not all cancellations were directly caused by the ground stop.

The FAA said its legacy equipment became unstable when data flooded its network at a rate of 1,000 connection attempts every 4 to 5 seconds. The initial investigation points to a radar site in Amarillo, Texas, and a radio communications site in El Dorado, Arkansas. L3Harris, the FAA's network service provider, had been working at the El Dorado site, including deploying a new router.

The FAA said it has no indication of a cyberattack. It said it disabled the broadcasting function on the originating routers and on more than 60 similar routers, and that it and L3Harris are still investigating the root cause.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford provided an update on the restoration of airspace. Duffy said officials have not determined whether contractor error or a faulty router caused the flood. Bedford said the router replacement was routine maintenance of the existing telecommunications network and not part of the $12.5 billion modernization effort.

Duffy would not rule out another ground stop while upgrades to the system are under way, according to CBS News. Asked about a Government Accountability Office report on the modernization effort, Duffy told CBS News: “We are going, I think, at the right speed. We have to get off old network, old telecom.”

The GAO report, issued in September, found that the FAA has advanced the effort but may be favoring quick action over cost control and the risk of disrupting air traffic, according to CBS News. The GAO also found that the FAA has neither a total cost estimate nor a master schedule covering related projects. Duffy is asking Congress for $50 billion for the updates.

President Donald Trump blamed the previous administration for an "old and broken" FAA system and urged Congress to provide money after the ground stop. Nationwide ground stops are rare. The previous two followed the Sept. 11 attacks and a brief FAA computer failure in January 2023.

#5481. Sumo Logic expands AWS Observability Solution with one-click deployment and new regions

Data analytics software firm Sumo Logic Inc. today released an expanded AWS Observability Solution, a monitoring package for Amazon Web Services Inc. users that can now be deployed in one click from AWS Marketplace.

Sumo Logic is pitching the update at cloud teams that would otherwise have to build their own dashboards before they can properly watch an AWS environment. Much of the company’s recent product work has gone into artificial intelligence agents that take on incident investigations.

Support for AWS regions in Zurich, Melbourne and New Zealand takes the number covered by the solution to 20. Workloads running in those three regions can now be watched with the same prebuilt alerts Sumo Logic offers elsewhere on 12 core AWS services. Lambda, DynamoDB and Application Load Balancer are among them.

Zurich has been on the company’s list since February, when Sumo Logic said its security products would come to the AWS Europe (Zurich) Region for customers bound by Switzerland’s Federal Act on Data Protection.

Anyone signing up through Quick Launch, the AWS Marketplace option behind the one-click deployment, can now do the whole thing — buying the package, setting it up and getting it deployed — without stepping outside their own AWS account. Sumo Logic says the deployments themselves are versioned, in Terraform and CloudFormation alike, which the company expects will mean less configuration drift over time.

Root Cause Agent, which Sumo Logic put into preview for operations teams on Oct. 13, is where much of the telemetry the package collects ends up. When an alert fires, the agent goes digging through the data on its own. A company blog post from the launch says every finding it turns up can be rerun as a search in one click.

The agent belongs to Dojo AI, the agentic AI platform Sumo Logic introduced for security operations teams in September 2025. Root Cause Agent carries that investigative work over into observability. Alongside it in October came new Dojo AI packages that bill all of a customer’s agent use, with Mobot, the SOC Analyst Agent and Root Cause Agent included, against one monthly credit pool.

“AI agents are only as good as the telemetry and context provided to them,” said Keith Kuchler, chief product and technology officer at Sumo Logic. Kuchler added that teams on AWS shouldn’t have to keep “working around regions their tools can’t reach.”

Back in September, Sumo Logic gave customers a way to trim telemetry before ingestion when it expanded its Data Pipelines service. The company, taken private by Francisco Partners in 2023 for $1.7 billion, will show the AWS package at AWS re:Invent in Las Vegas Nov. 30-Dec. 4.

Through Sumo Logic’s listings in AWS Marketplace, version 3.0.0 of the solution is available now to customers that monitor AWS infrastructure.

#5480. Markley Lowell Data Center Certified as Arboretum, the First of its Kind

Once a vacant dumping ground, the Lowell campus now holds about 1,500 trees and more than 400 plant species, projected to remove an estimated 3.8 million pounds of carbon dioxide from the air over the next 50 years

LOWELL, Mass., Nov. 17, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Markley's Lowell data center campus has been accredited as a Level I arboretum by the ArbNet Arboretum Accreditation Program, the world's only international accreditation program specific to arboreta. According to ArbNet, it is the first time a data center has earned the designation.

The recognition places a working digital-infrastructure campus â one that keeps hospitals, first responders, universities and more than 500 organizations online â alongside botanical gardens, public parks and college campuses. Locally, Markley joins UMass Lowell, which earned ArbNet accreditation in 2023.

"We're proud to be the first accredited arboretum on a data center campus," said Jeff Markley, founder and CEO of Markley Group. "The digital infrastructure our region depends on now shares its ground with a thriving tree canopy that helps clean the air and supports local biodiversity. ArbNet accreditation gives us an outside standard to hold ourselves to as we care for this land for decades to come."

Measurable climate benefitsPreliminary findings from a study by AECOM, a global infrastructure consulting firm, project that the campus trees will sequester approximately 3.8 million pounds â about 1,900 tons â of carbon dioxide over the next 50 years.

According to AECOM, that is equivalent to taking more than 400 gasoline-powered cars off the road for a year, or the energy use of 231 homes for a full year.

The canopy also strengthens urban tree cover within the Concord River Watershed, supports pollinators and wildlife, and gives employees, visitors, and neighbors a green space to enjoy.

Seven landscapes, one living collectionWorking with Stantec, a global design and engineering firm, Markley turned the site cleanup into a designed landscape of about 1,500 trees and more than 400 plant species. Stantec describes the project as starting as just a corporate campus landscape that has evolved into a curated collection of trees and diverse plant communities, chosen for form, texture and ecological value.  The campus access loop, once purely utilitarian, now leads visitors through a sequence of seven distinct outdoor rooms that change with every season.

The collection spans maples, deciduous ornamentals, Japanese cultivars, weeping specimens and evergreens. Together, the seven rooms show that meaningful habitat, urban forestry and critical technology infrastructure can share a single, seamless landscape.

What's nextThis spring, Markley, in partnership with AlvÃ©ole, will add beehives, wildflower meadows and milkweed to draw pollinators and monarch butterflies to the Lowell campus. The company also plans to extend the arboretum program to its other properties.

"Data centers power the digital economy, but they also sit on real land in real communities. With its investment in AlvÃ©ole's nature program, Markley Group is putting itself at the forefront of biodiversity data collection," said Alex McLean, Co-founder and CEO of AlvÃ©ole. "Nature is becoming something companies have to measure and report on, and the operators who act now and can prove it's working will set the standard for the industry."

The Jeff Markley Arboretum will open to the public each year to celebrate Arbor Day. ArbNet accreditation is valid for five years and can then be renewed.

For more information, visit  https://www.jeffmarkleyarboretum.com/.

Markley Lowell is committed to investing in and strengthening the Lowell community.

#5479. HSBC sold a slice of an Oracle-linked data center construction loan at a steep discount

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The bank sold about $300 million of an $18 billion loan for Oracle's New Mexico campus at prices in the mid-80s

HSBC Holdings sold about $300 million of an $18 billion construction loan for an Oracle $ORCL-linked data center in New Mexico at a discount, according to Bloomberg. The sale followed a force majeure notice that Oracle sent to the project's developer, a unit of Blue Owl Capital.

The slice changed hands at mid-80s levels, according to Bloomberg. The campus is in Doña Ana County. An HSBC representative declined to comment, and an Oracle representative did not have an immediate comment.

About 20 banks provided the loan, which goes by the name Project Miner and is divided into tranches that correspond to individual buildings on the campus, according to Bloomberg.

In the syndicated loan market, lenders can typically offload their positions on the secondary market, according to Bloomberg. Banks that fund construction projects usually hold the debt on their own books, and some are barred from selling until a pooled sell-down agreement runs out. A bank that leaves before the build is finished often has to accept a price cut that outweighs the upfront fees it collected.

The sale comes as lenders reconsider how much AI debt they hold amid fresh regulatory resistance after a Democratic sweep, according to Bloomberg. Jensen Huang’s departure as Nvidia $NVDA CEO has also fed worries over how quickly AI can keep expanding.

Oracle sent the force majeure notice in September, a move that would allow it to delay payment on the campus if it does not come online as expected in 2028. Oracle said at the time that the project remained on its planned schedule. Blue Owl said the notice did not change the financial commitments to the project.

The project has also faced a pipeline setback. The gas pipeline serving the site had to be rerouted after state regulators rejected its original path, which pushed the targeted in-service date to next year.

The campus, known as Project Jupiter, forms part of the Stargate AI infrastructure build-out, which leaders of Oracle, OpenAI and SoftBank Group joined President Donald Trump in announcing in early 2025. The campus is planned to have a capacity of 2.45 gigawatts, and slow approvals of its air and pipeline permits have set it back, according to Bloomberg.

#5478. Alecto raises $20M seed funding to make UK property law more accessible to consumers with AI

Alecto Conveyancing Ltd., a London-based artificial intelligence-native law firm, today announced it raised $20 million in seed funding led by Insight Partners to make the law more accessible to the general public.

Firstminute Capital, Blue Lion Global, Andrena Ventures, FJ Labs, Antiportfolio Ventures, the Rigby Group and Mischon de Reya LLP also joined in the round. Angel investors participating in the round included Octopus Group Chief Executive and founder Simon Rogerson and SwiftKey founder John Reynolds.

Founded in September 2025 by CEO Will Rice (pictured), a serial entrepreneur who previously built fintech mortgage lender Gen H, Alecto’s first service targets the United Kingdom conveyancing market, the legal work required to buy and sell property. Rice drew on his experience building a mortgage company and decided to focus initially on bringing more people into ownership. With that expertise, Alecto aims to use AI to help give everyday people greater access to the law.

Alecto argues that traditional legal services are starved, with too few qualified attorneys and too few hours a day. Billing is based on hours, not outcomes and the service model doesn’t lean toward customers; this leads to unpredictable costs and a process that leaves customers in the dark.

The law firm said it’s using AI and legal experts to explain opaque legal processes in plain language and help clients make informed decisions. The company intends to target the property conveyancing market, which represents almost $3.3 billion in the U.K. alone, and aims to become the number one leader in property legal services by 2027.

“For too long, the legal industry has expected customers to work on its terms; now, AI presents the opportunity to put the consumer in control,” Rice said. “People don’t want to buy a lawyer’s time; they want results. Alecto exists to make the law accessible to everyone, giving control back to the consumer.”

Consumer legal services in the U.K. value growth pushed revenue over £55 billion, around $72.5 billion, in 2026, according to a report from Research and Markets. Business and commercial practices lead with 51% market value, followed by growth in the injury and conveyancing law markets.

“Property is where we prove the model. We’re building the technology and operations to rapidly break into new countries and new areas of law,” Rice added. “Ultimately, access to exceptional legal support should not depend on how much money you have or how confidently you can navigate the system.”

#5477. NAR saved for his $541K exit; now it won’t pay, ex-CFO says

License under the Creative Commons Attribution 2.0 Generic license.

Former National Association of Realtors Chief Financial Officer John Pierpoint has sued the organization for unpaid retirement compensation totaling more than $541,000, according to a complaint filed on Tuesday.

Pierpoint alleged NAR has paid senior vice presidents one year of their base salary at retirement since 2005. To avoid booking the full expense when a senior vice president retired, NAR created a Compensation Reserve that let it steadily set aside funds throughout the executive’s tenure, which it would release at retirement. Pierpoint helped establish the reserve in 2005 at the direction of former NAR CEO Dale Stinton, court documents said.

Pierpoint retired from NAR on March 31, 2025 — a date he chose with the 2023 Sitzer | Burnett buyer-broker commission lawsuit in mind. The former CFO said he was key in executing the buyer-broker commission settlement payout, which totaled $418 million. The first settlement payment, totaling roughly $200 million, was issued in February 2025, with subsequent payments of $72 million per year until the full $418 million is paid.

Pierpoint said he notified NAR of his impending retirement in late 2024 and requested his retirement payout. However, six days before his last day with NAR, Pierpoint alleged that a Grant Thornton auditor named White — there is no first name listed in the court documents — emailed him and said that “NAR had been ‘unable to locate any policy or verify any consistent practice’ concerning the Compensation Reserve or ‘the payout to executives of a full year of salary upon retirement.'”

White also allegedly said that the Compensation Reserve “was not used to fund” the exit packages of eight other senior vice presidents who retired before Pierpoint, which are listed in the court documents as L.J., F.S., B.M., D.H., J.G.,  J.B., D.G. and B.G. Real Estate News said L.J., D.G. and B.G. are likely former general counsel Laurie Janik, former SVP of talent development and resources Donna Gland, and former senior vice president and CEO Bob Goldberg.

As a result, Grant Thornton said it was “unable to approve the payout of a full year’s compensation without any concrete proof that such act is mandated by an employment agreement, policy or plan.”

Pierpoint claimed NAR had the funds to pay his retirement benefit and provided a ledger outlining what the Association allegedly reserved from December 2014 to December 2024. He also said the trial balances NAR provided to outside auditors, including Grant Thornton, included evidence of the Compensation Reserve’s existence and purpose.

“NAR carried its obligation to Pierpoint at approximately 97.6 cents on the dollar three months before it refused to pay him anything,” the complaint read. “The practice NAR now claims it cannot verify is documented in NAR’s own ledger, its own year-end schedules, its own payroll records and its own audit files, and was paid to every one of Pierpoint’s predecessors who retired. NAR did not stop believing in its obligation; it stopped wanting to pay it.”

Pierpoint’s counsel accused NAR of shirking its obligation to pay the former CFO due to its financial woes after the settlement. In December 2025, former NAR president Kevin Sears said the buyer-broker commission settlement saved the Association’s finances — the other option was to file an appeal and declare bankruptcy.

“John Pierpoint helped guide NAR through an extraordinarily challenging period in its history, including the financial consequences of the antitrust litigation,” said David Fish, an attorney with Workplace Law Partners, P.C., who represents Pierpoint. “After nearly four decades of service, he expected the organization to honor the same retirement compensation practice it had followed for other senior executives.”

“We believe the evidence will establish that the financial pressures following the antitrust verdict did not relieve NAR of its obligation to pay compensation earned by its employees,” he added.

Pierpoint’s counsel is requesting that NAR pay the $541,059 retirement payout, statutory damages of 5 percent of the unpaid amount for each month it remains unpaid, attorneys’ fees and costs, and prejudgment and post-judgment interest. They also seek a jury trial.

NAR denied Pierpoint’s claims, saying that the former CFO has “[mischaracterized] a varied set of individual arrangements with departing executives as a uniform and guaranteed retirement benefit.”

“Mr. Pierpoint was not entitled to the payment he now seeks, and NAR’s decision was unrelated to its antitrust settlement or its financial condition,” an NAR spokesperson told Inman in an emailed statement. “NAR is committed to appropriate financial controls and responsible stewardship of its members’ dues dollars. NAR pays compensation and benefits that are actually owed, not just because a former executive requests payment. No such obligation exists here, and we intend to vigorously defend against these claims through the appropriate legal process.”

#5475. Democrats are preparing multiple probes of Trump's Venezuela oil deal

Free daily briefing on global business news.

House and Senate committees are laying groundwork to examine the 35% U.S. stake in North American Blue Energy Partners

Congressional Democrats are lining up several investigations of the Trump administration’s agreement with Alejandro Betancourt’s North American Blue Energy Partners (NABEP), according to Bloomberg. Democrats on panels including the House Oversight Committee and the Senate Armed Services Committee have started preparing for those inquiries.

The agreement, announced in August, would hand NABEP a century-long concession covering 17 oil fields in Venezuela, while the U.S. would receive a 35% ownership share of the company, according to Bloomberg. The U.S. would be entitled to buy a fifth of what the fields pump, priced at cost.

Rep. Robert Garcia, a California Democrat expected to take the helm of the House Oversight Committee next year, said the aim is to establish the facts. “We want to go in there and find out exactly what happened,” Garcia told Bloomberg. He added that Democrats also want to pass legislation to prevent any abuse in the future.

Sen. Jack Reed, a Rhode Island Democrat and the top Democrat on the Senate Armed Services Committee, said his panel is among those planning investigations. “If we went in there with Maduro as an excuse, but the real goal is to take oil, that is to me wrong,” Reed told Bloomberg. Sen. Richard Blumenthal, a Connecticut Democrat set to chair the Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, said he is concerned about “the potential for corruption.” A spokesperson for Sen. Martin Heinrich, a New Mexico Democrat expected to take over the Senate energy panel next year, said he plans to keep overseeing the deal, according to Bloomberg.

Following their midterm election victories, Democrats in both chambers will have the authority to summon administration officials for testimony, demand records and, if needed, issue subpoenas, according to Bloomberg. Their questions center on the contract's provisions, the compensation the U.S. extended to NABEP for its equity stake and the mechanism for supervising oil revenue. Democrats have also faulted the administration for keeping the text under wraps and questioned Betancourt's role, citing money-laundering and corruption probes that have targeted him in the U.S., Spain and Switzerland. Betancourt denies any wrongdoing and has faced no charges.

House Natural Resources Committee Democrats intend to carry on an inquiry launched earlier in the year, a staffer on the committee told Bloomberg. The Senate Foreign Relations Committee is also expected to launch an investigation.

Four ranking Senate Democrats, including Reed and Heinrich, had challenged the legality of the Pentagon's plan to take a 35% stake in NABEP in a letter to top administration officials. They demanded the full text of the deal before it was finalized. House Democrats sent a similar letter.

White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers defended the deal. "This deal is a major win for both the United States and Venezuela," Rogers said, according to Bloomberg. "If Democrats choose to pursue sham investigations over commonsense victories, they are choosing to work against the American people."

The administration has argued the deal would cut gasoline prices for Americans and give the government a route to restocking the strategic oil reserve, according to Bloomberg. A NABEP spokesperson told Bloomberg taxpayers paid nothing for the U.S. stake and that U.S. citizens must hold most of the seats on NABEP's board.

#5474. At KubeCon 2026, the illusion of AI control meets the reality of implementation

GUEST COLUMN by Jason English

I revisited Salt Lake City for KubeCon/CloudNativeCon NA 2026 hoping to find practical approaches to delivering customer value amidst a rapidly shifting kaleidoscope of artificial intelligence-driven solutions that are making it increasingly difficult to trust our own eyes and ears.

This year, the host Cloud Native Computing Foundation set its theme as “Cloud Native Without Limits,” and judging by the record-shattering pace of new community developments with more than 230 active projects, and the increasing adoption rate of AI for building and consuming applications, the momentum will only grow.

“If you look back at last year’s KubeCon in Atlanta, OpenClaw was not released yet, MCP was less than a year old, and inference in cloud native was just getting started,” Chris Anzyzcyk, chief technical officer of CNCF, said in the opening remarks.

“We knew we were moving out of a phase where most of the AI compute was used for training and we were going to massively ramp up inference,” said Jonathan Bryce, executive director of CNCF. “Just in the last eight months, we’ve seen a 4X increase in inference traffic across the industry. That’s really an incredible increase in the AI footprint. Inference is no longer just an opportunity, it’s now a cloud-native production workload.”

With more than 350K CNCF contributors and 21.2 million cloud-native developers worldwide, fully three-quarters of them are already using AI coding agents, according to the latest State of Cloud Native Development Q3 2026 report, and a show of hands in the room hinted at a much higher presence of AI tooling on the engineer’s desktop.

Likewise, two-thirds of self-described AI-driven organizations are standardizing on Kubernetes and related open-source technologies.

There’s a clear connection here, but AI is not the whole story. Enterprises still need to modernize their application fleets, and deploy, scale, secure and observe their most critical systems, in order to get beyond the AI hype and realize business value.

With an open mind and a skeptical eye, here were some of the interesting new perspectives and vendor solutions I encountered at the show.

With the rapid enterprise rollout of agentic AI, every developer is being challenged to apply human decision insight while working at agent speed, one of the major themes of the show.

Getting there will take more than new technologies, it will also require a lot of collaboration and understanding. The Kubernetes AI Conformance Program launched at KubeCon NA 2025 now has 42 major participating vendors agreeing to consistent standards, and this year there are new Kubernetes AI Certifications for upskilling engineers, whether they are just starting out, or if they are “Golden Kubestronauts” who already passed every course CNCF offers.

“Kubernetes has become the standard API for deploying a workload to a computer, including AI,” said Dan Ciruli, vice president and general manager for cloud native at Nutanix Inc. “The reason, in my opinion, is because the CNCF gave a safe haven for anyone from the smallest startup of two people to the largest companies on Earth to feel safe in donating labor, and code, and IP, and agreeing on things. And that, in turn, gave everybody, from governments to financial services to hot startups, the confidence that they could consume it.”

The firm recently introduced their Nutanix Agent Gateway and an NKP Metal solution that allows Kubernetes clusters and workloads to run on bare metal as well as virtual machines in EKS, AKS or GKE for what they call a “dual-native” experience.

“How are you going to safely and sustainably connect thousands of agents to the systems of record that actually run the business such as customer loyalty or inventory?” asked Matt DeBergalis, CEO, Apollo Graph Inc., doing business as Apollo GraphQL, which supports the popular open source GraphQL query language, presenting a new semantic domain model for deterministically interpreting AI prompts and controls for each record.

Last year CNCF announced a Dynamic Resource Allocation or DRA capability, which unlocked new possibilities for the community to optimize AI workloads running in Kubernetes. This year, sandboxing, or running agents in secure instances to prevent escapes, hijacking and overprovisioning, was the watchword.

Development has moved fast in this area, with two new projects: a Agent Substrate layer contributed by Google that optimizes resource consumption of thousands of agent sandboxes, and OpenShell, an Nvidia Corp.-contributed project for secure sandboxed runtimes.

Startup Apelogic Inc. doing business as HyperShell built an operational agent envelope based on OpenShell that defines guardrails what systems an autonomous agent can access, and what actions it can take, based on the business or system intent the agent was intended to serve.

Cast AI started out as a cloud cost optimization layer for rightsizing clusters on major hyperscalers, but as cloud native infrastructure started taking over enterprise environments, it now finds itself automating and optimizing more AI workloads across CPUs and GPUs, memory and storage. New at KubeCon, their Kimchi code agent governs and deploys application infrastructures from a prompt, which allows developers shift left agentic reviews before production tuning.

Floxdev Inc., which I covered as a startup with their Nix-based lean containerized environment deployments in 2025, put its Flox platform directly in the AI delivery path, giving agents skills to stamp out identical complete environments that include all dependencies, without reproducing any element of the software supply chain inventory that wasn’t intended to change. This moves agentic loops faster with lower compute costs, but the real value is when human engineers can reduce future maintenance and security remediation costs.

This year’s CNCF graduation of the OpenTelemetry project couldn’t come at a better moment, making OTel the lingua franca of application performance, scalability and reliability.

While observability was traditionally considered the domain of engineers and operators, now everyone from data analysts to business executives may be using an LLM or an agent to interact with enterprise applications, potentially changing software, or delivering more agents, in the process.

Splunk, a division of Cisco Systems Inc. has added to its agent observability suite with a specialized language model called Eval-G1 that can run prompt-and-response evals in sub-second times at sub-cent costs, giving engineers the ability to interrupt a faulty response in real time, before it reaches customers. A new Evaluation Studio helps teams generate guardrails in a low-code graphical environment. Also cool, a tokenomics feature (from the recent acquisition of Galileo, which we just covered) that analyzes token spend versus system and business performance metrics.

“It’s been exciting to see how OpenTelemetry, which started out as tens of thousands of adaptors for every application and client, has transitioned with the AI revolution so that now, we have frameworks that just emit OTel natively,” said Morgan McLean, senior director of product management at Splunk and OpenTelemetry co-creator. “So Splunk, and our competitors, can just launch new observability features without putting 30 people on writing new integrations.”

Since a lot of AI projects start out as experiments, observability stalwart Dynatrace LLC has made several moves to meet smaller teams where they are in validating each feature for performance and reliability before enterprise-scale rollouts. It recently acquired Bindplane for OTel-native telemetry pipelines, BlueBox, which gives developers a custom agent for debugging and checks within a coding IDE, and Arize, which maintains the popular Phoenix open-source tool for AI evaluations.

New Relic Inc. released a new Autopilot Kubernetes Agent, a virtual SRE that users can interact with via natural language to look across telemetry and APM data to assess the health of the cluster and application, triage issues with a complete stack trace, and recommend resolutions.

“Especially when you bring agents into your environment, you can’t just take your telemetry and throw it over to a general-purpose LLM, because there are known deterministic patterns and historical insights about Kubernetes we’ve been working to resolve for years,” said Jemiah Sius, vice president of market strategy and developer relations at New Relic.

A lot of the governance difficulty with agents and sandboxes and policies isn’t a technical problem; it is about user experience. Human engineers don’t like being “in the loop” for AI, aka “Meat Proxies,” that continuously pass along approvals. Humans need to be in control, with less toil and more focus on what customers want out of AI applications.

“You can try to create a secure agent sandbox with a policy where everything is disabled by default until a human approves it, but eventually, someone gets tired of being in that approval loop,” said Simone Morellato, senior director of product marketing, Rafay Systems Inc., an AI infrastructure delivery platform used by leading neoclouds. “So you give an agent access to one thing, and eventually you end up giving them access to everything. And at that point, you are back at square one.”

Since I covered Edera Inc. last year, this hardened runtime container vendor is finding new traction in this agentic age by continuing to strengthen the stack from the bottom up, with an agent runtime and OCAP bounded authority that acts as a switchboard for discretely defined agent capabilities, rather than assigning agents credentials or access to MCP servers or APIs or other agents that can be expanded or exploited for another HuggingFace-type incident.

“You can consume capabilities in our system and publish capabilities,” said Edera founder and Chief Technology Officer Alex Zenla. So, for example, for an MCP server, we publish each tool call as a capability. And then when you spin up your agent, you ask for the tool calls that you want. And then it consumes just those capabilities. And we’re able to enforce policies because we have one central pathway for everything to go through, so we can know exactly which agents are using which capabilities.”

“I love the focus on reliability that I’ve seen in the talks and on the floor here at KubeCon,” said Kolton Andrus, CEO of Gremlin Inc., which was there demonstrating their new Foresight AI solution that proactively injects failure conditions in order to identify and remediate failure risks. “You can no longer wait for things to fall apart before taking action. “Everyone’s moving 100 miles an hour trying to keep up with AI, and waking up to the fact that reliability can’t be an afterthought anymore. You can no longer wait for things to fall apart before taking action.”

This being my eighth KubeCon, I keep coming back because the community atmosphere here is unparalleled. There’s a real sense of camaraderie among developers and engineers from wildly different backgrounds, as they build new fundamentals and enjoy the journey toward a cloud native future.

We’ve come a long way over the last eleven years since Kubernetes was introduced. Interoperability, portability, control planes, observability, networking, identity, security and many more mature capabilities are there for the taking. Now AI is being layered on top. But that’s not the story here.

What really impresses me is how much this open source community gives back for the benefit of everyone. All of these people have real jobs to do, and yet they invest their own time, as much as the software industry invests in them.

Indeed, as CNCF’s own Jonathan Bryce said: “Some problems can only be solved in the open.”

Jason English is a principal analyst and chief marketing officer at Intellyx. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE. At the time of writing, Gremlin and Rafay are current Intellyx customers, Dynatrace, New Relic, Nutanix and Splunk are former customers, and none of the other companies mentioned here is an Intellyx customer. #5473. Bitcoin Price at a Turning Point: Nvidia Earnings, Anthropic IPO, and Trump-Xi-Putin Diplomacy Shake Markets

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Bitcoin price is entering a potentially decisive week as Wall Street prepares for three major events likely to reshape sentiment. Nvidia’s earnings, Anthropic’s enormous IPO, and an unprecedented Trump-Xi-Putin meeting are arriving almost simultaneously. Together, they could trigger a wave of capital rotation, putting pressure on crypto before potentially opening the door to a recovery.

Bitcoin price has already suffered a brutal correction, falling toward $65,000 after losing more than 20% over the past month. But the coming days could introduce a very different market dynamic. Institutional investors are preparing for one of the largest technology listings ever, bigger than SpaceX.

Anthropic upcoming IPO has likely become an enormous liquidity-absorption event, a butterfly effect across traditional markets and crypto. Claude developer has proposed selling 825 million Class A shares at $70 to $78 each. The offering could raise between $57.75 billion and $64.35 billion, implying a fully diluted valuation of $1.4 trillion.

Anthropic has launched the roadshow for its proposed initial public offering: https://t.co/oE6TA0vt3ELegal disclaimer: A registration statement relating to these securities has been filed with the SEC but has not yet become effective. These securities may not be sold, nor may…

The capital ambitions are extending beyond the public offering. Anthropic has separately arranged a $26 billion private placement involving major technology companies, including Google, Nvidia, Microsoft, AMD and Broadcom. Combined proceeds could reach $84.6 billion to $93.7 billion.

That is an extraordinary amount of capital competing for investor attention. Reuters reported that institutional investors are already preparing for the IPO alongside Nvidia’s earnings, making both events major tests for an increasingly vulnerable AI trade.

Anthropic’s private-market valuation has also attracted speculative trading on platforms such as Hyperliquid, where pre-IPO exposure has traded at a premium, highlighting just how aggressively investors are positioning for its public debut.

The consequences extend beyond technology stocks. Bitcoin, with its around-the-clock liquidity, could become an unintended source of funding.

But what have we learned from this? Before the June SpaceX IPO, Bitcoin experienced a huge sell-off, falling nearly 20% during the 30-day pre-IPO period. Fast forward a couple of months, Bitcoin price grinded higher as SpaceX’s attention faded.

Now, Anthropic could be just another test. If its IPO absorbs substantial investment capital, Bitcoin could face additional selling pressure. Once allocations settle, however, that temporary competition for liquidity could ease, allowing investors to reconsider previously abandoned positions.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

While Anthropic potentially competes for liquidity, Nvidia could provide the catalyst needed to restore confidence across technology markets. Nvidia will report its third-quarter fiscal 2027 results on November 17. London Stock Exchange Group expects $109 billion in revenue and 90% earnings growth.

The expectations are enormous, particularly after Nvidia’s market valuation declined from $5.8 trillion in early October to $3.9 trillion. Investors are looking for evidence that AI infrastructure spending remains sustainable despite the company’s leadership transition.

A strong earnings report could nevertheless change the narrative. Higher revenue guidance, resilient data center demand, and confidence in future AI spending could help stabilize technology valuations. Nvidia has repeatedly beaten analyst expectations for 8 straight earnings reports.

Why does this matter for Bitcoin? Institutional risk appetite often moves across multiple asset classes. When investors become comfortable taking risks in equities, speculative assets like crypto can benefit from renewed capital allocation.

If Nvidia surprises positively, Bitcoin price could receive an unexpected boost just as the Anthropic IPO reaches its public debut.

The 33rd Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders' Meeting will be held in Shenzhen, south China, from Nov. 18 to 19, marking the first time in 12 years that China is hosting the APEC meeting, following Beijing in 2014. pic.twitter.com/Wx74CFc2YR

Donald Trump, Xi Jinping, and Vladimir Putin are expected to meet on Thursday, November 19, during the APEC summit in Shenzhen, China.

According to Reuters, Trump plans to raise nuclear arms reductions and the Iran conflict. However, US officials do not expect an immediate agreement on nuclear disarmament, making the meeting more of an opening diplomatic conversation. Nevertheless, constructive signals between three major geopolitical powers could improve investor confidence.

The technical picture also offers an intriguing contrast. Bitcoin’s daily RSI recently climbed from 19.7 to 24.3, remaining deeply oversold. Fear and Greed stands at just 10, indicating extreme market pessimism. Negative futures-spot spreads still tell us that bearish positioning remains aggressive.

#5472. Roth 401(k) employer match is becoming mainstream, new report finds

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Share of employers adding Roth treatment of employer contributions rose to 42.4% from 19.7%, the Plan Sponsor Council of America said

The Plan Sponsor Council of America reported in its 69th annual survey that 42.4% of organizations have already adopted, or will adopt, a Roth option for employer contributions in their 401(k) plans, compared with 19.7% a year earlier.

The survey draws on responses from 753 plan sponsors about how their plans performed during 2025. Another 11% are considering the option, according to CNBC.

“The Roth era is here. SECURE 2.0’s mandatory Roth catch-up made Roth essential for nearly every plan, and sponsors aren’t stopping there,” Will Hansen, the council’s executive director, said in a statement.

Roth use is also growing among employee contributions, the survey found. Among the surveyed plans, 96.9% give participants a Roth option, and 24.5% of participants now use it, compared with 22.1% before. Among plans with Roth deferrals available, 65.0% let participants shift existing balances into Roth money without leaving the plan, compared with 61.0% before.

Workers used to receive their employer's matching dollars solely on a pretax basis, according to CNBC. The SECURE 2.0 law, signed in 2022 by then-President Joe Biden, allows employers to provide a Roth match if they choose. A plan that offers one does not apply it automatically, and workers must opt in.

Hattie Greenan, the council's research director, told CNBC she expects the share of employers offering the option to keep rising. "Roth is becoming mainstream," she said.

Financial advisers told CNBC the choice between Roth and pretax savings varies by person. Roth contributions carry no up-front tax break, but qualified withdrawals in retirement are tax-free. “It’s personal preference,” said Philip Chao, who holds the certified financial planner designation and serves as chief investment officer at Experiential Wealth, in comments to CNBC.
