#5470. Talkdesk’s life sciences play shows why industry depth beats AI cost-cutting

GUEST COLUMN by Zeus Kerravala

The customer experience arena, specifically the contact center, has been the low-hanging fruit for artificial intelligence deployments, with much of the focus on cost-cutting. The goals include fewer agents, shorter calls, higher containment and lower cost per interaction.

Those are legitimate goals, but they lead every vendor to the same pitch. When everyone sells the same savings, the market becomes a price war that favors the companies with the deepest pockets.

Talkdesk Inc. is taking a different path, and today’s announcement reinforces that. This week, the company introduced Talkdesk Life Sciences Experience Cloud, a platform designed for biopharmaceutical companies’ patient services operations. The goal is not to make calls cheaper. It is to move patients from a written prescription to therapy faster and keep them there.

That outcome is one a pharma executive will pay for, and one a generic contact-center-as-a-service platform is poorly equipped to deliver. This adds to Talkdesk’s portfolio of industry clouds, including financial services, government, retail, travel and others.

The new offering connects AI agents, human specialists, systems, and workflows across the specialty care journey, which typically includes enrollment, prior authorizations and specialty pharmacy handoffs. Talkdesk cites IQVIA research showing that nearly one in three commercially insured patients cannot access a prescribed therapy within 30 days, and Boston Consulting Group data indicating that 90% of biopharma leaders view fragmented platforms as their primary bottleneck.

The platform analyzes patient service conversations to pinpoint where patients get stuck, assists specialists in real time, and coordinates tasks among hubs, providers, payers, specialty pharmacies and safety teams. It supports the U.S. Food and Drug Administration’s 21 CFR Part 11 requirements for electronic records and signatures and integrates with existing customer relationship management, hub, pharmacy and safety systems.

One of the world’s five largest pharmaceutical companies has already deployed it. That customer uses AI to classify and route inbound calls and to monitor live conversations for potential reportable events, or PREs, which are adverse event signals that must be captured and sent to pharmacovigilance systems. When the system detects a PRE, it guides the frontline agent to collect the required details, preserves the source conversation and triggers approved workflows to document and route the information.

“A prescription should mark the start of healing, not the beginning of an administrative maze,” said Patty Hayward, general manager of healthcare and life sciences at Talkdesk. “We are focusing first on Therapy Access because quickly getting patients onto prescribed treatments is one of the most urgent, measurable challenges in healthcare today.”

Hayward’s choice of the word “measurable” is the key point. Time to therapy is a metric that appears on a drug maker’s revenue line and in patient outcomes, not just on a contact center dashboard.

Talkdesk competes in a crowded market against much larger companies. NiCE Ltd. and Genesys Cloud Services Inc. have scale in the contact center, while Microsoft Corp., Salesforce Inc., and Amazon Web Services Inc. can bundle customer service capabilities into platforms that customers already own. A smaller company cannot outspend those rivals on horizontal features, and it should not try.

What it can do is go deeper into specific industries than the giants are willing to go. Talkdesk has been building industry-specific clouds for several years, and life sciences is a logical next step from its healthcare work. Pharmacovigilance workflows, Part 11 compliance, hub services and specialty pharmacy coordination are not features a horizontal vendor casually adds to its roadmap. They require domain expertise, regulatory knowledge and integrations that take time to build, and that time becomes a competitive moat.

The industry approach also changes the sales conversation. A generic platform is evaluated on price per seat and feature checklists, usually by the information technology department and the contact center leader. An industry platform is evaluated on whether it solves a business problem the executive team already worries about.

In pharma, patient abandonment between prescription and first fill represents lost revenue and a failed treatment. That conversation happens with the head of patient services, which is a much better place for a smaller vendor to be.

The industry approach has helped channel partners sell Talkdesk. I asked Joe Rittenhouse, co-CEO of Converged Technology Professionals Inc., one of the premier communications resellers, about it.

“We’re no longer leading with features or price per seat,” he said. “We’re leading with the customer’s workflows, their compliance requirements and the outcomes they’re measured on. That industry approach is a key differentiator for us. It lets us skip the generic AI conversation and get straight to the problems that keep the business up at night, shortening the sales cycle and making the deployment stick.”

The bigger story is how this fits into Talkdesk’s customer experience automation or CXA strategy, which is not a typical contact center-as-a-service sell. The idea is to coordinate AI agents, people, knowledge and enterprise systems to resolve a customer need from start to finish, rather than simply answering or routing an interaction faster. Resolving issues across systems is a far bigger value proposition than call deflection, but it is also much harder to deliver in the abstract.

That is where industry depth becomes critical. End-to-end automation is only possible when the platform understands what “end” means. In a retail return, the end might be a refund. In specialty pharma, the end is a patient who has completed benefits verification, obtained prior authorization, had the drug shipped and is still taking it six months later.

Each step involves different systems, organizations and regulatory obligations. A horizontal AI agent cannot orchestrate that journey without someone first mapping it. Talkdesk is effectively packaging that work into the product.

This is also why the industry approach shifts AI from a cost story to a transformation story. Using AI to reduce handle time on patient service calls might save a few dollars per interaction, and identifying that patients in each program repeatedly stall at prior authorization, then fixing that bottleneck, can change how many patients start therapy. The first is an efficiency gain. The second changes the economics of the business.

The pharmacovigilance use case makes the same point. Missing a reportable adverse event carries regulatory consequences. AI that detects those signals and routes them correctly reduces risk and improves quality, rather than reducing headcount, a value proposition that is far easier to justify to a board.

For life sciences leaders, the lesson is to stop evaluating customer engagement technology based solely on contact center metrics. Start with the patient journey, identify where patients drop off and measure vendors on their ability to shorten time to therapy and improve adherence. Insist on proof of regulatory readiness, particularly for Part 11 and adverse event handling, and validate integration with the hub, CRM and safety systems already in place.

For buyers in other industries, the broader point still holds. AI that only cuts costs will eventually commoditize. AI that understands your business’s specific workflows, regulations and outcomes can transform it. Ask CX vendors how well they understand your industry, not just how good their models are.

For Talkdesk, life sciences is a smart focus area. It will not win every horizontal deal against larger rivals, but it does not need to. By targeting industries with complex, regulated journeys tied to clear outcomes, it can make CXA tangible and give customers a reason to buy that has nothing to do with price.

Zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.

#5469. U.S. retail sales edged up 0.2% in October, slowing ahead of the holidays

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The gain followed a 0.8% rise in September, and sales at motor vehicle and parts dealers fell 1.6% from the prior month

The Census Bureau reported on Tuesday that U.S. retail and food services sales rose 0.2% in October to $748.2 billion, a smaller gain than September's 0.8%.

The agency put the margin of error on the monthly change at plus or minus 0.4%. Its 90% confidence interval includes zero, so the data do not provide enough evidence to conclude the actual change differs from zero. Sales were up 6.8% from October 2025. The estimates are adjusted for seasonal variation and holiday and trading-day differences but not for price changes.

Motor vehicle and parts dealers posted a 1.6% decline from September. Excluding that category, total sales rose 0.6%. Gasoline stations gained 1.5%, nonstore retailers 1.2% and health and personal care stores 1.5%. Furniture and home furnishings stores fell 2.3%, and food services and drinking places rose 0.2%.

Sales at gasoline stations were up 30.3% from a year earlier.

The 0.2% gain matched what economists had forecast, according to Reuters. Households spent less on cars, trucks and other expensive purchases as prices rose, with the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran pushing inflation higher.

Retail sales in a narrower group that leaves out food services, building materials, gasoline and automobiles climbed 0.6% in October, according to Reuters. September's gain in that measure was revised up to 0.5% from 0.1%. Economists had forecast a 0.4% October increase.

The CNBC/NRF Retail Monitor, which draws on card spending data, showed U.S. retail sales rising 0.2% in October, the slowest monthly gain since November 2025. The National Retail Federation said Halloween sales and early holiday discounts prevented a weaker reading.

September's 0.8% gain was driven largely by receipts at gasoline stations. The Census Bureau's initial estimate put September sales at $745.0 billion. That figure has been revised to $746.6 billion.

The Census Bureau will release November retail sales data on Dec. 16.

#5468. Action1 Extends Microsoft Intune Capabilities Without Expanding the Attack Surface

At Microsoft Ignite 2026, Action1 will show how Endpoint Takeover Prevention lets enterprises extend Microsoft Intune with cross-platform patching and vulnerability management without adding takeover risk

SAN FRANCISCO, Nov. 17, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Action1, a leading provider of autonomous endpoint management (AEM) solutions, today announced it will demonstrate its platform at Microsoft Ignite 2026, including Endpoint Takeover Prevention (ETP), an industry-first security architecture designed to prevent threat actors from using a compromised management platform to take control of customer endpoints.

Action1 will demonstrate its industry-first Endpoint Takeover Prevention (ETP) architecture at Microsoft Ignite 2026.

Every endpoint management tool added to the environment can become another way in for threat actors. AI is making that exposure harder to ignore, shrinking the time between vulnerability discovery and exploitation. Action1's ETP architecture is designed to address that challenge: high-risk endpoint actions, including scripts, software deployments and remote sessions, require cryptographic authorization using private keys controlled exclusively by the customer. Action1 endpoint agents independently verify that authorization before carrying out a high-risk action, so compromise of the platform alone is not enough to act on customer endpoints.

As a result, organizations using Microsoft Intune can extend their environments with Action1 without expanding the attack surface that typically comes with adding another endpoint management tool. Action1 brings autonomous patching for third-party applications, real-time vulnerability assessment with risk-based prioritization, unified coverage across Windows, macOS and Linux, and continuous patch compliance visibility. Enterprises can build on their existing Microsoft investments while closing patching and vulnerability management gaps, achieving a cohesive approach to endpoint management.

"Strengthening endpoint management should not open a new path to takeover," said Mike Walters, President and Co-founder of Action1. "Enterprises with Intune environments need unified patching and visibility into vulnerabilities, but adding another privileged platform can increase risk on every endpoint. It is a tension we see across the cybersecurity industry, and ETP was designed to resolve it. With ETP, control stays where it belongs: with the customer."

A call for stronger endpoint management security

Recent vulnerabilities in N-able's N-central platform underscore the risks associated with centralized management tools and the broad access they can hold. Action1 believes endpoint management vendors should reduce risk for customers, not become a single point of failure. The company has called on endpoint management providers, including competitors, to adopt ETP principles and help establish a new security standard for the industry.

#5467. Three insights you might have missed from theCUBE’s coverage of GraphSummit 2026

AI agents need more than enterprise data to be effective; they also need the business context that data lives in. Knowledge graphs could consolidate the enterprise context currently fed to different AI agents into a single knowledge layer.

Developers are already providing AI agents with business context through prompts. But without a central source of truth, they must repeat that work every time they build a new agent, rather than drawing on a shared knowledge layer, according to Jesús Barrasa (pictured), field chief technology officer of gen AI at Neo4j Inc.

“This knowledge layer, this idea of capturing your enterprise knowledge and using it as the context engine for your agents, not only gives you the consistency … it gives you the explainability,” he said during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. “That’s the source of my data. These are the elements that I use to produce the answer.”

During interviews at GraphSummit, theCUBE Research’s John Furrier spoke with industry experts from Collibra BV, Blitzy Inc., Raymond James Financial Inc., and Qiagen N.V., among others. They discussed how knowledge graphs can ground AI agents in shared, traceable enterprise knowledge to improve explainability, enable safer coding at scale, support drug discovery and transform business operations. (* Disclosure below.)

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video interview with Jesús Barrasa:

Governance is a key question for enterprise AI deployments. How do you ensure AI agents behave appropriately as they become more autonomous? Judgment calls that used to be made by people now need to be made by agents in seconds, requiring a shift toward runtime governance, according to Felix Van de Maele, chief executive officer and co-founder of Collibra BV.

Collibra has introduced several capabilities – Live Map, Maestro, Guardian Agents and Agent Contracts – built on Neo4j’s graph database. Together, they form a control system that helps businesses make sure their AI agents use the right information and follow the rules.

“The challenge is: how do you govern at the speed of AI, which is different than the way we had to govern five years ago?” Van de Maele told theCUBE. “Maestro gives our customers the ability to build these governance steward agents that automate up to 80% of the governance work. You’re able to govern quickly and efficiently enough to keep up with the demands of new AI workloads.”

Other solutions, such as Agent Contracts, focus on enforcing boundaries around AI agents’ behavior. They monitor agents’ actions and block those that violate predefined rules, helping prevent unauthorized actions, according to Van de Maele.

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video interview with Felix Van de Maele:

Changing one small piece of software can unexpectedly break something somewhere else. For Blitzy Inc., which runs thousands of AI coding agents at once to help businesses make large-scale system changes, a knowledge graph can map dependencies and the risks of change within a system.

A knowledge graph gives agents the context they need to make changes safely without being overwhelmed by millions of lines of code, according to Neeraj Deshmukh, director of engineering at Blitzy. The company also uses human-approved action plans and automated testing to keep the coding process on track.

“On top of that, we have agents who are watching other agents to make sure that they abide by the spec, the plan that we had created and approved by the human in the loop,” Deshmukh told theCUBE. “That ensures that there is no drift or hallucination.”

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video interview with Neeraj Deshmukh:

A knowledge graph helps Raymond James Financial Inc. put AI agents to work on data from established sources, according to Naveen Mahankali, vice president of technology at Raymond James.

We have golden sources; we have systems that we can rely on today, and we’re able to use agents to build and compare what we are building against the golden sources,” he told theCUBE. “With the knowledge graph, even when we pull the data from different sources, it sits in the Neo4j, and we run evals compared to the golden sources and make sure they’re 100% accurate before launching.”

Raymond James is also exploring how AI agents can help financial advisors serve clients more efficiently. The company has already launched Raimond, its proprietary AI assistant, explained Jeff Griffith, vice president of AI engineering and data science at Raymond James, who joined Mahankali during the interview.

“We have an AI assistant … it’s gotten huge adoption, and it’s just going to get smarter,” Griffith said. “That’s part of the core evolution of what we’re doing in terms of engineering. We’re changing how people — how everyone — works with a desktop that gives people the best AI tools to move from doing all the menial tasks to managing agents that are doing those tasks. In terms of skills and what we are looking for, it is shifting just from people who can do tasks to people who have a drive to solve a meaningful problem.”

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video interview with Jeff Griffith and Naveen Mahankali:

#5466. Alex Vidal to oversee REMAX Canada as company clarifies remit

REMAX said its president role has always included oversight of Canada, confirming Alex Vidal also leads REMAX Canada. Don Kottick, president of REMAX Canada since April 2025, plans to leave the firm on Dec. 15.  AI Summary

Not only is Alex Vidal the new president of REMAX, but the company has clarified that his appointment to this position also encompasses REMAX Canada, making him the leader of REMAX’s Canadian operation.

Vidal was named president of REMAX in September, after The Real Brokerage completed its acquisition of REMAX, forming the Real REMAX Group.

In an emailed statement, a REMAX spokesperson told HousingWire that the president of REMAX has always overseen the company’s Canadian operation.

As Vidal moves into the Canadian leadership position, Don Kottick, who has served as the president of REMAX Canada since April 2025, has announced plans to leave the firm on Dec. 15. This information was conveyed to REMAX brokers and franchisees via an internal memo reviewed and confirmed by HousingWire.

“This move helps ensure every REMAX region around the world receives as much of the same focus, momentum and opportunities as possible,” the internal memo stated. “The next few months will be pivotal as we roll out new technology and invest in further strengthening the REMAX brand in Canada and around the world.”

Prior to joining REMAX, Kottick was the president and CEO of Sotheby’s International Realty Canada.

Before joining REMAX, Vidal served as the president of ERA Real Estate, helping lead the brand through Compass International Holdings’s acquisition of its parent company Anywhere Real Estate. Compass and ERA are currently suing Vidal, claiming that he violated non-compete agreements through his move to REMAX. In the legal complaint filed in mid-October, Compass claims that the non-compete agreement prevents Vidal from serving as president or providing service to any competing business for a period of one year from his departure from ERA.

#5465. Russia's crude exports hit highest since July as Ukraine targets refineries

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Overseas flows averaged 3.9 million barrels a day in the four weeks through Nov. 15, up 280,000 barrels a day from the prior period

Russia exported crude at an average pace of 3.9 million barrels daily over the 28 days ending Nov. 15, its biggest volume since late July, according to Bloomberg. That was 280,000 barrels a day more than in the four weeks through Nov. 8, according to Bloomberg's tanker data.

Ukraine has attacked 13 Russian refineries since the start of November, according to a Bloomberg tally, among them TAIF-NK's Nizhnekamsk plant and Ilsky, a refinery in the Krasnodar region. Strikes strand Russian oil that damaged plants can no longer handle, and those barrels end up being shipped abroad. Lulls in attacks give crews time to fix damaged units, which lets domestic plants take in more oil and reduces the volume heading overseas, according to Bloomberg.

President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said long-range strikes have disabled more than 55% of Russia’s oil refining capacity. He called the campaign a justified response to Russia’s refusal to de-escalate and its attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure. Bloomberg said it could not verify the claim.

Over the week ended Nov. 15, 39 tankers picked up Russian crude totaling 30.27 million barrels, versus 31 ships carrying 23.6 million barrels the prior week, according to Bloomberg. The weekly average of 4.32 million barrels a day was up 950,000 barrels a day and the highest since June. Weekly figures can swing sharply depending on when vessels depart, whether maintenance or bad weather interferes, and how sanctions and military action play out.

On a four-week basis, the gross value of Russia's oil shipments fell to $2.45 billion a week, the lowest in seven weeks, according to Bloomberg. Urals crude prices fell for a fifth straight week, which more than offset the higher volumes. Looking at the single week alone, export revenue climbed to roughly $2.29 billion.

China and India are still Russia's top crude customers, according to Bloomberg. Over the 28 days through Nov. 15, volumes bound for Asian buyers, counting cargoes that have no final destination listed, climbed to 3.72 million barrels a day, up from a revised 3.42 million barrels a day in the period ending Nov. 8.

Ukraine paused refinery strikes for two weeks in October before resuming attacks on major plants, including Kirishi, which is geared toward exports, and Omsk, Russia's biggest. Drone strikes in the first half of October had cut throughput at Russian refineries.

#5463. Alibaba launches Qwen4-Max with training, attention optimizations

Alibaba Group Holding Ltd. today introduced Qwen4-Max, its newest and most capable large language model.

The algorithm not only generates higher-quality output than its predecessor but also costs less. Those improvements are the result of a new architecture, Qwen4, that made the LLM’s training run more efficient. Additionally, Alibaba has equipped the model with an upgraded attention mechanism.

Qwen4-Max’s backbone, the part of an LLM that functions as its main processing engine, comprises 2.4 trillion parameters. The model activates only 71 billion at any given time. The backbone is supported by 328 billion so-called N-gram parameters, which function as a kind of cache. They save the results of oft-repeated calculations and thereby remove the need to compute them from scratch every time.

An LLM’s artificial neurons are organized into sets known as layers. When the model learns something new during training, a piece of data called a gradient travels through the layers and refines their output. The gradient moves through them one by one starting from the last layer, which finalizes and displays prompt responses.

Qwen4-Max includes a feature that enables the gradient to skip some layers. That feature, or residual, is effectively a shortcut inside the LLM. Its purpose is to reduce errors during the training workflow, which in turn lowers costs and improves output quality.

Residuals can also be found in many other LLMs. Historically, the mechanism was implemented as a single gradient transportation channel. Qwen4-Max’s implementation of the technology features four channels. Moreover, those channels have a “gate” that can adjust the movement of gradients to further improve the training process.

Qwen4-Max’s attention mechanism, a module that helps it understand user prompts, features two key customizations. The first is a technology called Gated DeltaNet that lowers the amount of hardware needed to process large prompts. The second optimization, QSA, skips pieces of data that the LLM doesn’t need to answer a prompt. That arrangement further lowers infrastructure costs.

Alibaba compared Qwen4-Max with its predecessor, Qwen3.8-Max, using an internal benchmark that includes knowledge work tasks. The former model achieved a higher score and used up to 35% fewer tokens to complete tasks. Those savings grew to 49% when the models were tested using the Terminal-Bench 4.0 suite of coding challenges.

Qwen4-Max is available through Alibaba’s cloud platform. The company plans to open-source a collection of smaller models based on the same technologies further down the line. It’s also open-sourcing Qwen-Live-Delivery-Plugin, an extension that makes Qwen4-Max better at performing time-consuming tasks.

When an LLM is assigned a long-horizon project, users often have to wait until the model completes its work before they can review the results. Alibaba’s plugin shortens the wait. It enables Qwen4-Max to quickly deliver an initial draft and then iteratively add improvements. Users can give the model feedback along the way to refine its work.

#5462. 'Big Short' investor warned AI cloud stocks are in trouble after Nvidia turmoil

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Steve Eisman said he thinks neoclouds are part of Nvidia's "vertical holding company" and are about to get ejected from it

Photo Illustration by Matteo Della Torre/NurPhoto via Getty Images

Steve Eisman, the investor known for "The Big Short," said on CNBC on Tuesday that the Nvidia $NVDA scandal now unfolding will hit AI neocloud stocks harder than any others.

Eisman described Nvidia as a "virtual vertical holding company and it's unwinding" during an appearance on "Squawk Box." "I think neoclouds are all in big trouble though because they are part of that vertical holding company and I think they're about to get ejected," he said.

Neoclouds borrowed money to build data centers. CoreWeave stock and Nebius stock have each fallen more than 50% over the past three months.

Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang stepped down last Thursday after a controversy erupted over an affair with a woman suspected of spying for China, according to CNBC. The Commerce Department has since acted to end a loophole that let China access data centers remotely, and Nvidia is due to report fiscal third-quarter earnings after the close on Tuesday, Nov. 17.

Anthropic is expected to go public on Thursday, according to CNBC. Eisman said the offering has lost its significance for the AI trade now that investor hopes for it have cooled. "I don't think anybody really cares," he said.

Eisman said he is focused instead on how severely Democrats will limit data center construction after they assume power in Congress and in a number of governors' offices in January.

"I think the biggest issues by far are how much are, how much are local and state governments going to slow AI data center construction? Is it going to be 100% moratorium? That would obviously be — that would put the country into recession overnight. Or is it something like 10% to 30%?" he said.

If construction slows by 10% to 30%, Eisman said, hyperscalers would fare best among AI-trade companies. "The group that makes out the best are the hyperscalers because they go cash flow positive again," he said, according to CNBC.

Eisman had said on Oct. 29 that he had cut risk in his own portfolio because he sees the AI trade nearing a tipping point. He said then that he had shorted against a number of his positions but was not net short any of them.

Elon Musk, the CEO of SpaceX and Tesla $TSLA, predicted on Oct. 25 that the more than 200 neocloud companies will see "guppy-level death and consolidation." Nvidia holds stakes in a number of neoclouds, and Huang had said the week before that demand for them is "off the charts."

#5461. Villa hires former Century Communities CFO Messenger as CEO

Villa has named homebuilding and real estate veteran David Messenger as CEO to lead the offsite homebuilder’s next growth phase. Villa says its integrated offsite model, which has delivered more than 425 homes since 2019, positions it to support larger communities. The move signals a push toward disciplined, community-scale growth and deeper partnerships with institutional housing players.  AI Summary

Villa, a San Francisco-based manufactured homebuilder, has appointed homebuilding and real estate veteran David Messenger as CEO, the company announced on Monday.

Founded in 2019, Villa says it has delivered more than 425 homes using an offsite construction model that spans accessory dwelling units (ADUs), multifamily projects and new neighborhoods. The company manages feasibility, design, permitting, site preparation and installation, and partners with a network of factories for production, according to the announcement.

Messenger brings decades of financial and operating experience in homebuilding and multifamily real estate, having spent more than 10 years as chief financial officer of Century Communities. During his tenure, Century expanded from about 150 to 1,800 employees across 18 states, grew to $4.5 billion in annual revenue and more than 10,000 annual closings, completed seven acquisitions and raised more than $3 billion in debt and equity capital, the company said.

He also led Century’s initial public offering and helped launch its mortgage, title and insurance subsidiaries, giving him direct experience with the vertically integrated models many large homebuilders use to manage costs and capture more of the housing value chain. Earlier in his career, Messenger spent roughly a decade at UDR, a publicly traded multifamily real estate investment trust, where he advanced through senior finance roles to become CFO.

Messenger’s appointment comes as Villa looks to expand beyond individual ADUs and small projects into larger communities in partnership with land developers and homebuilders. The company is already working on new neighborhoods including the 25-home Acacia Village in Santa Rosa, California, Alpine Village in Westminster, Colorado, and homes in Altadena, California, for families rebuilding after the Eaton Fire, according to the release.

Investors say his background in scaling a public homebuilder and in capital markets was a key factor in the decision.

“Villa has demonstrated its capabilities across ADUs, multifamily properties and new neighborhoods, and Dave is the right leader to build on Villa’s success and advance its growth strategy,” said Aaron Marsh, partner and CFO at Unless, an investor in Villa and member of Villa’s board of directors. “He brings deep housing experience, a track record of scaling businesses nationally and a clear understanding of what land and development partners need to move projects forward.”

Messenger said he sees an opportunity to apply processes from large-scale homebuilding to Villa’s offsite platform.

“This team has done what much of our industry has only talked about: delivering quality homes through offsite construction across individual properties, multifamily communities and new neighborhoods,” Messenger said in the announcement. “I see great potential to build on that foundation by bringing a large-scale homebuilder’s operating discipline to Villa, with an emphasis on predictable execution and profitable growth.”

Villa’s model aims to give homeowners, multifamily operators and developers a single partner from concept through completion. The company handles site feasibility, site and home design, permitting and on-site work and uses factory partners to build homes offsite, aiming for more predictable timelines and costs than traditional stick-built construction, according to the release.

“Dave has an exceptional track record spanning homebuilding, multifamily real estate, capital markets and land development,” said Heather Miksch, chief operating officer at Villa. “As we build on Villa’s momentum and pursue development opportunities, his experience will be invaluable in helping us grow our business while continuing to serve both homeowners and development partners.”

#5459. Noeri raises $110M to help companies build living AI systems that self-improve over time

Noeri Inc., a startup developing artificial intelligence systems that continuously improve their outputs as they learn from an organization’s data and work, is launching with $110 million in funding.

Today’s round was led by Menlo Ventures and saw participation from Seattle-based Madrona Ventures, Kindred Ventures, Wing Venture Capital and NEA. Snowflake and Cisco Ventures also took part in the round.

Noeri is the brainchild of Yejin Choi (pictured, left) and Carlos Guestrin (right), two prominent AI researchers from Stanford University, who spent years developing self-improving systems at the University of Washington prior to moving. The startup’s software is designed to study a company’s data, workflows and business processes.

Then as it learns about them, it will begin to propose changes regarding specific tasks, in order to make them more efficient. The co-founders refer to it as a “living” AI system that gets better at what it does over time.

For instance, it might offer different instructions, suggest different tools or switch out the model that handles each step of a workflow for another. Each of these suggestions comes with an explanation and is sent to a human for review before it’s accepted, similar to how AI-generated code changes are implemented.

Noeri is compatible with both open-weight and proprietary AI models and ensures that customers retain full ownership of their workflows and the AI systems they develop. Choi told Bloomberg in an interview that Noeri is trying to appeal to organizations that find themselves having to choose between either paying fees they can’t afford for the most capable AI models, or else accepting results from a less effective one.

The idea for the company stemmed from an effort to help a microbiology and immunology team at Stanford use OpenAI Group PBC’s models in a more cost effective way. According to Choi, she and Guestrin developed a small AI model that learned how to use OpenAI’s older models, and to their surprise, managed to fine-tune it to perform better than the more advanced GPT-5 on that research team’s projects.

The startup’s name was carefully chosen. Noeri means “intelligence, in the plural,” and it’s meant to reflect Choi’s and Guestrin’s belief that the future of AI won’t be dominated by just one or a handful of extremely powerful AI models.

Guestrin especially is a big proponent of choice in the AI industry. In a speech at Madrona Ventures’ IA40 Summit in September, he notably argued that the future of intelligence cannot be controlled by just one or two companies that own the models.

“Few companies would build their core operations on a single consultant who also advises every competitor, can change its terms at will and can never be brought in-house,” Choi and Guestrin wrote in a blog post outlining the startup’s mission. “A single, centralized AI offers exactly that arrangement.”

Noeri isn’t the only proponent of such a multimodel future. Similar arguments have been made by Mira Murati’s Thinking Machines Labs Inc., which last year debuted Tinker, a cloud-based service that anyone can use to fine-tune AI models and enhance their performance. Similarly, Applied Compute Inc. embeds engineers with its customers to help them fine-tune AI systems.

Guestrin previously helped develop a popular machine learning tool called XGBoost, which is used by researchers to boost the performance of AI models. He also co-founded an early machine learning startup GraphLab Inc., later known as Turi Inc., which was acquired by Apple Inc. in 2016.  After that, he joined Apple too and went on to lead that company’s machine learning and AI research organization.

Choi previously led the Allen Institute for AI’s common-sense reasoning research team before joining Nvidia Corp. in 2024 as a distinguished scientist. She quit about a year later to join Stanford in early 2025, from where she helped Guestrin start Noeri in May.

Noeri represents the culmination of two separate research projects. Guestrin pioneered a new self-distillation technique that allows AI models to become their own teachers, turning mistakes into lessons that allow them to improve their responses over time. Meanwhile, Choi’s work on agentic orchestration has shown that smaller models that conduct teams of AI agents and tools can outperform much larger frontier models at lower costs.

Those two projects are the foundation of Noeri’s systems. The startup says it’s now working with partners across multiple industries, including some of its investors, which were deliberately chosen to ensure its systems could be exposed to a wide variety of work.

“Most new AI labs ask the market to wait years for a breakthrough,” said Menlo Ventures Partner Venky Ganesan. “Carlos and Yejin are doing world-class research and putting it to work inside companies at the same time. That combination is rare, and it’s why we moved quickly to lead this round.”

#5458. Fund managers slashed tech exposure by the most since 2006, BofA survey finds

Free daily briefing on global business news.

A record net 38% of respondents say companies are overinvesting in AI, and 52% expect an AI hyperscaler to cut spending

Bank of America $BAC found that fund managers cut their technology allocations by the most since June 2006 in its November survey, according to Bloomberg.

Fund managers with an overweight position in tech made up a net 12% of respondents in November, down sharply from 37% in October. The survey covered Nov. 6 through Nov. 12 and drew responses from 169 participants who oversee a combined $461 billion in assets.

In a note, Bank of America strategist Michael Hartnett said the "big" takeaway from respondents is that companies ought to put the brakes on AI spending. A net 38% of respondents, the highest on record, say companies are putting too much money into AI, and 52% foresee an AI hyperscaler announcing a cut to capital spending within the coming half-year. "Euphoria on boom & AI over," Hartnett said, according to Bloomberg.

Respondents named an AI bubble as the top tail risk for markets, followed by an AI hyperscaler credit event, according to Reuters. Worries over a pullback in data center investment following the U.S. midterms have pushed technology shares down over the past few weeks.

The Nasdaq $NDAQ 100 is off by over 4% so far in November and is heading for its weakest showing for the month since 2008, according to Bloomberg. A gauge covering chip-sector shares has lost 27% of its value since the start of October.

Respondents showed less concern about the broader economy. Roughly 3% expect a recession within the next year, while cash positions have shrunk to 3.6% of total assets, the smallest share since August, according to Bloomberg.

Doubts about AI spending have weighed on tech stocks for weeks. Shares of Amazon $AMZN, Microsoft $MSFT, Alphabet $GOOGL and Meta $META had been sliding before the midterm elections because investors questioned whether the companies' computing outlays would pay off. Free cash flow has turned negative at Amazon, Alphabet and Meta, and the companies are turning to borrowing and share sales to finance the spending.

Democrats won majorities in the House and Senate in the midterms, having campaigned on curbing AI development and the large-scale building of data centers. Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet and Meta shares rose the day after the election as investors wagered that Congress would rein in AI spending.

Former Securities and Exchange Commission Chair Gary Gensler called the AI boom a bubble likely to burst and drag the economy into recession before the 2028 presidential election. "It's already a bubble," Gensler said.

#5457. Hedge fund pressures Invitation Homes to speed up home sales

Land & Buildings sent an open letter to Invitation Homes shareholders arguing the single-family rental REIT trades about 40% below the value of its homes and has underperformed major benchmarks for years. The activist investor is urging the company to sell homes individually at retail prices and commit to returning at least $2 billion a year to shareholders via buybacks or special dividends, while sharply reducing acquisitions and development. The clash could reshape capital allocation strategies in the institutional single-family rental sector and, if the plan gains traction, would push more homes from rental portfolios into the for-sale market.  AI Summary

Activist investor Land & Buildings Investment Management is pressing single-family rental giant Invitation Homes to accelerate home sales, sharply increase capital returns and scale back growth plans, arguing the company’s stock trades at a steep discount to the value of its houses.

In an open letter to shareholders released Monday, the Stamford, Connecticut-based hedge fund said it believes Invitation Homes is “among the most undervalued companies in the REIT sector” and criticized the board and management for what it called “complacency” and “half measures” in addressing the gap.

Land & Buildings, which owns an undisclosed stake in Invitation Homes, is led by Jonathan Litt, a longtime activist in the real estate investment trust sector. Invitation Homes (NYSE: INVH) is the nation’s largest owner of single-family rental homes, with more than 80,000 properties concentrated in Sun Belt and other high-growth markets.

Land & Buildings said the public market values Invitation Homes’ properties at roughly $270,000 per home, compared with an average sale price of about $460,000 on homes the company has sold since December 2025. That implies a discount of about 40%, according to the letter, which was disseminated via GlobeNewswire.

The firm said it separately valued more than 90% of the company’s wholly owned portfolio, “address by address,” and arrived at an estimated average value of approximately $425,000 per home. That analysis underpins its net asset value estimate of about $45 per share, which Land & Buildings said is more than 65% above Invitation Homes’ current trading price even after assuming 6% selling costs on every home.

“REITs with sound fundamentals and no distressed assets do not trade at such a discount indefinitely. Something has to give,” the firm said in the letter.

“Invitation Homes’ Board of Directors and management team are committed to acting in the best interests of the Company and its shareholders to deliver long-term, sustainable value,” says a prepared statement from the company. “Our focus is on strengthening our foundation and enhancing the resident experience that sets us apart. This focus has resulted in solid operational and financial performance in recent quarters, supported by consistent demand, strong retention, and continued execution across our core markets.”

“We are always open to hearing and considering the perspectives of our shareholders. Members of our Board and management team have had numerous discussions with Land & Buildings over the past several months to better understand its views, as we would with any shareholder. While we are disappointed that Land & Buildings has chosen to make its issues public at this time, we remain open to further engagement.”

Land & Buildings has highlighted what it described as sustained underperformance. Over the trailing one-, three- and five-year periods, Invitation Homes has lagged the S&P 500, the broader REIT index, its closest peer American Homes 4 Rent and the proxy peer group the board uses for benchmarking executive compensation, the letter said.

Over the past three years, Invitation Homes ranks second to last in that compensation peer group, trailing the group average by more than 35 percentage points, according to Land & Buildings. Shareholders who held the stock for five years have lost more than 20% of their investment, including dividends, the letter said, even as U.S. home prices have continued to climb.

The firm noted that Invitation Homes’ shares now trade at an implied capitalization rate of about 7%, roughly 60 basis points wider than American Homes 4 Rent, and at a lower multiple of adjusted funds from operations. The stock trades only modestly above its $20 IPO price from early 2017 while national home prices are up nearly 80% over that period, according to the letter.

Land & Buildings blamed Invitation Homes’ strategy for much of the gap. The company was a net buyer of homes in every year from 2022 through 2025 despite “a poor cost of capital,” and earnings have “repeatedly fallen short of expectations,” the firm said.

The letter also pointed to legal and regulatory costs. Land & Buildings said Invitation Homes has paid more than $79 million to resolve four legal matters related to resident treatment and business practices, including a $48 million settlement with the Federal Trade Commission in 2024. At the same time, the board approved more than $25 million in special retention awards in March 2026 for the CEO and three other executives, according to the firm.

“This troubling misalignment and lack of accountability is deeply concerning,” Land & Buildings said.

The activist laid out a three-part plan it says could unlock value and narrow the discount to net asset value:

Land & Buildings estimated that a multi-year, programmatic asset sale and capital return program could deliver “substantial annual accretion” to both earnings and NAV per share, supported by what it pegged as nearly $40 billion of gross asset value.

The letter criticized what Land & Buildings characterized as incremental steps by Invitation Homes, including recent home sales and share repurchases, arguing those moves have not been sized or communicated in a way that would change how investors value the company.

“Half measures appear to be this Board’s modus operandi: do just enough to relieve pressure while preserving the status quo,” the firm wrote.

Land & Buildings also objected to the board’s Nov. 11 appointment of Colin Connolly, CEO of office REIT Cousins Properties, as a new director. The firm said the board had previously told it that refreshment was not needed and argued that adding another sitting REIT chief executive provided “duplicative skill sets” rather than shareholder alignment and capital allocation expertise.

The activist said independent research firm Green Street wrote less than a year ago that Invitation Homes should “shrink its portfolio, return capital to shareholders, and redirect the bulk of its energy internally on operations until its valuation improves.” Land & Buildings said it had urged management to outline a clear, multi-year capital return plan at REIT conferences in September but came away with “little more than lip service.”

Invitation Homes did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the letter or the firm’s proposals. The company has previously defended its strategy of balancing internal growth, acquisitions and select dispositions as it manages a large, geographically diverse portfolio in a tight housing market.

The campaign underscores how corporate decisions at large institutional single-family landlords can influence for-sale and rental supply in already constrained markets. Land & Buildings’ proposal would require Invitation Homes to sell thousands of homes a year to owner-occupiers or directly to existing tenants at retail pricing.

For homebuilders and real estate agents, a large program of individual home sales by Invitation Homes could add incremental existing-home inventory in high-demand metros where resale listings remain scarce. The suggested 6% down-payment rebate for tenants could create a new pipeline of first-time buyers but might also draw scrutiny from policymakers and tenant advocates who have criticized investor ownership of single-family homes.

For other single-family rental REITs and institutional owners, the dispute highlights growing pressure from investors to prioritize buybacks and capital returns over portfolio growth when shares trade at discounts to estimated property values. If Invitation Homes embraced or was forced into a multi-year shrink-to-grow strategy, it could reset expectations for capital allocation across the sector.

Land & Buildings said it prefers to work “constructively” with Invitation Homes but “will not hesitate to take whatever steps we believe are necessary to maximize value,” a signal that a proxy fight or board challenge is on the table heading into the 2027 proxy season.

iTransplantÂ® will help MTN strengthen coordination, improve operational efficiency and modernize collaboration across its donation network to accelerate its lifesaving work.

WESTWOOD, Kan., Nov. 17, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Midwest Transplant Network (MTN), a federally designated organ procurement organization (OPO), and InVita Healthcare Technologies today announced a new partnership following MTN's selection of iTransplantÂ®, InVita's comprehensive software platform for organ, eye and tissue donation operations. The partnership brings together two organizations committed to advancing donation and transplantation through technology, innovation and operational excellence.

MTN serves Kansas and the western two-thirds of Missouri, partnering with more than 240 hospitals and five transplant centers to facilitate organ and tissue donation throughout its service area.

iTransplant will provide MTN with a market-leading platform that centralizes donation workflows and critical information from referral through recovery and donor family aftercare, helping streamline operations and improve efficiency across its organ, eye and tissue donation programs. The platform's configurable, interoperable design connects systems, workflows and data across the donation process, giving teams and healthcare partners the visibility and secure access needed to make timely, informed decisions. Together, we can better serve our hospital partners and the donor heroes and families whose generosity gives hope and shares life."

"We look forward to working alongside MTN's team to build on that record and reach new heights together in our shared mission to save and heal more lives."

InVita Healthcare Technologies delivers the world's most comprehensive human biologics software solutions managing blood, organ, and tissue workflows, enabling unmatched visibility and compliance to improve patient outcomes and save lives. Every day, healthcare organizations rely on InVita's software to carry out their missions and support the communities they serve. For more information, visit invitahealth.com.

Midwest Transplant Network saves lives through organ, eye and tissue donation. Serving Kansas and western Missouri since 1973, Midwest Transplant Network is a federally certified, not-for-profit organ procurement organization. Midwest Transplant Network works with organ, eye and tissue donors, their families, hospitals, and other professional partners to extend legacies, provide hope and give life. Its central office is in Westwood, Kansas, with satellite offices in Wichita, Kansas, and Columbia and Joplin, Missouri. Midwest Transplant Network commemorated 50 years in 2023, and consistently ranks in the top 10 of organ procurement organizations in the country.

#5455. Corma raises $125M to train cybersecurity-optimized foundation models

Corma.ai Ltd., a startup that develops artificial intelligence models for cybersecurity teams, has raised $125 million in funding.

NEA led the Series A round. Corma stated today that returning backers Khosla Ventures, Coatue and Sequoia Capital chipped in as well. The company is now valued at $1 billion.

Corma, which has offices in San Francisco and Tel Aviv, says competing AI models are often better at launching cyberattacks than fixing them. The company recently conducted a test in which it asked several large language models to hack a simulated corporate network. They succeeded at installing a malicious file across 85% of the test runs. In contrast, the models found only 12% of the malicious files that they themselves installed.

According to Corma, the gap between LLMs’ offensive and defensive capabilities can give hackers an edge over cybersecurity teams. That’s the issue the company is tackling with its cybersecurity-optimized AI models. Corma says that the algorithms can speed up some breach response workflows by a factor of 100 while reducing the associated costs.

The company benchmarked one of its models against the competition using an evaluation called DefenseBench V5. The test measures two metrics: how reliably a model performs defensive cybersecurity tasks and how fast it completes them. Corma says that its model outperformed GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus 5.5 and several other cutting-edge LLMs.

The company’s algorithms find breaches by analyzing data from other cybersecurity tools. Corma can ingest telemetry generated by firewalls, network monitoring software and a range of other applications. The company says that its models not only find threats but also generate remediation guidance for each one.

Automating breach response tasks is difficult because it requires LLMs to filter numerous false positives and duplicate alerts. Moreover, models often have access to only partial information about breaches. Many companies discard cybersecurity logs after a relatively short amount of time to reduce data storage costs.

Corma says that its algorithms can perform breach investigations on a fully autonomous basis. If human input is needed, they alert a relevant member of the cybersecurity team. It’s also possible to manually steer Corma’s models via a Slack chatbot. An administrator could, for example, ask Corma to double-check whether a recent effort to remove malware from a compromised server was successful.

“Since we came out of stealth, demand from the world’s largest organizations has been overwhelming, and one of our hardest problems has been securing capacity fast enough to keep up with the demand,” said Corma co-founder and Chief Executive Officer Alon Pluda.

Corma will use its newly raised funds to buy more infrastructure and enhance its AI models.

#5454. CZ Fires Back at Binance Dump Claims as Vitalik Bullish on Ethereum Quantum Upgrade

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Two of the industry’s most influential figures are pushing back against very different concerns. Binance co-founder Changpeng Zhao, known as CZ, has rejected accusations that the exchange sold crypto during the latest market crash. Meanwhile, Ethereum co-founder Vitalik Buterin is backing a faster approach to protecting the network against future quantum computing threats.

Their comments arrive as crypto suffers a sharp correction, leveraged traders absorb billions in liquidations, and Ethereum developers reconsider how quickly the network should prepare for a post-quantum future.

Changpeng Zhao has directly rejected speculation that Binance contributed to the latest cryptocurrency sell-off by selling digital assets.

“No, Binance did not sell crypto,” CZ wrote in a post on X.

Instead, the former Binance CEO said he had personally been buying crypto after receiving stablecoins over the past few days.

His response came as Bitcoin plunged toward $62,000, marking its lowest level since July. The wider market experienced approximately $2.02 billion in liquidations over a 24-hour period, with long positions accounting for $1.68 billion.

CZ also offered several possible explanations for the market weakness, including institutional ETF outflows, expectations of another Federal Reserve rate hike, security concerns, and investors potentially moving capital toward Anthropic’s anticipated IPO.

Why are crypto prices down?No one knows for sure. Correlation does not prove causation. Here are some potential reasons.Money shifting to the Anthropic IPO: https://t.co/jYwVi4huAYETF outflows: U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs saw about $1.9 billion in outflows over seven trading… pic.twitter.com/XL2aB1ZL9W

U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded $1.91 billion in net outflows across seven consecutive trading sessions through November 13. Spot Ether ETFs also suffered $398.9 million in weekly withdrawals.

The Binance selling allegations carry particular weight following the exchange’s October 29 security breach, but CZ public denial provides a clear counterargument to speculation that exchange selling accelerated the market decline.

His personal buying comments also show that he sees the current weakness differently from traders rushing to exit their positions. Defending the exchange’s reputation during a period of market stress is becoming just as important as explaining the direction of crypto prices.

While CZ is addressing immediate market concerns, Vitalik Buterin is looking much further ahead.

The Ethereum co-founder has dramatically changed his assessment of leanPCS, a proposed cryptographic technique designed to make Ethereum more resistant to quantum computing attacks.

“Over the past few weeks I’ve gone from thinking leanPCS is total bull to being a total bull,” Buterin wrote on X.

Over the past few weeks I've gone from thinking leanPCS is total bull to being a total bull. So let me explain some of these buzzwords in more detail.At the core, 8288 is about hyper-scaling data and execution for any computation that needs to get performed on a piece of data…

The statement shows growing confidence in an approach that could help Ethereum introduce quantum-resistant cryptography without dramatically increasing transaction costs and blockchain storage requirements.

The proposal, outlined in EIP-8288, focuses on combining individual digital signatures and cryptographic proofs into a shared mathematical proof. This is good for Ethereum because quantum-resistant signatures can be considerably larger than the cryptographic signatures Ethereum currently uses.

A standard Ethereum signature occupies approximately 65 bytes. Some proposed quantum-resistant alternatives could require between 1,000 and 6,000 bytes. Storing those larger signatures individually could consume substantial block space, potentially increasing network costs.

LeanPCS attempts to solve that problem by allowing computers to aggregate multiple signatures and verification checks before submitting a compact proof to Ethereum. Rather than permanently storing every bulky signature individually, the network could verify a shared proof covering multiple transactions.

Buterin favors this approach because it could provide a practical route toward quantum resistance without requiring Ethereum to commit immediately to a much larger architectural redesign.

Ethereum’s quantum preparation is already underway, with the Ethereum Foundation targeting 2029 for core post-quantum infrastructure milestones. The potential threat remains years away, but Ethereum developers increasingly recognize that replacing cryptographic foundations requires considerable preparation.

CZ and Buterin are confronting different problems, but both developments highlight the pressures facing the crypto industry. Binance needs to maintain market confidence while investors question exchange activity, security, and institutional capital flows.

Ethereum needs to strengthen its cryptographic foundations before quantum computing potentially threatens the security assumptions underlying today’s blockchain infrastructure.

CZ’s comments offer reassurance during an immediate market downturn, while Buterin’s endorsement could accelerate an important technical discussion within Ethereum.

#5453. Fed Governor Lisa Cook's lawyer signals she won't attend Dec. 14 White House hearing

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Lawyer Abbe Lowell says Cook would appear before an unbiased panel with fair procedures, but calls the current process unfair

Abbe Lowell, the lawyer for Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook, wrote to the White House that she is under no legal duty to attend a Dec. 14 hearing on unproven mortgage fraud allegations, according to Bloomberg.

The letter, which carries a Nov. 16 date and became public Tuesday, suggests more plainly than anything before it that Cook intends to stay away from the hearing, according to CNBC. Lowell addressed it to Will Scharf, presidential counsel.

Lowell argued that the committee President Donald Trump created last month serves as a pretext and endangers the central bank, according to CNBC. "Governor Cook has no legal obligation to participate in an unfair hearing — and indeed, has a duty to the Federal Reserve to decline to participate in any proceeding that would undermine the institution's unique status and independence," he wrote.

Lowell also called the process "a façade designed to obscure a predetermined decision to fire Governor Cook," according to Bloomberg. He said recent White House correspondence did not address her concerns.

Lowell left open the possibility of an appearance, according to Bloomberg. "If the White House establishes an unbiased panel and implements fair procedures that do not prejudge the outcome — such as providing the evidence it claims to have gathered with sufficient time for review and response — Governor Cook would be prepared to appear," he wrote. He added that the White House's Nov. 2 letter, with its ultimatums, fails to offer a workable way to move ahead.

CNBC's request for comment on the letter did not get an immediate reply from the White House.

Trump established a three-member committee in October to investigate allegations that Cook made false statements on mortgage documents. A White House memo said the hearing would be closed to the public but transcribed, and that the committee would then recommend whether cause exists to remove her from the Fed's Board of Governors. The hearing was first set for Nov. 5.

Lowell later asked the White House to postpone that hearing, citing what he called "demonstrably biased members" on the committee. He said Cook had official obligations in Europe and could attend no earlier than after the Fed's Dec. 8-9 policy meeting.

Cook denies wrongdoing, has not been charged with a crime and has sued to keep her job. Trump's effort to remove her began in August 2025. In June, the Supreme Court ruled 5-4 that she was entitled to notice and a chance to respond before any removal, and it left open what legally qualifies as cause.

#5452. Ackman says Trump can still end GSE conservatorships, relist this term

Bill Ackman and Pershing Square CIO Ryan Israel argue in a shareholder letter that Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac can exit their 18-year conservatorship and relist on the NYSE during the remainder of President Trump’s second term using executive authority, without Congress.  AI Summary

Bill Ackman still believes Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac can be relisted on the New York Stock Exchange and exit their conservatorships before the end of President Donald Trump’s second term, even after Democrats won control of both chambers in the midterm elections.

In a letter to Pershing Square Holdings shareholders signed in early November, Ackman, the company’s founder and CEO, and chief investment officer Ryan Israel wrote that “a relisting and release from conservatorship can be accomplished by the President using his executive authority without any involvement of Congress.”

They argue that the administration has a political incentive to act before 2029 to avoid “handing control” of the government-sponsored enterprises (GSEs) to a future administration, given the influence they have over housing policy.

Ackman and Israel said the GSEs can be released “in a manner that maintains and enhances mortgage affordability while maximizing the long-term value of American taxpayers’ 79.9% ownership of the two companies.” The Department of the Treasury holds warrants to acquire 79.9% of each enterprise’s common stock.

Pershing first detailed a road map in November 2025. The plan begins with a new agreement between the Treasury and the Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA) that addresses repayment or restructuring of Treasury’s senior preferred stock. The next step would be for the Treasury to exercise its warrants to purchase 79.9% of the GSEs’ common shares. The final step would be FHFA approval for the GSEs to relist on the NYSE as privately owned operating companies.

“The relisting and release of F2 will be one of the few major pieces of economic policy the President can still achieve after the midterms,” Ackman and Israel wrote. “We believe that there is no credible alternative to F2 exiting conservatorship and relisting on the NYSE as private-sector-owned operating companies.”

The memo also says Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has indicated the administration will focus on the GSEs and their future ownership status in 2027 and 2028.

Fannie and Freddie have been in conservatorship for 18 years. According to the Pershing memo, they now have more than $200 billion of shareholder equity. Over the past decade, average annual credit losses have been “only 0.05%,” and current capital levels are described as roughly 50 times that loss rate.Ackman and Israel estimate that combined capital could grow to more than $375 billion over the next five years, or more than 4% of the mortgage-backed securities guaranteed by the enterprises.

On valuation, the memo says the GSEs currently trade at about 1.5 times their earnings. From Trump’s election through the end of last year, when talk of a relisting was more active, their share prices rose by about eight times. This year, by contrast, their share prices have fallen more than 60% as the administration has remained “silent” on the issue, the investors said.

Pershing Square is heavily exposed to the outcome. The fund holds about 99 million shares of Fannie Mae, with a market value of roughly $422.5 million, along with roughly 95 million shares of Freddie Mac valued at about $386.9 million, according to the memo.

#5450. At SC26, Nvidia debuts new Rubin HPC chip, scientific research libraries

Nvidia Corp. today introduced a set of offerings designed to speed up scientific research across a range of fields.

The lineup is headlined by Rubin HPC, an upcoming graphics card with significantly more cores than the company’s current flagship chip. It’s joined by more than a half-dozen software tools geared toward scientists and engineers. The technologies made their debut at the SC26 high-performance and supercomputing conference in Chicago.

Nvidia’s flagship Rubin graphics processing unit features 898 Tensor cores, transistor clusters specifically optimized for large language models. It also includes over 28,000 CUDA cores. Those circuits can run not only LLMs but also other workloads such as scientific simulations.

The Rubin HPC (pictured), the upcoming chip that Nvidia previewed today, will feature more than 50,000 CUDA cores. It will also ship with a new iteration of NVLink, the interconnect that Nvidia’s GPUs use to exchange data with central processing units. The current version of the technology can move 3.6 terabits per second per graphics card.

Nvidia stated that Rubin HPC will also include a “sparse data acceleration” feature. Sparse data is the technical term for datasets that contain a large number of zeros. Many scientific projects generate such data, particularly in fields such as biology and astrophysics. A telescope, for example, might use zeros to represent sections of space without any visible stars.

“For agents tackling science and engineering, faster simulation means faster discovery,” said Ian Buck, Nvidia’s vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing. “Rubin HPC accelerates the simulations agents use to test ideas and guide their next steps, helping scientists and engineers explore more possibilities and bring breakthroughs closer.”

Nvidia plans to ship Rubin HPC in 2028. In the meantime, customers can speed up their scientific workloads using the software tools that debuted alongside the chip today.

Nvidia ships its GPUs  with a collection of libraries called CUDA-X that is designed to ease scientific research projects. The company’s SC26 announcement introduced several new additions to the suite.

Astrophysicists are gaining access to cuPhoton.xBeam, a library that makes it easier to analyze data from the Event Horizon Telescope network. It’s a collection of observatories used study black holes. According to Nvidia, cuPhoton.xBeam can perform data analysis tasks that historically took a month in eight minutes. It’s rolling out alongside cuPhoton.xLens, a library for simulating the plasma that fusion reactors use to generate electricity.

On the biology research side, Nvidia is open-sourcing cuSpa. It speeds up cell polygon calculations, which are used to study the structure of cells and the manner in which they interact with one another. Plus, an existing cellular analysis tool called rapids-singlecell is now available to Nvidia users in a containerized format.

Nvidia’s new biology research tools are joined by an AI bundle called Nemotron for Science. It’s built on Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, an open-source LLM the company introduced last month. The model features 124 billion parameters and activates about a 10th of them at any given time. It’s partly based on Mamba-2, a more hardware-efficient alternative to the ubiquitous Transformer model architecture.

Nemotron for Science pairs the LLM with a set of pre-packaged post-training workflows. Researchers can use them to optimize Nemotron 3.5 Super VL for specific scientific tasks. Additionally, Nvidia has added in nearly 50,000 chemistry-related questions. They can be used to post-train AI models and evaluate the capabilities of models that have already gone through the process.

“Nemotron for Science gives researchers open models, scientific data and post-training recipes to build specialized agents that reason through scientific problems and use CUDA-X accelerated tools to turn ideas into discoveries,” Buck said.

Quantum computers rely on a conventional processor to manage their qubits. Nvidia provides a set of software tools called CUDA-Q that makes it easier to link quantum hardware to its GPUs and CPUs. The company today expanded the suite with new building blocks for developing quantum software and an algorithm that can mitigate qubit errors.

Nvidia is teaming up with IBM Corp. and the U.S. Energy Department’s Fermilab to create a “modular quantum codesign platform.” It will combine the chip giant’s DGX B200 systems with quantum hardware from IBM. According to the companies, the goal is to create an environment that researchers can use to develop new qubit error correction algorithms and other quantum software.
