#5449. 4 takeaways from the Chargers' 23-20 win over the Ravens

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Four lessons from the Chargers' first win of 2026 in Baltimore, from a late forced fumble to a run defense that held the Ravens to 16 yards.

A team that keeps losing has to stop losing before anything else about it can be judged fairly. For the Chargers, the losing outlasted an entire offseason. Their last win before Monday came against the Cowboys in Week 16 of 2025, according to NBC Sports. The drought spanned two seasons, not just a bad start to one. Ending it was a genuine release for a team that had gone most of a calendar year without a victory. The relief also makes it tempting to treat everything that worked on that one night as the start of a turnaround, and that temptation is worth resisting.

The team across the field was struggling, too. The game was Baltimore's fifth straight loss, according to NBC Sports, and ESPN reports that it dropped the Ravens to 4-6. Monday night matched two slumping teams rather than handing the Chargers an upset of a contender. Baltimore was also without its star quarterback. Lamar Jackson was out with a right thumb injury, according to ESPN, and Jacoby Brissett played his first game for the Ravens after Baltimore acquired him in a trade. The Chargers' defense faced a quarterback who was still new to his offense. The win counts in the standings, but it came in a softer test than a typical Monday night in the NFL. The useful question for each lesson from the game is whether it would hold up against a healthier, sharper opponent.

The Los Angeles Chargers set out on the team's website to draw the key lessons from the Monday night win over Baltimore, from a defense that shut down the Ravens' running game to a late forced fumble and a ground attack that the offense relied on. Each of those lessons holds true for that one night. They differ in how much of each result the Chargers earned on their own and how much came from the condition of the team they played. Some rest on choices the coaching staff can make again next week, while others depended on what Baltimore could and couldn't do. The Chargers get their first chance to find out quickly, when they host the Jets at SoFi Stadium in Week 11.

The Chargers led the Ravens from start to finish on Monday night, according to NBC Sports, and still had to hang on for their first win of the season. A road win in Baltimore in prime time would usually point to a team that finally took control of a game. The Chargers instead won 23-20, according to chargers.com, and finished only one score ahead of an opponent that never once held the lead. They pulled ahead by double digits twice in the second half, and Baltimore kept closing the gap after each of those leads. The close finish did not come from a stronger team rallying late. It came from the Chargers failing to put away an opponent they were already beating.

Chargers head coach Jim Harbaugh credited his offense, defense and special teams alike for the win, but Baltimore moved the ball better than his team did. The Ravens gained 347 yards to the Chargers' 287, according to NBC Sports, and the Chargers' offense did not carry the night. The defense helped make up for that gap by forcing two turnovers. Takeaways tend to rise and fall from week to week, while a yardage edge is a steadier sign of which team controlled play. The Chargers won without that steadier sign on their side. After eight straight losses, the result mattered more than the way the Chargers reached it. Whether a win built this way can hold up is the question the rest of the night's lessons have to answer.

The Chargers' first win of the season came down to one Baltimore possession, and their defense ended it by taking the ball away. Baltimore had the ball on its final drive with the Chargers up three, according to chargers.com. ESPN reports that Zay Flowers lost the ball with 2:03 left, after cornerback Tarheeb Still kept working for it following the catch and pulled it free. "That was huge. Tarheeb was able — the ball come away from the body, and he was right there to claw it out," Chargers coach Jim Harbaugh told ESPN. With the ball back, the Chargers' offense no longer needed to score. It only needed to keep possession, and Justin Herbert's pass to Charlie Kolar on the next play gave the Chargers the first down they needed to run out the clock.

The defense had to make that play because the offense had stopped scoring touchdowns after halftime. The Chargers managed only a field goal in each of the third and fourth quarters, according to ESPN, so the offense added nothing in the second half that could put the game out of reach. Baltimore's passing game was carrying its offense, with Jacoby Brissett finishing the night at 340 yards, and Flowers had just caught one of his throws when Still stripped him. Still took the ball away from the part of Baltimore's offense that had been working, at the last moment when Baltimore could still tie or win the game.

A single forced fumble, however well timed, does not yet make a pattern. Chargers safety Tony Jefferson says the defense discusses going after the ball every day and treats it as a habit to keep repeating. The coming weeks will show whether the defense takes the ball away from offenses that are moving it well. Until then, Still's strip saved one win but has not shown that this defense can produce more of them.

A team trying to finish off its first win of the season needs a way to move the ball without giving it back, and the Chargers chose to run it. They ran for 160 yards at Baltimore, a total they had not reached in any earlier game this season, according to chargers.com. The offense also played its most careful game of the year and finished without a turnover. USA TODAY reports that it was Justin Herbert's first game of 2026 without an interception. By running the ball, the Chargers kept moving it without putting it at risk, which is what a winless team holding a lead needed most.

The big rushing night came from a decision about who would carry the ball. Mike McDaniel, who calls the Chargers' plays, stopped splitting carries among his running backs for this game, USA TODAY reports, and Omarion Hampton answered with the team's first 100-yard rushing game of 2026. Hampton finished with 105 yards on the full workload of a featured back. His longest run went only 19 yards, so he built his total from steady gains, not from a single breakaway. "The downhill runs were extremely good," Chargers head coach Jim Harbaugh said. Runs like those depend on how the staff uses Hampton, not on luck, and the coaches can call them again as long as they keep giving him the ball.

Herbert also gave Baltimore a second runner to account for, and his scramble produced the Chargers' first touchdown. The run game did not build every score, though. Hampton's touchdown followed an interception of Jacoby Brissett that the Chargers turned into points, according to USA TODAY. The defense helped set up that score as much as the runners did, so the running game's clearest value on Monday was control and safety.

This lesson depends least on Baltimore's condition, because it rests on a choice the Chargers make for themselves.

Baltimore had no running game to fall back on at any point in the night. The Ravens finished with 16 rushing yards and gained none before halftime, the Chargers' best run defense of the season, according to chargers.com. That left Baltimore with an offense that could only throw. Stopping the run was the Chargers' plan from the opening snaps, and it worked before Baltimore had any chance to wear the defense down. "There was a heck of a run wall, big emphasis on that," Chargers head coach Jim Harbaugh said. The Chargers also stopped the back Baltimore trusted most. Derrick Henry gained 10 yards on 10 carries, according to ESPN, so Baltimore could not keep handing him the ball until he found room.

The defenders who stopped the run also reached the quarterback when Baltimore threw. Jacoby Brissett faced 23 pressures from the Chargers, according to ESPN, on a night when his team could give him almost no help on the ground. Together, those results point to a Chargers front that won at the line of scrimmage on running plays and passing plays alike.

One strong night does not yet show a lasting change. Holding Baltimore to 16 yards stands out against every earlier game this season, and a single game that stands out that much is hard to treat as the new standard. Harbaugh's emphasis on the run suggests the Chargers can bring the same effort again. They have not yet shown they can get the same result against other offenses.

#5448. Infill outlier Thomas James Homes ‘landmaxxes’ lots with ADUs

TJH leverages attached ADU options across Seattle area floor plans to increase usable square footage on small lots. The company points to state legislation allowing 2 ADUs per lot and local treatment of ADUs as 2 units that can increase allowable floor area.  AI Summary

Where new construction is scarce and lots are tight, luxury homebuilder Thomas James Homes (TJH) has pivoted to offering accessory dwelling units (ADUs) to entice its homebuyers by adding more square footage on parcels with little room to spare.

For the firm’s Pacific Northwest division, which operates in Seattle and nearby suburbs where lots are small and space is at a premium, the approach is a natural fit. While detached ADUs are the more common use case nationwide, TJH’s PNW division uses attached ADUs because they offer cost efficiencies and add functional living space to small infill lots without sacrificing as much yard.

Most TJH floorplans in the region, which typically sell for $2 million to $5 million, include an attached ADU option, according to PNW division president Adam Rohde. More than half of buyers choose to include one.

Founded in 2006, TJH is a high-end, scattered-lot homebuilder that operates in California, Washington and Arizona. The company specializes in building replacement homes on individual lots in established neighborhoods where new construction is limited, either on homeowner-owned lots or through spec home sales. The goal is to bring the efficiency and predictability of production building to the infill market.

ADUs, which TJH began incorporating into more floor plans around 2022 or 2023, nest within that strategy by helping owners get more out of limited space, a trend the builder calls “landmaxxing.” Luxury buyers increasingly want flex space, and as Washington has passed stronger ADU laws allowing more density, TJH has used the new rules to fit more square footage on its buyers’ lots.

For builders operating in dense urban and suburban markets, TJH’s playbook offers a case study in making every square foot of a lot count.

“It’s our job to work with buyers to figure out how to best maximize the building value on their land,” Rohde said in an interview. “Our view of ADUs is that it’s a great way to expand the amount of home you can build, which, in and of itself, is a good proposition.”

TJH’s ADU strategy varies by division and market. While other divisions build detached ADUs, the PNW division favors attached units, which function as independent living spaces connected to the main house or built within it.

Buyers use the extra space in varying ways, from a home office or gym to bonus square footage, a rental unit or a place for multigenerational living.

According to Rohde, attached or integrated ADUs make more sense than detached ADUs for two main reasons.

First, the company builds on smaller infill lots with limited outdoor space. A detached ADU cuts into that space more than an attached alternative.

“We’re typically acquiring lots that…already have limited yard space. So, to put a detached unit in, you’re then eating further into that ability to create a very livable yard,” Rohde explained.

Second, attached ADUs share walls with the primary residence, which reduces the amount of additional construction required. Unlike detached units, they don’t require a completely separate structure, additional siding or separate utility connections. That creates efficiencies and makes them more cost-effective, with a better return on investment.

“With the integrated system, you’re already having some shared wall space, so you’re already getting some economies of scale and efficiency that make it a lot more cost-effective than the detached-style units,” he explained.

Still, that efficiency doesn’t make ADUs a simple project, and Rohde argued against the notion that they are an easy add-on, particularly detached units.

“There’s this perception in the market, especially when the new regulations were hitting to allow the expansion of detached ADUs in particular, that, ‘Hey, it’s really easy. You just pick up a module, plop it in your backyard, and presto, you have additional living space,’” he said. “The reality is, it’s just frankly not that simple.”

He pointed to several reasons why ADUs can be challenging to build, including fire separation and building codes, utility connections, site access and logistics, zoning and permitting timelines and the burden of ongoing maintenance costs.

“What people found is that it’s not that simple. And then it became, ‘How do we integrate ADUs into a more thoughtful development process?’ I think we’re really seeing a lot of traction around that [strategy],” Rohde explained.

Washington House Bill 1337, passed in 2023, helped make TJH’s approach possible. Under the legislation, cities statewide must allow two ADUs per lot. The legislation requires municipalities to allow ADUs with a gross floor area of at least 1,000 square feet. That legislation made it far easier for TJH to offer an attached ADU in most of its Seattle floor plans.

The real density gain, according to Rohde, comes from how Seattle treats a home with an ADU as two units, which increases floor area ratio and lets TJH build more total square footage, including the integrated ADU, on the same lot within zoning limits.

To comply with the law, Seattle updated its ADU rules in 2025 to treat a home with an ADU as two units, which may allow additional floor area ratio (FAR) on the lot. That allows TJH to build more total square footage when including an integrated ADU.

“It allows us to build more home on a given lot,” Rohde said. “But it’s not just building square footage for the sake of building square footage. It’s building thoughtful, value-add square footage.”

Rohde also pointed to Washington House Bill 1096, passed in 2025, which requires qualifying cities to create an administrative process for splitting a residential lot in two. Cities are phasing it in ahead of the 2027 state deadline.

“That will allow existing landowners who want to extract some value from a large parcel that they own to split and sell. It will allow owners of larger lots to put two complete, independent single-family residences that will then have their own opportunities to enact the ADU laws and things of that nature. Those types of things are really going to help us drive value,” Rohde added.

#5447. Milton Hershey School Hosts Exclusive HERSHEY Movie Premiere

Founders Week Event Offers Students a First Look at the Film Through a Gold-Carpet Premiere Featuring Surprise Hollywood Guests, Immersive Exhibits, and Historic Artifacts

HERSHEY, Pa., Nov. 17, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Milton Hershey School (MHS) students became the first large audience to watch the HERSHEY movie during an exclusive premiere at Founders Hall on Sunday, Nov. 15. The milestone screening placed the students who carry Milton and Catherine Hershey's legacy forward at the center of a one-of-a-kind event that concluded the school's 2026 Founders Week.

"Our students are the Hersheys' heirs and the living embodiment of Milton and Catherine's dream."

"Our students were not simply invited to see the HERSHEY movie. They were given the distinction of experiencing it first," said MHS President Peter G. Gurt. "That made the premiere especially meaningful because our students are the Hersheys' heirs and the living embodiment of Milton and Catherine's dream. There could be no more fitting audience with whom to share this story."

The premiere transformed the MHS campus into a movie extravaganza designed specifically for students. They walked a 739-foot gold carpet reflecting one of the school's signature colors, explored immersive exhibits about Milton and Catherine Hershey's lives and contributions, viewed rarely shown artifacts and costumes from the film, and took part in a custom-designed LED floor activation connected to the MHS Alma Mater. The event also featured appearances by influencers, celebrities, and actors, including Alexandra Daddario and Candace Cameron Bure, before students gathered for the screening.

The premiere capped a weeklong celebration rooted in the Hersheys' signing of the Deed of Trust in 1909 that established the school. Founders Week also included a special chapel service; a tree-planting ceremony for high school seniors; Founders Feast, a meal of gratitude served by MHS staff to all 2,200 students; a Founders Day Assembly and parade; fireworks above Founders Hall; and a Student Government Association Leadership Conference featuring Hershey entity executives.

"Being at Milton Hershey School and seeing firsthand the impact that Milton and Catherine Hershey's vision continues to have on young people is incredibly moving," said Daddario, who portrays Catherine Hershey in the HERSHEY film. "MHS is an amazing home and school for children and brings to life the very best of the Hersheys' ever-inspiring influence on the world."

Founded 117 years ago, MHS has a mission to nurture and educate children in social and financial need to lead fulfilling and productive lives. Honoring the Hersheys' wishes, its students live on campus in family-style homes led by married houseparent couples. "At MHS, we are forever grateful for our founders, and we will never take lightly our responsibility to make them proud in how we live, learn, and serve," said Gurt.

#5446. Open AI hit with lawsuit in California over Hugging Face rogue agent incident

California Attorney General Rob Bonta today announced the state has launched a lawsuit against OpenAI Group PBC after the company’s AI agents earlier this year went rogue and hacked the open-source AI platform Hugging Face Inc.

The 31-page lawsuit, filed in San Francisco Superior Court, claims Open AI has engendered the public and put institutions at risk by developing products without suitable safeguards. Bonta likened Open AI’s behavior to being a “public nuisance,” asking the judge to order the company to change its practices while imposing financial penalties for any money the company made from the high-risk areas of its business.

“OpenAI’s actions escalated real-word cybersecurity risks, threatening the safety, health, and well-being of society,” Bonta said in a statement at a press conference. “The company knowingly tested a dangerous product without proper oversight or safety procedures and misled the public about it — this disregard for public safety violated California law.”

Bonta believes that without external pressure, the scope and frequency of such attacks will increase in the future. “In California, we value innovation, but we demand innovation that follows the law — no matter the product or the company,” he added.

The “unprecedented” rogue attack in question occurred on July 21 this year when one of Open AI’s agents escaped what was supposed to be an isolated testing environment — a sandbox. To break out of their restricted environment and access the internet, the AI models exploited a previously unknown security flaw in OpenAI’s systems. From there, they gained access to other parts of the company’s network, stole login credentials, and exploited further security weaknesses to break into Hugging Face’s servers.

In response to the lawsuit, OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said he believes the company has been singled out when similar challenges have been faced at other major AI firms. “Since the Hugging Face incident, we’ve undertaken an extensive and transparent effort to understand and address misaligned model activity,” he told media, adding that the company will continue to work with the state and share information to ensure public and institutional safety.

Nonetheless, Bonta has expressed skepticism about Open AI’s willingness to conform to safety practices, writing that through a “lack of transparency and misrepresentations” the company has continued to develop dangerous models with the ability to deceive and engage in malicious behavior.

Open AI is already facing lawsuits in eight states over a number of incidents. The company stands accused of developing technologies that have harmed the public by providing dangerous medical advice or steering people to make bad, sometimes harmful, decisions that threaten their safety.

#5445. 10 Grand Theft Auto milestones, from a Scottish studio's 1997 original to GTA 6

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Grand Theft Auto history in 10 milestones, from DMA Design's 1997 top-down original through GTA V and GTA Online to the Leonida-set GTA 6

Grand Theft Auto has changed its viewpoint and its format several times since 1997, yet it keeps returning to the same few fictional places. The series began as a top-down game made by DMA Design, a Scottish studio, and published by BMG Interactive on PC and PlayStation. Grand Theft Auto III, published by Rockstar Games, launched on PlayStation 2 in October 2001 and moved the series into a full 3D open world. Grand Theft Auto Online followed in October 2013 as a multiplayer mode, shortly after Grand Theft Auto V. It has been updated over the years. Those shifts in perspective and format form the backbone of the Grand Theft Auto history traced here.

The 1997 original was set in three fictional cities: Liberty City, San Andreas and Vice City. Each name came back later in a new form. Grand Theft Auto III rebuilt Liberty City in 3D. Grand Theft Auto: Vice City, released in 2002, used its name for a 1980s Miami-inspired setting. Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas, released in 2004, used its name for a state with three cities: Los Santos, San Fierro and Las Venturas. Grand Theft Auto IV went back to Liberty City in 2008 and ran on the RAGE engine. Grand Theft Auto V, released in September 2013, was set in Los Santos.

The series also moved through time. Grand Theft Auto: London, 1969, a 1999 expansion pack for the original game, placed the action in the London of 1969. Grand Theft Auto 2, another 1999 release, went the other way. That top-down sequel was set in a near-future city and used a gang-respect system. The San Andreas story was set in 1992.

The people at the center of the games changed as well. Tommy Vercetti led Vice City. Carl "CJ" Johnson led San Andreas. Niko Bellic, an Eastern European immigrant, led Grand Theft Auto IV. Grand Theft Auto V split its story across three playable protagonists: Michael De Santa, Franklin Clinton and Trevor Philips.

Grand Theft Auto VI, which Rockstar has announced, is set in the state of Leonida, with Vice City as a setting. Its first trailer was released in December 2023.

The 10 slides below cover a selection of milestones from the series, not every game it includes. They run in chronological order, from the 1997 original to Grand Theft Auto VI.

Grand Theft Auto launched in 1997 as a top-down game from DMA Design, a Scottish studio. BMG Interactive published it on PC and PlayStation.

The top-down view defined how the original looked and played. Players watched the action from a camera positioned above the city.

That viewpoint did not end with the first game. The 1999 sequel, Grand Theft Auto 2, kept the same top-down approach.

The 1997 game spread its action across three fictional cities. They were Liberty City, San Andreas and Vice City. All three appeared within that single release.

Those names outlasted the original. Each one returned in a later entry of the series.

The publisher also changed after the first game. BMG Interactive released the 1997 original. Grand Theft Auto III, released in 2001, was published by Rockstar Games.

Grand Theft Auto: London, 1969 is a 1999 expansion pack for the original Grand Theft Auto. It moved the action to London and set it in the year 1969.

An expansion pack adds new content to an existing game. It is not a new numbered entry in the series. London, 1969 built on the 1997 original, the top-down game that started Grand Theft Auto.

The expansion arrived two years after that first game.

Its setting broke with the original. The 1997 game took place in three fictional cities. London, 1969 used a real city instead.

It also tied the action to a specific year in the past. That year falls 30 years before the expansion's own release.

Grand Theft Auto 2, released in 1999, was a top-down sequel to the original Grand Theft Auto. It was set in a near-future city called Anywhere, USA, and used a gang-respect system.

The sequel kept the overhead perspective of the 1997 game. Players still saw the city from above.

The setting changed. The original game spread its action across three fictional cities: Liberty City, San Andreas and Vice City. Grand Theft Auto 2 placed its story in one city set in the near future.

The sequel came out in the same year as Grand Theft Auto: London, 1969. That expansion pack for the original game looked back to 1969 London, while Grand Theft Auto 2 looked ahead.

Grand Theft Auto III moved the series from a top-down view to a full 3D open world. Rockstar Games published it on PlayStation 2 in October 2001.

Liberty City was its setting. That made Liberty City the first location in the series built as a three-dimensional open world.

The main games before it showed their cities from overhead. The 1997 original used that top-down perspective. Grand Theft Auto 2, released in 1999, kept it. Grand Theft Auto III dropped the overhead map for a world built in three dimensions.

The city's name went back to the start of the series. Liberty City first appeared in the 1997 Grand Theft Auto as one of its three fictional cities.

The publisher had changed too. BMG Interactive published the 1997 original on PC and PlayStation. Rockstar Games filled that role for Grand Theft Auto III.

Grand Theft Auto: Vice City, released in 2002, set the series in a fictional city inspired by 1980s Miami. Its protagonist is Tommy Vercetti.

The game came out the year after Grand Theft Auto III, which was set in Liberty City. Vice City replaced that location with one drawn from Miami.

The setting combines a place and a period. The place takes its cues from Miami, a real U.S. city. The period is the 1980s, a past decade rather than the present day.

Tommy Vercetti is the character players control in that 1980s world.

Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas, released in 2004, casts players as Carl "CJ" Johnson in a story set in 1992. Its map is a fictional state that holds three cities: Los Santos, San Fierro and Las Venturas.

The state itself is called San Andreas, and the game takes its title from it. Los Santos, San Fierro and Las Venturas each have their own name, but all three sit on the same map.

The 1992 setting puts CJ's story 12 years before the game came out in 2004. The game is set in the recent past, not the present day.

Carl Johnson is the game's protagonist. He goes by the nickname CJ.

Grand Theft Auto IV, released in 2008, took the series back to Liberty City and ran on the RAGE engine. Its protagonist is Niko Bellic, an Eastern European immigrant.

The RAGE engine is the technical marker for this entry. Grand Theft Auto IV used it to build its version of Liberty City.

Liberty City was not a new location for the franchise. It was one of three fictional cities in the original 1997 Grand Theft Auto. The other two were San Andreas and Vice City. That first version of the city was shown from a top-down view.

Grand Theft Auto III used Liberty City again in 2001. That game moved the series into a full 3D open world. Grand Theft Auto IV came back to the same city seven years later.

Across this timeline, Liberty City is the setting for three entries: the 1997 original, Grand Theft Auto III and Grand Theft Auto IV. The 2008 game is the one in that group built on the RAGE engine.

Niko Bellic gives the game its point of view. He is an Eastern European immigrant. The two entries just before this one in the timeline each had a different lead. Grand Theft Auto: Vice City, from 2002, followed Tommy Vercetti. Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas, from 2004, followed Carl "CJ" Johnson.

In the GTA timeline, the 2008 game arrived four years after Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas. It came five years before Grand Theft Auto V, which was released in September 2013 and is set in Los Santos.

Grand Theft Auto V, released in September 2013, gives players three protagonists instead of one. They are Michael De Santa, Franklin Clinton and Trevor Philips, and all three are playable.

That structure departs from the entries that came before it. Grand Theft Auto: Vice City cast players as Tommy Vercetti. Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas followed Carl "CJ" Johnson. Grand Theft Auto IV centered on Niko Bellic, an Eastern European immigrant.

Each of those games was built around one named lead. Grand Theft Auto V divides its story among three characters instead. The design moves the series from a single point of view to several within the same game.

The game is set in Los Santos. That name already had a place in the series. Los Santos was one of three cities in Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas, alongside San Fierro and Las Venturas.

Grand Theft Auto V came out nine years after San Andreas, which was released in 2004. San Andreas spread its story across a fictional state with three cities. Grand Theft Auto V is set in one of them.

The release also followed Grand Theft Auto IV by five years. That 2008 game was set in Liberty City. Grand Theft Auto V moved the numbered series from Liberty City to Los Santos.

Grand Theft Auto Online is a multiplayer mode that launched in October 2013. It arrived shortly after Grand Theft Auto V, which was released in September 2013.

That timing puts the two releases side by side in the GTA timeline. Grand Theft Auto V came out first, and the multiplayer mode went live soon after.

Grand Theft Auto Online has been updated over the years since that 2013 debut. The mode players reach today is not the same as the one that first launched.

That pattern sets it apart from the entries before it. It has a single launch date, followed by years of further updates.

Grand Theft Auto VI is set in Leonida, a fictional state, and Vice City is one of its settings. Rockstar has announced the game, and its first trailer was released in December 2023.

Leonida frames GTA VI around a state rather than a single city. Vice City is one location within that state, not the whole setting.

That structure has a precedent in the series. Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas, released in 2004, was also set in a state rather than in one city. GTA VI takes up that wider framing again with Leonida.

The Vice City name runs deep in the GTA timeline. It first appeared in the 1997 original Grand Theft Auto, as one of that game's three fictional cities. In GTA VI, the name returns as part of a larger state.

#5444. NAMB opposes VA loan fee increases in Senate bill

NAMB launched an advocacy campaign urging mortgage professionals to oppose Section 104 of S. 4744, which would raise VA IRRRL and assumption fees and make them permanent. The group estimates $4 billion in added borrower costs and backs the Major Richard Star Act as an alternative.  AI Summary

The National Association of Mortgage Brokers (NAMB) is urging mortgage professionals to contact their senators and oppose proposed increases to fees for veterans using Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) home loans, arguing the changes would shift the cost of new benefits onto other veterans.

The advocacy campaign, posted on NAMB’s website, comes as the Senate considers S. 4744, its version of the Take Care of America’s Veterans Act (H.R. 9237), which passed the House by voice vote on Veterans Day. The Senate bill is on the calendar and is eligible for debate and a vote.

NAMB supports the legislation’s goal of providing additional benefits to combat-injured veterans but opposes Section 104, which would increase fees associated with VA loans.

“Our biggest issue is the fact that our veterans serving our country took an oath to serve and defend. They didn’t take or raise their hand to receive a bill to pay for benefits for their fallen or disabled brothers and sisters. That is not the obligation of the soldier. That’s the obligation of the taxpayer and the disbursement of those tax dollars on the appropriations,” NAMB President Michael Farrell said in a conversation with HousingWire.

Under the Senate proposal, the funding fee for Interest Rate Reduction Refinance Loans (IRRRLs) would increase from 0.5% to 1.42%, while the VA loan assumption fee would double from 0.5% to 1%. The increases would also become permanent, eliminating a 10-year sunset provision.

“For the veteran doing the IRRRL and raising that 1.42% from 0.5% on a $400,000 average loan is taking [the fee] from $2,000 to $5,680. And the the concept of, ‘Well, it doesn’t affect their recoupment’ in regards to justifying doing the loan … it does affect and impact the cost of doing the loan,” Farrell added.

NAMB estimates the changes would add $4 billion in costs for veteran borrowers, or an average of $3,780 per veteran. The association also argues the higher IRRRL fee could conflict with the VA’s 36-month recoupment requirement, potentially making some veterans ineligible for the refinancing program.

“It seems like there’s other solutions that can be looked into to raise the funding to support the benefit. … But to alienate it just to one aspect of the IRRRL, when home affordability is a huge concern and veterans are looking to step down their rate or step down their payment to better their family living expenses, now we’ve tripled the cost of getting that done,” Farrell said.

Instead, NAMB is advocating for passage of the Major Richard Star Act (H.R. 2102/S. 1032), a bipartisan, standalone measure that would allow approximately 54,000 combat-injured military retirees to receive both full retirement pay and VA disability compensation.

The legislation was introduced by Rep. Gus Bilirakis (R-Fla.) in the House and by Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) in the Senate. On Veterans Day, the House voted 245-175 to discharge a resolution to consider the legislation separately and, on Nov. 12, passed the act.

“We are supportive of every veteran receiving their benefit,” Farrell said. “And if this is going to help 54,000 combat injured military retirees receive both their retirement pay and their disability pay, we stand to support the standalone Major Star Act. We do agree with that, but [regarding] Section 104, we have huge concerns on the feasibility of putting this bill on the backs of fellow veterans.”

#5443. Cypris Introduces the First AI Agent Workforce for R&D

New agent workforce platform enables R&D organizations to deploy specialized AI agents across technical, scientific, commercial, and regulatory workflows, with persistent memory, performance reviews, and enterprise governance.

NEW YORK, Nov. 17, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Cypris today announced the launch of Agent Fleet, a new capability enabling R&D organizations to build, deploy, and manage their own workforces of specialized AI agents.

Rather than relying on AI as a tool for individual research tasks, R&D teams can now orchestrate fleets of specialized agents capable of executing complete workflows across technical, scientific, commercial, and regulatory intelligence. Each agent operates under the direction and governance of the organization's subject matter experts, with defined responsibilities, persistent memory, performance feedback, and the ability to improve its execution over time.

The launch marks a shift toward a new operating model for corporate R&D, where professionals increasingly act as orchestrators of AI agents, directing specialized digital workers to accelerate discovery, identify new opportunities, and reduce uncertainty across the innovation lifecycle.

Purpose-Built Agents for Chemicals and Advanced Materials

Unlike general-purpose AI assistants, Cypris agents are designed to execute specialized R&D workflows, with a particular focus on the complexity of chemicals, advanced materials, and industrial innovation.

Organizations can configure and deploy agents for functions including:

These agents work across Cypris's integrated intelligence ecosystem, connecting patents, scientific literature, chemical compounds, regulatory information, and commercial signals to deliver actionable research outputs.

Unlike traditional AI tools designed for isolated tasks, Cypris Agent Fleet enables organizations to develop a workforce that improves through continued use and human guidance.

Agents can adapt to organizational preferences, incorporate feedback, and become more effective with experience.

Over time, organizations can cultivate specialized agents that increasingly reflect their technical standards, research priorities, and institutional knowledge.

Enterprise Governance for a New Class of Digital Workers

As AI agents take on more complex responsibilities, organizations need the ability to manage and scale their deployment with confidence.

Agent Fleet provides enterprise-level governance, allowing organizations to manage agents across teams while maintaining consistent standards and human oversight.

The result is a new operating model in which R&D professionals increasingly direct, evaluate, and coordinate AI agents rather than manually execute every research task.

Agents That Work Across Applications and Deliverables

Cypris agents are designed to operate across the environments and workflows enterprise R&D teams already use.

Whether within Cypris or connected applications such as Microsoft Copilot, Claude, and electronic laboratory notebooks (ELNs), agents can execute research assignments across multiple environments.

Agents can deliver work in various formats, including technical reports, presentations, spreadsheets, and interactive research outputs, allowing organizations to integrate AI agents into existing R&D processes.

Building the Agentic Workforce for Corporate R&D

"The next generation of R&D professionals won't spend their days manually gathering and synthesizing information. They'll be orchestrating fleets of specialized AI agents that carry out this work on their behalf," said Steve Hafif, CEO and Co-Founder of Cypris.

"What's important is that these agents aren't simply one-off assistants. They have responsibilities, memory, performance expectations, and the ability to improve through feedback. We're building the infrastructure for R&D organizations to manage AI agents much like they manage teams today."

Agent Fleet represents the next step in Cypris's broader vision of building the agentic workforce for corporate R&D. The company plans to introduce additional agent capabilities, deeper workflow integrations, and expanded workforce management functionality as the platform evolves.

Cypris is the AI-powered R&D intelligence platform purpose-built for innovation, IP, and R&D teams. The platform aggregates more than 1B data points across global patents, scientific literature, chemical compounds, regulatory sources, and corporate activity, giving research organizations a single source of truth for technical and strategic decision-making. Cypris is trusted by thousands of enterprise R&D teams, government laboratories, and innovation teams worldwide.

#5442. 10 infamous video game delays, from Duke Nukem Forever to Grand Theft Auto VI

Free daily briefing on global business news.

These 10 infamous video game delays, from Duke Nukem Forever to Grand Theft Auto VI, show how game development can stretch across years, studios and console generations

A release date in the video game business is a promise made before the product exists. Studios often announce games years before the core work is finished. When development runs longer than planned, the date moves. Sometimes it moves again. In a few cases, the wait stretches past a decade.

The announcements and target dates in this list run from 1995 to 2026. In between are projects that changed engines, studios, names, directors and console generations before anyone could buy them. Some of the finished games were completed by teams that were not involved at the start. One shipped on a console that did not exist when it was first shown.

These 10 infamous video game delays are a selection, not a complete record. They are ordered by announcement date, oldest first. The four earliest were shooters announced between 1995 and 1998. Among the later entries, one game was pulled from a digital storefront eight days after launch.

Each slide covers one game and one kind of delay story. Prey and Duke $DUK Nukem Forever were both announced by 3D Realms in the 1990s. They took different routes to release. Valve appears twice: once for a nine-year gap and once for a target date that fell in the same month its source code leaked. Square $SQ Enix also appears twice, with one project renamed midway and another revealed years before it shipped. Sony $SONY's The Last Guardian was revealed for one PlayStation and released on the next. Cyberpunk 2077 shows how a run of shorter postponements can add up. Grand Theft Auto VI remains an open case, with its schedule set by Take-Two announcements rather than a completed launch.

The aim is not to rank failure or to explain away every slip. Delays are a routine part of software development. What sets these examples apart is their length, their visibility or the specific chain of events that kept them from shipping on time. Taken together, they show how wide the gap between a first trailer and a finished product can grow.

Prey reached players in July 2006, 11 years after 3D Realms announced the game in 1995. Human Head Studios built the version that went on sale.

That makes Prey a case where the studio that finished the game was not the studio that first announced it. 3D Realms put the project before the public in 1995. Human Head Studios delivered the release that players could buy in July 2006.

Daikatana missed its Christmas 1997 target by about two and a half years. Ion Storm, the studio led by John Romero, released the game on PC in June 2000.

Ion Storm planned to have Daikatana on sale for the 1997 holiday season. That window closed without a release. The holiday seasons of 1998 and 1999 also passed before the PC version reached stores.

Romero led the studio throughout the project. The game shipped under the same studio that had set the original Christmas target.

The game's pre-release advertising campaign drew criticism. That campaign ran before the finished game was available to buy. Players were reacting to Daikatana's marketing years before they could play it.

Daikatana's delay combines two separate threads. One is a specific holiday date that the studio did not meet. The other is an advertising campaign that met criticism well ahead of launch. The June 2000 PC release closed the gap between the two.

Team Fortress 2 reached players on October 10, 2007, nine years after Valve announced it in 1998. It did not arrive as a standalone release. Valve shipped it as part of The Orange Box.

Valve made the announcement in the late 1990s. Players could not buy the game until the late 2000s. The project was promised in one decade and delivered in the next.

The release format is the defining detail of this case. The long wait did not end with a launch date of its own. Team Fortress 2 instead reached the market as one part of a larger package.

Duke $DUK Nukem Forever was released on June 14, 2011, 14 years after 3D Realms announced it in 1997. The studio that announced the game was not the one that finished it.

The project changed technology in its first year. In 1997, the same year as the announcement, the team moved development to Quake II technology.

A second switch followed in 1998, when the team moved to Unreal technology. Within two calendar years of the announcement, the project had changed its technical foundation twice.

The next major event on the record came in May 2009, when 3D Realms laid off staff. That was 11 years after the move to Unreal technology.

The layoffs did not end Duke Nukem Forever. Gearbox Software took the project over from 3D Realms and completed development.

The game reached stores about two years after the layoffs. It shipped under a different developer from the one that first put its name in front of players.

Half-Life 2 was released on November 16, 2004, more than 13 months after Valve's original target of September 30, 2003. The game's source code was stolen and leaked in September 2003, the same month the planned launch was due.

Valve had set September 30, 2003, as the release date for the first-person shooter. That date passed without a finished game reaching players.

Source code is the underlying programming a studio writes to build a game. A leak of that material puts unfinished work in the hands of people outside the company before the developer chooses to release it. It can expose how a project is built and how far along it is.

On October 2, 2003, Valve's Gabe Newell publicly discussed the theft. His comments came two days after the original target date. By then, the scheduled launch had already been missed.

The record places the theft, the leak and the missed date close together on the calendar. Those dates do not show what pushed the release back. They show only that the events fell within weeks of one another in the fall of 2003. Any account that links them as cause and effect goes beyond what the timeline itself establishes.

Counted from the original target, players waited 413 days for the finished game. That stretch is measured from a fixed release date rather than from a first announcement. It tracks the slip of one specific promise.

The Half-Life 2 delay is defined by its sequence. A missed launch came first, followed within days by a public account from Gabe Newell about stolen code. More than a year later, the finished game arrived.

Final Fantasy XV was released on November 29, 2016, 10 years after Square $SQ Enix first announced it. At its 2006 announcement, the game had a different name, Final Fantasy Versus XIII, and was planned for PlayStation 3.

The original title tied the project to Final Fantasy XIII rather than giving it a number of its own. It was presented as a companion to another game, not as the next main entry in the series.

In 2013, Square Enix renamed the game Final Fantasy XV. The new number took it out from under Final Fantasy XIII and placed it in the main numbered series.

That same year, Hajime Tabata replaced Tetsuya Nomura as director. The director who brought the game to release was not the one attached to it during its years as Versus XIII.

The 2013 changes split the game's public history into two stretches of unequal length. The first ran from the 2006 announcement to the rename and lasted seven years. The second ran from the rename to the November 2016 release and lasted three years.

Most of the decade between announcement and launch passed under a name the finished game never carried. Players bought it as Final Fantasy XV.

Kingdom Hearts III was released on January 29, 2019, more than five years after Square $SQ Enix revealed it at E3 2013.

The reveal took place at E3, the Electronic Entertainment Expo.

Five full calendar years passed between the reveal year and the release year. The game did not reach players at any point from 2014 through 2018.

The Last Guardian was revealed at E3 2009 as a PlayStation 3 game and reached players on PlayStation 4 on December 6, 2016. About seven years separated its first public showing from its release.

Sony $SONY introduced the project at E3 2009. It was presented as the next game from Fumito Ueda and Team ICO.

At that reveal, the named platform was PlayStation 3. The game never came out on that console.

By the time it shipped in December 2016, The Last Guardian was a PlayStation 4 title. The machine named in the original announcement and the machine it launched on came from different PlayStation generations.

That made this delay a matter of hardware as well as calendar time. The game did not simply arrive late on the console it was announced for. It moved to Sony's next generation before anyone could buy it.

Cyberpunk 2077 missed its first release date of April 16, 2020, and was delayed three times before CD Projekt Red launched it on December 10, 2020. Eight days later, Sony $SONY removed the game from the PlayStation Store after complaints about its performance on older consoles.

CD Projekt Red announced Cyberpunk 2077 in 2012. The game went on sale eight years after that announcement.

April 16, 2020, was the first firm date attached to the project. It did not hold. The first delay moved the launch to September 17, 2020. That shift added 154 days, or about five months, to the schedule.

A second delay pushed the release to November 19, 2020. The new date sat 63 days after the September target.

The third delay was the shortest of the three. It moved the launch from November 19 to December 10, 2020, a gap of 21 days.

Each postponement was shorter than the one before it. The schedule moved in shrinking steps rather than in one long jump. Each step also named a specific new day rather than a season or a year.

The original April date and the actual launch ended up 238 days apart, or nearly eight months. Each new date replaced one that had already been announced. Two of the replacement dates, September 17 and November 19, also passed without a release.

Set against the full timeline, that stretch was short. Most of the time between announcement and launch passed before any firm date existed. The dated delays covered less than a year of a game first announced in 2012.

Sony took the game off the PlayStation Store on December 18, 2020. The PlayStation Store is the digital marketplace where PlayStation owners buy and download games. The removal came 246 days after the original April target.

Every date in this sequence, from the first target to the store removal, fell within 2020. The last entry was not a new release date but a removal from Sony's digital store.

Grand Theft Auto VI is scheduled for November 19, 2026, after Take-Two announced two delays. Rockstar Games and Take-Two had originally targeted 2025 for the game's release.

That original target named a year, not a day. The first delay changed both. Take-Two announced a new release date of May 26, 2026. The game left 2025 behind and gained a specific day on the calendar.

That date did not hold. Take-Two later announced a second delay, this time to November 19, 2026. The new date sits nearly six months after the May date.

The two delays did different work. The first took the game out of its original target year. The second kept it in 2026 but moved it late into that year.

Every date in this story so far comes from an announcement. None of them describes a finished launch. November 19, 2026, is the most recent target Take-Two has announced. It remains a scheduled date rather than a completed release.

#5441. With $5M in funding, Pretxt launches runtime oversight layer to supervise AI agents in real time

Artificial intelligence supervision pioneer Pretxt AI is launching with $5 million in seed funding today as it tries to contain the very real risk of unleashing autonomous agents in production environments.

It has created a new kind of “AI Supervision” tool that applies oversight at runtime to ensure those agents follow a company’s rules at all times. Today’s round was led by Deciens Capital and saw participation from Howdy Partners, Service Provider Capital and NSV Wolf Capital.

The startup is pitching the idea of a continuous runtime supervision layer that monitors AI agents as they’re getting work done, contrasting their behavior with the parent organization’s rules and policies. If it spots an agent is starting to drift off-course, it will immediately intervene to put it back on the right track, before it can make a critical mistake that hurts the business.

Real-time guardrails like Pretxt has designed are likely going to become a priority for enterprises as they begin to trust AI agents with more consequential work than simply drafting emails or creating images. For instance, if agents are to be trusted with handling customer refunds and accessing mission-critical databases and modifying records within them, companies will need the strongest reassurance that they’re not going to mess up those tasks.

But those assurances are few and far between. AI is notorious for “hallucinating” responses when it doesn’t know the answer to a question, and autonomous agents have shown erratic behavior time and again. They don’t need a malicious prompt injection to start missing critical required steps in a workflow or invent policy exceptions to simplify a task they’re trying to complete. They’ve shown they can do this in both labs and in the real world.

In response, most security tools take a heavy-handed approach, blocking agents outright, but this means that work slows down. The other approach is to flag errors after the fact, but by the time that happens they could have already caused massive damage.

Pretxt’s co-founders Brian Soby (pictured, left) and Aaron Costello (right) realized that companies need a more balanced approach to agentic security and oversight. Soby, who serves as the startup’s chief executive, previously held senior security roles at Salesforce Inc. and Mitre Inc. before founding the software-as-a-service security startup AppOmni Inc.

It was there that he met Costello, who now serves as Pretxt’s chief technology officer. During their time at AppOmni, they uncovered several major vulnerabilities in AI agents developed by Salesforce and ServiceNow Inc. and began to understand what’s required to ensure those agents can still work safely.

Many traditional agent monitoring tools use a second large language model as a “judge” to monitor the behavior of the main LLM that’s doing the work. But Pretxt’s co-founders shunned this idea because it creates latency, increases compute costs and involves too much guesswork.

Instead, their AI Supervision platform is powered by a near-deterministic engine that evaluates agent’s actions in milliseconds in order to spot those that break the rules and intercept them in progress. The company reckons it can do this up to 60 times faster than LLM-as-a-Judge-based security tools.

The approach is effective. In tests on Zapier’s AutomationBench, Pretext was able to reduce agent policy violations from around one in five to zero. The tool is designed to be easy to implement, so teams don’t need a thorough understanding of the models or agents they’re trying to supervise.

Instead, they simply choose which policies, standards and guardrails should apply to an agent, and then they can keep track of them in real time. The platform allows users to track approvals, roll back plan versions and escalate any tricky edge cases to human decision-makers.

That last capability is especially useful, because many organizations’ security plans have gaps when agents encounter situations that were not previously envisaged. In such cases, Pretxt halts the agent and asks a human to decide what the rules should be.

“Supervising an AI agent shouldn’t mean becoming an expert in everything it touches or in how it’s built,” Costello said. “Teams tell us in plain language how it should behave and where the boundaries are, and we supervise and steer the agent to stay within them. So there’s no untangling permissions or digging into the agent’s internals.”

Pretxt’s AI Supervision tool is available in early access now. It’s primarily targeting high-stakes regulated industries where mistakes and hallucinations simply cannot be tolerated.

For financial services and insurance companies, it can enforce borrower verification rules and route complex claims to humans, while in healthcare and life sciences it ensures that agents don’t step outside of strict boundaries. In customer support applications, it can prevent agents from offering unapproved discounts or refunds to customers.

AI Supervision can provide a lot of different benefits to a lot of different people. Chief information officers and other senior executives will be able to scale higher-value AI projects safely, while security teams, compliance officers and platform engineers can address gaps in risk management and ensure low-latency policy enforcement without needing to stack additional models.

Enterprise Management Associates analyst Chris Steffen said the thing that really sets Pretxt apart is its focus on the basics. Not only does it check that agents are behaving themselves, but it also makes sure they’re doing the work they’ve been assigned without breaking any rules or cutting any corners, creating what is effectively a new category of AI supervision tool.

“Most tools ask if an agent is secure, compliant or observable, but far fewer can show if the agent is correctly doing the job it was given,” Steffen said. “Most tools can only report what went wrong after the fact, when it’s too late. Pretxt intervenes while the outcome can still change to get agents back on track.”

#5440. The next housing crisis could be a cyberattack, not a rate shock

Mortgage servicing risk is increasingly tied to cyber resilience, not only rates or credit. The column argues for zero trust, secure-by-design engineering, faster vulnerability mitigation and constrained agentic AI to protect borrower data, escrow payments and platform integrity.   AI Summary

For decades, the mortgage industry has understood risk through interest rates, credit performance, liquidity and market volatility. We have sophisticated models to anticipate financial disruptions and regulatory frameworks designed to manage them. Often overlooked is the security and resilience of the digital infrastructure that makes American homeownership possible.

Every day, servicing platforms move escrow payments, safeguard homeowners’ data and support families through hardship. An attack on these systems is not just an IT problem. It represents a significant financial risk to millions of American families.

The next disruption to the housing market may not begin with a change in interest rates. It could start with a compromised identity, an exploited vulnerability or an attack on a critical technology provider. Protecting these systems starts with a mindset shift. Servicers should approach their platforms with a Zero Trust philosophy, trusting nothing by default and building and running every system under the assumption that it can be compromised.

One of the most persistent mistakes in enterprise technology is treating cybersecurity as something that happens after software is built, a gap that cybercriminals are quick to exploit. Weak architecture, excessive privileges, insecure integrations and misconfigured infrastructure get baked into a system, and fixing them after deployment costs far more than preventing them in design.

Cybersecurity must be integrated into the work of every team from day one as they build new products that make loan servicing more efficient. Security should not be the department that tells engineering why something cannot go to production. It should be part of the engineering process that ensures it can go to production safely.

For too long, enterprise cybersecurity has assumed that if you build a strong perimeter, you can trust what’s inside it. That approach is incompatible with today’s interconnected financial ecosystem, which runs on cloud infrastructure, third-party integrations, distributed workforces and constantly shifting data flows.

Zero trust is not a marketing slogan; it is an engineering philosophy that must be built in from day one and extend across the enterprise technology system. This means eliminating implicit trust and continuously evaluating access. A good lock on the front door doesn’t make a home secure if everything inside is open to anyone who gets past it. Zero trust starts with the assumption that someone eventually will get through, so every room, and the safe inside it, has its own lock.

For servicers, that means a single stolen password or compromised vendor connection can’t open every borrower file and escrow account. In mortgage technology, secure by design and default must become baseline expectations rather than competitive differentiators.

By adopting the Zero Trust mindset, servicers should continuously test their defenses and identify potential threats. Traditional cybersecurity programs have invested heavily in vulnerability scanning, security assessments, compliance reporting and incident response.

To do this, we must move from passive defense to proactive cyber operations. Threat intelligence should be more than vulnerability scans or security assessments in a weekly report. It should directly inform how security teams hunt for threats, test defenses, prioritize engineering work and anticipate adversary behavior.

Cybersecurity programs often measure success by vulnerabilities found, tickets opened and assessments completed, but those track activity, not security. Finding a vulnerability does not make an organization safer. Mitigating it does.

To effectively stand up to the growing danger of cybersecurity threats, leaders should focus on shortening the time between identifying a weakness and eliminating or containing the risk. That starts with preventing vulnerabilities from entering production and continues through automated detection, intelligent prioritization, remediation and validation throughout the life of a system.

The goal is not to produce a more comprehensive inventory of problems. It is to systematically reduce the opportunities available to attackers. That is the difference between vulnerability management and vulnerability mitigation.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is already changing the threat landscape, and defenders cannot expect to prevail by relying solely on human-speed defense. Agentic AI offers a solution. Security agents can continuously correlate threat intelligence with enterprise assets, identify exploitable attack paths, orchestrate approved mitigations, confirm they were successful and escalate complex decisions to human operators.

In software development, AI-enabled agents can identify insecure code, validate dependencies, evaluate infrastructure configurations, generate security tests and propose remediations before vulnerabilities reach production, helping security expertise scale across development teams.

That capability must operate within carefully engineered boundaries: Zero trust identities, least-privilege access, auditable actions, appropriate testing and human oversight for consequential changes. AI-generated code and directed actions must be tested for security risk, and any AI built into products needs its access to data and systems governed from the start.

None of this matters if we lose sight of whom we are protecting. Behind every mortgage account is a person or family making one of the most significant financial commitments of their lives.

This Cybersecurity Awareness Month, the mortgage industry should move beyond familiar conversations about passwords, phishing, and annual security training. Those fundamentals matter, but the next era of cybersecurity demands more: that we stop treating cybersecurity as a function that protects technology after it has been built and start recognizing it as an essential part of how trustworthy technology is created through Zero Trust architectures and AI-integrated systems.

Kyle Draisey is the Chief Information and Security Officer of Sagent.This column does not necessarily reflect the opinion of HousingWire’s editorial department and its owners. To contact the editor responsible for this piece: [email protected].

#5439. 80% of Merchants Use AI for Chargebacks, but Only 11% Have Automated, Chargeflow and Juniper Research Finds

Merchants who use AI report a chargeback dispute media win rate of 38%, up from 27.75%

NEW YORK, Nov. 17, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Chargeflow, the AI chargeback platform used by more than 20,000 merchants, according to the report "The State of Chargeback Management: How AI Is Reshaping Performance," a survey of 121 enterprise merchants in the U.S. and U.K. conducted by Juniper Research. Merchants that use AI win a median 38% of the chargebacks they dispute, against 27.75% for those that don't. Yet the median merchant in both groups disputes and wins the same share of its eligible chargebacks: 6.65%.

AI users also contest the same median share of their eligible chargebacks as non-users. Juniper Research points to a gap between adopting AI and changing how the work gets done: 80% of respondents use AI in chargeback management, but only 11% have mostly or fully automated it.

The report's findings come as pressure on merchants grows. Chargebacks rose over the past 18 months for 65% of respondents, and nine in 10 of those saw growth of 10% or more. Almost half put the annual cost of chargebacks at 0.5% to 1% of revenue. Friendly fraud is a large part of the problem: 43% believe it accounts for more than a quarter of their chargebacks.

"Most merchants have added AI to a manual process," said Dan Moshkovich, VP of Go-to-Market at Chargeflow. "It helps them win more of the disputes they file, but people still decide which ones to file, so they fight the same small share. That's the next step for AI in chargebacks: knowing which disputes are worth fighting and building a case for each one."

Merchants want evidence of higher win rates to justify AI investment

Asked what would justify spending on AI for chargebacks, 39% of merchants chose a higher win rate and 34% chose more revenue recovered. Fewer than one in five chose time saved or lower costs. Most want a big gain before they buy: 69% said a tool would need to lift their win rate by at least 11 percentage points, taking a merchant that wins 30% of its disputes to 41% or more. AI hasn't cleared that bar yet: AI users report a median win rate 10.25 percentage points higher than non-users, just short of the 11-point mark. Juniper Research concludes that "while AI has delivered incremental improvements, it is not yet enough to meet enterprise expectations." When choosing a provider, 72% rated the quality of its data as very important and 70% said the same of security and compliance, against 31% for total cost.

Of respondents, 77% said chargebacks rise over the December holidays. Most are still optimistic: 58% expect lower chargeback losses in the 2026 season than in 2025. Chargeflow's own data shows what changes over that peak. The Chargeflow Data Lab, launched Oct. 22, studied about 3 million disputes across the last three peak seasons. Over the 2025 Black Friday to Cyber Monday weekend, 34.7% of chargebacks said the order never arrived, up from 19.9% in a normal week. Fraud claims fell to 27.2% from 37.8%, and the same shift appeared in 2023, 2024 and 2025.

As AI matures, chargeback tools will be judged on whether they turn intelligence into better decisions and measurable financial gains," said Nick Maynard, VP of Research, Juniper Research. "The opportunity is not simply to automate chargeback management. It is to make chargeback management materially more effective."

Juniper Research surveyed 121 C-level executives and senior managers at U.S. and U.K. businesses with at least $100 million in annual gross merchandise value in September 2026: 80 in the U.S. and 41 in the U.K. The full report is available at chargeflow.io/data-lab/the-state-of-chargeback-management.

Chargeflow is the industry-leading AI Chargeback Platform, with more than $50 billion in transactions protected. It operates on a simple belief: every business has the right to keep the revenue it has earned.

Many businesses write off chargebacks as a cost of doing business. Chargeflow fights for that revenue instead. Its data-driven AI catches fraudulent orders before fulfillment, resolves eligible disputes before they become chargebacks, and builds the strongest case on the chargebacks that get through. Representment comes with no upfront cost and no financial commitment: merchants pay only when Chargeflow wins.

Trusted by more than 20,000 merchants and more than 300 enterprise customers, Chargeflow is the No. 1-ranked provider on G2 for both chargeback management and e-commerce fraud protection.
