#5438. Blockbuster games now earn and cost like big films, and 10 forces explain why

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Why video game budgets have exploded, from Grand Theft Auto V to Marvel's Spider-Man 2 and Concord, explained through 10 cost drivers shaping how blockbuster games get made

Grand Theft Auto V passed $1 billion in sales within three days of its September 2013 release, according to publisher Take-Two Interactive $TTWO. Returns on that scale give publishers a reason to spend heavily on the next potential hit.

The spending behind those hits is harder to see. Most publishers do not disclose what an individual game costs to make. Public figures are scarce. One of the clearest comes from leaked Insomniac Games documents. Press reports on those files put the cost of the 2023 game Marvel's Spider-Man 2 at $315 million. That number comes from the leak, not from a company announcement.

Explaining why video game budgets have exploded means looking at several pressures at once. Hardware is one. The PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X $TWTR both launched in November 2020. Each new console generation asks studios for more detailed art, animation and environments. People are another. Big games depend on actors for motion capture and voice work. Video game performers represented by SAG-AFTRA began a strike on July 26, 2024.

Release gaps show how long the work can take. Rockstar Games released Red Dead Redemption 2 in October 2018, eight years after the first Red Dead Redemption arrived in May 2010. Every year in production adds to the bill.

Marketing is a separate expense on top of development. Publishers rarely say what they spend on it.

The companies behind games have grown larger as well. Microsoft $MSFT announced its $68.7 billion deal for Activision $ATVI Blizzard in January 2022 and closed it in October 2023. Prices have moved too. A $60 price was standard for new games for many years. Nintendo priced Mario Kart World at $79.99 when it announced the game in April 2025.

Higher spending also raises the cost of failure. Firewalk Studios released the live-service shooter Concord on August 23, 2024. Sony $SONY pulled the game on September 6, 2024, and closed Firewalk in October 2024.

The 10 slides below cover a selection of the forces behind modern game budgets. They end with Larian Studios' Baldur's Gate 3, which won Game of the Year at the 2023 Game Awards, as a different route to a hit.

Grand Theft Auto V showed how much money one blockbuster game can make in its first days. Rockstar Games released it in September 2013. Its parent company, Take-Two Interactive $TTWO, reported that the game brought in $800 million in sales on its first day and passed $1 billion within three days.

Those totals came from the publisher itself. That matters in an industry where hard numbers are scarce. Publishers often keep detailed sales data private. A confirmed launch figure gives outsiders one of the few clear public reference points for what a top-tier release can earn.

The game arrived on PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360. Rockstar North, the Edinburgh studio that has long led the series, built it around three playable protagonists named Michael, Franklin and Trevor. Players could switch among them during the story. The plot was structured around how their lives overlapped.

The setting was Los Santos, a fictional city modeled on Los Angeles. Around it sat the countryside, desert and coastline of the fictional state of San Andreas. Filling a map of that size with streets, buildings, traffic and characters is the kind of work that demands large teams of artists, designers, writers and engineers.

The launch gave the industry a public benchmark. Publishers planning their own flagship projects now had a confirmed example of how large and how fast the return on a major bet could be.

That payoff is part of the logic behind larger spending. When a single title can bring in that much revenue so quickly, the argument for funding bigger teams and more detailed worlds becomes easier to make inside a publisher.

Rockstar also kept selling the same game for years. It later released versions for PlayStation 4, Xbox One and PC. It then released versions for PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X $TWTR and Series S. Each release extended the commercial life of a game first sold in 2013.

Red Dead Redemption 2 came out in October 2018, eight years after the original Red Dead Redemption launched in May 2010. Long gaps between major releases are one sign of how long blockbuster production can run.

Rockstar Games made both games. Between the two Red Dead launches, the studio also released Grand Theft Auto V.

A long production cycle raises a budget in a direct way. A studio pays its staff for every year a game is in development. Those salaries build up before a single copy is sold. A project that runs for many years has to recover all of that spending after release.

Time adds costs beyond payroll, too. Office space, software licenses and equipment are paid for across the full life of a project. A studio also carries the risk that player tastes or technology will shift before the game is finished.

Long cycles create a trade-off as well. A studio that spends years on each game releases fewer games. Each release then has to cover a larger share of the studio's costs.

The gap shapes the series itself. Without a new release, a franchise has no fresh launch to drive a wave of sales. Players who finished the first game have to wait for the story to continue. The publisher has to keep interest in the name alive across that wait.

Take-Two Interactive $TTWO, Rockstar's parent company, reported that Red Dead Redemption 2 earned $725 million in its first three days on sale. That opening came after a stretch of years in which the series had no new main entry to sell.

The $725 million figure measures sales, not profit. Take-Two did not report a production cost alongside it. The number shows how quickly a long project can bring money in. It does not show how much of that money remained after years of spending.

Leaked Insomniac Games documents, as reported by the press, put the cost of making Marvel's Spider-Man 2 at $315 million. The 2023 game's budget became public through that leak, not through an announcement by the studio or its publisher.

A leaked internal figure is a reported cost, not a confirmed one. It shows the scale of one project. It does not show how the money was counted, which expenses it covers or how it was spread across the production.

Those gaps matter when the number is set beside other games. Two studios can define a budget in different ways. One might include years of salaries, outside contractors and licensing. Another might leave some of those items out. The figure also leaves open whether marketing falls inside the total. Without the underlying accounting, a single total cannot be lined up cleanly against another project's cost.

Hard budget numbers rarely surface in the games business. Sales milestones often get public announcements. Production spending usually stays inside the company.

That leaves public discussion of rising costs resting on a small set of data points. A single document from inside one studio can carry a lot of weight in that discussion. The Spider-Man 2 number became one of those reference points after the press reported on the leaked Insomniac Games files. For readers trying to gauge how expensive blockbuster games have become, it offers a rare concrete number tied to a named title.

The game itself also shapes what the figure represents. Marvel's Spider-Man 2 is a sequel built around a licensed Marvel character. The total therefore belongs to a franchise project, not a new property built from scratch.

The $315 million covers one title. It is not a figure for a studio's annual spending or for a publisher's full slate of games.

Without confirmation from the company, the $315 million remains a reported budget. It rests on the leaked documents and the press coverage of them, not on an official disclosure.

The PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X $TWTR launched in November 2020, and both were built to run games at 4K resolution. Higher resolution raises the level of detail that every character, building and texture must hold up to, and artists have to create that detail.

A 4K image measures 3,840 by 2,160 pixels. That is four times the pixel count of a 1080p image, which measures 1,920 by 1,080 pixels. On a large television at that resolution, a blurry texture or a blocky, low-polygon object is easier to spot. Art teams respond by building assets with finer geometry and higher-resolution textures.

That work does not scale automatically. A rock, a jacket or a car door still has to be modeled, textured, lit and checked. When the target resolution rises, each of those steps involves more data and more review. Each object also needs several versions at different levels of detail so it can render efficiently at a distance. Large open-world games contain many thousands of such objects.

Both consoles also added hardware support for ray tracing. The technique simulates how light bounces, reflects and casts shadows. It can make scenes look more physically accurate. It also gives developers another lighting system to build, test and tune alongside traditional methods.

Fast solid-state drives are standard on both machines. They let games stream large amounts of data quickly, which cuts down on loading screens. Faster streaming also lets designers place denser, more detailed environments in front of the player. More detailed environments mean more assets to produce.

In the years after the 2020 launch, many studios shipped games on two console generations at once. Building for both the older PlayStation 4 and Xbox One and the newer machines meant supporting different performance targets within a single project. Each version needed its own optimization and testing.

None of this adds up to a single published price tag. Publishers rarely break out how much of a budget goes to art or graphics work. What the hardware shift did change is the baseline of detail a blockbuster release has to meet.

Motion capture and voice acting make blockbuster games depend on large casts of paid performers, specialized capture stages and long recording schedules. That labor was at the center of the strike SAG-AFTRA video game performers began in 2024.

Performance capture records an actor's body, face and voice together. Performers wear tight suits dotted with reflective markers. A ring of cameras around the stage tracks those markers as the actors move through a scene.

Facial work adds another layer. Head-mounted cameras pointed at the performer's face record expressions in detail. Animators later map that data onto a digital character so its face matches the original performance.

The raw capture is only the starting point. Animators and technical artists clean up the recorded motion, correct errors and fit it to each character model. A single cinematic scene can pass through several departments before it reaches the finished game.

Naughty Dog's The Last of Us, released in 2013, relied heavily on this kind of work. Troy Baker and Ashley Johnson played Joel and Ellie on a capture stage, supplying both movement and voice. Their performances shaped the characters as players see and hear them.

Casting extends well beyond the lead roles. Large productions hire stunt performers for fights and action sequences. They also cast separate voice actors for supporting characters, enemies and crowds.

Voice work grows with the size of the script. Open-world and role-playing games can contain many thousands of recorded lines across main stories, side quests and background chatter. Publishers that release a game in several languages often record new voice tracks for each market. That repeats much of the casting and studio work.

The SAG-AFTRA strike centered on protections against artificial intelligence tools that could replicate performers' voices and likenesses, alongside compensation. The walkout fell under the union's Interactive Media Agreement, which covers work for major game companies.

Performer costs rise with the scope of a production. Every added scene, language or retake means more hours on a capture stage, more time in a recording booth and more animation work afterward.

Marketing is a separate cost from development for big-budget AAA games, and it sits on top of what a studio spends building the game. A publisher rarely reveals how much it spends promoting one title. As a result, the full cost of most games stays out of public view.

A development budget pays for the people, tools and technology that make the game. A marketing budget pays for making sure buyers know the game exists by launch day. That work includes cinematic trailers, gameplay reveals, paid advertising, retail promotion and partnerships with streamers and video creators.

For a blockbuster release, a campaign can begin long before the game ships. A first teaser may appear years ahead of launch. The publisher then has to keep attention alive through later trailers, preview events and preorder pushes. Each stage carries its own production and media-buying costs.

Live showcases are one common stage for that work. The Game Awards and Summer Game Fest both feature world premieres of new game trailers. Platform holders run their own broadcasts as well, including Sony $SONY's State of Play and Nintendo Direct. A reveal at one of these events puts new footage in front of a large live audience at a single moment.

Platform holders also sign marketing agreements with publishers. These deals can attach a console brand to a game's advertising or give one platform's players early or exclusive content. Such arrangements add another party to the campaign. Their terms are rarely made public.

The timing matters because big-budget games depend on strong opening sales. A publisher that has funded years of development needs a large audience ready to buy as soon as the game appears. Marketing is how it builds that audience in advance.

Publicly traded publishers such as Electronic Arts $EA and Take-Two Interactive $TTWO report marketing spending in their financial filings. They report it as a company-wide expense rather than game by game. That makes it hard to set one title's promotional spending against its development cost. Any specific ratio between the two is a guess unless a company discloses it.

A reported game budget, when one surfaces at all, may leave out much of what a publisher spent to bring that game to market.

Microsoft $MSFT agreed to pay $68.7 billion for Activision $ATVI Blizzard, a sign of how much money now surrounds the video game business. The company announced the deal in January 2022 and completed it in October 2023.

The figure is the price of a whole publisher, not the cost of making any one game. The money bought a company with many studios, a catalog of existing titles and the rights to future releases. Reading it as a game budget would misread what the number measures.

Those holdings include some of the largest franchises in the business. Activision publishes Call of Duty. Blizzard Entertainment makes World of Warcraft, Diablo and Overwatch. King, the mobile arm, makes Candy Crush Saga. Each of those series has its own studios and release schedule.

The purchase did not stand alone. Microsoft had already bought ZeniMax Media, the parent of Bethesda Softworks, for $7.5 billion in a deal that closed in March 2021. Bethesda's franchises include The Elder Scrolls and Fallout. Together, the two acquisitions moved several major franchises under one owner. Microsoft also runs the Xbox console business and the Game Pass subscription service. Both draw on the games its studios produce.

The gap between announcement and completion was about 21 months. Regulators examined the deal during that period. The U.S. Federal Trade Commission sued to block it in December 2022. The U.K. Competition and Markets Authority blocked the original version in April 2023. Microsoft then restructured the deal. It sold the cloud streaming rights to Activision Blizzard games outside the European Economic Area to Ubisoft. The CMA cleared the revised version in October 2023.

The acquisition is a story about consolidation. Fewer, larger owners now hold more of the studios and franchises behind big-budget games. The most expensive productions increasingly sit inside companies large enough to fund them. Microsoft's purchase of Activision Blizzard is one of the clearest examples of that concentration.

Concord shows how quickly a live-service bet can come apart. Sony $SONY's Firewalk Studios released the game on August 23, 2024, and Sony pulled it on September 6, 2024. Sony then closed Firewalk Studios in October 2024.

The game was pulled 14 days after its release date. That left the development spending behind Concord a two-week window to start earning money back.

A live-service game is designed to run for years rather than ship once and be finished. Publishers plan seasons of new content, such as maps, characters and cosmetic items, to keep players returning and spending. The model ties revenue to an active player base over a long period, not to a single sale at launch.

That structure changes the cost math. A traditional single-player game spends most of its budget before release. A live-service game also needs servers, a team that keeps producing updates, and staff for balance changes and player support after launch. Those costs start on day one, whether or not players show up.

Multiplayer design adds another pressure. Matchmaking depends on enough people being online at the same time. When a player base is small, queues get longer and matches are harder to fill. That can push the remaining players away.

Live-service titles also compete for a limited resource: player time. A game built around seasonal play asks people to commit for months. Many players already split that time among online games they have played for years.

The result of a failed launch is lopsided. A single-player game that sells poorly still keeps the revenue from the copies it sold. A live-service game that loses its audience may no longer be worth running at all. Taking it offline means the planned years of post-launch income never arrive.

For a publisher, the loss from a case like Concord covers more than the money spent building the game. It also includes the team behind it. In Concord's case, that meant the end of Firewalk Studios as well.

For many years, $60 was the standard price for a new console game in the U.S. That ceiling has since moved higher. Nintendo priced Mario Kart World at $79.99 when it announced the game in April 2025.

The sticker price of a new release is one of the few levers a publisher controls directly. Revenue from a full-price game comes down to two numbers: how many copies sell and what each copy costs. When development spending rises, a publisher can try to sell more copies, charge more for each copy or do both.

The $60 standard held for a long stretch in which production work grew much larger. Across those years, one base price had to cover projects with bigger teams, longer schedules and more detailed art. Inflation also eroded what a fixed $60 was worth over time.

Publishers found other ways to raise what each player spends while the base price stayed put. Deluxe and collector's editions sell the same game at higher prices, usually bundled with extra content. Downloadable expansions and in-game purchases bring in money after launch. These options let the headline price stay fixed while the total a player could spend kept climbing.

The $70 price point moved part of that burden back onto the base game. At $70, each standard copy brings in $10 more than at $60, before retailers and platform holders take their share. A buyer who wants only the standard edition now pays more up front than under the old norm.

Mario Kart World pushed the figure further. Its $79.99 price is $19.99 above the long-running $60 standard.

A higher price raises revenue per copy only if enough players still buy at that level. The extra amount applies to every copy sold, so the gain grows with a game's sales. Publishers rarely disclose how sales respond to each increase. That makes it hard to measure from the outside how much of a game's budget a price change actually recovers.

Baldur's Gate 3, released by Larian Studios in August 2023, won Game of the Year at the 2023 Game Awards. Larian has not disclosed what the game cost to make.

That missing figure limits any direct comparison with blockbuster spending. What can be compared is how the project was organized and paid for along the way.

Larian is a Belgian developer headquartered in Ghent. It is not owned by Sony $SONY, Microsoft $MSFT, Nintendo or Take-Two Interactive $TTWO. Larian published Baldur's Gate 3 itself rather than handing release decisions to an outside publisher.

The studio built the game on an existing foundation. Baldur's Gate 3 adapts the fifth edition rules of Dungeons & Dragons under a license from Wizards of the Coast. It is a turn-based, party-based role-playing game. Larian had already worked in that genre with Divinity: Original Sin and Divinity: Original Sin 2.

Larian also developed the game in public for years. Baldur's Gate 3 entered paid early access on PC in October 2020, nearly three years before the full launch. Early buyers could play an opening portion of the game and send feedback while work continued. That arrangement brought in revenue and player data well before the finished version shipped.

The full release arrived on PC in August 2023. A PlayStation 5 version followed in September 2023, and an Xbox Series X $TWTR|S version came in December 2023.

The Game Awards win came against nominees from some of the industry's largest companies. The 2023 Game of the Year field included Marvel's Spider-Man 2 from Sony's Insomniac Games and The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom from Nintendo. Capcom's Resident Evil 4, Remedy Entertainment's Alan Wake 2 and Nintendo's Super Mario Bros. Wonder were also nominated.

The case does not show that blockbuster games can be made cheaply. It shows another route to Game of the Year: a long public development period, a licensed rule set, prior genre experience and self-publishing.

#5437. SuperDial revamps its healthcare voice agent platform to stop AI bots wasting time calling each other

SuperDial Inc., the creator of voice-first artificial intelligence agents for automating healthcare workflows, is overhauling its platform with a new Agent-to-Agent RCM architecture.

The goal is to eliminate the compute inefficiencies that have arisen as autonomous workers become more prevalent in the industry.

The startup, which raised $15 million in a Series A funding round last year, is best known for its voice agents that automate payer operations, revenue cycle management and administrative outreach. It aims to alleviate the time-consuming burden of having to call health insurance providers, waste time on hold, navigate phone trees and check online portals for information. Traditionally, SuperDial has seen itself as a voice-first platform that’s focused on call automation, but the shift to its Agent-to-Agent RCM architecture suggests it wants to deemphasize phone calls as much as possible.

The company is addressing the friction that has emerged from the slightly dystopian reality that both healthcare providers and insurance payers have largely replaced humans with AI agents in order to automate routine calls. But the fact that agents are handling the calls on both sides creates huge inefficiencies, resulting in those bots wasting time and compute resources as they engage in unnecessary robotic conversations. Rather than streamline insurance eligibility checks, claim follow-ups and prior authorizations, those agents find themselves stuck in multi-minute phone exchanges to relay structured data verbally that both sides already possess.

SuperDial founder and Chief Executive Sam Schwager refers to these scenarios as the “bot wars,” and says they’re increasingly engaging in relentless and destructive battles with one another that cost both healthcare providers and insurance companies money.

“One side deploys AI to secure approvals and payment for care,” he said. “The other deploys AI to review those requests and, at times, deny them. Neither has a reason to stop. Every extra round costs more in AI spend, pulls in staff on both sides to handle what the bots can’t settle, and can delay payment and care. The result is more friction, not less.”

With Agent-to-Agent RCM, SuperDial is trying to sidestep the bot wars by no longer defaulting to outbound calls. Instead, it acts as a kind of omnichannel orchestration layer, where success is determined by the number of requests resolved, rather than completed phone calls. When a revenue cycle team initiates a request, SuperDial’s agents will first check the relevant electronic data interchange feeds and application programming interfaces to find the information they need.

If they find it, great, but if not, they will then try the payer’s web portals. If they’re still out of luck after exhausting all options for digital retrieval, only then will they proceed to place a voice call. Those calls are more efficient too, since SuperDial’s agents will retain all of the context from their initial search, so they only need to query the agent on the other side of the line for the information that’s missing.

Schwager said Agent-to-Agent RCM puts more emphasis on resolution, allowing a provider’s agent and a payer’s system to connect and work together to resolve administrative requests with less work on both sides.

“The difference between this and the bot wars is the definition of done,” he said. “Two agents were optimizing for their own side of the exchange, but now those two agents are optimizing for a usable answer — that is, the information the provider needs to move the account forward, delivered in response to a request the payer can actually answer.”

For customers, life becomes much simpler. All they have to do is tell SuperDial what it needs to know, and its agents will work to get the answers in the fastest time and most efficient manner possible. “How we get the answer is our problem, not theirs,” Schwager said.

Schwager said the industry needs to move away from the idea that healthcare administration can be improved by having two bots argue with each other faster. “If an agent already has the information, that context should travel with the request,” he explained. “If a digital channel can answer it, there should be no call. The goal is fewer exchanges, not faster ones.”

The company’s long-term goal is to create an AI-native network that facilitates seamless, automated payer-provider communications. The goal is to eliminate repetitive inquiries and cut down on the administrative delays that can negatively impact patient outcomes, Schwager added.

SuperDial says it’s already having a big impact. Since it founded its platform in 2021, it has handled more than 10 million automated calls between healthcare providers and insurance firms – interactions that would once have been made by humans. Had humans made those calls, it would have been much slower, because SuperDial says its agents average about four minutes per call when dealing with insurers’ automated voice systems, compared with 17 minutes or more when reaching a human representative.

With its architectural overhaul, SuperDial is now targeting insurers, in addition to the healthcare providers it already serves. Earlier this year, it announced it had signed a key deal with Guardian Life Insurance Co. of America to modernize its dental provider data attestation workflows.

#5436. When mortgage reviewers disagree with AI: A practical adjudication protocol

Lenders should predefine how to adjudicate disagreements between AI findings and human reviewers. The protocol keeps original evidence, separates observation from policy interpretation, assigns decision authority, allows unresolved status and measures time and rework.   AI Summary

An AI system flags a problem in a mortgage file. The reviewer looks at the documents and disagrees. During an evaluation, this can become a discussion about whether the technology works. In production, it becomes a decision someone has to make while the file is waiting.

The system may have identified a genuine issue. The reviewer may have information the system did not receive. Both may be looking at the same evidence and interpreting a requirement differently. Putting a person in the process does not settle any of this. The team still needs a reliable way to establish what is correct.

In my recent HousingWire article, I argued that lenders should measure how much human attention a loan consumes. Disagreements between AI and reviewers deserve particular attention because resolving them can take far more effort than identifying the original issue.

I believe lenders should agree on how to resolve these cases before an evaluation begins. Otherwise, the evaluation can end with a long list of overrides and very little clarity about what the results mean.

The original finding should remain available after a reviewer challenges it. That record should include the document and page involved, the data used, the requirement being tested and the relevant system or rule version. The reviewer’s response should sit alongside it, with the evidence supporting the disagreement.

Consider an illustrative example in which a system flags a missing signature, but the reviewer says it is present on a later version of the document. Before deciding whether the finding was wrong, the team needs to establish which version the system reviewed and when the later version became available.

If the document arrived after the review, the finding may have been correct when it was raised. If the document was already available but the system failed to select it, there is a different problem to fix. A final status of “cleared” would hide that distinction. Preserving the original evidence gives the team something concrete to investigate and prevents a later reviewer from having to reconstruct the entire discussion.

A finding often contains more than one conclusion. In the signature example, one question is whether a signature appears in the relevant location. Another is whether that signature is required for the document, transaction and stage of the process being reviewed. The first is an observation, while the second depends on the applicable requirement.

A system could get the observation right and apply the wrong requirement. A reviewer could correctly question the requirement but overlook that the document being reviewed is incomplete. These should be recorded as separate issues.

I would ask the team to identify exactly where the disagreement sits: document selection, extracted information, applicable requirement or judgment about the issue’s significance. That distinction helps the team choose the corrective action. Improving document recognition will not resolve an unclear policy, and more reviewer training will not repair a system that consistently selects an outdated document. It also keeps the discussion focused on evidence rather than on whether the reviewer or the technology should be trusted more.

Every disputed finding needs an owner who can make the relevant decision, with that authority established before the disagreement occurs. A straightforward document-selection error may be resolved within the review team. A question about how a requirement applies may need a designated policy owner, while a recurring technical error should reach the team responsible for the system.

For material cases, I would use a second qualified reviewer rather than leaving the original reviewer to be the sole judge of their own decision. The same principle applies to the technology provider. A provider can explain its output, but should not be the only party deciding whether that output meets the lender’s requirements.

The resolution should state what was decided, the evidence relied upon and who approved it. “Reviewer disagreed” tells the next person very little. The process should also be proportionate. An obvious extraction error should not require a committee. A disputed issue that could affect a consequential decision deserves more scrutiny.

Sometimes the available evidence will not support a decision because a document is unreadable, a required page is missing or the relevant requirement needs clarification. Forcing the case into “AI correct” or “reviewer correct” in those circumstances creates certainty the team has not earned. The case should remain unresolved, with the missing evidence or clarification identified and the next action assigned.

That status should have an owner and a review date. It should also have a defined consequence for the workflow, based on the nature of the issue and the lender’s existing controls. An unresolved disagreement should not silently disappear because the file has moved to another team.

During an evaluation, unresolved cases should remain visible in the results. They should not be counted as successes or quietly removed from the reported sample. This matters when comparing systems. A strong accuracy figure is difficult to interpret if the hardest cases have been excluded because no one could establish the correct answer.

The resolution itself is only part of the result. Lenders should also examine how much time the reviewer spent finding the evidence, whether another person had to repeat the review and whether the file was reopened. They should track whether the same issue returned on the next loan. These questions reveal whether the technology is making the work easier.

A finding that is ultimately correct can still be poorly presented. If the reviewer has to search hundreds of pages to understand it, there is a workflow problem worth fixing. A high override rate also needs investigation rather than an immediate conclusion. It could reflect poor system performance, unclear requirements, inconsistent reviewer decisions or several of these together.

I would review disputed cases by cause and severity, alongside the time and rework required to resolve them. I would also sample cases where the reviewer and system agreed. Agreement alone does not establish that both were correct.

The findings should inform changes to the technology, the instructions or the review process. Those changes need testing before they are applied more broadly. An individual override should not automatically become a new rule or a training label.

Lenders should ask technology providers to demonstrate a disputed case, including how the evidence is retained, who can challenge the finding and how the final decision is recorded. That demonstration may be more revealing than another clean file moving through the system without intervention.

Mortgage operations will continue to need experienced people who can question an output and explain their judgment. Those people need evidence, authority and a workable route to resolution. When the next reviewer opens the file, they should be able to understand what was questioned, how it was resolved and why the decision can be relied upon. If they have to start the investigation again, the disagreement was never properly closed.

Alok Bansal is Founder and CEO of Logikality.This column does not necessarily reflect the opinion of HousingWire’s editorial department and its owners. To contact the editor responsible for this piece: [email protected].

#5434. Bitcoin Bottom? Is the Market Preparing for a Reversal or One Final Crash?

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Bitcoin found its bottom? Bitcoin is fighting to hold $65,000 after a brutal weekend selloff pushed BTC USD below $62,000. The rebound offers bulls some relief, but the market is showing signs of a much deeper liquidity problem.

The world’s largest crypto has lost 13% since the 8th of November, with Ethereum and XRP also hitting multi-month lows. Billions in leveraged positions have disappeared as traders rush to reduce exposure.

Yet the selloff has created an interesting setup. Extreme fear, forced liquidations, and heavily discounted prices could signal that much of the speculative excess has finally been removed.

The problem is that capital continues leaving the crypto market. Stablecoin supply has contracted for five consecutive weeks, while US spot Bitcoin ETFs have recorded seven consecutive sessions of outflows.

Bitcoin now faces a defining question: has the market finally found its bottom, or is another crash waiting around the corner?

The latest liquidation wave has given the Bitcoin bottom argument some credibility. When leveraged traders are forced out, selling pressure can eventually exhaust itself, leaving the market with fewer speculative positions vulnerable to another cascade. What comes down must go up, and vice versa.

The weekend recovery also shows that buyers are willing to defend the $62,000 region. BTC rebounded to $64,000 – $65,000 after briefly touching $62,006 this morning.

Market sentiment has also deteriorated sharply. Extreme fear is returning as investors abandon riskier positions and traders become increasingly defensive. This is often where market reversals begin. Sellers who wanted to exit have already sold, while longer-term investors start looking for attractive entry points.

Galaxy Research has also presented a bullish argument. In an October 26 report, the firm said it believed Bitcoin’s bottom was already in, pointing to diminished selling pressure, reduced speculative positioning, and stronger long-term fundamentals.

However, a convincing recovery needs more than a short-lived bounce. Bitcoin must attract fresh spot demand and reclaim important resistance levels before bulls can claim victory.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

The biggest obstacle to a Bitcoin bottom is the lack of fresh money entering the market. Stablecoin supply has contracted for five consecutive weeks. Glassnode puts the 30-day decline at $17.1 billion, marking the fastest contraction since June 2022.

Stablecoins provide much of the dollar liquidity used to purchase cryptocurrencies, so when investors redeem stablecoins for traditional dollars, the market loses potential buying power.

Bitcoin ETFs are sending another warning. US spot Bitcoin ETFs have lost $2.35 billion over two weeks, extending a difficult period for institutional demand. Corporate buying has weakened too. Public companies collectively sold 11,647 BTC worth approximately $869 million. Strategy remained a buyer, adding 1,037 BTC, but the wider corporate treasury trend has turned negative.

Macroeconomic conditions are making the situation worse. Hotter-than-expected US inflation and employment figures have pushed interest-rate expectations higher. Futures markets now fully price a 25-basis-point Federal Reserve rate hike in December.

BREAKING: October PPI Inflation rises to 6.5%, its highest level since November 2022.Core PPI Inflation was 5.0%, in-line with expectations of 5.0%.CPI, PPI, and PCE inflation continue to push higher in the US.All signs point toward a December rate hike.

Higher rates strengthen the dollar and make non-yielding assets like Bitcoin less attractive. Meanwhile, the dollar index has climbed to 102.9, adding another headwind for crypto markets.

Coinbase Institutional also warned that Bitcoin could struggle to recover without renewed crypto-native demand. Its analysis places $62,000 among the important support levels, with $58,000–$59,000 emerging as another potential downside target.

The technical picture remains fragile. Bitcoin needs to reclaim the $66,000–$68,000 region before bulls can establish a convincing recovery. A sustained move above $73,000–$75,000 would provide a much stronger reversal signal.

Bitcoin has already experienced a substantial correction, but the rebound hasn’t settled the argument. The bullish case rests on exhausted sellers, reduced speculative exposure, extreme fear, and buyers defending the $62,000 region. The bearish case rests on shrinking stablecoin supply, ETF withdrawals, weaker corporate accumulation, and rising borrowing costs.

For now, liquidity remains the deciding factor. A genuine Bitcoin bottom needs more than liquidation-driven relief rallies. It needs fresh capital entering the market, institutional demand returning, and spot buyers absorbing available supply.

If stablecoin supply stabilizes and ETF flows turn positive, Bitcoin could build a foundation for its next recovery. But if capital continues leaving the ecosystem, the $62,000 floor could give way to another painful correction.

Bitcoin may be approaching its bottom, but the market hasn’t yet shown that buyers are ready to take control.

#5433. Three insights you might have missed from theCUBE’s coverage of Dell’s “AI Leadership Symposium”

Moving enterprise AI workloads into production introduces practical challenges for chief information officers. Those challenges include managing costs, scaling enterprise AI infrastructure and establishing governance models to keep agents in check and data secure.

Cost and control were major themes of discussion at Dell Technologies Inc.’s “AI Leadership Symposium.” Expanding AI workloads can drive up infrastructure and model costs, while deploying autonomous agents introduces new questions about security, oversight and data access.

At the same time, organizations are exploring different ways to run AI, from private cloud environments to models operating directly on devices. That is creating demand for enterprise AI infrastructure and partnerships that can accommodate a wider range of deployment needs.

“No one is asking whether to adopt AI; that’s pretty much a done deal,” said John Furrier, executive analyst at theCUBE Research. “They’re asking who controls it, where it runs and whose law it operates.”

Furrier spoke with industry experts from Dell, Deepgram Inc., Singulr AI Inc., MisaLabs Inc. and Intel Corp., among others, during the AI Leadership Symposium. The interviews covered the infrastructure, partnerships and computing power needed to scale AI. (* Disclosure below.)

Here’s theCUBE’s complete keynote analysis from John Furrier:

Cloud token bills remain a major pressure point on enterprise AI budgets. That’s leading some businesses to look for ways to relieve that pressure, according to Helen O’Sullivan, AI business development manager and solutions specialist at Dell.

“A lot of our customers I support in the Bay Area, they’re dealing with this real immediate struggle of running through their token budget in a matter of weeks that they had allotted for months,” she told theCUBE. “You still use those frontier models, but you use the open source and infrastructure on-prem to at least eliminate some of the token stress and token maxing going on right now.”

Organizations can also make better use of existing data center capacity when evaluating enterprise AI infrastructure investments. Dell and Intel are helping customers evaluate those options, according to Tim Wood, sales director for the Northwest region at Intel, who joined O’Sullivan during the discussion.

“A lot of enterprises already have [central processing units] in their data center,” he said. “There may be existing resources and headroom in the infrastructure they already have that’s capable of doing some of these next-generation apps and workloads.”

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video interview with Helen O’Sullivan and Tim Wood:

As companies deploy more AI agents, they need better ways to monitor what those agents actually do and ensure their actions align with company policies and intentions. That means introducing runtime governance that can assess AI agent behavior during execution, according to Shiv Agarwal, co-founder and chief executive officer of Singulr AI Inc., who spoke alongside Sri Viswanath, founder and chief executive officer of Sycamore Labs Inc., and Victor Jakubiuk, co-founder of MisaLabs Inc.

“[It’s] as simple as an action where it reaches out to the internet to get some data or sends out an email to a private account or something,” Agarwal told theCUBE. “That could be deeply hidden inside an agentic action.”

Good AI governance also means setting boundaries around where models can access data and how they process it. CIOs often prefer virtual private clouds to keep sensitive information within a controlled environment, according to Viswanath.

“They’re also trying to architect in a way that all of the data stays there,” he said. “They don’t trust sending it outside because then we don’t know where it goes.”

The pace of AI development complicates those governance efforts. Companies need to ensure their systems behave as intended even as AI capabilities evolve, according to Jakubiuk.

“AI has no limit to the speed of development, speed of progress,” he said. “As an enterprise, as that AI lead, you want to be able to take the latest and greatest and stay on top.”

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video interview with Victor Jakubiuk, Shiv Agarwal and Sri Viswanath:

Deepgram is working with Dell and Fortanix Inc. to bring its voice AI models beyond the cloud and onto customer devices. Potential applications range from interactive voice response systems for small businesses to AI-enabled laptops for students, according to Nick Mann, staff technical program manager at Deepgram.

“I want our models on those, on the hardware, to run natively,” he told theCUBE. “Air-gapped. That’s where we want to get to. That’s where AI as a whole needs to start meeting people where they are and how they’re going to use it.”

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video interview with Nick Mann:

Deepgram’s plans reflect a broader push to develop AI solutions tailored to how customers want to build and deploy the technology. In Silicon Valley, where technically sophisticated buyers often prefer building their own solutions over buying packaged products, Dell is expanding its partner ecosystem to help meet that demand, according to Sean O’Connor (pictured), regional manager of ENT West, large enterprise and acquisition, at Dell.

“For us, that notion of ecosystem is starting to change,” he told theCUBE. “Today we’re here with Intel [Corp.], we’re here with SHI [International Corp.], we’re here with Microsoft [Corp.]. But that ecosystem also now is starting to bleed into private equity and venture capital.”

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video interview with Sean O’Connor:

#5432. Hackers have cut power in Ukraine, but could they take down the U.S. grid? 10 cases

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Whether hackers can take down the U.S. power grid has no simple answer, and these 10 cases, safeguards and weak points show what cyberattacks have done and what limits them

A cyberattack has already caused a blackout — just not in the U.S. In December 2015, attackers took over operator workstations at three regional distribution companies in Ukraine and opened breakers. The breaches cut power to roughly 225,000 customers. The outage lasted hours, not days. A year later, malware called Industroyer cut power for about an hour at a transmission substation near Kyiv.

Those attacks raise a question that returns with each new federal warning: could hackers take down the U.S. power grid? The answer depends on what an attacker can reach, how far a failure can spread and how quickly operators can restore service. None of those factors reduces to a simple yes or no.

Stuxnet, discovered in 2010, showed that code can physically damage industrial equipment. It targeted Siemens control systems and damaged centrifuges at Iran's Natanz enrichment plant. It was not aimed at a power grid. In 2023 and 2024, CISA, the FBI and other agencies issued warnings about a China-linked group called Volt Typhoon. The agencies said the group had pre-positioned itself in U.S. critical infrastructure networks, including some in the energy sector. The U.S. government said the aim was the ability to disrupt operations in a future crisis. That kind of access is not the same as an outage.

The shape of the U.S. grid matters too. It consists of three major interconnections, Eastern, Western and Texas, run by thousands of utilities with different systems. That fragmentation limits how far a single intrusion can spread. It also makes uniform defense hard. The North American Electric Reliability Corporation, or NERC, sets mandatory Critical Infrastructure Protection standards for the bulk power system, and FERC approves them. Smaller distribution utilities face fewer mandatory requirements.

Large outages do not require an attacker. The 2003 Northeast blackout affected about 50 million people in the U.S. and Canada. A software bug in an alarm system at FirstEnergy $FE in Ohio, along with overgrown trees touching power lines, contributed to the cascade. Recovery tools exist as well. Black start procedures let utilities restart plants without outside power. GridEx, a NERC-run exercise held every two years, tests how utilities respond to cyber and physical attacks.

The 10 items below are a selection, not a ranked list of threats. They explain what cyberattacks on electric utilities have done, where the weak points sit and what limits the damage an intrusion can cause.

In December 2015, hackers cut electricity to roughly 225,000 customers in Ukraine. It was the first publicly confirmed case of a cyberattack causing a power outage.

The intruders did not need to destroy any equipment to cause the outage. They took control of operator workstations at three regional distribution companies. These are the computers that control-room staff use to monitor and operate equipment across a utility's network from a central location.

From those screens, the attackers opened breakers. A breaker is a switch that stops current from flowing along a line. Operators open breakers as a routine step during maintenance or to isolate a fault. In this case, that ordinary command was the method of the attack.

The method is central to the question of whether hackers could take down the U.S. power grid. The attackers turned the utilities' own control tools against them. Once they held the workstations, they could send the same kinds of commands a legitimate operator would.

The targets were distribution companies. These utilities handle the final stage of electricity delivery. They carry power from the high-voltage network to homes and businesses in their regions. The outage therefore reached customers served by three separate companies.

The U.S. government and the E-ISAC later attributed the attack to Russian-linked actors. The E-ISAC, the Electricity Information Sharing and Analysis Center, gathers and shares threat information for the power sector. The center is operated by NERC, the North American Electric Reliability Corporation.

The outage lasted hours, not days. Remote access to control systems was still enough to switch off electricity for a large number of people. Both facts bear on the question of what a cyberattack on the electric grid can and cannot do.

So far, Ukraine is the only country where cyberattacks have been publicly confirmed to cause blackouts. No confirmed cyber-caused blackout has occurred in the U.S.

In December 2016, malware known as Industroyer, also called CrashOverride, cut power from a transmission substation near Kyiv, Ukraine, for about an hour. The tool itself set the attack apart. It was code that could send commands directly to substation equipment in that equipment's own industrial protocols.

Industrial protocols are the languages control systems use to communicate with physical devices in the field. A utility's control software relies on them to read the status of equipment and to issue commands, such as opening or closing a breaker. Most everyday malware has no use for these languages. It steals data, encrypts files or spreads across office networks. Industroyer was written to talk to the hardware that moves electricity.

That was a step beyond Ukraine's first grid hack a year earlier. The December 2015 attack depended on intruders operating utility controls themselves. Industroyer moved much of that work into software. A program that issues breaker commands on its own reduces the need for attackers to work the controls by hand. It also packages the knowledge needed to manipulate grid equipment into code.

The level of the grid that was hit also differed. The 2015 attack struck distribution companies, the utilities that deliver power to homes and businesses at lower voltages. The 2016 attack struck a transmission substation. Transmission is the high-voltage part of the grid that carries electricity in bulk over longer distances. Power is stepped down from there for local delivery. A transmission substation therefore sits upstream of the lines that serve customers.

The physical result was limited. The outage was brief, and the incident did not become a lasting regional blackout. For anyone asking whether hackers could take down the U.S. power grid, the case points in two directions. Malware built specifically for grid equipment exists and has worked against a real substation. That single strike still produced a short outage rather than a prolonged collapse.

Industrial protocols are not unique to Ukraine. Utilities in many countries, including the U.S., use control systems that communicate with field equipment in this way.

Stuxnet, discovered in 2010, was malware that damaged centrifuges at Iran's Natanz enrichment plant. It did this by targeting Siemens control systems. That made it a clear case of software breaking physical machinery.

Many cyberattacks stay inside the digital world. They steal data, lock files or knock websites offline. Stuxnet went further. It reached the systems that tell industrial machines how to behave, and the harm landed on the equipment itself.

Centrifuges at an enrichment plant spin at very high speeds to enrich uranium. Control systems govern that motion. Stuxnet attacked that control layer. The result was broken hardware, not only a disrupted network.

That difference shapes recovery. A disrupted network can often be brought back once malicious code is removed and systems are rebuilt. Damaged machinery cannot be restored that way. It has to be repaired or replaced before it runs again.

Stuxnet was not aimed at the power grid. It did not cause a blackout. Its target was a uranium enrichment facility in Iran, and no electric utility was involved.

Its relevance to electricity comes from what it demonstrated. Power plants and substations also run physical equipment through industrial control systems. Circuit breakers open and close on command. Generators respond to control signals. Stuxnet proved that malicious code can reach that kind of control layer and turn digital commands into physical consequences.

The same distinction would apply on the grid. An intrusion that only opens breakers leaves equipment that operators can close again. An intrusion that damages generators or substation hardware would leave a repair job behind it.

That proof has limits. The code targeted Siemens control systems, and its known damage was at Natanz. An attack on a U.S. utility would have to match the equipment and software that utility actually uses. That is a separate challenge, and the Natanz case does not answer it.

The U.S. power grid is not one machine that a single switch could turn off. It is made up of three major interconnections — Eastern, Western and Texas, known as ERCOT. Thousands of utilities run the equipment inside them.

That structure shapes any answer to whether hackers could take down the U.S. power grid. An attacker who breaks into one utility's network has reached one operator, not the country. The division into separate interconnections also sets boundaries on where trouble can travel.

Those boundaries change what a nationwide outage would require. An attacker aiming at the whole country would need footholds inside all three interconnections, not just one of them.

The utilities inside those interconnections do not share one common set of computers or software. Each runs its own systems. An intrusion built around one company's setup may not carry over to the company next door.

For anyone trying to cause a nationwide blackout, that variety is an obstacle. One piece of malicious code or one stolen login does not open every control room at once. Reaching more operators means getting past more separate systems.

The same fragmentation creates a problem for the people defending the grid. With thousands of operators running different systems, there is no single standard setup to lock down. Security work has to happen utility by utility rather than all at once.

The result is a trade-off rather than a simple answer. The grid's patchwork design limits how far one breach can spread. It also makes it hard to raise defenses evenly across the whole network.

The three-interconnection layout is part of the answer to how vulnerable the power grid is. A breach at one utility reaches that utility's systems. Spreading an outage beyond it runs into separate operators, different technology and the boundaries between the Eastern, Western and Texas interconnections.

NERC, the North American Electric Reliability Corporation, sets mandatory cybersecurity rules for the bulk power system. These rules are the Critical Infrastructure Protection standards, known as CIP. FERC, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, approves them.

The arrangement splits the job in two. NERC writes the requirements, and a federal regulator signs off on them. Utilities within their scope must follow them. They are not optional guidance. The mandatory status means compliance does not rest on each company's own judgment about what is worth doing.

The bulk power system is the high-voltage backbone of the grid. In general terms, it includes large power plants along with the transmission lines and substations that carry electricity over long distances. A failure at that level can affect customers across a wide area.

The CIP standards are written for that backbone. A compromised control system at a major transmission substation can affect far more people than a fault on one neighborhood line. The rules concentrate on the equipment where a breach would reach the most customers.

That focus leaves a gap. Smaller distribution utilities face fewer mandatory requirements. Distribution utilities deliver power over local lines to homes and businesses. Distribution is also the level where an outage reaches customers directly.

Fewer requirements do not mean none. A smaller utility still runs systems that keep power flowing to its customers. The difference lies in how much of its protection is set by a mandatory standard and how much depends on choices the utility makes for itself.

The result is uneven coverage. The CIP standards set a mandatory floor for the parts of the grid with the widest reach. They do not apply to every utility to the same degree. For anyone weighing grid cyber risk, the question is not only whether rules exist but which parts of the system they cover.

Colonial Pipeline shut down its pipeline operations in May 2021 after a DarkSide ransomware attack. The case shows that a breach on the business side of a company can stop physical operations.

Colonial Pipeline is a fuel pipeline company, not an electric utility. The attack did not cause a power outage, and it was not a strike on the grid. It still belongs in a discussion of grid cyber risk. It shows how critical infrastructure can stop working without an attacker ever taking control of physical equipment.

Ransomware is malicious software that encrypts a victim's files or systems and then demands payment to restore access. A typical infection locks up data. It does not send commands to valves, pumps or circuit breakers.

Industrial companies generally run two kinds of networks. Information technology, or IT, covers the business side: email, accounting, billing and corporate records. Operational technology, or OT, covers the systems that monitor and control physical equipment. In a pipeline, OT controls the equipment that moves fuel. In a utility, it controls the equipment that generates and delivers electricity.

Colonial's breach was on the IT side, yet the operational side still stopped. The company halted pipeline operations itself, as a precaution. A company that cannot yet confirm how far an intrusion has spread may choose to halt operations on its own.

That distinction bears directly on whether hackers could take down the U.S. power grid. Electric utilities run IT and OT networks, as pipeline operators do. Ransomware confined to a utility's business systems would not, by itself, send commands to grid equipment. It could still lead operators to disconnect systems or pause some operations while they assess the damage.

The attacks on Ukraine's grid in 2015 and 2016 took a different route. In those cases, attackers acted on grid equipment directly. Colonial shows a second route to disruption — one in which the stoppage comes from a defensive choice rather than an attacker's command.

The case moves the question of electric grid cyber risk beyond control rooms. Protecting OT networks covers one path to an interruption. Keeping ransomware out of corporate networks covers another. A precautionary shutdown still halts service, whatever triggered it.

Volt Typhoon is a China-linked hacking group that U.S. agencies said in 2023 and 2024 had pre-positioned itself inside U.S. critical infrastructure networks. Some of those networks belong to the energy sector.

The warnings came from several federal agencies. CISA, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, issued them alongside the FBI and other agencies. The alerts covered critical infrastructure broadly rather than the power grid alone.

The energy sector's place on that list carries extra weight. Electricity supports most other critical services, from water treatment to communications.

The U.S. government also described the group's purpose. It said the aim was the ability to disrupt operations in a future crisis. That stated goal separates the campaign from intrusions built only to steal data. The concern is less about what intruders copy out of a network. It is about what they could do later from inside it.

Pre-positioning means gaining access to a network in advance and keeping it. An intruder who already holds a foothold does not need to break in when a crisis begins. The access stays in place until someone decides to use it — or until defenders find and remove it. Access that sits unused also produces little activity for defenders to notice.

Access is not an outage. The public warnings described intrusions and intent. They did not report any U.S. blackout caused by the group. Holding a position inside a network and cutting power to customers are separate steps.

That distinction shapes where the Volt Typhoon warnings fit in the question of grid risk. By the U.S. government's own description, the group was preparing an ability to disrupt. The warnings did not say that ability had been used against the power grid. For grid operators, the gap between access and action is the window in which an intrusion can still be found and removed.

The 2003 Northeast blackout cut power to about 50 million people in the U.S. and Canada, and no hacker was involved. A software bug in an alarm system at FirstEnergy $FE in Ohio, along with overgrown trees touching power lines, helped set off a cascade that spread across a wide area.

The blackout matters for grid cyber risk because of how it spread. It shows the scale an outage can reach once a local problem moves through connected parts of the system.

A cascading failure follows the physics of a connected network. Electricity flows along every available path between generators and customers. When a line trips offline, the power it was carrying shifts onto neighboring lines. If those lines become overloaded, protective equipment can disconnect them too. Each loss pushes more load onto what remains.

Both contributing causes were common kinds of failure. Trees that had grown too close to transmission lines made contact with them, and that took lines out of service. The alarm software problem at FirstEnergy meant operators did not get the warnings that would normally flag that kind of trouble. Missing alarms make it harder for a control room to act while a problem is still small.

The pairing is what links 2003 to the cyber question. A failure in software, not in steel or wire, played a part in turning local line trips into a regional blackout. In 2003 that software failure was a bug. Operators losing an accurate view of their own system is also an effect that an intrusion into utility control systems could produce.

Fragmentation does not seal every part of the grid off from its neighbors. Sections that are connected share power, so they can also share failures.

The blackout marks a limit on what the comparison proves. It was an accident with physical triggers, not a coordinated attack. It does not show that a hacker could reproduce it. It shows that the grid's interconnected design can carry a local fault far beyond where it started, with or without anyone intending it.

U.S. utilities prepare to recover from a major outage with black start procedures, which restart power plants without any electricity from outside. They also rehearse responses to cyber and physical attacks in GridEx, an exercise that the North American Electric Reliability Corporation, or NERC, runs every two years.

A grid that has gone dark cannot simply be switched back on. If an attack or a failure leaves a region without power, operators need a way to get generation running again with no outside supply to draw on. Black start procedures provide that path.

The procedures are worked out before any emergency. Utilities do not have to invent a restart plan in the middle of a blackout. The plan already exists, and operators know which steps come first.

This bears directly on the question of whether hackers could take down the grid. Causing an outage is one problem for an attacker. Keeping power off is a separate one. A restart plan prepared in advance is aimed at the second problem. It gives operators a known route back.

GridEx covers the human side of recovery. The exercise puts utilities through simulated attacks and tests how their staff respond.

The exercise treats digital and physical threats as part of the same planning problem. A utility facing an intrusion in its networks may also face damage to equipment in the field. GridEx asks participants to handle both kinds of attack rather than one in isolation.

The two tools address different parts of recovery. Black start is about the machines and how generation comes back from zero. GridEx is about the people and organizations that have to make decisions under pressure.

Neither one stops an attack from happening. Both are built for what comes after an attack succeeds. They are designed to shorten an outage rather than to prevent the intrusion that caused it.

Ukraine's power companies restored service faster after their grid hacks partly because operators could switch to manual control. In the U.S., utilities pursue a layered set of defenses — network segmentation, multifactor authentication and monitoring of operational technology — with support from federal agencies.

Manual control matters because the Ukrainian attacks worked through remote systems. An intruder who controls the software that opens and closes breakers makes that software untrustworthy. The fallback is to run the equipment without the compromised network. A utility with trained staff and ready procedures for hands-on operation can restore power while its digital tools are still in doubt.

Network segmentation addresses a different problem. Utilities run two broad kinds of networks. Information technology, or IT, covers email, billing and business software. Operational technology, or OT, covers the systems that monitor and control physical equipment such as substations and generating units.

Segmentation divides these networks and limits the connections between them. The goal is to keep a breach on the business side from becoming a direct path to the machines that move electricity. An attacker who lands in an accounting system should still face barriers before reaching anything that controls power flow.

Multifactor authentication targets the risk of stolen login credentials. It requires a user to confirm their identity with something beyond a password, such as a code from a separate device or a physical security key. A password captured through a phishing email is then not enough on its own to open an account.

Monitoring OT networks means watching the traffic inside control systems for activity that does not match normal operations. Control networks generally carry routine, repetitive commands. An unexpected instruction to a breaker, or an unfamiliar device communicating on the network, can signal an intruder.

The federal government also backs utilities on this front. CISA, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, works with utilities on cyber defense. The Department of Energy supports them through CESER, its Office of Cybersecurity, Energy Security, and Emergency Response.

None of these measures makes a grid immune to intrusion. Together, they aim to make an intrusion harder to achieve, quicker to detect and less likely to reach the equipment that keeps power flowing.

#5431. EXCLUSIVE: California officials urged to examine Zillow Preview, referral model

Consumer and advocacy groups asked California’s housing regulators to investigate Zillow’s pre-market Zillow Preview program and its agent referral model. The letter also alleges steering toward Zillow Home Loans and argues renters faced higher costs after the Redfin rentals deal.  AI Summary

A coalition of consumer and advocacy groups is urging California housing regulators to investigate Zillow Group’s listing, agent referral and mortgage practices, arguing the company is distorting the state’s housing market and overcharging buyers and renters.

Demand Progress, Revolving Door Project, Americans for Financial Reform, Children’s Advocacy Alliance and the Consumer Federation of America sent a letter to Californian officials alleging that Zillow has leveraged its position in listings, buyer representation and mortgage lending to “soak homebuyers” and renters, and call for enforcement under multiple state laws.

The letter, addressed to Rohit Chopra, secretary of the California Business and Consumer Services Agency, and Chika Sunquist, commissioner of the California Department of Real Estate, contends that “the California housing market is broken” and that Zillow is “one of the most aggressive actors in distorting the market, to its own profit and to the detriment of the public.”

The groups focus heavily on Zillow Preview, the firm’s pre-marketing program launched in March 2026 that allows major brokerages to promote listings on Zillow before they hit the broader market. Keller Williams, REMAX, HomeServices of America, Side and United Real Estate were among some of the first firms to sign on to the program. More than 400 brokerages have entered exclusive agreements with Zillow, the letter states, arguing that the arrangement locks “freshest inventory” on Zillow and, more recently, Realtor.com, while sidelining competing platforms. The coalition urges California regulators to scrutinize these vertical agreements and what it characterizes as “monopsonistic capture of pre-market listings.”

The coalition also targets Zillow’s long-running agent referral model. The letter alleges that when consumers click “Contact agent” or “Request a tour” on many listings, they are often routed to Zillow-affiliated buyer agents rather than the listing agent, citing prior academic research and litigation.

A Wharton School study found most consumers believed those buttons would connect them to an agent associated with the property and that “almost none” could correctly identify who would contact them based on Zillow’s interface, according to the letter.

The groups highlight Zillow’s Flex program (now known as Zillow Preferred), which charges participating buyer agents a “success fee” reportedly as high as 40% of the buy-side commission. They argue that this structure reduces incentives for agents to compete on price and aligns agent incentives more closely with Zillow than with consumers.

The letter notes that Zillow has faced class action litigation over these practices, including claims that its referral and commission structures constitute a racketeering “enterprise.” The case, filed in federal court in Washington state, challenges both the referral flows and undisclosed fees as deceptive under federal and state law.

On the listing side, the group says Zillow offers listing agents a 10% share of the buy-side commission on deals that close from Preview leads, including when the buyer ultimately purchases a different property. They argue that this unilateral setting of referral compensation could conflict with the spirit or letter of the National Association of Realtors’ (NAR) commission lawsuit settlement, which sought to decouple listing and buyer-broker compensation.

On the financing side, the letter accuses Zillow of using its agent network to steer borrowers toward Zillow Home Loans. It cites allegations in the amended complaint in the renewed Taylor lawsuit that affiliated buyer agents risk losing leads or expulsion from Flex if they do not prioritize Zillow’s lending arm.

Most buyers do not shop widely for financing. Zillow’s own research has found that roughly 72% of buyers submit just one mortgage application, according to the letter. Separately, Zillow research has shown that rate shopping can save borrowers thousands of dollars over the life of a loan.

The coalition points to an empirical analysis by Georgetown University Law Center professor Steven Salop, which concluded that Zillow Home Loans borrowers paid about $4,600 more on average than comparable borrowers at other lenders between 2025 and 2027. Salop’s work estimates $186 million in projected overcharges over that period, with even higher average costs for military veterans and Black and Asian borrowers.

The letter compares the alleged steering to the in-house mortgage referral arrangements that drew a 2024 lawsuit from the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) against Rocket Homes. That case, brought under the Real Estate Settlement Procedures Act, focused on alleged kickback and referral schemes between affiliated real estate and mortgage businesses and has since been dismissed.

The advocacy groups also raise concerns about Zillow’s expansion in rentals. They note that renters tend to have lower incomes and less bargaining power than buyers, and argue that Zillow has long tried to prioritize its own rental listings while limiting rivals’ visibility.

The letter references Zillow’s $100 million multifamily rental syndication deal with Redfin, claiming that it paid Redfin to shutter its multifamily rental advertising business and transfer clients to Zillow. That agreement later triggered an antitrust complaint by the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) and five states, which alleged Zillow illegally paid a competitor to exit the rental listings market.

FTC staff estimated that landlords using Zillow paid an average 14.5% more per listing after the deal, according to public statements cited in the letter. The coalition says renters ultimately bore those higher marketing costs.

Zillow and Redfin settled with the FTC in August 2026 without admitting wrongdoing. The order requires changes to certain agreements but allows the companies to maintain some form of partnership through at least 2030.

The coalition urges California officials to deploy what it calls the state’s “strongest toolkit in the nation” against Zillow’s business model. Specifically, the letter asks Chopra and Sunquist to use the Department of Real Estate’s licensing and rulemaking authority to investigate alleged steering by licensees that may violate fiduciary duties, and to consider rules requiring privately marketed properties to be listed concurrently on public platforms, drawing on legislation passed in Connecticut and New York.

Additionally, they ask officials to investigate and, where warranted, bring actions under the state’s Cartwright Act and Unfair Competition Law against Zillow Preview’s exclusive agreements, Zillow’s arrangement with Realtor.com and any “re-coupling” of commissions after the NAR settlement.

They also want officials to pursue enforcement under the Consumers Legal Remedies Act and Unfair Competition Law targeting Zillow’s “Contact agent” and “Request a tour” interfaces, alleged nondisclosure of Preferred referral fees and failure to disclose that agent recommendations can be driven by Zillow’s financial interests and to coordinate with the multistate coalition that brought the Redfin rental action, to avoid jurisdictional gaps that could allow similar conduct to persist in California.

The groups argue that while the FTC settlement with Zillow over its Redfin agreement “closed one case,” it did not address what they describe as a broader pattern of conduct spanning purchase, financing and rental markets. They frame California, the nation’s largest housing market, as a critical venue for testing new state-level responses.

If regulators accept the coalition’s framing, California could move to restrict or reshape referral fee structures and pre-market listing programs, directly affecting how agents source leads and are paid. In addition, a California investigation into Zillow’s referral flows could set new guardrails on when and how real estate professionals can recommend affiliate lenders, particularly around disclosure and independence requirements.

Zillow did not immediately respond to HousingWire’s request for comment on the letter.
