#5429. SiMa.ai’s Palette 3.0 runs many AI models on one chip and lifts throughput up to 3.5 times

Physical artificial intelligence chip startup SiMa Technologies Inc. today released Palette 3.0, a new version of its Palette software suite intended to allow many AI models to run concurrently on one chip.

According to the company, the release, which builds on the Palette Neat agentic development environment launched in June, can raise model throughput by as much as 3.5 times.

Developers building drones, robots and other autonomous machines, which need to run AI models on the device rather than in a data center, are a primary focus of the release. SiMa.ai argues that while industry incumbents rely on adapting legacy data center technology, it builds its software and silicon exclusively for physical AI.

Leading the new capabilities in Palette 3.0 is improved concurrent model execution on SiMa.ai’s Modalix MLSoC. Maintaining what the company describes as a low-power profile, a single chip can handle complex reasoning and multimodel workloads at the same time. The platform can also run separate Docker containers on the chip. Supported workloads include large language models and vision-language models.

Perception, depth and reasoning models used by drones and robots are also said to run faster on the new version. Working with ecosystem partners, SiMa.ai has added unified sensor fusion, dense neural depth fields and closed-loop digital twin simulation to the platform. The goal of the additions, SiMa.ai says, is to remove the integration and validation bottlenecks that slow down autonomous development.

Performance figures for those models are published in a new Model Registry, which SiMa.ai says measures every result within real-world power constraints. The company is offering competitive benchmarking details on request.

Also new in the release is a set of open-source capabilities for generative AI application development. Behind the 3.5-times throughput figure is speculative decoding, using the EAGLE3, DFlash and Gemma 4 MTP algorithms. Support has also been added for large mixture-of-experts models such as OpenAI Group PBC’s GPT-OSS-20B, which can now run on the Modalix MLSoC 16GB system-on-module.

Developers are free to adapt the open-source code, which is available on GitHub. Documentation for Palette 3.0 is provided through SiMa.ai’s Developer Center.

Founded in 2018 by Chief Executive Krishna Rangasayee, SiMa.ai offers a platform that combines purpose-built silicon with software for AI on physical devices. Notable customers and partners include Robert Bosch GmbH, Emerson Electric Co. and Synopsys Inc.

SiMa.ai raised $150 million in a Series C round at a $1.45 billion valuation in September. Fidelity Management & Research Co. and Amplify Partners co-led the round. The company has raised $500 million to date.

#5428. How buyer objections shape listing strategy in 2027

A veteran listing agent argues the strongest listing strategy starts by identifying likely buyer objections before marketing begins. He outlines pre-listing steps including permits, condition, insurance costs, and active competition to set pricing expectations and reduce renegotiation.  AI Summary

The longer I work in real estate, the more convinced I become that some of the most important work in selling a home happens before the first photograph is taken. I’ve represented sellers through very different housing markets, and one thing hasn’t changed: Even the best marketing campaign can’t overcome every concern a buyer may have.

Photography, descriptions and online exposure matter. But they’re only part of the equation.

Before listing a home, I try to answer a simple question: What might cause a qualified buyer to hesitate, negotiate aggressively or walk away? I’d rather uncover those concerns before losing a good buyer.

Earlier this year, I listed a four-bedroom pool home in Oakland Park, Florida, that needed considerable updating. Frankly, I was concerned about how buyers would react to its condition. It wasn’t turnkey, but it had real strengths: an attractive location and a walkable neighborhood.

We priced the property at $660,000. Within four days, we received five offers, and the home sold above asking price. The transaction was reported by Paul Owers for Homes.com in May 2026.

That experience reinforced something I’ve observed repeatedly: Buyers will accept imperfections when they believe the overall value makes sense. Not every home needs extensive improvements before selling. Conversely, a desirable neighborhood doesn’t excuse unrealistic pricing. Our job is to recognize a property’s strengths and shortcomings, then help sellers decide how to proceed.

I wonder whether our focus on marketing sometimes crowds out essential preparation. We can produce photographs, videos and descriptions quickly. But if we haven’t researched the property, understood the competition or identified potential insurance concerns, we may be beautifully marketing a problem we should have investigated first.

Today’s buyers face affordability challenges, costly financing and, in many markets, more competing homes. Here in South Florida, insurance costs, property taxes, maintenance and condition can significantly influence purchasing decisions. A house may appear affordable, but the monthly cost of ownership can tell a different story.

As listing agents, we need to look at properties through the buyer’s eyes. Could an older roof create insurance or financing problems? Are improvements properly permitted? What might surface during an inspection? What else could buyers purchase for the same money?

We won’t always have every answer. But we should know which questions to ask.

I like to start with the property itself.

That doesn’t necessarily mean expensive improvements are needed. But it calls for an honest conversation about price, condition and expectations. I don’t pretend we can anticipate every problem. Yet experience helps us recognize what might give buyers second thoughts.

One of the harder parts of representing sellers is telling homeowners something they’d rather not hear. Perhaps their anticipated price isn’t supported by the market. Maybe an expensive renovation won’t produce the return they expect. Those conversations aren’t easy.

For many sellers, their home represents years of memories, hard work and financial investment. We owe them empathy, but also honesty. I’d rather have that conversation before listing than watch a seller become discouraged after weeks of limited activity and repeated price reductions.

Technology can help with this preparation. I use artificial intelligence to research properties, study competing listings and organize information. But technology doesn’t replace walking through a property, asking difficult questions or recognizing when something deserves further investigation.

Sometimes you have to put the computer aside, visit the property and bring in someone who knows more about a particular problem than you do.

There’s wisdom in acknowledging another professional’s expertise. As we approach 2027, I believe listing agents should spend less time emphasizing how widely they can advertise a home and more time explaining how they’ve prepared it for the market.

Good marketing gets buyers through the door. What we’ve done before they arrive can make a real difference in what happens next. Even a well-prepared listing can encounter unexpected problems. There are no guarantees in this business. But sellers deserve to know we’ve done our homework, considered the competition and anticipated difficult questions.

For me, it comes down to this: The best listing strategy doesn’t begin by asking how we can make a home look more appealing. It begins by understanding what might keep a buyer from saying yes.

Gary Lanham is a broker associate with LoKation Real Estate and an AI-certified Realtor specializing in residential listings in the Fort Lauderdale area. With 22 years of real estate experience, he founded Lanham & Associates, acquired by Coldwell Banker Realty in 2014. A member of the Master Brokers Forum, Lanham writes and teaches about listing strategy, real estate technology and professional representation.

#5427. Visa and Mastercard pushed for final approval of $38 billion swipe fee deal

Free daily briefing on global business news.

A federal judge in Brooklyn withheld a ruling after Monday's hearing as Walmart and the National Retail Federation object

Visa $V and Mastercard $MA urged U.S. District Judge Brian Cogan on Monday to give final approval to their $38 billion deal with merchants, who accused the networks of overcharging to handle credit card transactions, according to Reuters.

Cogan withheld a decision on final approval at the hearing in Brooklyn, New York. He said a decision to turn down the settlement might set off a "protracted process" if the case then went to trial, according to Reuters.

The settlement obliges Visa and Mastercard to trim their swipe fees by a tenth of a percentage point for five years, while limiting charges on standard consumer cards to 1.25% for eight years. It ends the "Honor All Cards" rule, which requires merchants to accept all of a network's cards or none. Merchants would, for the first time, be able to pick which of three categories to accept: standard consumer cards, commercial cards, or premium consumer cards such as rewards cards.

The proposed settlement would apply to over 12 million merchants, although some of its opponents put the number of businesses affected at more than 20 million.

Visa lawyer Michael Shuster described the deal as delivering "potent" relief to merchants, while acknowledging that Visa is hardly "jumping with joy" over the changes. "It's going to change life for the networks," Shuster said.

Two experts retained by the plaintiffs, economist Joseph Stiglitz and Keith Leffler, a University of Washington professor, estimated that the changes could deliver $224 billion in total benefits, including for consumers, with merchants saving $38 billion by 2031.

Swipe fees, which are also called interchange fees, added up to $118.8 billion for Visa and Mastercard across the United States in 2025, according to the Merchants Payments Coalition. The average rate came to 2.36%.

The court logged just over 1,000 objections, among them filings from Walmart $WMT and the National Retail Federation. Some opponents say merchants would keep paying steep fees to take rewards cards and would lack the ability to pick among issuers, for instance by taking one bank's cards while turning away another's.

Mithun Mansinghani, a lawyer for the National Association of Convenience Stores and Circle K, told Cogan that the deal contains no structural changes that would foster real competition among card issuers. He said charges would stay excessive for commercial cards and premium consumer cards, which together account for over 90% of the market for cards. "Competition should be the North Star ... and this settlement is way off course," Mansinghani said, according to Reuters.

The Electronic Payments Coalition, whose members include Visa, Mastercard, Bank of America $BAC, Capital One $COF, Chase and Citibank, supports the settlement.

Cogan granted preliminary approval in June and said he expected to grant final approval, describing the terms as "fair, reasonable, and adequate." He acknowledged that some objections raised legitimate points but said perfection was not the standard.

In June 2024, a different judge, Margo Brodie, refused to approve an earlier $30 billion deal because its size was inadequate. She concluded that swipe fees would not have fallen to pre-violation levels and that the "Honor All Cards" obligation would have remained intact.

#5425. Exclusive: Cogent Security’s DefenseOS adds policies and automations for AI agents

Vulnerability management startup Cogent Security Inc. today launched DefenseOS, an operating system designed for artificial intelligence agents that carry out defensive cybersecurity work inside the enterprise.

Arriving with DefenseOS are two new capabilities, Agent Policies and Agent Automations. The first is designed to give Cogent’s AI agents a deep understanding of the enterprise environment, while the second puts recurring security work on an automated schedule.

Cogent is pitching DefenseOS at security teams that are struggling to keep up as AI speeds up the discovery of vulnerabilities. In October, Microsoft Corp. fixed more than 1,400 security flaws in a single Patch Tuesday release, more than it fixed in all of 2025. The window between disclosure and exploitation has also shrunk, by Cogent’s count, from months in 2024 to only hours this year.

Prioritizing at that pace requires context such as which assets are business-critical, which are exposed to the internet and who owns them. According to the company, that information is spread across documents, teams and tribal knowledge, and most organizations see only a fraction of it.

In its role as the context engine for Cogent, DefenseOS ingests data from scanners, business systems and other security tools. Once the data has been normalized and deduplicated, DefenseOS encodes how the enterprise functions to deliver accurate risk scoring, prioritization and remediation. The platform serves as the AI harness that sets the working environment and limits for Cogent’s agents.

The first of the two new capabilities, Agent Policies, is described by Cogent as creating a context layer that builds and grows via agents, turning how an enterprise works into rules. Those rules then shape how the Cogent platform handles asset context, risk scoring, prioritization and remediation. The company claims the feature strips out much of the operational overhead that enterprises formerly had to put into running a vulnerability management program.

The second, Agent Automations, acts as the execution layer within DefenseOS. Using it, security teams can build agentic workflows that run automatically to generate alerts and reports, investigate vulnerabilities and deliver remediation guidance on a consistent basis.

Co-founder and Chief Technology Officer Geng Sng said recurring reports, known investigations and routine alerts take up a large share of a security team’s week. With Agent Automations, he said, teams can “define that work once” and have Cogent’s agents run it on their schedule.

“Every enterprise runs its security program differently, and moving at machine speed means grasping those differences,” said co-founder and Chief Executive Vineet Edupuganti. “DefenseOS unifies the context of an enterprise environment, surfacing rules into Agent Policies that a customer can codify, and creating the runtime environment for continuous cyber defense led by AI agents.”

The launch follows the release earlier this month of VR-1.1, a new version of Cogent’s frontier reasoning model that writes fixes for newly disclosed software vulnerabilities.

DefenseOS and Agent Automations are available now to all Cogent customers. Agent Policies has launched in beta for new Cogent deployments ahead of general availability at a later date.

Founded in 2025 and staffed by former researchers and operators from Google DeepMind, Abnormal AI Inc. and Coinbase Global Inc., Cogent says Fortune 500 security teams using its platform have cut the exposure window for critical vulnerabilities by 97%. The company has raised $53 million to date, including a $42 million Series A led by Bain Capital Ventures in February.

#5424. Anthropic is guiding its IPO price to the top of its range — or higher

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Anthropic would be valued at roughly $1.4 trillion on a fully diluted basis if shares priced at the upper end of the range

Anthropic is signaling to prospective investors that it anticipates pricing its IPO at or beyond the top of its range, according to Bloomberg.

The company filed an amended registration statement on Tuesday that lists 825 million shares of Class A common stock at an estimated $70 to $78 each. Anthropic is selling 801,351,354 of those shares, and selling stockholders are offering 23,648,646. The stock has been approved to list on the Nasdaq $NDAQ Global Select Market under the symbol "ANT."

Google $GOOGL, Nvidia $NVDA, Advanced Micro Devices, Broadcom $AVGO, Micron $MU Technology, Microsoft $MSFT and TSMC $TSM have agreed to buy a combined $26.0 billion of Anthropic's Class N common stock in a private placement at the IPO price, the filing said. The placement closes immediately after the IPO and depends on the offering being completed. Anthropic estimated net proceeds from the IPO and placement at about $84.6 billion at a $74 share price, the midpoint of the range.

Including the private placement, the offering could bring in as much as $90.4 billion at the top of the range, according to Bloomberg. Anthropic would be valued at roughly $1.4 trillion on a fully diluted basis if shares priced at the upper end of the range.

Banks plan to close their order books at 4 p.m. ET on Tuesday, according to Bloomberg. The IPO is slated to be priced Wednesday, with trading starting a day later, though terms may still shift. Goldman Sachs $GS and Morgan Stanley $MS are leading the offering, and the filing lists 20 other banks.

Orders have climbed to almost seven times the supply of stock on offer, according to Bloomberg. Bankers have told prospective investors that current backers will get priority and that some buyers will receive smaller allocations than they anticipate, according to Bloomberg. The filing said up to 20% of the shares offered are expected to go to retail investors.

Anthropic's run-rate revenue stood at roughly $81 billion at Oct. 31, an increase of $10 billion since Sept. 30, the filing said. The company reported revenue of $17.0 billion for the three months ended Sept. 30.

Anthropic also disclosed about $900.9 billion in purchase commitments and lease agreements, substantially all tied to compute and infrastructure. About $70.7 billion of that is due in the 12 months after Sept. 30, 2026.

#5422. Semperis updates Lightning identity security platform to defend against AI agent attacks

Enterprise identity protection and cyber resilience company Semperis Ltd. today released the latest version of its Semperis Lightning identity security platform, which is designed to help organizations defend against identity attacks by artificial intelligence agents and conventional attackers alike.

Delivered through a single console, the new version of Lightning is said to combine exposure management, attack-path analysis and detection-and-response workflows. Along with Microsoft Corp.’s Active Directory and Entra ID, the new release supports Okta Inc.

Semperis says organizations using Lightning can adopt AI tools for productivity while reducing the risk of agents compromising critical resources. According to Chief Executive Mickey Bresman, identity systems have become “the main control plane” in the agentic age.

Though AI agents move at machine speed through the enterprise, Bresman said, they still depend on the identity fabric for access. With Lightning, organizations are said to be able to create, enforce and monitor what he called “agentic execution boundaries.”

Chief Product Officer Alex Weinert, who joined Semperis in April 2025 after serving as vice president of identity security at Microsoft, said security teams “do not need another flat list of identity findings.” Context on what can actually reach the identity control plane is what they need instead, he said. Agentic identities, he added, are opening new routes to privileged systems.

On the exposure side, Lightning, which now comes with a growing catalog of more than 220 security indicators, continuously scans identity infrastructure for exposures in human and nonhuman identities. The results are then scored, according to Semperis, before being triaged in a single workflow.

The platform’s live identity graph, which Semperis describes as a map of relationships and attack paths, covers routes to domain administrators, privileged accounts and other critical assets. According to the company, remediation guidance from the graph is prioritized by risk so that teams can respond faster.

Nonhuman and agentic identities are discovered automatically, Semperis says, and added to a searchable inventory of every identity in an environment. The company claims Lightning can scale to the largest multitenant, multiforest environments.

Built-in rule templates are designed to detect suspicious activity in Active Directory and Entra ID, such as unusual logons over Kerberos and NT LAN Manager. The company is also offering what it calls generative assistance alongside the templates.

Semperis introduced Lightning in April 2024 with Lightning Identity Runtime Protection, a machine learning-powered identity threat detection service. The company extended its resilience offerings to Okta and Ping Identity Corp. environments in February, when it acquired MightyID Inc.

More than 1,200 organizations, including over 25% of the 100 largest U.S. companies, are said to use Semperis. The company last raised $125 million in growth financing from JPMorgan Chase & Co. and Hercules Capital Inc. in June 2024. Earlier investors include Kohlberg Kravis Roberts & Co. LP, Insight Partners, Ten Eleven Ventures and Paladin Capital Group.

#5421. The Dow falls 337 points as Home Depot weighs and the Nasdaq holds flat before Nvidia’s earnings

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Home Depot stock fell close to 2% after a CEO change, while chip stocks kept the Nasdaq flat before Nvidia reports after the bell

The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 337 points, or 0.7%, on Tuesday as Home Depot $HD stock dropped close to 2% ahead of Nvidia $NVDA's quarterly earnings report. The S&P 500 slipped 0.2%, and the Nasdaq $NDAQ Composite was little changed.

Home Depot's decline followed word from the retailer that a new chief executive will be stepping into the role, according to CNBC. The stock's move weighed on the Dow and overshadowed quarterly results that beat Wall Street expectations.

Chipmakers helped the Nasdaq hold steady, leaving it close to unchanged. Marvell Technology stock rose 2%, while Arm Holdings and Broadcom $AVGO stock each gained 1%. Semiconductor names rose on a report that Anthropic planned to set its IPO price higher than the $70 to $78 range currently marketed, according to CNBC.

Nvidia is due to report fiscal third-quarter results after the bell Tuesday, Nov. 17. Its shares are down almost 24% so far in November, on track for the steepest one-month drop since April 2022, according to CNBC. Nvidia stock showed little direction in the opening hours of the session.

Jensen Huang stepped down as CEO last week following reports of two extramarital affairs, one of them with a woman suspected of spying for China, according to CNBC. Colette Kress, the company’s interim CEO, is expected to pull back on Nvidia’s dealmaking, according to The Wall Street Journal. Nvidia is projected to deliver yet another quarter of robust revenue gains.

Chip stocks in Asia declined Tuesday after the Commerce Department unveiled a rule meant to curb exports of chips made by Nvidia and other American firms to China. European stocks also fell.

Sales at U.S. retailers and food service businesses grew 0.2% in October to $748.2 billion, matching forecasts, according to CNBC. Excluding gas and autos, retail sales were up 0.6% compared with September, topping the 0.4% increase Wall Street had forecast. Import prices were also due Tuesday.

The Dow gave up over 700 points on Monday, a 1.4% decline, while the S&P 500 fell 1.9%. The Nasdaq Composite fell 2.5%, marking its steepest single-session drop since Nov. 5, according to CNBC.

#5419. Spara’s Scout AI assistant acts on sales opportunities before reps know to look

Artificial intelligence sales agent startup Spara Inc. today introduced Scout, an AI assistant designed to act on sales opportunities before salespeople know to look for them.

Working around the clock, the new service analyzes context from customer conversations, emails and customer relationship management data to identify opportunities, prepare personalized outreach and complete work before reps realize it needs doing.

Scout is aimed at addressing a limitation of most AI assistants, which still require users to tell them what to do, according to Spara. The service instead works within the daily workflows of salespeople, providing an always-on partner that keeps track of customers and helps move work forward without constant direction.

Signals analyzed continuously by Scout include job changes, company news, buying signals and CRM activity across a salesperson’s accounts. From there, the service determines when to engage customers and prospects, as well as who to contact. Instead of requiring another platform to manage, Scout delivers its findings through Salesforce Inc.’s Slack and text messages.

Over time, Scout retains what it learns about each account, along with the salesperson’s preferences and previous outreach. Doing so is said to allow the service to anticipate next steps and deliver more relevant recommendations.

Outreach messages are drafted in the salesperson’s voice, with reps kept in control of what gets sent. Going beyond recommendations, Scout can join customer calls and contribute to conversations in real time, helping salespeople move opportunities forward.

“Sales has always been a game of speed, timing and relationships, but there’s only so much one person can keep track of in a day,” said David Walker, co-founder and chief executive of Spara. “Even the best sales organizations can’t realistically give every rep the support they need to act on every opportunity at exactly the right moment.”

Spara also released early results from users of the new service. Salespeople using Scout were found to have increased the number of personalized emails sent eightfold in their first two weeks of use. Outreach generated by Scout drew a 10.5% reply rate, against 3.5% for traditional sales sequences, according to the company. Early users also booked 29% more meetings.

Chris Brown, a partner at Spara investor Inspired Capital who has worked with the team since the beginning, said Spara has built agents that go-to-market teams trust with their most important customer conversations. Scout is now “putting that trust to work for individual sellers,” he added.

Scout is available for free starting today at spara.com/scout.

Founded by Walker and Zander Pease, Spara offers a platform for building AI agents that carry out sales work across chat, email, text messaging, voice and interactive product demos. The agents handle tasks ranging from engaging and qualifying leads to following up with prospects, booking meetings and managing renewals. Notable customers include Justworks Inc., Rho Technologies Inc. and Mindbody Inc.

Spara launched in September 2025 with $15 million in seed funding. Including additional funding since then, the company has raised $20 million to date, with Radical Ventures and Inspired Capital leading the seed round.

#5418. Leaked Deutsche Bank files reveal $582 million in suspicious Epstein payments

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The bank's 2019 reports to U.S. authorities covered 3,200 transactions, and it says some matters date back as much as two decades

Deutsche Bank flagged roughly $582 million of Jeffrey Epstein-linked transactions as suspicious, more than twice what Senate investigators identified, according to the Financial Times.

The bank submitted 21 suspicious activity reports to U.S. authorities in 2019 that spanned 3,200 transactions connected to Epstein and his businesses, according to the Financial Times. Among the flagged transactions were payments to women, transfers routed through shell companies, donations to charity that may have been misused, and money received from billionaires such as Leon Black and Glenn Dubin.

The figure comes from about 15 million leaked bank files that range from internal email traffic and compliance reports to financial documentation. A journalist consortium numbering over 200 reviewed the files and released its findings Tuesday, according to Forbes.

An August Senate Finance Committee investigation led by Sen. Ron Wyden, an Oregon Democrat, found wire transfers tied to Epstein that it deemed suspicious and that totaled $250 million, according to Forbes. Deutsche Bank's internal review also took in checks and transactions that passed through other banks, which explains part of the gap.

Epstein signed on as a Deutsche Bank client in 2013, five years after being convicted of soliciting a minor for sex, according to the Financial Times. The bank told him in December 2018 that it was ending the relationship, the Financial Times said in its account. Deutsche Bank shut the last two accounts he held three days after he was arrested in July 2019, according to Financial Mail. An internal probe found no fewer than 112 "high-risk transactions," according to Financial Mail.

Deutsche Bank said in a statement that the reporting refers to purported internal documents that whistleblowers allegedly disclosed. “The matters which are in focus of the media reports date back many years and in some cases as much as two decades,” the bank said, according to Bloomberg. It said it had examined the issues when they arose and collaborated closely with regulators. The bank said it invested €7 billion ($7.8 billion) in its control environment between 2019 and 2025.

The bank said testing with a security firm found no indication that its current IT environment was compromised or that account information, login credentials or payment data were accessed. It said it has informed the relevant authorities, including the data protection authority.

Lawmakers led by Sen. Elizabeth Warren, a Massachusetts Democrat, and Rep. Robert Garcia, a California Democrat, in October introduced a bill that would require federal financial regulators to release records on Epstein and investigate banks and executives tied to him. The Wyden investigation concluded there was “significant evidence that JPMorgan $JPM Chase, Deutsche Bank, and Bank of America $BAC violated federal anti-money laundering laws by failing to screen and report Epstein’s suspicious financial transactions in a timely manner.”

Deutsche Bank has spent upward of $200 million on penalties and legal settlements connected to its Epstein dealings, without admitting wrongdoing, according to Bloomberg. Suspicious payments do not, on their own, establish that each transaction amounted to a crime, according to CNBC.

Deutsche Bank stock slid by upwards of 6% during the opening hours of trading Tuesday.

#5417. Lighter Halts Crypto Withdrawals After $15.5M Security Breach as LIT Falls

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Lighter has suspended crypto withdrawals after a suspected security breach drained $15.5 million from two market-maker accounts. Its LIT token fell more than 15% as traders assessed the damage.

The decentralized perpetual futures exchange halted withdrawals and new liquidity pool creation on November 16. The incident reportedly involved compromised API keys belonging to two market makers, rather than a vulnerability in Lighter’s core smart contracts.

Update: Our investigation indicates that today’s incident was caused by a leaked API key for a specific trader's account. The Lighter protocol and smart contracts are unaffected.As a precaution, we have enabled Guardian mode on our smart contract. Our main priority is to… https://t.co/LUuFiY5cK0

On-chain investigators identified a $10.39 million USDC withdrawal from Lighter’s Ethereum settlement contract. Another $5.09 million loss was reported from a second account, although investigators had not independently verified that amount leaving the platform.

The incident has raised fresh questions about security across decentralized derivatives platforms, particularly how exchanges protect large trading accounts and their liquidity infrastructure.

The suspected attacker reportedly gained access to API keys associated with two market-maker accounts. These credentials allegedly provided enough permissions to manipulate their trading positions and liquidity pool activity.

The reported losses were split between two accounts, with $10.39 million and $5.09 million in USDC taken from their respective balances. The alleged attack involved closing existing positions before creating a zero-fee liquidity pool under a compromised account. Attacker purchased nearly all its shares, transferred the victim’s funds into the pool, and redeemed those shares.

Bitquery independently tracked the first major withdrawal through Ethereum. The attacker converted $10.36 million in USDC into ETH within four minutes.

LIVE: tracking the Lighter hack walletAs of 11:36 UTC, 16 Nov:• 10.39M USDC out of @Lighter_xyz → 5,764 ETH• 10 payments of 160 ETH → Hyperliquid → 5,583 XMR1• 4,165 ETH still in the walletWe update as it moves:https://t.co/NZvBlmMEeP https://t.co/JcD3AOQ8Bs

The wallet received 5,764 ETH, subsequently distributing 960 ETH across six fresh wallets. Those wallets moved funds through Hyperliquid and purchased XMR1, while approximately 4,805 ETH remained in the original wallet during Bitquery’s investigation.

Lighter initially described this crypto incident as involving a compromised external party. It suspended withdrawals and new liquidity pool creation while investigating the breach.

The team subsequently clarified that its protocol and smart contracts were not compromised. Instead, the incident reportedly originated from a leaked API key belonging to a specific trader.

As of now, Lighter activated Guardian mode on its smart contracts and announced plans to upgrade its contracts through its Security Committee. The exchange also identified recovering funds associated with additional withdrawal attempts as a priority. Its stated target was completing the upgrade and restoring withdrawals by the end of November 16.

LIT traders now face another question: whether the exchange can restore withdrawals quickly enough to prevent a prolonged confidence crisis.

Lighter builds its derivatives ecosystem around Ethereum, while ASTER taps into BNB Chain and Hyperliquid operates its own blockchain. Bitcoin, meanwhile, still has considerable room to develop its decentralized derivatives infrastructure.

Bitcoin Hyper ($HYPER) is positioning its Layer 2 network around that opportunity, combining Bitcoin’s settlement infrastructure with Solana Virtual Machine (SVM) execution for faster transactions and lower fees.

The idea is to bring more sophisticated DeFi applications to Bitcoin, potentially including decentralized perpetual futures trading. Rather than relying exclusively on Ethereum-based liquidity or another standalone derivatives chain, the project aims to connect Bitcoin’s liquidity with high-speed execution.

Its presale has raised more than $33.2 million. The current advertised token price stands at $0.0136, with buyers offered a 35% annual percentage yield (APY) through its staking program.

The project also has a live testnet featuring a bridge, faucet, explorer, and wallet infrastructure. Its roadmap targets further development of its Bitcoin bridge and DeFi ecosystem.

November 26 is the presale closing date, putting the token’s next major launch milestone just days away. So, for those watching the next generation of decentralized derivatives, Bitcoin’s potential role in that market remains an interesting opportunity.

Bitcoin Hyper is betting that combining Bitcoin’s liquidity with Solana-style execution can help establish that missing infrastructure.

Lighter’s immediate challenge is restoring withdrawals and demonstrating that its security upgrades address the vulnerabilities exposed by the incident. The $15.5 million loss is big, but the bigger issue is whether users and market makers remain comfortable keeping capital on the platform.

The coming sessions could prove decisive as traders monitor withdrawal availability, recovery efforts, and further disclosures from the exchange.

#5416. 16 Robert Pattinson films, from Twilight to Bond-era blockbusters and art-house risks

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Sixteen Robert Pattinson films show a career split between franchises and director-driven risks, from Twilight to The Batman Part II.

Credit: Georges Biard / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 3.0)

Robert Pattinson did not build his career by climbing from small parts to big ones. He made big-studio films such as The Batman, Dune and Tenet in the same years as bleak, odd films such as The Lighthouse, Good Time and High Life. An actor who leaves teen-idol fame for art-house work risks losing his place in the franchise business, but Pattinson kept his. Amazon $AMZN MGM Studios has named him to replace Daniel Craig as 007, according to Parade, which puts him at the center of the James Bond franchise. His move away from his Twilight image led him back to the biggest kind of franchise role, not away from it. "He hasn't been defined by Edward Cullen," film critic Luke Goodsell told ABC News. The strange films were not a retreat from big-studio work. Pattinson made them alongside it, and viewers should see his films as two careers running at once.

Pattinson takes on Bond during the busiest stretch of his career. Dune: Part Three, The Odyssey, Primetime and The Drama all come out in 2026, according to ABC News. The Bond job adds a major franchise film to that crowded calendar without a fixed place on it, because the next Bond film has no title and no announced release date, according to CNBC. That leaves the order of his coming projects uncertain. Viewers no longer need to ask whether Pattinson can move between blockbusters and director-driven films. The open question is which kind of work his next few years will favor, and nothing announced so far answers it.

Wikipedia surveyed Pattinson's notable films across blockbusters, independent work and upcoming projects. Its entries include his brooding lighthouse keeper in The Lighthouse, his role in Christopher Nolan's film about reversing time, Tenet, Bong Joon Ho's satire Mickey 17 and The Take, a New York heist film with Denzel Washington. The franchise hits, the art-house gambles and the films still to come appear side by side, in the same mix in which Pattinson made them. Viewers who look at them together can see which choices kept him in the franchise business, which directors came back to work with him again, and which risks critics valued more than their scores suggest. The films he has yet to release show what his two-track career now has to balance.

Pattinson's unusual, director-driven choices all came after one defining part: Edward Cullen, the brooding vampire at the center of a teen romance. His fame built over a series of films rather than from a single hit. His role as Cullen in the Twilight films, released from 2008 to 2012, made him a worldwide star, according to Wikipedia. ABC News reports that he finished five films in the saga before he turned to independent work. His stardom and the role grew together over the same stretch until the public had trouble telling them apart. That closeness was the risk in his success. An actor who plays one part through a long series can become that part in the minds of the people watching.

The fame came with a forecast that his career would end when the series did. Pattinson and his Twilight co-star Kristen Stewart were "assumed, I think, to be doomed after that, and both of them went out and said, 'OK, we're going to revive our careers in different ways'," film critic Luke Goodsell told ABC News. Failure was the expected outcome for both actors, and each took a separate path away from it. His move away from franchises was not a fall from stardom. He made that move at a time when many people had already written him off.

He came out of the saga famous and widely expected to fade.

Pattinson's turn as Batman placed him in a gloomy crime story rather than a bright superhero spectacle. He plays Bruce Wayne in Matt Reeves' dark 2022 noir reboot of the character, according to Wikipedia. The tone matters for an actor known for bleak, odd films. In The Batman, his two tracks meet: the film carries the name of one of the best-known franchises, and its dark noir style matches the brooding work he made away from franchises.

Batman is no longer the only defining franchise role on his calendar. Pattinson is due back as Bruce Wayne, and USA Today reports that his newest casting makes him the eighth James Bond in the film series. He is now committed to two of cinema's best-known characters at the same time, so his Batman run is one half of a pair rather than the peak of his career. He spoke about the new job in the grandest terms. "James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime," Pattinson said.

Pattinson took on Bond before the Batman sequel existed as anything more than a planned release. The Batman Part II is set to reach theaters in 2028. His Bond casting became public on Nov. 16, 2026, according to USA Today. The two franchises now overlap in his future. Nobody can yet say whether the sequel will anchor his franchise career or get squeezed by the newer role.

For now, the 2022 film is the only finished chapter of his Batman.

Pattinson's first big break came inside a franchise that was already running at full scale, not in a new project built around him. He played Cedric Diggory in Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire, his early breakthrough in 2005, according to Wikipedia. Parade reports that the film was the fourth installment in the Harry Potter series. Pattinson joined a story whose world and audience were already in place, and he did not have to launch anything himself. His part still carried real weight in that story. Cedric is selected as a Triwizard Tournament champion, which puts Pattinson's character in the competition at the center of this installment rather than in the background. His first prominent credit was a franchise credit, and his career began on the blockbuster side well before he took on strange, director-driven films.

Pattinson made his Potter film under a producer who is also part of his Bond future. David Heyman, the producer behind Goblet of Fire, oversaw every one of the eight Harry Potter films, Parade reports, and he is among the producers of the coming Bond film. Pattinson's first franchise and his newest one share a key producer. He will work again with a man who has already guided one long series from its first film to its last. Pattinson acted in Heyman's 2005 film and will work with him again on the Bond film announced in November 2026. The connection spans every film Pattinson made in between.

The Potter credit is less a youthful footnote than the first film Pattinson made with a producer who is now behind his Bond film.

In Tenet, Pattinson works on one of Christopher Nolan's biggest productions as the hero's partner rather than the hero. He plays Neil in Nolan's 2020 science-fiction film about reversing time, according to Wikipedia, and The Associated Press reports that John David Washington leads the cast as The Protagonist. Pattinson is billed as a co-star, second in line on a spectacle that Nolan built around his own ideas about time. That matters for an actor whose career runs on two tracks, because it shows he did not wait for lead roles before taking on blockbuster work. He reached a Nolan event film through a supporting part, and he took it without needing his name at the top of the poster.

The second billing still placed Pattinson among the largest productions of his career. The film had a $200 million budget in 2020, according to The Associated Press, and it belongs with his major franchises and blockbusters rather than with his small, strange films for art-house directors. The filmmakers' record shows why a supporting role was worth taking. By 2020, audiences had spent nearly $4.8 billion over 20 years on films directed by Nolan and produced by Emma Thomas. For Pattinson, joining their cast in a secondary part still meant working at the top of the commercial film business, alongside people with a long record of hits.

Tenet showed that Pattinson could share the screen at the largest scale without having to carry the film himself.

Christopher Nolan has cast Pattinson twice, which makes The Odyssey a sign of a director's trust more than a star vehicle. Nolan had already worked with him on Tenet, where Pattinson played Neil. For The Odyssey, a separate film, Nolan cast him as Antinous, according to the Arizona Daily Star. That second casting is the reason the film stands among his notable credits. A director who had already worked with him wanted him back for an unrelated project, and repeat casting is the plainest sign that a working relationship held up.

Pattinson does not lead the film. Matt Damon plays Odysseus, the title character, according to the Arizona Daily Star, so the center of the story belongs to someone else and Pattinson's Antinous is a supporting part. He still stands out in the role. Bruce R. Miller, a reviewer for Lee Enterprises, singled him out as "the sharp, sly Robert Pattinson." The choice resembles his art-house work on a smaller scale, because he took a distinct supporting character over the largest share of the screen.

Miller's verdict on the film itself is strongly favorable. He gave The Odyssey 3½ stars and judged it worth its running time of about three hours, according to the Arizona Daily Star. In his view, the film covers a great deal of ground while keeping its focus, landing each moment quickly and then moving on. For a film of that length, his review suggests the hours do not drag.

For anyone following Pattinson, The Odyssey is worth seeing as proof that Nolan wanted him back, not as a measure of what he can carry alone.

Dune: Part Three puts Pattinson beside the director who will make the next James Bond film, and that pairing matters more than the trilogy the film completes. On its face, the film belongs to the franchise side of his career at full scale. Pattinson joined Denis Villeneuve's 2026 film, which closes the director's science-fiction trilogy, according to Wikipedia. CNBC reports that Villeneuve will also direct the next Bond film, the one Pattinson will lead as 007. Dune is the first of Pattinson's two Villeneuve projects and the one audiences will see first, while the Bond film still has no title and no announced release date.

Audiences will watch the film already knowing that its director and its star have a Bond film ahead of them. The Bond casting was announced Nov. 16, 2026, according to CNBC. Dune: Part Three is due in theaters Dec. 18, according to ABC News, so the Bond news reached the public first. Villeneuve openly welcomed the actor into the larger franchise. "He has the timeless soul of 007 and brings a spirit that is completely new," Villeneuve said. His praise carries more weight than a studio statement would, because he has already directed Pattinson on a film. The last chapter of a science-fiction saga is also the first big-screen result of a partnership whose next assignment is 007.

The Lighthouse is the clearest case of Pattinson betting on a film made to provoke viewers and winning their approval anyway. He won acclaim for his 2019 horror turn opposite Willem Dafoe, and the film is rated 7.3 out of 10, according to Wikipedia. Its early reception surprised the man who made it. Before the film's release in 2019, director Robert Eggers said he was shocked it had not divided audiences more, given how many bold and exaggerated choices went into its story and its filmmaking, according to CBC News. The extremity extended to the film's form. It is a psychological horror film shot in black and white, and Dafoe said at the time that the film had stayed with the people who saw it. The festival audiences Eggers described were receptive rather than split, even with those choices on screen. For an actor still shedding a heartthrob image, this was no safe detour.

The praise for Pattinson here belongs partly to the place where the film was made and to the actor he played against. The cast filmed at Cape Forchu in Yarmouth County, Nova Scotia, according to CBC News, so the isolation on screen is a real stretch of coastline rather than a studio set. In a psychological horror film, the actors took their tone from that coast. "The location really told us how things had to be played, what kind of story we were telling. It informed everything," Dafoe said in 2019. Pattinson worked in that same setting, which Dafoe credited with shaping how the cast played the story.

His boldest gambles have worked partly because of whom he chose to work with and where, not on nerve alone.

A few years after the vampire saga, Pattinson took a part with none of a heartthrob's shine. In Good Time, he played a desperate robber for the Safdie brothers in 2017, and the film carries a 7.3/10 rating, according to Wikipedia. The Chicago Sun-Times reports that the brothers' earlier features were Daddy Longlegs and Heaven Knows What. Both sides of the camera took a real risk, because a star with worldwide fame trusted his post-Twilight career to filmmakers with only a short list of features behind them. The gamble held up. A rating of 7.3 marks a film that people respected rather than one they adored.

Not every critic offered that respect when the film opened. Richard Roeper, a Chicago Sun-Times reviewer, gave Good Time 2.5 stars in 2017, according to the Chicago Sun-Times. His verdict was mixed rather than dismissive, and he found both strengths and faults in what the Safdies and their star had attempted.

Roeper's score is one critic's view from the year of release, and the film's 7.3 rating sits well above that welcome. Good Time has kept its place among Pattinson's notable work despite the cool reception from a major critic. Playing a man whom audiences might not like was the risk he chose to take, and he took it while he was still working to move past Twilight.

Here he showed he was willing to be disliked on screen, which asks something different of an actor than being liked in a franchise.

Pattinson took a part in The Lost City of Z that keeps him beside the story rather than at its center. He played Corporal Henry Costin, a British explorer, in James Gray's 2016 adventure, a film rated 6.6/10, according to Wikipedia. That rating points to a reception that was favorable but far from enthusiastic. In a 2017 feature, Smithsonian magazine reports that Costin serves as aide-de-camp to the expedition's leader, Percival Fawcett, and that Charlie Hunnam plays Fawcett. Gray, the film's writer and director, set out to tell a straightforward story about Fawcett. The film follows the leader, and Pattinson's corporal works at his side.

The supporting part came with a demanding shoot. The production spent eight weeks filming in Colombia, according to a Smithsonian magazine feature published in 2017, so the cast worked on location rather than on a soundstage. Gray made clear before the film's release that the production had faced real danger. "We escaped catastrophe on a few occasions," he told Smithsonian magazine. For viewers, that means the expedition on screen was filmed far from a studio, under conditions its director describes as dangerous at times.

The Lost City of Z belongs among Pattinson's notable films as a supporting role in a director's own project, made years before his biggest franchise parts. It gave him no franchise and no starring role. Viewers who come for Gray's account of Fawcett will find Pattinson as the explorer's aide, working in the background of someone else's story.

Cosmopolis is the strongest case that Pattinson's art-house choices cost him. His 2012 film with David Cronenberg carries a 5.1/10 rating, according to Wikipedia, a score barely above the middle of the scale. He plays a billionaire asset manager on a trip across Manhattan, CBC News reports, and nothing about the part resembles the teen romance that made him famous. Viewers still have to decide whether the film's craft earned that score or whether people reacted to how hard it is to watch.

Cronenberg built the film around talk. He adapted Don DeLillo's 2003 novel and took its dialogue from the book, according to CBC News, and long conversations take up most of the screen time that a thriller would give to action. He saw that choice as the film's main strength. "It's the dialogue first of all which carries everything...It's incredibly funny, incredibly profound, incredibly adept and very philosophical. I mean, you don't get that very often," Cronenberg told CBC News. Viewers who want plot are likely to find long philosophical exchanges hard going, and a film made this way tends to split its audience. Seen in that light, the low rating looks more like a divided response to a demanding film than proof that Cronenberg and Pattinson made a bad one.

Pattinson also took this risk in public. Cronenberg's film was first shown to anyone at the Cannes Film Festival, according to CBC News, so the gamble was on view from its first screening. Pattinson has said he was deeply frightened when filming began. That makes Cosmopolis the hardest case against the idea that the strange films did him no harm, because a film with such a modest rating is also one that unsettled him from the first day on set. Still, the rating shows how people received the gamble. It does not show that taking the gamble was a mistake.

Of all the risks Pattinson has taken, High Life makes the least effort to please, and that is why it belongs here. Wikipedia reports that he starred in Claire Denis' 2018 art-house space drama, a film rated 5.7/10. Stephanie Zacharek, a film critic at TIME, called it "brilliant if not exactly likable" in 2019. The middling score and her praise describe the same quality, because Denis made a film that is difficult on purpose. For a viewer, the 5.7 is a warning about how hard the film is to sit through, not a sign of weak craft. It does not make High Life a lesser entry in his art-house work.

The difficulty is built into the setup, which gives Pattinson almost no one to play against. In the opening scene, his character, Monte, repairs the ship and talks to an infant over a monitor, TIME reports, so he begins the film alone with a baby who cannot answer him. With no adult scene partner, the starring role rests on what he can show without words. In 2019, Zacharek found tenderness, suspicion and ruthlessness in his expressions alone. Plot and spectacle carry little of the weight in this film, and his face carries most of it. His franchise roles never asked that of him, since those parts surround him with action, dialogue and large casts.

For fans who came to Pattinson through The Batman, High Life is a test of whether they follow the actor or the franchise.

Bong Joon Ho uses science fiction in Mickey 17 to tell a satire about a worker whose life is treated as cheap. His 2025 film casts Pattinson as that disposable worker, according to Wikipedia. The Korea Times reports that the film is science fiction. That genre runs through much of Pattinson's big-studio work, including Dune and Tenet. In this film, a director with his own ambitions sets the terms instead of a studio series. Pattinson does not have to choose between the two sides of his career here. He works in the genre of his blockbusters for a filmmaker known for satire.

The character's disposability is both the film's joke and the hardest part of Pattinson's job. Mickey is an "expendable" worker, and in this story being expendable means being duplicated, so Pattinson has to play more than one version of the same man. Bong praised the way Pattinson handled the two versions, according to The Korea Times. That praise carries weight because the director who designed the challenge is the one judging the result. The part asks Pattinson to keep two versions of one character distinct on screen, and it tests his range more than his star presence.

Viewers who know him from Dune or Tenet will find the same genre in Mickey 17, put to a satirist's purpose and built around a role that asks more of the actor than of the star.

Pattinson's coming years are crowded with epics and franchises, yet he still made room for the kind of small, odd film that built his reputation for risk. In The Drama, a 2026 black comedy directed by Kristoffer Borgli, he stars opposite Zendaya, according to Wikipedia. ABC News reports that the independent studio A24 made the film and that Borgli earlier cast Nicolas Cage in Dream Scenario. That puts one of the biggest young stars around in a director's project rather than a spectacle, with a filmmaker who has built a film around an offbeat star before. It is the trade Pattinson keeps making: he goes where a demanding director wants a stranger version of him.

At the center of The Drama is a couple, not a world to save, and Luke Goodsell, a reviewer for ABC Arts, judges Pattinson's work in it the strongest of his career. Pattinson plays Charlie, a museum head curator, an ordinary professional in an intimate story. That makes it a rare character-driven part among the franchise films and director-led epics he has lined up next. Goodsell keeps the film's plot twist out of his review, so audiences can still come to the film without knowing it. The small films may show more of his acting than the big ones do.

Borgli is Norwegian, ABC News reports, and the film looks at America from the outside. Some viewers may find its handling of race and the U.S. clumsy, though Goodsell argues the clumsiness is deliberate, a portrait of a European misreading the country. The likely response is a split rather than a consensus, with some viewers seeing satire and others seeing carelessness.

That is the bargain of the second track. Pattinson accepts that a film like this may be judged a misstep in public, and that willingness has kept his franchise career from fixing him as one type.

Primetime is a Pattinson film that audiences know by its director's name, not by his character's. Pattinson appears in Lance Oppenheim's 2026 thriller, according to Wikipedia. That filmmaker, that genre and that year make up the whole public picture of the project for now. Before anyone knows whom he plays, they already know whose film it is and what kind of story it tells. This is the director-first side of his career in its plainest form. On the smaller, stranger half of his work, Pattinson has repeatedly signed on for a filmmaker's project, and the part has mattered less than the person making the film. Here that choice shows clearly, because the film's identity starts with Oppenheim, with no character or plot to point to.

Nothing about his character is on record yet. The film's entry lists no character name, co-stars, plot or release status for his part, so viewers have no way to weigh the role itself. Anyone curious about Primetime has only the pairing of actor and director to go on. Pattinson has asked for that kind of faith throughout his art-house work, and he asks for it here in its simplest version. Viewers who have followed him into odd, demanding films for years will recognize the request. They back the director now and find out about the role later.

The Take has not reached audiences yet, so the reason to watch for it is the people attached. Pattinson stars opposite Denzel Washington in the heist film, which Meirelles is directing in New York City for release in 2027, according to Wikipedia. He signed on for a director and a co-star before there was anything on screen to point to, and many of his other choices followed the same logic. The film is due after his already crowded 2026. For now, The Take is best read as a sign of the kind of work he intends to keep doing rather than as a finished entry in his career.

The Take fits neither of his two tracks neatly. It is not one of his giant franchise parts, and nothing known about it so far marks it as one of his bleak, strange gambles. It is a heist thriller, a mainstream genre meant to entertain, made under a director's name rather than a franchise's banner. That makes it a quieter test of how Pattinson divides his time. The question is whether a director-led genre film with no franchise behind it still has room on a schedule he now has to share with the Bond job.

Pattinson's next few years will show which side of his career The Take ends up on, and how much room he keeps for a film with no franchise behind it once he is 007.

Of all the films still ahead of Pattinson, his return as Batman is the one with both a year and a shoot behind it. The sequel is scheduled for 2028 and brings him back as the caped crusader, according to Wikipedia. CNBC reports that Pattinson is already in production on it, so this is a film being made, not a project waiting to begin. For now, Batman is the most secure part of the blockbuster side of his career and the big-studio role fans can most confidently expect to see him in next. The sequel also keeps him with the same filmmaker, because Matt Reeves, who directed the first film, is directing this one as well. Pattinson has a habit of working with directors who come back for him, and Reeves is one more of them.

Batman is no longer the only major franchise role in Pattinson's future. The Bond casting gives him a second famous character to carry alongside Bruce Wayne, and he speaks about the new part with open reverence. "James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime," Pattinson said, as reported by USA Today. The sequel remains scheduled for 2028, but his time now has to stretch across two franchise productions. How he will divide it between them has not been made public.

The Batman Part II will be one of the first tests of whether Pattinson can keep both franchise roles going without one pushing the other aside.

#5415. Exclusive: Envoy targets defense contractors and semiconductor fabs with Visitors Critical

Workplace management platform company Envoy Inc. today launched Visitors Critical, a new tier of its visitor management service for defense contractors, semiconductor fabs and other high-security sites.

The new tier is aimed at a problem Envoy says is common at those sites, where visitor security is still run across email, spreadsheets and separate systems and letting the wrong person in can be costly. Penalties, debarment or a lost facility clearance are all possible after a wrong entry at a compliance-driven site. The person who signed the authorization can also be held liable, according to the company, which noted that settlements under the International Traffic in Arms Regulations have reached $51 million.

“We’ve spent the last 13 years building Envoy to deliver the highest levels of security, safety and compliance in a way that feels natural to the people using it,” said founder and Chief Executive Larry Gadea, who worked as an engineer at Google LLC and Twitter Inc. before starting the company in 2013.

Visitors Critical scans a visitor’s government-issued ID and matches their face to the photo on it. Names are also screened against denied-party and export-control lists through Visual Compliance and Descartes MK, both from The Descartes Systems Group Inc. Contractor qualifications are checked through ISN Software Corp. From there, visits are sent for approval based on the organization’s own written policies. The approver’s reasoning is then kept on record in case of an audit.

Among Envoy’s existing customers is Attalon Inc., the former aerospace and defense business of Coherent Corp. Every visitor to all 12 of Attalon’s sites has their ID scanned by Envoy before being screened against denied-party lists. Tim Carr, Attalon’s director of security and environment, health and safety, said that an auditor who inspects one site “has effectively inspected them all.”

The launch comes as new Envoy research of 1,000 security leaders found that 62% of enterprise leaders are very confident they would pass a physical security audit without preparation. Some 63% of that group had a security incident in the past year. At sensitive workplaces, 44% of leaders could not say with confidence who was in their building the previous day.

Visitors Critical is available now. Hardware-based ID verification, which uses supported readers to authenticate the document itself and catch forged IDs, is being offered through an early access program.

Envoy claims more than 16,000 workplaces in 170 countries as customers, including 92 of the Fortune 500. The company launched Response, a threat intelligence and incident management product, in August. It raised $111 million in a Series C round in January 2022 at a $1.4 billion valuation.

#5414. Reconciling the OCC’s Final Stablecoin Reserve Floors Against the Fed’s Proposal

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

The OCC's final GENIUS Act rule sets a 5% cash floor and a 40% cap on any one counterparty. The Fed's open proposal uses neither figure, and its comment window runs until November 30.

Issuers now face two sets of reserve rules that share a redemption deadline and differ on almost everything else.

Ask a stablecoin issuer what its reserves must look like in 2027, and the honest answer is now: it depends which regulator you ask.

The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) gave its answer on October 21, the final rule implementing the GENIUS Act. Our October 19 piece on staggered agency filings expected that rule "before the end of October," and it came two days later. The rule sets specific numbers: at least 5% of reserves in demand deposits or similar instant-access funds, and no more than 40% of reserves with a single counterparty.

The Federal Reserve's answer is still a proposal. Its GENIUS Act rulemaking remains open for comment until November 30, and it contains neither of those numbers. Until the Fed finalizes its rule, any company planning to issue under both agencies' rules, or deciding which one to apply to, is working with one fixed set of numbers and one open-ended set of principles.

The OCC's final rule was published in the Federal Register on October 23 and takes effect on January 18, 2027, the same day as the GENIUS Act itself. Comptroller Jonathan V. Gould called it "a clear, practical framework for payment stablecoin innovation, with strong standards for reserve backing, redemption, and risk management."

The reserve rules are looser than the March proposal in several places:

The OCC also removed the rebuttable presumption that some affiliate yield arrangements break the GENIUS Act's ban on paying interest, though it kept its broader anti-evasion powers. The agency received about 328 comments.

For existing issuers, the timeline is short. Under OCC Bulletin 2026-51, firms already operating in the United States that file a "substantially complete" application by January 18 can generally expect a waiver of the prior-approval requirement.

The Fed released its two proposals on September 24. They were published in the Federal Register on September 29 under Docket No. R-1899, and comments are due November 30.

The main requirements proposal would require Board-supervised issuers to "fully back their stablecoins with certain permissible reserve assets". The reserves' fair value would have to equal or exceed the stablecoins' outstanding value at all times. Permissible assets include:

On diversification, however, the Fed sets no numbers. Reserves must be "sufficiently diverse" to keep one-to-one backing at all times, and issuers must manage concentration in uninsured deposits and repo counterparties. The Board says it generally expects reserves to be mostly Treasuries, but it sets no cash floor and no counterparty percentage.

Redemption is where the two agencies agree most closely. Both define timely redemption as no later than two business days after a request. The difference lies in what happens under stress.

The FDIC, in its own proposal, uses a third approach: issuers would report on their own when redemption requests exceed 10% of issuance within 24 hours.

The clearest conflict is not about how much cash an issuer must hold, but how each agency treats bank deposits.

Under the OCC rule, at least 5% of reserves must be held in demand deposits or similar balances. That is a direct requirement to hold bank money.

The Fed proposal has no deposit floor. Instead, it would charge 2% capital against reserves held as uninsured deposits at an insured bank, and the same charge applies to undercollateralized reverse repo. One agency requires a minimum amount in deposits, and the other makes issuers hold extra capital against the deposits they choose to keep.

Concentration works the same way. An issuer with 60% of its deposit reserves at one bank would breach the OCC's 40% cap, unless one of the custodian or government exemptions applies. Under the Fed's current text, that issuer would face only a judgment by its supervisor about whether it has managed concentration risk properly.

The rules for a reserve shortfall also differ:

The difference is largest on capital. The OCC sets an individualized capital requirement measured in GAAP tangible equity. It has a $5 million floor that now lasts for the issuer's whole life, plus an operational backstop equal to 12 months of total expenses, up to half of which can be funded with qualifying subordinated debt.

The Fed proposes a fixed formula. On top of the 2% charges on deposits and repo, it adds an operational-risk charge on outstanding issuance:

It also adds 25% of three-year average revenue from sources other than reserves, adjusted by a loss scalar.

For an issuer with $50 billion in circulation, the issuance charge alone works out to $850 million under the Fed's proposal, before the revenue add-on. The OCC rule has no comparable fixed figure. Its capital depends on the issuer's own risk profile, with the $5 million floor as the only set minimum.

For now, the OCC's figures are final and the Fed's are not. Issuers and banks that hold reserves can still argue for changes until the Fed's comment period closes on November 30, and the Fed has asked 277 questions.

The decisions that matter most are clear from the comparison above:

Both sets of rules apply from the same date, January 18, 2027. If the Fed's final rule keeps its current approach, the United States will begin regulating stablecoins with a common redemption deadline and two different reserve rulebooks, decided by which agency charters the issuer.

#5413. Tech Moves: Wizards of the Coasts names president; new execs at Skydance, Pulumi, Marchex and Syndio

Tech Moves covers notable hires, promotions and personnel changes in the Pacific NW tech community. Submissions: [email protected]

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 11, 2026 at 10:24 amNovember 11, 2026 at 11:04 am

— Dan Ayoub, the past head of Dungeons & Dragons, has been named president of Wizards of the Coast & Hasbro Digital Games. Ayoub joined the Renton, Wash.-based Wizards of the Coast in 2022 and counts himself among the longtime players of D&D and Magic: The Gathering.

“D&D is 52 years old. Magic is 33. Brands don’t last that long because of any one leader; they last because generations of creators and fans keep choosing them,” Ayoub said. “We owe it to them to protect what makes these worlds special.”

Earlier in his career, Ayoub spent more than a decade at Microsoft, primarily with its 343 Industries video game studio, now called Halo Studios.

— Farah Ali has joined the media company Skydance as vice president of engineering, based at its Bellevue, Wash., office. She previously spent a decade at Electronic Arts over two stints, most recently as vice president of AI transformation and technology.

Ali has also served as an affiliate professor at the University of Washington, teaching courses in software entrepreneurship, and as a technical advisor for Madrona Venture Labs. She was co-founder and chief technology officer of FreightWeb, a Seattle-based logistics technology startup.

Paramount Skydance last month completed its acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery (WBD), with the combined company taking the name Skydance. Shortly after, the company announced the departure of two WBD leaders from the Bellevue site: Avi Saxena and Tyler Whitworth.

— Irene Chang has joined Pulumi as chief revenue officer. The Seattle startup automates cloud infrastructure tasks such as managing networks and databases, optimizing costs and ensuring compliance.

Chang said Pulumi’s culture and product won her over. “We automate deployments so teams can provision resources in seconds and scale from simple apps to enterprise architectures without losing control or compliance,” she wrote on LinkedIn.

Chang was previously Postman’s VP of corporate sales for the Americas and before that held VP roles at Cloudflare.

Pulumi is No. 15 on the GeekWire 200, a ranked index of the Pacific Northwest’s top startups.

— Marchex, the Seattle-based, publicly traded call and conversation analytics company, has named Travis Fairchild as president. The news was disclosed in an SEC filing. Fairchild was previously with Marchex for 18 years in strategy and business development roles.

He left in 2021 to become CEO of Archenia, a Las Vegas-based customer qualification and acquisition company, which Marchex acquired in July.

Troy Hartless, who in September 2025 added president to his role as chief revenue officer, will return to serving solely as CRO.

— General Fusion has named David Janashvili as chief financial officer, effective Nov. 30. The Vancouver, B.C.-based company is developing fusion energy devices and became the first fusion venture to go public, through a SPAC. It trades on Nasdaq as GFUZ.

Janashvili joins from Surami Partners, which provides financial services for clean tech companies, and previously led climate tech investment banking at CIBC Capital Markets. Across numerous roles, he has advised boards and management teams of public and soon-to-be public companies.

— Gravity Payments has appointed CEO Tammi Kroll as chairman of its board of directors while she continues to lead the digital payments company.

“Her appointment as Chairman recognizes more than a decade of leadership at Gravity and her role in helping the company grow while remaining focused on the independent businesses and employees it serves,” the company said.

Kroll joined the company in 2015 as CTO, chief operating officer and chief information officer. She took over as CEO in 2022 after founder Dan Price resigned while facing assault and reckless driving charges. That case and a second were dropped, and Price maintained his innocence.

— Syndio, a Seattle-based pay equity startup, has two more leadership changes following the addition of seven new executives in April:

Syndio is No. 45 on the GeekWire 200, a ranked index of the Pacific Northwest’s top startups.

— Seattle-based real estate brokerage Redfin has named Andy Swanton as general manager of rentals. He returns to the company after a short stint in 2022 as VP of properties. Swanton has also worked for Opendoor and BYD.

— Seattle cybersecurity company ExtraHop has appointed Rupert Clayson as head of sales for Europe, the Middle East and Africa (EMEA). The company reports growth in sectors including financial services and energy, and offers defense against AI-assisted security attacks. Clayson, who is based in London, joined from TeamViewer and was previously with Fortinet.

— POSaBIT Systems, a Seattle-based company providing point-of-sale and payments technology for the cannabis industry, has named Emily Eagon as CFO. Eagon joined POSaBIT last year as vice president of finance and has more than 25 years of experience in finance and accounting roles, including leadership at Verdigris and predictis.

— Benjamin Mullins has returned to Amazon as head of program management for the Devices Brand Studio. Mullins spent four years with Prime until 2019, when he left for a role at Oracle. He then joined Meta, where he was head of product for Reality Labs.

— Debra Bouchegnies has announced she is retiring from the University of Washington’s CoMotion Labs at the end of the year. Bouchegnies is CoMotion’s associate director of marketing and has been with the program since 2018. A replacement has not been named.

— Aman Dhingra has been appointed to the Technology Alliance board of directors. Dhingra has been with McKinsey & Co. for 17 years and serves as a partner.
