#5412. Can bank deposits be affected in a cyberattack? 10 things to know

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Bank deposits can be affected in a cyberattack through blocked access, data breaches or account takeover, and FDIC insurance and Regulation E protect money in different ways.

A cyberattack on a bank and a theft from one customer's account are separate events, and U.S. rules treat them differently. The first targets the institution's systems. The second targets a specific balance, and it is the more direct path from a hacker to a depositor's money.

So can bank deposits be affected in a cyberattack? The answer depends on the kind of attack. Banks record balances in ledgers and keep backups. An attack on their systems does not by itself erase what customers hold. Ransomware or a distributed denial-of-service attack can still lock people out of online banking and apps for a time. A data breach can expose names, account numbers or Social Security numbers. That exposure does not move money on its own. It does give criminals material for later fraud.

Protection also depends on details that are easy to overlook. Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation coverage applies when an insured bank fails. It covers up to $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, per ownership category. It is not built to repay money a criminal takes from an account at a bank that stays open. Credit unions carry comparable coverage through the National Credit Union Share Insurance Fund, run by the National Credit Union Administration. The standard limit is the same $250,000.

Recourse for theft comes from elsewhere. Regulation E, which implements the Electronic Fund Transfer Act, limits consumer liability for unauthorized electronic transfers. How much a customer can lose depends partly on how quickly the problem is reported. Credit cards fall under a separate federal law, the Fair Credit Billing Act. Business accounts generally sit outside Regulation E. They rely largely on the Uniform Commercial Code and the account agreement.

Scams add another layer. When a criminal tricks a customer into sending money, the payment is generally not treated as an unauthorized transfer under Regulation E. That distinction can shape what a bank is required to do.

The 10 slides that follow cover ways cyberattacks and fraud can reach a deposit account, along with the protections that apply to each. They run from insurance limits and reporting deadlines to account takeover, ransomware and data breaches. The last slide covers everyday habits, such as transaction alerts and stronger login security. Those habits help catch fraud early and make stolen credentials harder to use.

A cyberattack on a bank's own systems does not, by itself, wipe out the balance recorded in a customer's account. The larger risk to an individual depositor is a criminal getting into a specific account and moving money out of it.

A bank hack and a theft from one person's checking account can sound like the same event. They work through different mechanisms and lead to different remedies. Knowing which one happened determines how a deposit was exposed and which protections apply.

A deposit balance is a record. It is the bank's accounting of what it owes a customer. Banks keep that record in ledgers and back it up. When a bank's computer systems go down, the obligation does not disappear. The money a customer deposited is still owed, even if the screen showing it is temporarily unavailable.

Cyberattacks reach depositors along three broad paths. The first is disruption. An attack can knock out online banking, mobile apps or transfers for a period. Customers may not be able to see or move their money while systems are restored. Losing access for a time is not the same as losing the balance.

The second path is data exposure. A breach hands criminals personal and account details, but stolen data does not move money on its own. What it provides is material for later impersonation or for opening accounts in a customer's name.

The third path is account access. This is where deposits are most directly at risk. A criminal with working login credentials can start transfers that pull real funds out of a real account. Unlike the other two paths, this one can reduce a balance directly.

Each path calls for a different response. Disruption mostly means waiting until service returns. Data exposure calls for watching for follow-on fraud. Unauthorized access calls for contacting the bank as soon as the activity is spotted.

Which rules apply after a loss depends on what happened. The answer turns on whether the institution failed and whether the transfer was authorized. It also turns on whether the account is a consumer or business account, and how quickly the problem was reported.

FDIC insurance protects deposits up to $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, per ownership category. It pays out when an insured bank fails. A hack affects this coverage only if the bank itself fails.

The Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation is an independent agency of the U.S. government. Congress created it through the Banking Act of 1933, after a wave of bank failures in the early 1930s. Its insurance is backed by the full faith and credit of the U.S. government. Coverage is automatic. A depositor does not need to apply for it or buy a policy.

The trigger is the failure of the institution, not the cause of the trouble. A bank could close because of bad loans, a run on deposits or, in theory, damage tied to a cyberattack. In each case the insured amount is the same. The FDIC generally either arranges for a healthy bank to take over the failed bank's deposits or pays insured depositors directly.

Ownership category sets the effective ceiling. The FDIC separates accounts by how they are owned. Common categories include single accounts, joint accounts, certain retirement accounts such as individual retirement accounts, trust accounts and business accounts. Each ownership category at the same bank carries its own $250,000 limit. A person with a single account and a share of a joint account at one bank can be insured for more than $250,000 in total.

The coverage applies to deposit products. Those include checking accounts, savings accounts, money market deposit accounts and certificates of deposit. It does not extend to stocks, bonds, mutual funds, annuities, crypto assets or life insurance policies. That holds even when those products are sold through an insured bank. The contents of a safe deposit box are not covered either.

Credit unions use a parallel system. The National Credit Union Administration insures member deposits through the National Credit Union Share Insurance Fund. Its standard limit is also $250,000. As with the FDIC, the fund pays out when an insured credit union fails.

A depositor can confirm whether a bank is insured through the FDIC's BankFind tool. The NCUA offers a similar search for federally insured credit unions.

FDIC insurance pays depositors when an insured bank fails, not when a criminal takes money from an account at a bank that stays open. If a fraudster drains a checking account at a healthy bank, deposit insurance is not the tool that restores those funds.

Deposit insurance has a single trigger: the failure of an insured institution. When a bank fails, the FDIC steps in so insured depositors can reach their money. An account emptied by a hacker does not meet that condition. The bank is still solvent and still operating.

Credit unions work the same way. The National Credit Union Administration insures member deposits through the National Credit Union Share Insurance Fund. That fund also responds to the failure of an insured credit union. It does not reimburse a member whose savings a criminal moved out of an account at a credit union that remains open.

The two situations raise different questions. A bank failure asks whether an institution can meet its obligations to all of its depositors at once. Theft from one account asks who bears the loss, the customer or the bank. Deposit insurance was designed to answer the first question, not the second.

For theft, recourse comes from three other places. The first is the bank's own obligations to its customer. The second is federal law on electronic payments. Regulation E, which implements the Electronic Fund Transfer Act, sets rules for unauthorized electronic transfers on consumer accounts. The third is the account agreement, the contract a customer accepts when opening the account. It spells out how disputes, errors and security responsibilities are handled.

A balance well under the insurance limit can still be stolen. The size of a deposit says little about protection from fraud. What shapes the outcome after a theft is the type of account, the type of payment and how fast the customer tells the bank.

Regulation E, which implements the federal Electronic Fund Transfer Act, limits how much a consumer can lose when someone moves money out of an account without permission. The rule sets liability in tiers, and each tier is tied to a reporting deadline.

The rule applies to electronic fund transfers on consumer accounts. These are accounts held by individuals for personal, family or household purposes. Debit card purchases, ATM withdrawals and online transfers out of a checking or savings account all fall within its scope.

An unauthorized transfer is one started by someone without the account holder's permission. The account holder also receives no benefit from it. A thief using a stolen debit card fits that definition. So does a criminal who logs in with stolen credentials and sends money elsewhere.

The first liability tier is the narrowest. It applies when a debit card or other access device is lost or stolen. If the consumer tells the bank within two business days of learning about it, liability is capped at $50. If the unauthorized transfers before that notice total less than $50, the consumer owes only the smaller amount.

Waiting longer raises the ceiling. Reporting after the two-business-day mark can push the consumer's liability up to as much as $500. The clock starts when the consumer learns of the loss or theft, not on the day the card went missing.

These figures are legal maximums, not amounts a consumer automatically owes. Bank or card network policies can be more generous than Regulation E requires. The account agreement spells out which terms apply to a given account.

Regulation E also requires banks to investigate errors that consumers report. Unauthorized transfers count as errors under the rule. A prompt, specific report gives the bank what it needs to begin that review.

The protections have limits on who they reach. Business accounts are generally not covered by Regulation E. Disputes over unauthorized transfers on those accounts are governed largely by the Uniform Commercial Code and by the terms of the account agreement. A company and an individual customer at the same bank can face different rules for the same type of fraud.

A consumer who misses the 60-day deadline to report an unauthorized electronic transfer can face larger losses on later transfers. Under Regulation E, the clock starts when the bank sends the statement that shows the problem.

This deadline is separate from the rules about a lost or stolen card. It does not depend on the customer knowing that a card is missing. It turns on what appears on the periodic statement, whether that statement arrives on paper or electronically. Once the bank transmits a statement showing an unauthorized transfer, the consumer has 60 days to flag it.

The rule carries the most weight when nothing physical goes missing. A criminal can copy card details at a compromised terminal, steal an account number in a data breach or log in with stolen credentials. The customer may still hold the debit card and have no reason to suspect anything. The statement then becomes the first record of the theft.

The larger exposure applies to transfers that happen after the 60-day period ends and before the consumer reports. For those later transfers, the consumer can be held responsible. To hold the consumer liable, the bank must show that the transfers would not have occurred if the consumer had reported in time.

The logic is about prevention. A thief who goes unnoticed for months can keep moving money out of an account. Regulation E places part of the cost of that delay on an account holder who had a statement in hand and did not act on it.

The regulation allows the time limit to be extended for extenuating circumstances. It names extended travel and hospitalization as examples. In those situations, the bank must extend the period to a reasonable time.

The window covers electronic activity on consumer accounts. That includes debit card purchases, ATM withdrawals, online bill payments and electronic transfers between accounts.

Reviewing every statement, or the transaction history in a banking app, keeps the deadline from coming into play. Contacting the bank by phone or in writing as soon as an unfamiliar transaction appears gives the bank notice. Notice ends the consumer's exposure to further losses under this rule. Keeping a record of the date, the person contacted and what was said creates evidence of when that notice was given.

Federal law caps a consumer's liability for unauthorized credit card charges at $50. Fraudulent credit card charges also draw on the card issuer's credit line, not on money sitting in a bank deposit account.

That difference matters most for anyone worried about their deposits. A stolen credit card number gives a criminal access to borrowed money. The charges show up as a balance owed to the issuer. The cash in the cardholder's checking or savings account stays where it is.

The $50 cap comes from the Fair Credit Billing Act. The Federal Trade Commission and the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau both describe that limit in their consumer guidance. Card networks and issuers can also set policies that are more generous than the legal minimum.

Debit cards work differently. A debit card is tied directly to a checking account. When a criminal uses a stolen debit card number, the money leaves the customer's own account. The customer then has to dispute the charges to recover those funds.

That difference has practical consequences. While a debit dispute is being resolved, the money is missing from the account. A lower balance can cause other payments, such as rent, bills or automatic transfers, to be declined. Depending on the account's terms, it can also trigger overdraft fees.

Debit card disputes fall under Regulation E, which implements the Electronic Fund Transfer Act. Under that rule, the customer's share of a loss depends on how quickly the problem is reported. The credit card cap under the Fair Credit Billing Act does not rise in tiers based on reporting speed.

For online shopping and other card-not-present purchases, the type of card determines where the exposure sits. A stolen credit card number puts the issuer's credit line at risk. A stolen debit card number puts the cardholder's own deposits at risk.

Both protections still depend on the cardholder. Unauthorized charges have to be spotted and reported to the bank or card issuer.

Account takeover happens when a criminal gains working login access to someone's online banking and then moves money out as if they were the customer. The attack usually starts with stolen credentials, gathered through phishing, reused passwords or malware on the victim's device.

Phishing is the most direct route. A message poses as the bank, a delivery company or a payment app. It sends the target to a fake login page. Whatever the person types there goes straight to the attacker.

Reused passwords open a second door. When one website leaks its login data, criminals try the same email and password combinations on banking sites. This tactic is known as credential stuffing. It works only when a customer has used the same password in more than one place.

Malware takes a quieter path. Keyloggers record what a user types. Some banking trojans can capture login details or display fake screens inside a real session. The customer may see nothing unusual while the software collects what the attacker needs.

Once inside, the criminal tends to act fast. Common moves include adding a new payee, changing the contact email or phone number on file and sending transfers to accounts the attacker controls. Changing contact details can divert alerts and verification codes away from the real account holder. That buys the attacker time to move money before anyone notices.

On a consumer account, a transfer started by a criminal who logged in without the customer's permission is generally an unauthorized electronic transfer under Regulation E. The customer did not initiate the payment and did not agree to it.

A different scam can look similar on a bank statement but is treated differently. In an authorized push payment scam, the criminal never takes over the account. The customer is persuaded to send the money personally. The person doing the persuading often poses as a bank employee, a government official or a romantic partner.

Because the customer initiated the transfer, these payments are generally not treated as unauthorized under Regulation E. The central question after a loss is who actually started the transfer — the account holder or someone who broke into the account.

Ransomware or a distributed denial-of-service attack can shut off online banking, mobile apps or transfers for a time. Losing access is not the same as losing money. A disruption alone does not erase the balances a bank has recorded.

The two attacks work differently. Ransomware is malicious software that encrypts a target's files and systems, locking the owner out of them. The criminals behind it typically demand payment for a decryption key. A distributed denial-of-service attack, usually shortened to DDoS, does not break into systems at all. It floods a website or app with so much traffic from many sources that legitimate customers cannot get through.

For a depositor, the visible effect of either attack can look similar. A login page may fail to load. A banking app may show errors. Transfers, bill payments or card transactions that depend on the affected systems may stall until service returns.

The records behind those screens determine what each customer owns. Banks keep ledger records of every account and maintain backups of that data. Those records define how much money each customer holds. An outage on the customer-facing side interrupts the ability to view or move funds. It does not rewrite the underlying account history.

Ransomware can be the more disruptive of the two for a bank's operations. It can lock internal systems rather than just block the front door. Recovery can take longer as a result. Backups can let a bank rebuild its systems without relying on the attackers for a key. A DDoS attack usually subsides once the traffic stops or is filtered out.

The practical risk for customers during an outage is timing. A payment due on a specific date may not go through while systems are down. Knowing which bills are coming up, and having another way to pay them, reduces that exposure.

An outage can also become a lure for scammers. Messages claiming to come from the affected bank may ask customers to confirm account details or log in through a link. Contacting the bank through a phone number or website already known to be genuine avoids that trap.

A data breach at a bank exposes information, not money. The stolen records do not move a single dollar on their own. The danger to deposits comes later, when criminals use that data to commit other kinds of fraud.

A breach happens when an outsider gains access to records a bank holds about its customers. The exposed material can include contact details, account numbers and government identifiers. None of this changes the balance recorded in a customer's account. What changes is how much a criminal knows about that customer.

That knowledge makes phishing more convincing. A fraudulent email, text or phone call that cites a real account number or a correct home address looks far more legitimate than a generic message. The goal is usually to get the customer to reveal a password, a one-time code or a card number. Each of those can then open a path into the account itself.

SIM swapping is another follow-on risk. In a SIM swap, a criminal persuades a mobile carrier to move the victim's phone number to a SIM card the criminal controls. Personal details taken in a breach can help the criminal pass the carrier's identity checks. Once the number moves, text messages meant for the victim go to the criminal. That includes the security codes many banks send by text.

New account fraud uses exposed data in a different way. The criminal does not break into an existing account. The criminal opens a new one in the victim's name instead. A Social Security number combined with a name and birth date can be enough to apply for credit. The victim may not learn of it until a debt collector calls or a credit report shows an unfamiliar account.

A credit freeze is the response most specific to this risk. A freeze restricts access to a person's credit report. That makes it much harder for a criminal to get new credit approved in that person's name. A U.S. consumer places it separately with each of the three nationwide credit bureaus: Equifax, Experian and TransUnion. A freeze does not affect existing accounts or the credit score. It also does not stop fraud on a deposit account whose details a criminal already holds.

Timing is part of the risk. Stolen data can be sold, traded or reused. Fraud tied to a breach can therefore surface long after the incident itself. A breach notice signals a higher chance of suspicious contact, not a loss that has already happened.

Four habits do much of the work of protecting money in a bank account. They are real-time transaction alerts, unique passwords, phishing-resistant multi-factor authentication and reporting problems to the bank right away.

Transaction alerts are an early-warning system that many banks and credit unions offer. Customers can often set notifications for any withdrawal, any transfer above a chosen amount, a new payee, a password change or a login from an unfamiliar device. Alerts arrive by text, email or push notification from the bank's app. Their value is speed. A customer who sees an unexpected transfer within minutes can contact the bank while the problem is still small.

Alerts work alongside a regular look at the account itself. Checking recent activity in the app every few days can catch small test charges. Fraudsters sometimes use these to confirm that a stolen card or login works before trying a larger withdrawal.

Reused passwords are a common way into accounts. When one website is breached, criminals try the same email and password combination on other sites. This technique is called credential stuffing. A password used only for the bank account means a leak somewhere else cannot unlock it.

A password manager makes unique passwords practical. It generates long random passwords, stores them in an encrypted vault and fills them in automatically. Many password managers autofill only on the exact website where a password was saved. That behavior can help expose a lookalike phishing page.

Multi-factor authentication adds a second check beyond the password, but the methods differ in strength. Codes sent by text message can be intercepted if a criminal gets a mobile carrier to move the victim's phone number to a new SIM card. Authenticator apps generate codes on the device itself, so a hijacked phone number does not expose them.

Passkeys go further. A passkey is a cryptographic credential linked to one specific website and stored on the user's own devices. It cannot be typed into a fake site. That design makes it resistant to phishing. Where a bank offers passkeys or an authenticator app, those options are stronger than SMS codes.

Reporting a problem is safest through a trusted channel. The phone number on the back of a debit card or on the bank's official website is the reliable choice. Calling a number from an unexpected text or email risks reaching a scammer instead of the bank. Writing down dates, the names of staff spoken to and any case numbers creates a record if the dispute takes time.

If a bank does not resolve a problem, consumers can file a complaint with the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau. The agency forwards complaints to the company involved and asks it to respond.

#5411. AWS gives developers a free local stand-in for its cloud, built from scratch by AI agents

by Todd Bishop on Nov 11, 2026 at 10:51 amNovember 11, 2026 at 10:51 am

AWS says its engineers didn’t write or review a single line of code in its newest developer tool, and the company is touting that as a selling point.

AWS Emulator, released Wednesday, simulates AWS services on a developer’s own machine. It’s built from more than 400 API models covering more than 200 AWS services. Developers and AI coding agents can use it to test code without a network connection and without paying for the real cloud.

The tool addresses a problem that coding agents such as Amazon’s Kiro and Anthropic’s Claude Code have made worse. Agents can write code faster than teams can test it against the real cloud. Agents check their work by running the code and reading the results, over and over, and doing that in the cloud adds delays and costs.

The emulator lets them run that loop on a developer’s own machine.

In an ironic or perhaps appropriate twist, AWS used AI agents to build the emulator. Agents also maintain it, testing it against real AWS and fixing the gaps they find.

“The emulator was written entirely by autonomous agents. Our team hasn’t written or reviewed any of the code,” wrote Matt Goldberg, the AWS senior principal engineer behind the project, in a blog post.

Goldberg compared his agents to himself as a kindergartner, too young to hold a crayon properly, who got yelled at by classmates for ruining a group drawing of dinosaurs. The problem wasn’t bad intent, he wrote, just a lack of competence. The answer, for agents, is clearly defined areas to fill in.

“I think agents also need coloring books,” he wrote.

The agents work from AWS’s public API models, which describe how each service should behave, and check their work against the real AWS cloud.

The agents run on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore in three teams. One writes “fidelity tests” — real-world scenarios such as creating a queue, sending a message and deleting the queue — and checks each against real AWS. A second runs those tests against the emulator and files issues for failures, and a third fixes them, one agent per issue.

Every change passes through an automated gate where other agents check coding standards and security. Goldberg wrote that hundreds of agents now fix thousands of issues a day.

The project started as a weekend experiment, inspired by Anthropic’s demonstration earlier this year in which a team of Claude agents built a C compiler. Goldberg gave Kiro a three-step prompt and got a passable first version of Amazon SQS, AWS’s message queuing service, in 15 minutes.

By the end of the weekend, Goldberg wrote, Kiro had built a rough version of the rest of AWS, with obvious gaps, and his team started using it to test its software that Monday.

Swami Sivasubramanian, AWS vice president of agentic AI and emerging tech, tied the project to a lesson he described to GeekWire in June. He spent four nights babysitting Kiro as it tried to rebuild a replication engine he and Allan Vermeulen built by hand nearly 20 years ago.

Once he gave the agent a spec and a way to test its work, the job took about two hours.

“When agents write the code and check their own work, the engineer’s job is to give them room to work on their own and to build the specs, tests, and merge gates that decide when that work is correct,” Sivasubramanian wrote in a guest post on CTO Werner Vogels’ blog.

It’s the same idea behind Amazon’s recent move to rewrite its engineering playbook for an era when AI writes the code.

The emulator has limits. Devin Pratt, an IDC analyst, told InfoWorld that it doesn’t yet simulate throttling, outages or differences in which services and features are available by region, and that it doesn’t sandbox the code it runs. The agents’ backlog of known gaps is public, in a GitHub folder called “things-that-do-not-work.”

Other AWS emulators exist, most notably LocalStack, which this year put its free version behind an account requirement and limited it to noncommercial use. AWS released its emulator for free under CC0, a public domain dedication, with the full commit history on GitHub.

The company says it will share more at its upcoming re:Invent conference.

If AI can’t understand the business context trapped inside legacy systems, moving them to the cloud just moves the problem. See how Thoughtworks and AWS combine AI/works™ with AWS Transform to modernize for the AI era.

#5410. Can the internet go down? 10 facts on how it breaks and why it holds together

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Can the internet go down? These 10 slides, from undersea cable cuts to routing errors, explain how outages happen and why the whole network rarely fails

The internet has no off switch. It is a collection of many independently run networks that agree to pass traffic to one another using shared rules. That design shapes the answer to a question people tend to ask after a major outage: can the internet go down?

The short answer is yes, in pieces. Parts of the internet fail regularly. A single website can vanish for an afternoon. A popular app can stop loading across a continent. A whole country can lose access when its government orders providers to cut service. The other kind of failure has never been recorded: a total, simultaneous shutdown of the internet worldwide. The gap between those two outcomes — a local or service outage versus a global collapse — is the thread running through this list.

The weak points sit at several layers. Some are physical, such as fiber-optic cables on the seabed and the electricity that powers data centers, cell towers and home routers. Others are logical. Routing systems tell networks where to send traffic, and the Domain Name System turns web addresses into the numbers computers use. A mistake in either can make working services unreachable.

Then there are deliberate disruptions. Attackers can flood a target with junk traffic until it stops responding. Governments can cut or slow national access. Concentration adds its own risk. Many unrelated websites rely on the same few content delivery and cloud providers. One fault at such a provider can take them offline together. The sun adds another variable. A strong solar storm raises open questions about long-distance power lines and other equipment.

The 10 slides that follow start with how the internet is built, then work through the failure points one at a time. Each one includes documented examples where they exist. The final slide explains the redundancy that usually keeps a failure contained. For businesses that depend on constant connectivity, these mechanisms show why an outage at one provider can halt logins or payments while the rest of the internet keeps running. For everyday users, they show why a site can be down for some people and working for others.

No single company, government or machine runs the internet. It is made up of separately managed networks that connect by following common technical standards, and control is spread across all of them.

Each of those networks is called an autonomous system. One might belong to a broadband provider, a mobile carrier, a university, a cloud company or a large corporation. Each operator runs its own equipment and decides how traffic moves inside its own network.

The common standards are protocols. The Internet Protocol gives every connected device an address. The Transmission Control Protocol helps data arrive complete and in the right order. Any network that follows these rules can exchange traffic with any other network that does the same.

Autonomous systems are identified by numbers. Five regional internet registries hand out those numbers, along with blocks of IP addresses: ARIN, RIPE NCC, APNIC, LACNIC and AFRINIC. The registries coordinate addressing. They do not carry traffic or control what flows across the networks they register.

The design traces back to packet-switching research in the 1960s. Paul Baran at the RAND Corporation in the U.S. and Donald Davies at the National Physical Laboratory in the U.K. developed the idea independently. A traditional phone call held open one dedicated circuit between two points. Packet switching instead breaks data into small chunks.

Each packet carries its own addressing information. It can travel separately and be reassembled at the destination. Packets from the same email or video stream do not have to follow the same path. If one route is congested or broken, traffic can move along another.

The ARPANET project, funded by the U.S. Defense Department's Advanced Research Projects Agency, put these ideas into practice. It began operating in 1969, first connecting computers at the University of California, Los Angeles and the Stanford Research Institute. ARPANET switched its hosts to TCP/IP on Jan. 1, 1983. Those protocols still underpin the internet.

That layout explains the pattern of most outages. No one network is the internet. A fault tends to stay with the provider, service or region where it started, while traffic elsewhere keeps flowing. Partial failures of this kind happen often. A complete, simultaneous worldwide shutdown has never been recorded.

A single incorrect Border Gateway Protocol announcement can redirect or drop traffic meant for networks that had nothing to do with the mistake. A fault inside one company's network can make a major service unreachable for users far beyond that company's own customers.

BGP is the system that independent networks use to tell each other which blocks of IP addresses they can reach. Each network announces the address ranges it handles. Its neighbors pass those announcements on to their own neighbors. Over time, every participating router builds a picture of which path leads to which destination.

The weakness lies in trust. BGP was first specified in 1989, when far fewer networks used it. The protocol has no built-in way to confirm that a network announcing a set of addresses is entitled to them. A router generally accepts what its neighbors tell it and passes it along.

Routers also prefer the most specific route available. If one network announces a large address block and another announces a narrower slice inside it, traffic for that slice follows the narrower announcement. That rule keeps routing precise. It also lets a bad announcement override a legitimate one.

A well-documented example came in 2008, when Pakistan Telecom tried to block YouTube inside Pakistan. It did this by announcing a route for part of YouTube's address space, intending to send domestic requests nowhere. The announcement leaked to its upstream provider, which passed it to the wider internet.

The false route was more specific than YouTube's own. Many networks around the world followed it as a result. YouTube became unreachable for many users outside Pakistan for a time, until the false route was withdrawn and filtered out.

Network operators now use route filtering and Resource Public Key Infrastructure, known as RPKI, to reduce these risks. RPKI lets address holders publish signed records stating which networks may originate their addresses. Other networks can then reject announcements that do not match those records.

Adoption of these safeguards is voluntary and uneven across networks. A misconfigured announcement can still spread before anyone catches it.

Undersea cables carry most international internet traffic between countries and continents. When one is cut on the seabed, connections across a whole region can slow down or drop out until a repair ship fixes it.

These cables are fiber-optic lines. They carry data as pulses of light through thin strands of glass wrapped in protective layers. Specialized ships lay them along surveyed routes on the ocean floor. Each cable ends at a coastal landing station, where it connects to networks on land.

Most damage is accidental. A ship dragging its anchor can snag a cable in shallow water. Bottom trawling and other fishing activity can catch and break one in the same way. Cables near the shore are often armored or buried for this reason. In deep water, they usually rest on the seabed with lighter protection.

Natural events pose a separate risk. The 2006 Hengchun earthquake off Taiwan damaged multiple undersea cables in the surrounding waters. Connectivity across parts of Asia was disrupted afterward. Cables running through the same stretch of sea can fail together. One earthquake can remove backup routes along with the main ones.

Fixing a cable is slow work. Operators first have to locate the fault. A dedicated repair ship then travels to the site. The crew raises the damaged section to the surface, splices in a replacement length and lowers the cable back down. Weather, water depth and the ship's distance from the fault all affect how long the job takes.

While a cable is out of service, network operators shift traffic onto other cables that still have spare capacity. Users in well-connected regions may notice slower speeds rather than a complete loss of access. Places served by only one or two cables have far fewer options. For them, a single cut can remove most international connectivity until repairs are finished.

Satellite links offer another path for data. They carry only a small share of international traffic compared with seabed fiber, however.

A cable cut is a regional problem, not a global one. It can isolate a country or slow service across part of a continent while networks elsewhere keep running.

When the Domain Name System fails, websites can look broken even though their servers are running normally. A browser cannot reach a site until it turns the site's name into a numeric address. DNS is the service that performs that lookup.

DNS works like a directory for the internet. A person types a name such as quartz.com. Computers, however, route traffic using IP addresses, which are strings of numbers. DNS connects the two. Without a working answer from DNS, a browser has nowhere to send its request.

A lookup passes through several layers. A device first asks a recursive resolver. That resolver is often run by an internet service provider or by a public service such as Google $GOOGL Public DNS or Cloudflare's 1.1.1.1. If the resolver does not already know the answer, it works down a chain. It queries the root servers, then the servers for a top-level domain such as .com. The last stop is the authoritative name servers for the domain itself. Those authoritative servers hold the official record.

That chain creates a weak point. Many companies hand their authoritative DNS to an outside provider. If that provider stops answering, resolvers cannot get the address for any domain it hosts. The websites, apps and servers behind those domains may be fully intact. Users still see error messages. Their devices simply cannot locate those servers.

Caching softens the effect for a while. Resolvers store recent answers for a period called the time to live, or TTL. The TTL is set in the domain's DNS records. Once a cached record expires, the resolver must ask again. During a provider outage, those fresh requests fail.

The disruption at Dyn on Oct. 21, 2016, followed this pattern. Dyn provided DNS for many well-known sites. An attack on its infrastructure left resolvers unable to get answers for the domains it served. Access to those sites was disrupted, mainly for users in North America and Europe. The sites' own servers were not the target.

DNS failures do not require an attack. A mistyped record can make a site unreachable. So can a configuration change pushed to the wrong place, or a domain registration allowed to lapse. In each case, the problem sits in the naming layer rather than in the site itself.

The usual defense is to spread DNS across more than one provider. A domain can list name servers run by two separate companies. If one stops responding, resolvers can try the other. That setup can turn a DNS failure into a slowdown or a partial outage instead of a complete loss of access.

A distributed denial-of-service attack, or DDoS, floods one target with more traffic than it can handle until it stops answering legitimate users. It knocks out a particular website, server or service. It does not shut down the internet as a whole.

The word "distributed" separates a DDoS from an ordinary denial-of-service attack. A single attacking machine can be identified and blocked by its address. A DDoS sends traffic from a large number of machines at once, often spread across many networks and countries. That makes hostile requests hard to separate from real visitors.

Attacks come in several forms. Volumetric attacks try to fill the target's bandwidth with raw data. Protocol attacks exhaust resources on servers, firewalls or load balancers by abusing the way connections are set up. Application-layer attacks send requests that look like normal page loads. Each request forces the target to do real work, and that work piles up.

Most of the machines in a large attack do not belong to the attacker. They are compromised devices grouped into a botnet and controlled remotely. Their owners usually do not notice. A hijacked device can keep working normally while it sends attack traffic on command.

The Mirai botnet showed how far this could reach. Mirai infected internet-connected devices such as IP cameras, digital video recorders and home routers. Many of those devices still used factory-default usernames and passwords. Mirai scanned the internet for them and logged in using lists of common credentials. It was used in the 2016 attack on the DNS provider Dyn.

Mirai's source code was posted publicly in 2016. Other attackers copied and adapted it. Variants built on it have continued to appear. The episode drew attention to cheap connected devices that often go without security updates.

Defenders respond by filtering traffic before it reaches the target. Specialized mitigation services absorb attack traffic across large networks and pass clean requests through. Network operators can also drop all traffic aimed at a victim's address further upstream. That stops the flood, but it also takes the victim offline.

The limits of a DDoS help answer whether the internet can go down. An attack on one service can disrupt everything that depends on that service. The attack still needs working networks to carry its traffic. A DDoS cannot switch the internet itself off.

A national government can take its own country offline. Most countries reach the global internet through a limited number of providers and international links. An official order to those companies can cut access for an entire population.

Egypt showed how this works in January 2011. During mass protests, authorities had the country's internet access cut. Most users inside Egypt lost their connections to the outside world. Websites hosted inside the country also became unreachable from abroad.

The shutdown starts as an administrative order rather than a technical attack. A government does not need to sabotage cables or break into servers. It instructs licensed operators to stop carrying traffic. In practice, providers can withdraw the routing announcements that tell other networks how to reach their customers. Once those announcements disappear, the rest of the internet no longer has a path into the country.

Concentration determines how easy this is. A country with a single state-controlled gateway can be disconnected quickly. A country with many competing providers and many cross-border links is harder to isolate. Each additional independent connection is another company that must receive and follow the order.

A full cutoff is the bluntest option. Throttling is a quieter alternative. Authorities slow connection speeds until video, voice calls or file uploads stop working, while basic access technically remains. Governments can also block specific apps or websites instead of the whole network. These partial measures can be harder for users to recognize as deliberate.

Mobile networks are part of the same picture. In many countries, people go online mainly through phones rather than fixed broadband. An order aimed at mobile operators can disconnect a large share of users without touching home or office lines.

A national shutdown is still a local event in global terms. Traffic between other countries keeps flowing, and the wider network routes around the missing region. The people inside the affected country bear the cost. Their businesses, banks, schools and families lose every service that depends on a connection.

When many websites rely on the same infrastructure company, one fault at that company can take unrelated sites offline together. Shared dependence on content delivery networks and cloud providers helps explain why large parts of the web sometimes fail at the same moment.

A content delivery network, or CDN, keeps copies of a website's pages, images and video on servers in many locations. When a reader asks for a page, the CDN sends it from a nearby server instead of from the site's own origin server. The data travels a shorter distance. Pages load faster as a result. The CDN also spreads incoming traffic across many machines, which helps a site cope with sudden surges in visitors.

Cloud providers play a related role. They rent out computing power, storage and databases. Companies can then run their services without building data centers of their own. Websites, apps and internal business tools often sit on rented infrastructure of this kind.

The trade-off is concentration. A small number of large providers carry much of this work. A news site, a retailer and a government portal may share nothing except the company standing between them and their readers. If that company's systems fail, all of them can go dark at the same time.

On June 8, 2021, a configuration issue at the CDN Fastly caused errors across sites that used its service. Reddit $RDDT was among the sites that went down. So was gov.uk, the U.K. government's main website. The disruption lasted a short period before Fastly restored service. During that window, visitors saw error messages where pages should have been.

To an ordinary user, an outage like this can look as if the internet itself has stopped. The underlying networks, cables and routing systems kept working. The fault sat in one layer of infrastructure that many sites happened to share.

That distinction sits at the center of whether the internet can go down. A CDN or cloud outage is a service-level failure, not a collapse of the network. Sites that did not route their traffic through Fastly were not affected by its fault.

Companies can limit this exposure by splitting traffic across more than one CDN or cloud provider. The approach is known as multi-CDN or multi-cloud. It adds cost and complexity. Each business weighs how much downtime it can accept against the expense of maintaining that extra redundancy.

A large power blackout can take the internet offline across a whole region. Data centers, cell towers, network switching sites and home routers all run on electricity. The network stops working wherever that supply fails for long enough.

The weakest point is often inside the home. A Wi-Fi router and the modem beside it go dark the moment the power cuts out. A laptop with a fully charged battery still cannot reach the internet if the box linking it to the provider has no electricity.

Mobile data can keep working for a while. Cell towers commonly carry battery backup, and some sites also have generators. Once those batteries drain and no generator is available, the tower drops off the network. Phones nearby then lose both calls and data, even if the handsets themselves are still charged.

The provider's own network has the same dependency. Cable, fiber and DSL systems rely on powered equipment in local exchanges, street cabinets and regional hubs. Some of that equipment has backup power and some does not. A household running its own generator can still lose service if a cabinet down the street goes dark.

Data centers are designed to ride through outages. They typically use uninterruptible power supplies, which draw on banks of batteries to bridge the first moments of a cut. Diesel generators then start and take over the load. That arrangement keeps servers running, but only as long as fuel lasts and deliveries can arrive.

A long or widespread blackout tests those limits. Roads may be blocked, fuel trucks may be delayed, and generators need maintenance to keep running. Cooling systems also draw heavy power, and servers cannot run safely once they overheat.

Even a severe regional blackout remains a local failure. The rest of the internet keeps running, and traffic flows around the affected area. For the people inside it, the result can look like the internet itself has gone down.

A strong geomagnetic storm could damage long-distance power lines and other equipment the internet depends on. The best-known historical example, the Carrington Event of 1859, disrupted telegraph systems in Europe and North America.

The event is named after Richard Carrington, a British astronomer who observed an intense solar flare on Sept. 1, 1859. A powerful geomagnetic storm reached Earth soon after. Telegraph operators reported sparks and failed lines. Some lines kept carrying messages after their batteries were disconnected. Auroras appeared much farther from the poles than usual.

Storms like this begin on the sun. A coronal mass ejection sends a cloud of charged, magnetized gas into space. If that cloud strikes Earth's magnetic field, it can set off a geomagnetic storm. The storm induces electric currents in long conductors on the ground. Power lines, pipelines and old telegraph wires all fit that description.

Power grids face the most direct risk among modern infrastructure. Induced currents can overheat large transformers, which are slow to replace. In March 1989, a geomagnetic storm triggered the collapse of the Hydro-Québec power grid in Canada. Millions of people lost electricity. For the internet, the main risk from a storm of that kind runs through the loss of power.

The cables that carry data are a separate question. Fiber-optic strands carry light, and light is not affected by induced currents. Long undersea cables differ in one respect. They contain copper conductors that power repeaters spaced along the seabed to boost the signal. Those powered components are the part of a subsea cable that a storm could affect.

Space weather also reaches equipment in orbit. In February 2022, SpaceX said a geomagnetic storm increased atmospheric drag on a batch of newly launched Starlink satellites. Many of them fell back into the atmosphere. GPS signals and high-frequency radio can also degrade during strong storms.

Whether a modern Carrington-scale storm would cause lasting damage to the internet remains an open question. No storm of that strength has been recorded since the modern network was built. The U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's Space Weather Prediction Center tracks solar activity. It rates geomagnetic storms on a five-level scale from G1 to G5. Spacecraft that watch the sun can spot a coronal mass ejection as it leaves. That gives grid and network operators advance warning before it arrives.

The internet rarely fails everywhere at once because its core pieces are duplicated and spread out. Redundant routes, many separate cable systems, multiple root server operators and distributed hosting usually keep a failure inside one region or one service.

Redundancy starts with the way networks connect to each other. Large networks typically buy connectivity from more than one upstream provider, a practice called multihoming. They also exchange traffic directly at internet exchange points, where many networks meet in one facility. When one link drops, traffic can shift to another path.

The physical layer follows the same logic. Many cable systems cross oceans and continents, and different groups of companies build and own them. Losing one route puts more load on the remaining ones. It does not usually cut a whole continent off from the rest of the world.

The Domain Name System applies the same principle at its top level. At the top of DNS sit 13 root server identities, labeled with the letters A through M. Each identity is a single name and address, but it is not a single machine. Independent organizations run them, including Verisign, NASA and the University of Southern California's Information Sciences Institute.

Anycast routing turns those 13 identities into a worldwide system. With anycast, the same address is announced from many locations at once. A query goes to whichever copy is closest in network terms. Many servers around the world answer for the root this way. If one site goes offline, routing sends its queries to another.

Caching adds a further layer of protection. DNS resolvers store answers for a set period of time. Most lookups never need to reach the root servers at all.

Hosting has spread out as well. Large sites often run copies of their content in data centers on several continents. If a fire or flood shuts one facility, the others can take over its traffic.

None of this makes outages impossible. Redundancy only protects the places where it has been built. Some regions have fewer routes than others. Shared dependencies can still tie together systems that look separate on paper. What the design does is make a simultaneous, total shutdown far harder to trigger than a local one.

#5409. Rand Fishkin’s Seattle game studio serves up first trailer for ‘The Snackbar at the End of the World’

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 11, 2026 at 11:21 amNovember 11, 2026 at 11:21 am

If the eventual release of “The Snackbar at the End of the World” is a full-on meal for video game fans, news this week of the game’s first trailer should at least suffice as an appetizer.

Seattle-based Snackbar Studio, co-founded by SparkToro founder Rand Fishkin and his wife, writer Geraldine DeRuiter, unveiled its debut title and Steam page on Tuesday. The hand-drawn narrative adventure RPG puts players in the role of a chef trying to save a struggling family restaurant in a magical version of 1960s Italy.

The studio now plans to launch the game late next year, after originally targeting the second half of 2026. Snackbar raised $2.15 million from 38 angel investors two years ago, and the project began four years ago, according to Fishkin. The team includes five co-founders (Fishkin, DeRuiter, game designer Nicolas Kraj, lead programmer Miriam Cabrera and art director Francesco Mazza) plus about 10 contractors.

In the studio’s description on Steam, players forage for ingredients in the “forbidden wilds” outside town, battling explosive tomatoes, chaotic zucchini and vendetta-driven poultry. They then cook dishes back at the restaurant before a tyrannical mayor known as the Sindaco can shut it down. The game mixes combat and stealth with cooking mini-games based on real-world recipes.

The trailer is set to “’O surdato ’nnammurato,” a classic Neapolitan song performed by professional musicians recruited by the studio’s music director. Fishkin said he and DeRuiter both cried the first time they heard it.

Fishkin is best known in Seattle tech circles as co-founder of SEO software company Moz and audience research startup SparkToro, and he more recently launched Alertmouse, a tool for tracking online mentions. DeRuiter, a writer and author, is Snackbar’s head writer.

In a LinkedIn post this week, Fishkin recalled telling DeRuiter during the COVID lockdown that he wanted to fulfill a childhood dream of making a video game. Her reply: “Don’t wait. Do it now. I’ll do it with you.”

In the same post, he said the game’s themes include found family and fighting fascism “even when there’s no hope you’ll win.” He called it a love letter to DeRuiter’s small family village in the mountains outside Naples, to that era of Italy, to video games, and to the many people both of their families have lost in recent years.

Moments like hearing that song come often in the work, Fishkin said, such as when a new feature clicks or a new animation brings DeRuiter’s characters to life. He has always loved art without being good at any form of it. “I may not be able to create art, but I can enable it,” he said. “What a wonderful feeling.”

There have been lows, too. The team spent its initial 18 months on the project with a contract agency that didn’t work out, losing money with nothing to show for it. Fishkin is glad they kept going, “even when it felt financially irresponsible.”

The game is entirely human-made, and Snackbar’s no-AI stance is firm. “Geraldine hates AI with the fury of a thousand suns,” Fishkin said. He once suggested, just once, that she use Google’s AI Mode to find a synonym, and she was mad at him for the rest of a six-hour flight home from Philadelphia. Even if players, the rest of the team and the games media were fine with AI (and they’re not), DeRuiter alone would make it a no-go, he said.

Still ahead are 10 to 12 months of finishing the game’s content, playtesting, bug fixing, marketing and launch prep. Fishkin called it daunting, but said team members have done it many times before, “even though it’s our first rodeo.”

Fishkin is still juggling Snackbar with SparkToro and Alertmouse, and describes his role at the studio as mostly oversight and management. SparkToro is growing again, and Alertmouse recently hit a big milestone in annual renewals with high retention. He and his Alertmouse co-founders are putting more money into the company to fund growth.

Balancing the three roles is a challenge, he said, but only rarely completely overwhelming. “Like this week.”

In just a few weeks, AWS re:Invent brings advanced and expert-level sessions on the services you build on every day, from serverless and containers to databases and developer tools. Go hands-on with new launches the same week they’re announced, and hear directly from the engineers who built them. Experience the depth you won’t find anywhere else.
