#5408. From Millerites to Y2K: 10 end-of-the-world dates that passed

Free daily briefing on global business news.

These 10 failed doomsday predictions, from the Millerites' 1844 date to Y2K and viral blackout hoaxes, show how precise end-of-the-world dates came and went

Every end-of-the-world claim carries a built-in test: a date. The preacher William Miller's followers settled on Oct. 22, 1844. Harold Camping named May 21, 2011. Popular accounts of the Maya Long Count calendar pointed to Dec. 21, 2012. Each date arrived, and each one passed.

That pattern makes failed doomsday predictions easy to check. A vague warning about decline is hard to disprove. A specific date is not. Once the calendar moves on, the claim either holds or it does not. In every case on this list, it did not.

The sources of these predictions vary more than their outcomes. Some came from religious date-setting, built on readings of scripture such as the Book of Daniel. Others drew on astronomy and physics. In 1910, the detection of cyanogen gas in the spectrum of Halley's Comet fed fears that Earth's passage through its tail could poison the air. A 1974 book called The Jupiter Effect tied a 1982 planetary alignment to possible earthquakes. In 2008, critics warned that the Large Hadron Collider at CERN could create black holes.

Technology produced its own version. The Y2K bug was a genuine programming problem rooted in two-digit year fields. Governments and companies spent years fixing it. The collapse of power grids and banks that some predicted did not follow. More recent claims have spread mainly online, from the supposed hidden planet Nibiru to recurring hoaxes that say Earth will go dark for days.

This list is a selection of 10 cases, not a complete record or a ranking. The cases run in chronological order. Each is explained on its own terms: who made the prediction, what it rested on, what date it named and what happened next. Several share a second pattern. When the first date failed, the prediction was often revised rather than abandoned, with a new date set further out.

That history offers a few questions for apocalypse claims circulating now. Who is making the claim? What evidence does it cite? Has a scientific body such as NASA already addressed it? And what happened the last time someone set a date?

The Millerite movement predicted that Christ would return on Oct. 22, 1844. When the day passed without incident, followers called the letdown the Great Disappointment. Some of them went on to help build the Seventh-day Adventist Church.

The forecast began with William Miller, a farmer and Baptist preacher from Low Hampton, New York. He spent years studying the Bible. He concluded that the Book of Daniel contained a timetable for the Second Coming.

His key passage was Daniel 8:14, which speaks of 2,300 days before the sanctuary is cleansed. Miller read each prophetic day as a year. He started the count in 457 B.C., the date he assigned to a Persian decree to rebuild Jerusalem. That arithmetic pointed to roughly 1843.

Miller began preaching his conclusions publicly in the 1830s. Joshua V. Himes, a Boston minister, turned the message into an organized campaign. Himes launched the newspaper Signs of the Times. He also arranged camp meetings and lecture tours across the northeastern U.S.

Miller avoided a single date at first. He described a window that ran from about March 1843 to March 1844. When that period ended without the expected return, the movement needed a new answer.

Samuel S. Snow, a Millerite preacher, supplied one. He tied the prophecy to the Jewish Day of Atonement. By his reckoning, it fell on Oct. 22, 1844. The date spread quickly through the movement in the late summer and fall of that year. Some believers left crops unharvested or closed their businesses to prepare.

The day ended like any other. Many followers left the movement. Others faced ridicule from neighbors and the press.

A smaller group reinterpreted the prophecy instead of abandoning it. They argued that Oct. 22 marked an event in heaven rather than on Earth. From that group came figures such as Ellen G. White and James White. The Seventh-day Adventist Church was formally organized in 1863. Miller died in 1849, years before the church took formal shape.

Earth passed through the tail of Halley's Comet around May 18–19, 1910, and nothing happened to the planet or its people. The scare behind that date grew from a real observation. Astronomers had found cyanogen, a poisonous gas, in the comet's light.

Halley's Comet is a periodic comet that returns to the inner solar system roughly every 75 to 76 years. It is named for the English astronomer Edmond Halley. He calculated that comets recorded in 1531, 1607 and 1682 were one object, and he predicted its return. The comet reappeared in 1758, years after Halley's death.

By 1910, astronomers had a tool Halley never used: spectroscopy. Splitting a comet's light into its component colors reveals the chemical signatures of the gases it contains. When observers studied Halley's Comet this way, cyanogen showed up in its spectrum.

Cyanogen is a compound of carbon and nitrogen, and it is toxic. Its presence gave a doomsday story something that sounded like scientific grounding.

The French astronomer Camille Flammarion pushed the finding further. He suggested that Earth's passage through the comet's tail might poison the atmosphere. Flammarion was a widely read author on astronomy, and his warning traveled well beyond scientific circles.

Newspapers covered the fear. Some sellers looked to profit from it, marketing so-called comet pills and gas masks to people anxious about the encounter.

The physics never supported the alarm. A comet's tail stretches across millions of kilometers but holds very little material. The gas in it is far too thin to alter the makeup of Earth's atmosphere.

Mark Twain was born in 1835, during the comet's previous appearance. He died in April 1910, as it came back. In 1909, he had remarked that he expected to go out with the comet.

Halley's Comet returned in 1986. That March, the European Space Agency's Giotto probe flew past its nucleus and sent back close-up images. Its next return is expected in 2061.

The Jupiter Effect, a 1974 book by John Gribbin and Stephen Plagemann, argued that a 1982 alignment of the planets could set off earthquakes, including along California's San Andreas fault. The planets arrived in position. The disaster never came.

The forecast stood apart from most end-of-the-world claims because it was framed as physics rather than prophecy. Gribbin trained as an astrophysicist. The book laid out a chain of physical causes and asked readers to follow each link to a year on the calendar.

The chain began with the Sun. The authors reasoned that when most of the planets gathered on one side of it, their combined gravity would raise tides on the Sun and stir up solar activity. A more turbulent Sun would then slightly alter the speed of Earth's rotation. That small change, they suggested, could release strain already built up in stressed faults.

Every step depended on the one before it, and the first step was the weakest. The planets are tiny next to the Sun. Their tidal pull on it is minute. On Earth, the Moon's tidal pull far exceeds that of any planet, Jupiter included. Grouping the planets together adds very little to forces Earth already feels every day.

The word "alignment" also promised more than the sky delivered. The planets did not form a straight line. They clustered within the same broad stretch of the solar system on one side of the Sun. That grouping carried little gravitational consequence for Earth.

The San Andreas fault gave the warning its local force. It marks the boundary where the Pacific Plate and the North American Plate slide past each other. Movement along it caused the 1906 San Francisco earthquake. Californians already knew the fault could produce another large quake.

The year 1982 came and went without the predicted catastrophe. The San Andreas did not rupture on the planets' schedule. California's earthquake risk remained what it had been before the book appeared: real, ongoing and still not predictable to a specific date.

Edgar Whisenant, a former NASA engineer, predicted that the Rapture would come between Sept. 11 and Sept. 13, 1988. The three days passed without incident.

Whisenant set out his case in a booklet titled 88 Reasons Why the Rapture Will Be in 1988. Each numbered reason was meant to support the others and point to a single three-day window.

In the teaching of many evangelical Protestants, the Rapture is the moment when Christian believers are caught up to meet Christ in the air. The term comes from rapiemur, the Latin for "we shall be caught up" in the Vulgate translation of Paul's first letter to the Thessalonians.

In the dispensationalist reading popular among many of these believers, the Rapture comes before a seven-year period of tribulation. Whisenant attached that event to specific days on the calendar.

The September window overlapped with Rosh Hashanah, the Jewish New Year, which fell on Sept. 12 and 13 in 1988. The holiday is also known as the Feast of Trumpets, a name drawn from the Hebrew Bible. Paul's letter also describes a trumpet sounding at the moment believers are caught up.

Another strand of the timing rested on a count of years. The modern state of Israel was founded in 1948. Whisenant's reasoning treated 40 years as one biblical generation and counted forward from 1948 to reach 1988. The idea drew on Matthew 24, where Jesus tells his disciples that "this generation" will not pass away until the events he describes take place.

Sept. 13, 1988, ended with no Rapture. Whisenant then published a follow-up, The Final Shout: Rapture Report 1989, which moved the prediction to 1989. That year also passed without a Rapture.

The same chapter of Matthew records Jesus saying that no one knows the day or hour of his return. Whisenant's first booklet named a three-day window, and his second named a full year.

The Y2K bug was a real software flaw. Many older computer systems stored years as two digits, which meant "00" could be read as 1900 instead of 2000. Years of repair work came first, and the predicted breakdown of power grids and banks did not come.

The name is shorthand. Y stands for year, the 2 for the number and K for kilo, the metric prefix for a thousand.

The two-digit habit dates to early computing, when memory and storage were expensive. Dropping the "19" from a year saved space on punch cards, magnetic tape and mainframe records. Programmers writing code in the 1960s and 1970s generally did not expect it to still be running decades later. Much of it was.

The risk lay in date arithmetic. A program that calculates a person's age, a loan's interest or a license's expiration subtracts one year from another. If 2000 is stored as "00," that math can return a negative number or a result that is off by a century. Systems that sort records by date can also place new entries ahead of old ones.

A second, smaller issue involved leap years. Years divisible by 100 are usually not leap years, but years divisible by 400 are. That made 2000 a leap year. Software that applied only the century rule could get Feb. 29 wrong.

Public warnings went further than the code itself. Some forecasts said failures would spread from computers to utilities, banks and other services at midnight.

The repair work involved auditing old code, then rewriting or replacing the parts that handled dates. In the U.S., the President's Council on Year 2000 Conversion coordinated the federal effort.

When midnight passed across the world's time zones, the large-scale failures did not arrive. Some minor glitches were reported. A number of websites displayed the year as "19100." The code behind them placed the digits "19" in front of a year counter that had reached 100.

The quiet rollover left a question that is hard to settle: whether the remediation prevented failures or the risk had been overstated. A failure that does not happen leaves little evidence behind.

A related date limit still lies ahead. Many systems count time as seconds elapsed since Jan. 1, 1970. A 32-bit signed version of that counter runs out on Jan. 19, 2038.

Nancy Lieder predicted that a hidden planet called Nibiru, or Planet X $TWTR, would approach Earth in May 2003 and cause a global catastrophe. The month passed without incident. NASA astronomers have said no such object exists.

Lieder spread the claim through ZetaTalk, a website she ran. She said the information came from aliens she described as beings from the Zeta Reticuli star system. That gave her prediction an unusual basis. It rested on neither scripture nor a published scientific paper. It rested on what Lieder presented as messages relayed to her.

The scenario she described was physical rather than spiritual. A large body would move through the inner solar system, and its close pass would bring disaster to Earth. Lieder tied the event to a specific month, which made the claim easy to check. When May 2003 arrived, no planet appeared.

The name Nibiru did not originate with Lieder. It comes from ancient Babylonian astronomy, where it referred to a celestial body associated with the god Marduk. The writer Zecharia Sitchin popularized a reworked version of the idea in his 1976 book The 12th Planet. Sitchin argued that an unseen planet orbits the sun on a very long cycle.

Planet X has a separate and legitimate history in astronomy. Percival Lowell used the term in the early 20th century for a planet he believed lay beyond Neptune. The search at Lowell Observatory in Arizona led Clyde Tombaugh to discover Pluto in 1930. The phrase later drifted from that research into fringe claims.

NASA astronomers have pointed to an observational problem with the claim. A planet large enough to threaten Earth within months would have been visible in the night sky long before it arrived. Astronomers around the world would have been tracking it. No such object was ever observed.

The missed date did not retire the prediction. The date was later pushed back. The claim kept circulating online for years, attaching itself to fresh deadlines as earlier ones passed. NASA astronomers have kept giving the same answer: no hidden planet is on a collision course with Earth.

Fears that the Large Hadron Collider would create a black hole and swallow Earth peaked when CERN started circulating beams in the machine on Sept. 10, 2008. The planet carried on. CERN's safety assessment had already concluded that the collisions posed no danger.

The collider is a 27-kilometer ring of superconducting magnets buried beneath the French-Swiss border near Geneva. It was built to smash protons together at energies no earlier accelerator had reached. Physicists designed it to probe the basic structure of matter, including the search for the Higgs boson.

Those record energies gave critics their opening. Some argued that the collisions could produce microscopic black holes. In their scenario, a tiny black hole would sink toward the center of the planet. It would then grow by absorbing the matter around it. Other warnings involved hypothetical particles called strangelets.

The concern moved beyond online forums. Before startup, two critics, Walter Wagner and Luis Sancho, filed a lawsuit in U.S. federal court in Hawaii seeking to delay the collider. The case was dismissed.

CERN answered with a formal safety assessment. Its central argument rested on nature rather than on theory alone. Cosmic rays — high-energy particles from space — have struck Earth and other bodies for billions of years. Many of those impacts produce collisions at energies similar to or higher than anything the collider could reach.

The reasoning followed directly. If such collisions could create dangerous black holes, the damage would already be visible. Earth, the sun and other astronomical objects have absorbed that bombardment and still exist. The collider was repeating, under controlled conditions, something that happens in nature all the time.

Physics offered a second line of reassurance. Under Hawking radiation, a theory proposed by Stephen Hawking, a microscopic black hole would be expected to evaporate almost instantly rather than grow.

The Sept. 10 startup passed without trouble. On Sept. 19, 2008, a faulty electrical connection between magnets caused a helium leak that damaged part of the machine. Operations stopped for more than a year. The fault was mechanical and unrelated to black holes.

The collider resumed work in late 2009. In July 2012, CERN announced the discovery of a particle consistent with the Higgs boson.

Harold Camping, the head of the Family Radio network, predicted that the Rapture would take place on May 21, 2011, with the end of the world following months later. The date passed without incident. So did the revised end date he set for Oct. 21, 2011.

Camping was not a trained theologian. He studied civil engineering and ran a construction business before turning to religious broadcasting. Family Radio, a Christian network based in Oakland, California, carried his teaching to listeners across the U.S. and abroad.

His forecast grew out of a numerical reading of the Bible. Camping treated dates, numbers and time spans in scripture as clues that could be combined to build a calendar of the end times. On his count, May 21, 2011, fell 7,000 years after Noah's flood.

The prediction reached far beyond his regular listeners. Supporters paid for billboards in cities across the U.S. announcing Judgment Day. Some followers left their jobs or spent their savings spreading the warning.

When May 21 passed, Camping reinterpreted it. He said the day had brought an invisible, spiritual judgment rather than a visible one. He then set Oct. 21, 2011, five months later, as the date for the physical end of the world.

He suffered a stroke in June 2011, between his two announced dates. He later stepped back from hosting his regular broadcast program.

In March 2012, after both dates had passed, Camping acknowledged in a statement that his prediction had been wrong. He also called the attempt to name a date sinful.

The 2011 forecast was not his first. Camping had earlier made a prediction centered on 1994, laid out in a book titled 1994? When that year ended without the return he expected, he went back to his calculations. Those calculations later produced the 2011 dates.

Dec. 21, 2012, marked the end of the 13th baktun cycle in the Maya Long Count calendar, and popular claims recast that date as the end of the world. Maya scholars said the calendar simply rolled into a new cycle. The day passed without incident.

The Long Count is a day-counting system the ancient Maya used to track long spans of time. It records dates in nested units, much as a modern calendar nests days inside months and months inside years. The baktun is the largest unit in everyday use. One baktun equals 144,000 days, or roughly 394 years.

In Long Count notation, the date reached in December 2012 was written as 13.0.0.0.0. The string of zeros looks like an odometer rolling over. To some readers, it suggested that time itself was running out.

A completed baktun closed one counting period. It did not end the count, any more than Dec. 31 ends time. Maya inscriptions also refer to dates well beyond 2012. One text at Palenque, in southern Mexico, refers to a date in A.D. 4772.

The doomsday version spread through books, websites and television documentaries in the years before the date. The 2009 disaster film 2012, directed by Roland Emmerich, used the date as the backdrop for a global catastrophe. The movie put the idea in front of a mass audience.

Popular accounts tied the date to scenarios unrelated to Maya timekeeping. These included a collision with a hidden planet, a sudden reversal of Earth's magnetic poles and a special alignment with the center of the Milky Way. None of these ideas came from the Long Count itself.

NASA published material ahead of the date rebutting the doomsday claims. The agency explained in plain terms that no planet was on a collision course with Earth and that a magnetic pole reversal does not happen suddenly. It also released a video, framed as if from the day after, explaining why the world had not ended.

Dec. 21, 2012, fell on a Friday. The next day, the count moved to 13.0.0.0.1, and the 14th baktun was underway.

Viral posts claiming that Earth will go dark for several days have circulated online for years, and the predicted darkness has never arrived. One version spread around 2015 and claimed that NASA had confirmed days of darkness. NASA denied it.

These claims tend to follow a set pattern. A post names an upcoming date, attaches the name of a space agency or a scientist, and describes days without sunlight. The details change from one version to the next. The core promise stays the same.

Attaching NASA's name gave the 2015 post an air of official backing it did not have. The sun kept rising and setting on its normal schedule.

Basic astronomy shows why the claim cannot work as described. Earth turns on its axis about once every 24 hours. At any moment, roughly half of the planet faces the sun and is in daylight. For the whole planet to stay dark for days, the sun would have to stop lighting it.

Natural darkness during the day is brief and local. A total solar eclipse happens when the moon blocks the sun. Totality at any one spot lasts no more than about seven and a half minutes. The moon's shadow covers only a narrow path across Earth's surface.

Longer darkness does occur, but only in some places. Above the Arctic Circle, the sun stays below the horizon for at least one day around the winter solstice. Near the North Pole, that stretch lasts for months. At the same time, land south of the Antarctic Circle has round-the-clock daylight.

A blackout hoax is not the same thing as a power blackout. On April 28, 2025, the Iberian blackout cut electricity across Spain and Portugal. It was a real failure of the power grid. It had nothing to do with predictions that Earth would go dark.

The two ideas can blur when a real outage makes headlines. A grid failure is a problem with the electricity supply on the ground. The hoax describes the planet itself losing its light.

#5407. Lila Bio lands $3.65M grant to fight pulmonary hypertension with AI-designed proteins

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 11, 2026 at 2:31 pmNovember 11, 2026 at 2:31 pm

Lila Bio, a startup spun out of Nobel laureate David Baker’s lab at the University of Washington, has received a $3.65 million grant from the National Institutes of Health to develop a treatment for pulmonary hypertension.

The condition causes high blood pressure in the arteries that carry blood from the heart to the lungs. It forces the heart to work harder and can lead to heart failure.

The Small Business Innovation Research fast-track award supports Lila’s efforts to develop a protein-based treatment for pulmonary hypertension that could be given by injection a few times a year.

“Most approved therapies only manage symptoms, such as vasodilators,” Lila CEO Jake Kraft said in a LinkedIn post, referring to drugs that widen blood vessels. “Lila Bio is pursuing clinically-validated, disease-modifying mechanisms that treat the underlying disease.”

The funding comes from the NIH’s National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute and is divided into two phases. The initial $605,981 will support early testing in mice, rats and non-human primates. The second phase, totaling $3,049,462, will support further animal testing and studies using lung tissue from patients.

Kraft and chief scientist Anindya Roy co-founded Lila in 2023. Both worked as postdoctoral fellows at UW’s Institute for Protein Design, which Baker directs. Lila raised $10 million in seed funding the year it was founded. Last year, it announced a collaboration with pharmaceutical giant Eli Lilly to develop treatments for solid tumors.

The startup uses AI and machine learning to design therapeutic proteins through two platforms. One supports the pulmonary hypertension project, creating long-acting injectable drugs designed to remain active in the body for weeks or months. The other focuses on targeted radiotherapy, using proteins to deliver radioactive isotopes to tumors.

“We want to bring medicines to patients,” Kraft told GeekWire in an earlier interview. “We don’t want to just say we’ve designed a protein, but we actually want to be able to say we’ve saved lives.”

The AWS re:Invent livestream runs November 29–December 3, so you can follow the week from wherever you are. Choose from 60+ sessions across topics and skill levels, from introductory overviews to advanced deep dives. Catch every major launch as it is announced. Customers share what they learned, and select sessions include live Q&A. Livestream registration is free.

#5406. From frequency to cold-load pickup: 10 things to know about rolling blackouts

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Rolling blackouts are planned, rotating power cuts that grid operators order during shortages, and these 10 explainers cover how they work and why utilities rely on them

Electric utilities sometimes switch off power to their own customers on purpose. They do it to keep a much larger share of those customers connected. That trade sits at the center of rolling blackouts, one of the last tools grid operators use during a supply emergency.

The logic starts with a constraint built into the power system. Electricity cannot be stored cheaply at grid scale. Power plants have to produce what homes, offices and factories draw at every moment. When demand climbs past what generators can deliver, the gap has to close somehow. Operators can close it in a controlled way, or the grid can close it on its own terms.

The second path carries far more risk. A shortage shows up first as a drop in grid frequency, the steady rhythm of alternating current. Generators can trip offline to protect themselves when frequency keeps falling. Each one that drops off makes the shortage deeper. That chain reaction can end in a widespread, uncontrolled blackout.

A planned, rotating outage interrupts that chain. Operators cut a defined amount of demand, then rotate the cuts among groups of customers. No single neighborhood absorbs the whole shortfall. The rest of the system stays protected.

The practice is not limited to one country or one kind of crisis. California's grid operator ordered rotating outages during an August 2020 heat wave. The Electric Reliability Council of Texas ordered load cuts during a February 2021 winter storm. South Africa's state-owned utility, Eskom, has used scheduled outages, which it calls load shedding, since 2007–2008.

The 10 slides that follow explain the mechanics behind those events. They cover why supply and demand must stay balanced and what grid frequency reveals. They also explain how automatic relays and human operators each shed load. Later slides look at how utilities pick which circuits go dark and how a brownout differs from a full cutoff. The final slides cover the heat, cold and equipment failures that trigger shortages, along with the real cases above. They close with the steps operators try first and the staged process of turning the power back on.

An electric grid has to generate exactly as much power as its customers use, moment by moment. There is no large, low-cost reserve to draw from when demand runs ahead of supply.

That sets power apart from most other commodities. Oil can sit in tanks, and natural gas can be held in underground storage for months. Electricity on the grid is produced and consumed almost at the same instant. Pumped hydro plants and large battery systems do store energy. That storage adds cost on top of generating the power in the first place.

Demand never stays still. It typically climbs as homes and businesses start their day, holds through working hours and falls overnight. Weather and holidays can shift that pattern. Every switch flipped, motor started and charger plugged in adds to the load the system must serve.

Grid operators plan for this by forecasting demand ahead of time and scheduling enough power plants to meet it. Some plants run steadily for long stretches. Others, such as natural gas peaking plants, are built to start quickly and cover short spikes. Operators adjust output throughout the day as actual demand moves away from the forecast.

Operators also hold operating reserves. These are generators kept ready to ramp up or come online if another plant fails without warning. Reserves give the system a cushion, but that cushion is finite.

The balance matters in both directions. When supply exceeds demand, operators cut back generation, sometimes by curtailing wind or solar output. When demand exceeds supply, the gap affects the entire connected system almost immediately, not one isolated area.

A supply gap can close in only two ways. Operators can add generation or import power from elsewhere. The alternative is to reduce how much customers draw. If extra supply cannot arrive fast enough, cutting demand becomes the only option left.

Grid operators accept a planned, limited cut in demand because an unresolved imbalance threatens the stability of the whole system. That controlled reduction is the core of a rolling blackout.

A rolling blackout is a deliberate, temporary power cut that moves from one group of customers to the next. Each group loses electricity for a limited stretch, then gets it back while another group is switched off.

The word "rolling" describes that movement. A shortage is not handed to a single town or neighborhood for its full length. The outage instead passes through a sequence of customer groups, and the loss is shared among them.

That sharing is the purpose. A grid in shortfall has to remove a certain amount of demand to stay in balance. Rotation keeps that total cut in place while changing who carries it. One group's power comes back only as another group's power goes out. The overall reduction holds steady through each cycle.

The planned nature sets these outages apart from more familiar ones. A storm that brings down a line or a transformer that fails causes an outage nobody chose. A rolling blackout is a decision. A grid operator has judged that cutting some customers on purpose is safer than letting the shortage run unchecked.

The decision and the work of carrying it out often sit with different organizations. A regional grid operator can set how much demand must come off the system. Local utilities then choose which of their own customers take each turn without power.

The practice goes by other names. Rotating outages means the same thing. Load shedding is a broader term that covers any deliberate removal of demand from the grid. That includes cuts made automatically by protective equipment.

Each rotation is meant to be temporary in two ways. Every group's turn without power is limited. The rotation itself also ends once supply can again cover demand. Short, shared outages are the price a grid pays to avoid an uncontrolled blackout that could leave far more customers without power.

Grid frequency is the clearest real-time sign that a power system is running short. When customers draw more electricity than power plants produce, frequency sinks below its target of 60 hertz in North America or 50 hertz in Europe.

Frequency measures how many times per second alternating current changes direction. Conventional generators on a large grid spin in step with that rhythm. A turbine on the North American grid turns at a speed tied directly to 60 hertz.

That physical link turns frequency into an early warning. If demand suddenly exceeds supply, the missing energy comes from the rotating mass of turbines and generators across the system. Those machines slow slightly, and frequency falls with them. When supply exceeds demand, the machines speed up and frequency rises.

Generators on an interconnected grid run in synchrony. Frequency is therefore essentially the same everywhere on that grid. An operator watching a single reading can spot an imbalance affecting the whole system. There is no need to tally the output of every plant and the use of every customer.

Small deviations happen all day as demand shifts. Generators carry controls called governors that raise or lower output automatically as frequency drifts. That response steadies the system and buys time for operators to bring more supply online.

A larger or longer drop carries more risk. Power plants run protective systems that disconnect them if frequency strays too far from normal. Running well away from design speed can damage turbines and other costly equipment.

Every protective trip pulls more supply from a grid that was already short. Frequency then falls further, which can push other plants past their own limits. That sequence is how a manageable shortage turns into a system-wide collapse.

The amount of spinning mass on a system shapes how fast this unfolds. Heavy rotating machines resist sudden changes in speed, which slows the slide in frequency. Solar panels and batteries connect through power electronics called inverters rather than large rotating machines. On grids with less rotating mass, frequency can change more quickly after a sudden loss of supply.

For grid operators, a falling frequency reading shows the gap between supply and demand as it opens. It arrives before plant trips can compound the shortage, which leaves a narrow window to act.

Under-frequency load shedding is an automatic safety system that cuts power to blocks of customers when grid frequency falls to preset levels. It acts faster than any human operator could, and it serves as the grid's last line of defense against collapse.

The core equipment is the protective relay. A relay watches electrical conditions on a line and trips a circuit breaker when those conditions cross a set limit. An under-frequency relay watches one measurement: how fast the grid's alternating current is cycling.

In North America, the normal value for that measurement is 60 hertz. Each relay is programmed with a threshold somewhere below that mark. If frequency sinks to the threshold, the relay opens a breaker and disconnects the load connected behind it. No dispatcher has to approve the action.

The settings come in steps. A scheme is built with several preset levels, and each one removes another block of load. If the first step stops the decline, the later steps never fire. If frequency keeps falling, the next relays trip in turn. This staged design sheds only as much demand as the emergency requires.

Speed is the reason the system exists. The sudden loss of a large power plant can pull frequency down within moments. That leaves too little time for a control room to assess the problem and order cuts by hand. The relays are set to act first, while the decline can still be stopped.

Automatic shedding differs from the rotating outages that grid operators order during a supply crunch. Those manual cuts are timed and moved from one customer group to the next. Automatic shedding is decided in advance. Engineers choose which feeders to wire into the scheme and the frequency setting for each one. In the moment, the relays respond only to frequency.

In North America, the North American Electric Reliability Corp. sets reliability standards that govern how these schemes are designed and coordinated across a region. Coordination matters. Relays in neighboring areas need settings that work together rather than against one another.

An automatic trip means the measures that come earlier did not close the gap. Operators aim to balance supply and demand well before frequency nears the relay settings. When the scheme does operate, it buys time. Operators use that time to bring back generation and steady the system before customers are reconnected.

Manual load shedding is a power cut that a grid operator orders on purpose when supply can no longer cover demand. In North America, that order follows a tiered warning system. The North American Electric Reliability Corp., or NERC, defines it as Energy Emergency Alert levels one through three.

NERC sets and enforces reliability standards for the bulk power system across the U.S., Canada and part of Mexico. Its alert levels give grid operators, utilities and neighboring systems a shared vocabulary. When one region declares an alert, others can tell how tight its conditions have become.

The first level signals that all available generation is in use or committed to run. The operator has little room left if demand climbs further or a plant fails. At this stage, the alert is a warning. Customers see no change in service.

The second level means the operator has put its load management procedures into effect. It is drawing on emergency resources to keep generation matched to demand. Power still flows to every customer, but the system has almost no margin left.

The third level means firm load interruption is imminent or already under way. Firm load is the ordinary demand of homes and businesses that utilities have committed to serve. At this point, operators expect to cut some of it or have already started.

Regional grid operators use their own names for these tiers. The California Independent System Operator, which runs most of the state's high-voltage grid, calls its top tier a Stage 3 emergency. The meaning lines up with NERC's level three. Rotating outages are imminent or already in progress.

Manual shedding works on a slower timescale than the automatic relays built into the grid. The operator sends instructions to the utilities in its area, telling each one to drop a set amount of demand. The utilities then switch off chosen parts of their distribution systems. The process takes minutes rather than fractions of a second.

That human step has a purpose. A deliberate order lets the operator size the cut to the actual shortfall. It can then divide the reduction among the utilities it oversees. Each utility decides how to spread its share across its own customers. When supply catches up with demand, the operator lowers the alert level and lifts the order to shed load.

Utilities usually pick which neighborhoods lose power by distribution circuit, not by individual home or street. Each circuit is a distribution line that serves a set group of customers. The utility switches that whole line off and on as a unit.

A household is not singled out or spared on its own in a circuit-based rotation. Whether a home goes dark depends on which circuit it sits on. It also depends on whether that circuit is in the rotation.

The grid operator and the local utility play different roles. The operator decides that load must come off the system. The utility then carries out the cut on its own lines. It chooses circuits that together add up to the reduction the operator ordered.

Some circuits are typically kept out of the rotation where possible. These are lines that serve hospitals, emergency services and other critical loads. The aim is to keep facilities tied to health and public safety running through the shortage.

Because the circuit is the unit, the exemption reaches beyond the critical site itself. Homes and businesses on the same line as a hospital keep power along with it. Neighbors a few streets away may sit on a different circuit and take their turn in the rotation.

Exempting circuits also affects everyone else. Each line removed from the pool leaves fewer circuits to share the shortage. With a smaller pool, the remaining circuits can face longer or more frequent turns without power.

These exemptions apply where possible, not in every case. Sparing a critical facility means sparing its whole circuit. That protection is a goal in each utility's plan rather than a guarantee for every site.

No single rulebook sets which circuits go into rotation. Each utility works from its own load-shedding plan. The details differ from one company to the next. Customers who want to know where they stand generally need to check their own utility's plan. A neighboring provider's rules may not apply.

A brownout lowers voltage without cutting service, a rolling blackout switches power off completely for a set period, and a cascading failure is an uncontrolled collapse. Operators control the first two. The third is the result both are meant to prevent.

The term brownout comes from the way incandescent bulbs dim and turn yellowish when voltage sags. Customers stay connected throughout. Lights glow weaker and some appliances behave oddly, but service never fully stops.

Lower voltage still affects some equipment. Many electric motors, such as those in refrigerators and air conditioners, try to do the same work at reduced voltage. They draw more current to compensate. That extra current makes them run hotter. Sustained low voltage can shorten the life of the equipment.

Grid operators in some regions can order a small, deliberate voltage reduction as an emergency step. It trims demand slightly without taking anyone offline. The effect is modest. A voltage reduction cannot close a large gap between supply and demand on its own.

A rolling blackout takes the opposite approach. Power to a group of customers drops to zero, then returns after a fixed window while another group takes its turn. The cut is total, but it is scheduled, limited and shared. Operators accept short, full outages for some customers so the rest of the system keeps running normally.

A cascading failure has no schedule and no rotation. It starts when one failure pushes extra strain onto the remaining equipment. Overloaded transmission lines can disconnect under that strain. Each loss shifts more burden onto what is left. The outages then spread across a connected region faster than operators can respond.

Recovery marks the sharpest difference. After a rolling blackout, operators switch a circuit back on. The rest of the grid is still energized, so the returning circuit has live power to reconnect to. After a full collapse, there may be no live grid at all. Operators must rebuild it from black-start units, which are power plants able to start without drawing electricity from the grid. They then extend power outward piece by piece. That process can take far longer than any planned rotation.

Brownout is sometimes used loosely to describe planned power cuts. In grid engineering, the three terms describe distinct events with different causes, controls and consequences.

Rolling blackouts usually begin with one of two problems. Demand climbs faster than generation can follow, or supply drops without warning. Extreme heat, extreme cold, plant failures, fuel shortfalls, transmission limits and drought can each open that gap.

Heat waves push demand up mainly through air conditioning. When high temperatures last for several days, buildings hold more heat and cooling systems run longer. Homes, offices and stores across a wide area all draw on the grid for cooling at the same time. Hot weather also lowers how much current transmission lines can safely carry.

Cold snaps strain both sides of the balance. Electric heaters, heat pumps and other heating equipment raise demand as temperatures fall. Freezing weather can also force power plants offline. Water lines, sensors and valves at a plant can freeze if the site was not built or weatherized for severe cold. A single cold snap can raise demand and cut supply at once.

Unplanned generator outages remove supply with no notice. A mechanical or electrical fault can trip a large plant offline in seconds. Grid operators hold reserve capacity to cover the loss of a big unit. Trouble starts when several units fail together. It also starts when one unit fails during peak demand and reserves are already thin.

Fuel supply problems can idle a plant whose equipment works normally. Gas-fired plants depend on pipeline deliveries. A drop in pipeline pressure or flow can leave them short of fuel. Coal plants depend on stockpiles and rail shipments. When fuel cannot reach a plant, the plant cannot generate, whatever the condition of its machinery.

Transmission limits create shortages that are local rather than systemwide. Each power line can carry only so much electricity. A region can run short even when a neighboring area has spare generation. That happens when the lines between them are already at capacity. The same constraint caps how much help an operator can bring in from outside during an emergency.

Drought cuts into hydroelectric output. Lower river flows and reservoir levels leave less water to run through dam turbines. Grids that lean heavily on hydropower lose part of their supply in dry years. That kind of shortfall can persist through a whole dry season rather than a single afternoon.

These triggers often overlap. A broad heat wave can raise demand in several regions at once. That leaves neighboring grids with less spare power to share. A severe freeze can push up heating load while also disrupting gas deliveries to the plants that need it.

California in August 2020, Texas in February 2021 and South Africa under Eskom show three different ways planned power cuts can play out. California ran a brief rotation. In Texas, the rotation broke down. South Africa turned scheduled cuts into a long-running practice.

The California Independent System Operator ordered rotating outages on Aug. 14 and 15, 2020, during a heat wave. These were the first such orders in the state since the 2000–2001 energy crisis.

The California episode follows the standard pattern for a rolling blackout. The grid operator directed the cuts. They rotated among groups of customers instead of falling on a single area. Each group lost power for a limited stretch. Service then came back while another group took its turn.

Texas shows what happens when that pattern fails. In February 2021, during a severe winter storm, the Electric Reliability Council of Texas, known as ERCOT, ordered utilities to cut load. The outages that followed lasted far longer than a planned rotation would. For many Texans, the cuts did not arrive as brief, shared turns without power.

That breakdown shows the limit of the method. Rotation depends on having enough supply to restore one group before cutting the next. When the shortage runs too deep, there is not enough power to bring groups back on schedule. The planned rotation then gives way to long outages for the customers who were cut.

South Africa follows yet another model. Eskom, the country's state-owned utility, has used scheduled outages since 2007–2008. It calls them load shedding. That is the same term grid operators in North America use for deliberate cuts to demand. Eskom labels each round of cuts by stage.

The South African program differs from the U.S. cases in its duration. California's orders came on two days in August 2020. Eskom's scheduled outages have recurred in the years since they began. That makes them a repeated practice rather than a single emergency.

Taken together, the three cases cover the range of what the term means in practice. A rolling blackout can be a short emergency step, a rotation that collapses under strain or a long-running schedule.

Grid operators try several measures before ordering rolling blackouts: importing power from neighboring grids, paying large customers to cut their use and asking the public to conserve. When outages do happen, service returns in stages to limit a demand surge known as cold-load pickup.

Imports are one of those options. A grid connected to neighboring systems can draw extra electricity over transmission lines when its own plants fall short. That option has limits. Transmission lines can carry only so much power. Neighboring regions may also be facing the same heat wave or cold snap. A shortage that covers a wide area leaves less spare power for anyone to sell.

Demand response works on the other side of the balance. It removes demand instead of adding supply. Utilities and grid operators enroll large customers, such as factories and commercial buildings, in programs that pay them to reduce electricity use when the grid is strained. A manufacturer might pause an energy-intensive process. An office complex might scale back its cooling. Each of these customers uses a large amount of power. A small number of them cutting back can free up capacity that would otherwise require outages for many homes.

Public appeals reach everyone else. California's Flex Alert is a named example of this kind of request. It asks residents and businesses to use less electricity during periods of grid stress, for instance by putting off running major appliances. Participation is voluntary. That makes the effect of an appeal harder to predict than a paid demand-response contract.

Restoration after an outage is not a single flip of a switch. Operators bring circuits back in stages. Each step lets them confirm that supply can keep up with the demand coming back online.

The main hazard during this phase is cold-load pickup. In normal operation, refrigerators, air conditioners, water heaters and furnaces cycle on and off at different times. That staggering keeps total demand on a circuit relatively steady. After an outage, many of these devices have been waiting for power. They all start at once when it returns. Electric motors and compressors also draw extra current as they start up.

The combined surge can push a circuit well above its usual load. That can strain transformers and trip protective equipment. A tripped circuit would put customers back in the dark and could add stress to a grid that is still recovering. Reconnecting load in measured blocks spreads that surge out over time.

#5405. AI voice company WellSaid retools for agents while keeping its commitment to human actors

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Todd Bishop on Nov 11, 2026 at 2:56 pmNovember 11, 2026 at 3:09 pm

WellSaid, the AI voice company that spun out of Seattle’s Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence in 2019, is reinventing itself for the era of AI agents.

The company this week launched WellSaid Producer, which connects its voiceover direction tools directly to AI assistants such as Claude and Microsoft Copilot.

Instead of logging into WellSaid’s app, corporate users can ask the AI assistant for a voiceover to accompany a training or marketing video, for example. The assistant then sends the script to WellSaid, which generates the audio using its licensed voices.

It’s part of a broader overhaul and refocusing of WellSaid’s business. The company has spent the past two years moving away from individual users to focus on businesses. It now has about 30 employees, down from more than 70 in late 2024.

Along the way, WellSaid has turned profitable, CEO Benjamin Dorr told GeekWire.

“We’ve been calling this adventure Act II, so I guess Producer is Scene I,” Dorr said. Extending the metaphor, he acknowledged that “the cast is a lot smaller,” and noted that many of the company’s leaders are new, recruited from his own network.

Dorr joined WellSaid as CFO in 2024 and became CEO in spring 2025. He was previously chief operating officer of Cordial, a San Diego marketing software company, and earlier worked in tech investing and banking at The Carlyle Group, Morgan Stanley and Citi.

He succeeded Brian Cook, the former Nintex CEO who led WellSaid for about 16 months. Co-founder Matt Hocking, who was CEO until early 2024, remains on WellSaid’s board and is now chief product officer at Type, an AI startup for creative writers.

Dorr’s leadership team includes three executives who also worked at Cordial and joined WellSaid since last fall: Natalia Holts, senior vice president of finance and accounting; Jeni Bishop, vice president of marketing; and Bryan Keefer, vice president of product.

Chris Johnson, the chief product and technology officer, and co-founder Mixail Petrochuk, the chief technology officer, remain from the earlier leadership team.

The company is maintaining its longstanding practice of building its AI voices from recordings of professional voice actors, who are paid royalties when businesses use their voices to narrate training courses, marketing and other videos.

WellSaid drew widespread attention in 2023 when it created a spot-on synthetic version of former NPR “Planet Money” host Robert Smith’s voice, with his permission, as part of a special series by the popular radio show and podcast.

Its customers include nearly half of the Fortune 100, according to WellSaid. The company’s licensing approach stands out in a sector that remains a wild west, with models trained on audio scraped from the internet and tools used to fake the voices of public figures.

“We view [Model Context Protocol], and agents in general, to be as disruptive to software as the Web once was twenty years ago.”

How it works: Producer uses Model Context Protocol, or MCP, a standard way for AI assistants to connect to other software. It works with Claude, ChatGPT, Copilot and Atlassian’s Rovo, and Dorr said AI agents that work on their own will be able to use it by the end of the year.

Companies using WellSaid Producer can set up style guides so brand names, acronyms and technical terms are pronounced the same way in every file. When a product name or script changes, Producer can update every affected voiceover in one pass, and each finished file carries a record of its license.

WellSaid also says it’s the first voiceover platform to generate audio natively at 48 kHz, the standard for film and video. Producer is sold as a platform, with customers committing to buy credits for minutes of finished, licensed audio. WellSaid’s licenses today are mostly one-time buyouts, but Dorr said the company wants to price more like the traditional voiceover industry, where an ad voiceover is priced by its length, reach and how long it runs. WellSaid will continue to offer its Studio app for customers who want to work there directly.

The strategy: Dorr said voiceover is just one step in a larger production process, and many creative tools now include basic AI speech that is sometimes good enough. He sees AI agents letting companies combine specialized tools from vendors they trust, instead of settling for one all-in-one app.

“We view MCP, and agents in general, to be as disruptive to software as the Web once was twenty years ago,” he said.

Voice actors: Actors’ revenue share rates won’t change when their voices are used through AI assistants, Dorr said. One of his first moves as CEO was to open the company’s stock option pool to its top 20 voice actors, and WellSaid is building a voice actor advisory board, with more details expected to be released in December. Dorr said WellSaid plans to add custom royalty structures, “potentially all the way up to union rate cards.”

Customers will also be able to use voice models from other companies alongside WellSaid’s own, for features its models lack, such as one voice speaking several languages. The voices still come from WellSaid’s actors under its licensing terms. “We’re not moving from our position on commercial licensing,” Dorr said.

The business: WellSaid has about 1,000 business customers, and its top 25 customers each spend more than $100,000 a year, Dorr said. Moving away from individual users “did flatten our growth compared to a lot of AI companies growing at astronomical rates,” he said.

By comparison, rival ElevenLabs, which has offered voice generation through Claude since 2025, was valued at $22 billion in a recent employee tender offer.

WellSaid raised venture debt from Multiplier Capital in March but didn’t disclose the amount. Its most recent disclosed equity funding was a $10 million Series A round in 2021 that valued the company at $65 million, according to PitchBook.

Dorr said debt was a better fit than equity for a “modestly growing and, now, profitable company,” at a time when investors’ growth expectations “have become extreme.” He said WellSaid will consider other financing in 2027 “if our ambitions outstrip our ability to reinvest.”
