#5404. 10 cyberattacks that changed history, from the Morris worm to Colonial Pipeline

Free daily briefing on global business news.

These 10 cyberattacks that changed history, from the 1988 Morris worm to the 2021 Colonial Pipeline ransomware attack, show how digital threats reshaped security, policy and business

Each attack on this list exploited a weakness that defenders had not yet treated as real. In 1988, that weakness was the open, trusting design of the early internet. By 2021, it was the business computer systems behind a major U.S. fuel pipeline. In between, attackers turned trusting inboxes, industrial controllers, factory-default passwords and routine software updates into ways in. The fallout forced governments, companies and ordinary computer users to rethink what needed protecting.

This list of cyberattacks that changed history follows that progression in chronological order. It begins with a graduate student's self-replicating program and an email worm that spread through a love-letter subject line. It moves on to the denial-of-service attacks that flooded a whole country's government, bank and media websites in 2007. It then covers malware that damaged uranium enrichment centrifuges in Iran. Later entries include destructive attacks on a Hollywood studio and on global businesses such as the shipping firm Maersk. The list ends with a ransomware attack that led a pipeline operator to halt operations as a precaution.

These famous cyberattacks matter well beyond the security industry. They tested the law, producing the first conviction under the 1986 Computer Fraud and Abuse Act. The 2007 attacks on Estonia were followed by the NATO Cooperative Cyber Defence Centre of Excellence, set up in Tallinn in 2008. Governments also began naming names. The U.S. and the U.K. have publicly attributed several of the attacks below to North Korea or Russia.

For businesses, the lessons are practical. An unpatched Windows flaw let ransomware move across networks. A trusted vendor's software update carried intruders into customer systems. An attack on business IT systems, not on pipeline controls, still stopped fuel shipments.

The 10 attacks below are a selection, not a ranking or a complete record. Each slide explains what happened, how the attack worked and what it changed. Where a government has formally attributed an attack, the slide names that government.

On Nov. 2, 1988, Cornell graduate student Robert Tappan Morris released a self-replicating program that spread across the early internet and slowed many connected computers. Morris became the first person convicted under the 1986 Computer Fraud and Abuse Act.

The program was a worm. A virus needs a person to open a file or run a program. A worm copies itself to new hosts on its own. It looks for reachable machines, gets in through a weakness and starts the cycle again from its new location.

The network Morris released it onto was small by later standards. Its users were mostly universities, research labs and government and military sites. Many machines were set up to trust one another. Security practices assumed that the people on the network were colleagues.

The worm took advantage of that trust. It targeted computers running versions of the Unix operating system. It used flaws in common programs, including the sendmail email service and the finger utility. It also abused trust settings that let one machine log in to another, and it tried to guess weak user passwords.

A design error turned the program into an outage. The worm was meant to check whether a machine was already infected. It was also written to copy itself in some cases regardless of the answer. Computers ended up running many copies at once. Those copies consumed processing power until the machines slowed or stopped responding.

System administrators spent days isolating machines, analyzing the code and cleaning up. Some institutions disconnected from the network entirely while they worked.

The legal response set a precedent. Federal prosecutors brought the case under the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act, which targets unauthorized access to computers. The verdict showed that releasing self-spreading code onto a network could be prosecuted as a federal crime in the U.S.

The incident also changed how defenders organized. Within weeks, the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency funded the creation of the Computer Emergency Response Team Coordination Center at Carnegie Mellon University. Similar incident-response teams now operate inside governments and companies around the world.

Morris later joined the faculty of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and co-founded the startup accelerator Y Combinator. The worm that carries his name made self-spreading code a recognized category of security threat. It also showed that on a connected network, one flaw can travel far beyond the machine where it started.

The ILOVEYOU worm spread worldwide in May 2000 inside an email that looked like a love letter. It showed that a message from a familiar sender could carry malware across continents without exploiting any flaw in the operating system.

The worm originated in the Philippines. Its emails carried the subject line "ILOVEYOU" and a brief note asking the recipient to open the attached letter. The attachment was named LOVE-LETTER-FOR-YOU.TXT.vbs.

That file name was the core of the trick. Windows hid known file extensions by default at the time. Many users saw only "LOVE-LETTER-FOR-YOU.TXT" and assumed it was a harmless text file.

The real extension, .vbs, marked the file as a VBScript program. Windows ran it as soon as someone double-clicked it.

Once opened, the script did two things. It damaged files on the infected computer, overwriting many of them, including image files, with copies of itself. It also used Microsoft $MSFT Outlook to email itself to the contacts in the victim's address book.

That second step explains the worm's reach. Each new recipient got the message from someone they knew — a colleague, a relative, a client. A note that might have been deleted if it came from a stranger looked safe when it came from a friend.

Security professionals call this technique social engineering. It targets human judgment rather than a software bug. The ILOVEYOU worm did not need to break into a machine on its own. It needed a person to click.

The flood of copies overwhelmed mail servers. Many companies and government offices took their email systems offline to stop the spread and clean infected machines.

Microsoft released an Outlook security update later in 2000. The update blocked users from opening script attachments such as .vbs files directly from email.

The same formula drives phishing today. A trusted-looking sender, an emotional or urgent hook and an attachment or link that does the damage remain standard tools for attackers. Corporate security training that warns staff about unexpected attachments addresses the exact behavior the worm exploited in 2000.

In April 2007, websites run by Estonian government bodies, banks and media outlets were flooded with traffic after authorities in Tallinn relocated the Bronze Soldier, a Soviet war memorial. It was among the first cyberattacks to strike a nation's online services across so many sectors at once.

The Bronze Soldier is a bronze statue of a soldier in Red Army uniform. It was unveiled in Tallinn in 1947 to mark the Soviet victory in World War II. Many Estonians linked it to decades of Soviet occupation. Many of the country's Russian speakers saw it as a tribute to the war dead.

The government moved the statue from central Tallinn to the Defence Forces Cemetery of Tallinn. The decision set off riots in the capital in late April. The online assault ran alongside the street unrest.

A denial-of-service attack does not break into a system or steal data. It overwhelms a server with more requests than it can handle, so legitimate users cannot get through. When the traffic comes from many machines at once, often hijacked computers in a botnet, it is called a distributed denial-of-service, or DDoS, attack.

Estonia's heavy use of online services raised the cost of the disruption. After regaining independence in 1991, the country moved much of its public life online, from banking to government services. In March 2007, weeks before the attacks, it became the first country to allow internet voting in a national parliamentary election.

That reliance cut both ways. A population used to banking and dealing with the state online had fewer offline routines to fall back on when those sites slowed or went dark.

The attacks also raised a question NATO had not yet answered. Estonia had joined the alliance in 2004. The open question was whether a cyberattack on a member could count as an armed attack.

The NATO Cooperative Cyber Defence Centre of Excellence opened in Tallinn the following year. The center later convened the international experts who wrote the Tallinn Manual, first published in 2013. The manual examines how international law applies to cyber conflict.

At its 2014 summit in Wales, NATO declared that cyber defense is part of its core task of collective defense. The alliance has since treated a serious cyberattack as a possible trigger for its mutual-defense commitment, to be judged case by case.

Stuxnet, a piece of malware discovered in 2010, targeted Siemens industrial controllers at Iran's Natanz uranium enrichment plant and damaged centrifuges. It showed that computer code could cause physical destruction, not just steal or erase data.

The target was an industrial control system. This is the kind of equipment that runs machinery rather than office networks. Facilities like Natanz rely on programmable logic controllers. These are small dedicated computers that tell motors, valves and pumps what to do.

Stuxnet was built to look for Siemens controllers and the Siemens Step 7 software that engineers use to program them. Earlier malware typically stole information, sent spam or crashed computers. Stuxnet was written to change how machines behaved in the physical world.

At Natanz, that meant interfering with the centrifuges that spin uranium gas to enrich it. The malware altered the speed at which the centrifuges ran. The machines depend on precise, stable rotation, and the changes damaged them.

The code was also designed to conceal its work. It fed operators readings that suggested normal operation while the equipment was being pushed outside its settings. That deception meant the damage could look like mechanical failure rather than an attack.

Stuxnet could reach systems that were not directly connected to the open internet. It was able to spread through USB drives. That route let it cross from ordinary computers into isolated industrial networks.

Its sabotage was narrowly aimed. Stuxnet checked for a specific configuration of equipment before running its damaging routine. On computers that did not match that setup, it did not attempt the sabotage.

The malware first came to light through VirusBlokAda, a small antivirus firm in Belarus. Security researchers around the world then spent months taking the code apart to understand its purpose.

Reporting has widely linked Stuxnet to the U.S. and Israel. Neither government has officially acknowledged a role.

The same families of controllers run power grids, water treatment plants, factories and other heavy infrastructure. Stuxnet demonstrated that an attacker with enough resources could manipulate that equipment through software alone. For the operators of those systems, it turned a theoretical risk into a documented case. An isolated network is not automatically a safe one.

In November 2014, attackers broke into Sony $SONY Pictures Entertainment. They stole and leaked internal data and wiped company systems. The FBI publicly attributed the attack to North Korea in December 2014. That statement turned a corporate breach into a geopolitical event.

The timing tied the intrusion to a single film. Sony Pictures was preparing to release The Interview, a comedy built around a fictional plot to assassinate North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. The attackers called themselves Guardians of Peace.

The hack combined two kinds of damage. The first was theft. Attackers copied internal material and released it publicly. The leaks included private emails, employees' personal information and unreleased films.

Leaked data does not come back once it is public. Journalists, competitors and anyone else online could read it. The studio had no way to recall it.

The second kind of damage was destruction. Wiper malware erases or overwrites data on infected machines. It can leave computers unable to start or function. At Sony Pictures, ordinary business tools went dark while the studio's private records circulated online.

Each problem makes the other harder to handle. A data leak is easier to manage when internal systems still work. A system outage is easier to manage when sensitive records stay private. Sony Pictures faced both at once.

The target also mattered. Sony Pictures is a film studio, not a defense contractor or a government agency. The attack showed that a private company could be drawn into a dispute between states because of what it produced. For entertainment, media and other consumer-facing firms, that exposure became part of the security picture.

The FBI's December 2014 statement marked a shift in how the U.S. government handled state-linked hacking. Naming a foreign government in public, rather than responding quietly, became a policy tool in its own right. North Korea denied involvement.

In January 2015, the U.S. imposed new sanctions on North Korea in response to the attack and other actions by its government. Public attribution backed by economic penalties gave the U.S. government a way to respond to a cyberattack without military action.

On Oct. 21, 2016, the Mirai botnet hit the DNS provider Dyn with a denial-of-service attack and disrupted access to many major websites. Mirai was built from hijacked cameras, routers and other connected devices that still used their factory default passwords.

A botnet is a network of compromised machines that an attacker controls remotely. Each infected device takes commands from a central server. A single home camera has little computing power or bandwidth. In large numbers, such devices can send enough traffic to overwhelm a target.

Mirai found its recruits by scanning the internet for devices with open remote-login services. It then tried a built-in list of common factory usernames and passwords. Many devices shipped with the same credentials, and many owners never changed them. Once inside, the malware added the device to the botnet and kept searching for more.

The choice of target explains why the outage reached so far. DNS, the Domain Name System, translates the website names people type into the numerical addresses computers use to find each other. Without a working DNS lookup, a browser cannot locate a site. That holds even if the site's own servers are running normally.

Dyn handled these lookups for many companies at once. Flooding its infrastructure with junk traffic meant legitimate requests for its customers' domains went unanswered. Users trying to reach those websites saw failures, although the websites themselves had not been hacked. Trouble at one provider became an outage for many companies.

Before Mirai, a weak password on a webcam could look like a risk mainly to that device's owner. The Dyn attack showed that the same weakness, repeated across a large population of cheap Internet of Things devices, could be turned against unrelated companies and their customers.

The owners of infected devices often had no sign that anything was wrong. A hijacked camera or router could keep working normally while also taking part in attacks. That made the problem hard to fix from the user side.

The episode also carried a lesson about concentration. Companies that relied on a single DNS provider had a single point of failure outside their own systems. Spreading DNS service across more than one provider is one way organizations reduce that exposure.

Mirai's source code was posted publicly online shortly before the Dyn attack. That release let other attackers build their own versions. Malware derived from Mirai continued to circulate in the years that followed.

WannaCry ransomware spread around the world in May 2017 by exploiting a Windows flaw through EternalBlue, an exploit tied to leaked U.S. National Security Agency tools. The organizations it disrupted included parts of the U.K. National Health Service.

Ransomware encrypts the files on an infected computer and demands payment for the key to unlock them. WannaCry displayed a ransom note asking victims to pay in bitcoin. Most ransomware of that period depended on someone opening a malicious file or link. WannaCry did not need that step.

The malware behaved like a worm. Once inside a network, it searched for other Windows machines carrying the same weakness in the Server Message Block $SQ file-sharing protocol. It then copied itself to them. A single infected computer could spread the infection across an office network without anyone clicking anything.

That flaw already had a fix. Microsoft $MSFT released a security update for it in March 2017. A group calling itself the Shadow Brokers published EternalBlue online in April 2017. Organizations that had not installed the update were exposed. So were those still running unsupported versions of Windows, such as Windows XP. After the attack began, Microsoft issued an emergency patch for Windows XP, a system it no longer supported.

In the U.K., the NHS felt the effects directly. Infected computers at some hospitals and GP practices forced staff to cancel appointments and operations. Some ambulances were diverted to other hospitals. The episode showed that an unpatched office computer could interfere with patient care.

The spread slowed because of Marcus Hutchins, a British security researcher. While examining the code, he found that it checked whether a particular web domain existed. The domain was unregistered, and he registered it. Once the address went live, new infections stopped carrying out their attack. The domain had worked as a kill switch.

In December 2017, the U.S. and the U.K. publicly attributed WannaCry to North Korea.

The lasting lesson concerns patching. WannaCry exploited a vulnerability that already had a published fix. It hit hardest at organizations that had delayed updates or kept outdated systems in service. The attack also raised questions about government agencies holding on to software flaws. A tool linked to intelligence work had ended up powering a global outbreak.

NotPetya first spread in June 2017 through a compromised update to M.E.Doc, an accounting program used by businesses in Ukraine. It looked like ransomware, but it worked as wiper malware built to destroy data rather than hold it for payment.

The outbreak began on June 27, 2017, the day before Ukraine's Constitution Day. Organizations that had installed the tainted M.E.Doc update became the first victims. From there, the code moved across internal networks on its own, with no clicks required from anyone inside.

Its spread relied on more than one method. It used EternalBlue, the same leaked Windows exploit behind WannaCry weeks earlier. It also harvested administrator credentials from infected machines. Those stolen credentials let it reach computers that had already been patched against EternalBlue.

The damage did not stay inside Ukraine. Companies with offices or network connections in the country were exposed. The Danish shipping firm Maersk was among those hit, and its disruption showed how one infected foothold could reach a global operation. The drugmaker Merck $MRK, the snack maker Mondelez $MDLZ International and FedEx $FDX's TNT Express unit also reported damage.

Infected machines displayed a demand for bitcoin and an email address to contact after paying. The German email provider hosting that address shut the account down. That cut off any contact with the attackers. The larger problem sat in the code itself. The identifier shown to victims had no working link to a decryption key. Paying could not restore files.

That difference separates the two categories. Ransomware is a criminal business model that depends on returning data to victims who pay. A wiper has no such incentive. NotPetya was built to destroy, and its payment screen gave victims a false impression that recovery was possible.

In February 2018, the U.S., the U.K. and other governments attributed NotPetya to the GRU, Russia's military intelligence service. The attribution had consequences beyond diplomacy. Mondelez sued its insurer, Zurich American, after the insurer cited a war exclusion to deny coverage for NotPetya losses. The dispute put a direct question to insurers and corporate buyers. It asked how cyber policies treat attacks that governments link to a foreign state.

Attackers hid malicious code inside software updates for SolarWinds' Orion network-management platform. The security firm FireEye disclosed the intrusion in December 2020.

Orion is software that IT teams use to monitor servers, network equipment and applications from a single dashboard. To do that job, it typically runs with broad access to the systems it watches. That level of access made it a valuable place to plant a backdoor.

The method is known as a software supply-chain attack. Instead of breaking into each target directly, attackers compromise a vendor that many organizations already trust. The vendor's normal distribution channel then delivers the malicious code on the attackers' behalf.

In the SolarWinds case, the tampered code was built into Orion updates that the company shipped to its customers. Organizations that installed those updates were following standard advice to keep software current. The update process itself carried the compromise.

FireEye uncovered the operation while investigating a breach of its own network. It named the backdoor Sunburst. The firm then published technical details so other organizations could search their own systems for signs of it.

In April 2021, the U.S. government attributed the operation to Russia's Foreign Intelligence Service, the SVR. That attribution placed the campaign in the category of espionage by a foreign intelligence agency. It was not presented as the work of criminals seeking payment.

The incident changed how organizations think about the software they buy. A digitally signed update from a known vendor had long been treated as safe to install. SolarWinds showed that a signature confirms where code came from, not that the vendor's build process was clean.

That lesson moved supply-chain security into government policy. In May 2021, President Joe Biden signed Executive Order 14028, which set new security expectations for software sold to federal agencies. One measure it promoted was the software bill of materials, a list of the components inside a product.

For companies, the practical result was closer scrutiny of vendors. Reviews of how suppliers build and sign their code joined the usual security questionnaires. Organizations also began asking how much network access a monitoring tool really needs. The focus widened from whether a supplier was reputable to how its code was produced and delivered.

In May 2021, the DarkSide ransomware group attacked Colonial Pipeline's business systems. The company halted pipeline operations as a precaution. Fuel supply disruption and panic buying followed in parts of the U.S. Southeast.

Colonial Pipeline operates a fuel line that runs from the Houston area of Texas to the New York Harbor region. It carries refined products such as gasoline, diesel and jet fuel to markets along the East Coast. Many communities in the Southeast rely on that flow. When it stopped, shortages appeared at gas stations within days.

The attackers did not seize the pipes, pumps or valves. Their target was the corporate information technology network. That is the side of a company that handles email, billing, accounting and records. The systems that physically control fuel flow are a separate layer, often called operational technology.

Colonial shut down the physical operation anyway. The company said it took systems offline proactively to contain the threat. An operator in that position cannot be certain that an intrusion has not crept toward the control systems. Restarting before the network is understood carries that risk.

The incident showed that an attack on ordinary office computers could interrupt a piece of national energy infrastructure. Security plans that treat corporate IT and industrial operations as separate worlds do not account for that dependence.

The FBI identified DarkSide as the group responsible in May 2021. DarkSide ran a ransomware-as-a-service model. In that arrangement, developers build and maintain the malware. Affiliates use it to break into victims, and the two sides split any ransom payments.

The structure resembles a franchise business. A small core of developers can extend its reach through many independent operators. That model also makes the groups harder to disrupt. Removing one affiliate leaves the rest of the operation intact.

Federal regulators responded within weeks. In May 2021, the Transportation Security Administration issued a security directive for pipeline operators. It required companies to report cybersecurity incidents to the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. It also required them to name a cybersecurity coordinator. A second directive followed in July 2021. Before the attack, pipeline operators had worked under largely voluntary federal cybersecurity guidance.

#5403. Exchange Ledgers in the Middle as CFTC and SEC Diverge on What “Delivery” Means

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

A customer buys a token on a U.S. exchange and the app shows the balance. Under the CFTC's December 14 framework, nothing has been delivered yet.

Under the SEC's crypto proposal, delivery doesn't decide the question at all. An October 27 comment letter asks the two agencies to settle on one answer.

Open almost any crypto exchange app after a purchase and you'll see a clean number: 1.0000 ETH, available. To the customer, the asset is theirs. To the exchange's database, it's a row in an internal ledger. To federal regulators, that row is now being judged by two different tests that don't agree on what it means.

The Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) has opened an advance notice of proposed rulemaking on what it calls Regulation Crypto Asset Transactions (CTX) and Regulation Crypto Asset Markets (CAM). It sets out the agency's first formal view of "actual delivery" for crypto since it withdrew its 2020 guidance last December. Comments close on December 14.

The Securities and Exchange Commission's Regulation Crypto Assets proposal takes a different view of the same moment. Then, on October 27, a comment letter on the SEC's file raised the gap directly. It described the situation as "two conflicting definitions of the same physical facts" and asked the agencies to "please coordinate the definitions."

Delivery matters because it decides which rulebook applies.

For the CFTC, the answer comes from Section 2(c)(2)(D) of the Commodity Exchange Act. A leveraged, margined or financed retail commodity trade is treated like a futures contract unless "actual delivery" happens within 28 days. If delivery happens in time, the trade falls outside futures rules. If it doesn't, the exchange is effectively running a futures venue.

For the SEC, the question is whether a token is still part of an investment contract. Under the August proposal, a covered investment contract ends when the issuer has finished or permanently stopped its essential managerial efforts and files a Form TR transition report. Whether the buyer has received the token is not part of that test.

So one agency treats delivery as the deciding question, and the other barely considers it.

The CFTC's position is still preliminary, but it is detailed. Published in the Federal Register on October 13, the notice relies on the Monex case standard: actual delivery requires "the transfer of some meaningful degree of possession or control."

For crypto, the agency suggests that possession and control "may require possession of the credentials (e.g., private key(s))." It takes three positions that matter most to exchanges:

The agency is also asking whether control has to be exclusive, whether delivery can happen while a lien or security interest is outstanding, and how financing offered in an exchange's standard account documents affects whether a trade is covered at all.

The SEC's proposal, released on August 18, deals with a different question. It creates offering exemptions, including a $5 million startup exemption over four years, and a safe harbor for when a crypto asset's investment contract ends. Neither depends on where the token sits.

Under the proposal, a token held in a customer's self-custody wallet and a token recorded on an exchange's books are treated the same way. In both cases, the investment contract question depends on the issuer's managerial efforts and its filings.

That is the gap the October 27 letter tries to close. Its author, who describes themselves as a fintech founder designing a consumer platform, argues that "where the customer holds the private keys or execution is on-chain, with custody evidence, the asset should be treated as delivered and the covered-investment-contract analysis should end there."

Running four common exchange transactions through both frameworks shows where the tests split.

Trade one: a fully paid purchase left on the exchange.

Trade two: the same purchase withdrawn to a self-custody wallet on day three.

Trade three: a margined purchase kept on the exchange's ledger for 30 days.

Trade four: an on-chain swap that settles directly into the user's wallet.

The pattern is consistent. Self-custody is the only position that clearly counts as delivery under the CFTC's view and also ends the analysis under the letter's proposed SEC fix. Everything left on an exchange's internal ledger stays in an unclear position. The CFTC treats it as undelivered and the SEC's text doesn't address it.

The letter was filed on October 27, a week after the SEC's October 20 comment deadline. It is anonymous and brief, but its main concern is practical. If the definitions stay separate, it warns, founders will have to design products around whichever rule is stricter.

It is the only filing on either docket so far that sets the two definitions side by side.

The CFTC process is still at the advance-notice stage, so a formal proposal will follow. For U.S. platforms, though, the direction is clear. Under the CFTC's preliminary reading, an exchange that keeps customer assets in internal ledger accounts has not delivered them. If that exchange also offers margin or financing, it is on track to be treated as a futures venue.

The SEC's final rule could adopt the letter's custody-based approach or keep delivery out of its analysis entirely. Until one of those happens, the same ledger entry can be undelivered for one regulator and irrelevant for the other.

Exchanges and their customers have until December 14 to say which definition should prevail. The real decision is whether "delivered" ends up meaning the same thing at both agencies.

#5402. Ex-Seattle startup DeltaGen acquired by new AI company backed by Veeam co-founder

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 12, 2026 at 5:51 amNovember 12, 2026 at 5:51 am

DeltaGen, an AI startup that got its start in Seattle before moving to San Francisco this year, has been acquired by Worker.ai, a new small-business software company backed by Veeam founder Ratmir Timashev.

Worker, which launched Thursday, acquired all of DeltaGen for an undisclosed price that included a substantial cash component and equity in Worker, DeltaGen co-founder and CEO Rene Bystron told GeekWire.

Bystron joins Worker as co-founder and COO, and nine other DeltaGen employees are coming with him, including co-founders Michal Studnicka and Matus Ondreicka.

Worker, led by co-founder and CEO John Roberts, a former private equity operator based in Raleigh, N.C., is building software that lets small businesses hand off recurring work to AI agents. DeltaGen’s voice technology captures decisions made in conversations and turns them into assigned tasks.

Roberts had been a DeltaGen customer before Worker needed voice technology, Bystron said. “We could have raised another round and kept building independently, but this gave us the capital and experience to move faster with people we trusted,” he said.

Launched in 2024, DeltaGen raised a $1.2 million pre-seed round in early 2025 to build generative AI tools for financial professionals, with a focus on streamlining mergers and acquisitions. The company relocated from Seattle to San Francisco earlier this year.

“I still love Seattle and miss it like crazy,” said Bystron, who is keeping his apartment in Belltown. “But being closer to the AI founders, customers and investors in San Francisco makes a real difference at this stage. It also didn’t help that Washington has been chipping away at its tax advantage.”

Timashev, who co-founded data backup giant Veeam, is backing Worker to help small businesses such as manufacturers, service companies and family businesses grow.

“AI can now give small businesses more capacity without asking already stretched owners to work longer days,” he said in a statement. “Worker is my bet on that shift.” The size of his investment was not disclosed.

DeltaGen’s current product is an AI voice platform, which will continue as it’s integrated into Worker. DeltaGen’s AI voice platform will continue as it’s integrated into Worker, which is opening access gradually through a waitlist.

#5401. Viking stock slips after low river levels cut into cruise profits

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Adjusted earnings of $1.11 a share missed analyst estimates as low water cut an estimated $100 million from adjusted gross margin

Viking Holdings reported third-quarter adjusted earnings of $1.11 a share on Tuesday, down from $1.20 a year earlier, after unusually shallow stretches of European rivers upended sailing schedules and prompted passengers to cancel. Viking stock was down by up to 5% before the opening bell.

Analysts expected $1.27 a share on average, according to Bloomberg, which called the shortfall Viking's largest since 2024. The mean forecast from four analysts surveyed by Zacks Investment Research was $1.23, The Associated Press reported.

Total revenue rose 9.2% to $2.18 billion, which matched Wall Street forecasts, according to The Associated Press. Net income was $498.4 million, compared with $514.0 million a year earlier. Adjusted EBITDA fell 4.3% to $673.5 million. Net Yield, the company's per-passenger-day margin measure, slipped 0.8% to $612.

Occupancy dropped to 91.3% from 96.0%. Viking said the low water conditions reduced third-quarter revenue by an estimated $100 million and that the impact on adjusted gross margin was also about $100 million. The margin figure reflects lost margin from cancellations and extra direct costs to mitigate the disruptions. The company canceled no scheduled cruises.

"While prolonged periods of historically low water levels disrupted portions of our European river operations during the quarter, our nearly 30 years of experience operating on Europe's waterways allowed us to adapt to changing conditions and minimize the impact on our guests," CEO Leah Talactac said in a statement.

As of Nov. 8, Viking had sold 93% of its capacity for the 2026 season and 68% for 2027 across its core products. Advance bookings for 2026 totaled $6.2 billion, up 11% from the same point a year earlier. The company said that figure declined since its last earnings release, mainly because of cancellations tied to itineraries disrupted by low water. Advance bookings for 2027 stood at $5.83 billion, up 17% from the same point for the 2026 season.

Viking issued vouchers to certain guests on affected itineraries as a goodwill gesture. The company said redemptions count in advance bookings at net value. Viking said during the summer that the complete financial hit from honoring those vouchers would start in the current quarter and run across two years, according to Bloomberg.

Parts of the Danube, Elbe and Rhine remain unusually shallow, according to Bloomberg. Viking noted in a memo dated last week that conditions are getting better in certain stretches thanks to recent rain.

Viking furnished the results release to the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission in a Form 6-K filing.

#5400. Seattle’s Allen Institute helps create a ‘Rosetta Stone’ for brain cells to unlock clues to disease

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 12, 2026 at 8:00 amNovember 11, 2026 at 5:15 pm

A coalition of 56 institutions across nine countries is publishing groundbreaking research today on the basal ganglia — a group of brain structures that help control movement, emotions, motivation and habits. The region is linked to psychiatric and degenerative disorders, including schizophrenia, bipolar disorder and Parkinson’s disease.

The scientist have produced a biological Rosetta Stone that creates a shared system for naming and describing cells in the basal ganglia across species. The goal is to help researchers compare findings, collaborate and accelerate their understanding of this essential brain region.

“This is groundwork that is necessary to really make progress,” said Michael Hawrylycz, principal investigator with the Seattle-based Allen Institute who helped organize the consortium.

The project, called the BRAIN Initiative Cell Atlas Network, or BICAN, produced a basal ganglia atlas that is publicly available for basic researchers, clinicians and others to use.

The research is being presented in a package of 26 articles in a special issue of the journal Cell. The data comes from humans, macaques, marmoset and mice. One of the benefits of comparing the basal ganglia between species is understanding which components are uniquely human, providing potential insights into neurological diseases.

Despite the critical and wide-ranging roles, the basal ganglia is relatively small — it’s about 2% of the brain with a volume roughly the size of a large gumball.

For the project, the researchers pulled information from 25.5 million brain cells, including 21 million human cells. They used a variety of techniques to tease out insights, including RNA sequencing to identify gene activity from single cells in precise locations; epigenomic studies revealing where genes are switched on or off; and measurements of electrical activity combined with cell shape and genetic information.

It’s a lot of data to stitch together and make sense of, Hawrylycz said. “AI is a perfect tool” for the job, he said, because it excels at finding patterns.

The findings could help guide future treatments, but the work remains basic research rather than clinical research, Hawrylycz said.

The new research is the first major installment of the third phase of a brain-mapping effort that began in 2014. The first phase demonstrated that scientists could analyze individual cells on a large scale. The second produced an atlas of the mouse brain.

BICAN aims to create a standardized atlas describing cells throughout the brains of humans and other primates. Hawrylycz said the work is expected to take another two or three years.

#5399. Strategy Bitcoin vs. BitMine Ethereum: Which Crypto Treasury Is Better Positioned for a Market Recovery?

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Strategy is buying more Bitcoin while Tom Lee’s BitMine keeps loading up on Ethereum. Both companies are doubling down as crypto prices slide. But their latest purchases reveal two very different bets on the next bull market. Strategy added another 485 BTC, taking its treasury to 850,849 Bitcoin. Meanwhile, BitMine’s Ethereum holdings have climbed to more than 6.07 million ETH, worth $11 billion at current prices.

Neither company is backing away. In fact, both are positioning themselves for a recovery that could dramatically revalue their massive crypto treasuries. The question is which strategy has the better chance of delivering the biggest payoff.

Michael Saylor’s Strategy acquired 485 BTC for $33.4 million between November 9 and November 15, according to its latest SEC filing. The company paid an average of $68,887 per coin, bringing its total holdings to 850,849 BTC.

Strategy has acquired 485 $BTC and repurchased $228M of $STRC. As of 11/15/26, we hold 850,849 BTC and $4.9B of USD Assets. $MSTR https://t.co/cACnaFSMsr

Strategy has now spent $64.2 billion accumulating Bitcoin, with an average acquisition price of $75,452. At Bitcoin’s recent price near $64,200, the treasury is worth roughly $54.6 billion, leaving the company with an estimated $9.6 billion unrealized loss.

That is a substantial paper loss, but Saylor’s accumulation strategy has never depended on buying every Bitcoin at the bottom. Strategy continues using capital markets to expand its position, betting that Bitcoin’s long-term appreciation will eventually overwhelm short-term volatility.

Its latest filing also revealed $244.7 million in proceeds from common stock sales. Strategy allocated $33.4 million toward Bitcoin purchases, while spending $228.1 million repurchasing its STRC preferred shares.

That second transaction is worth watching. Strategy is managing its capital structure while maintaining its Bitcoin accumulation machine. It also reported $4.75 billion in its USD Reserve. The company already controls more than 850,000 BTC, giving shareholders enormous exposure to Bitcoin’s next major move.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

Tom Lee is playing a different game. BitMine’s Ethereum holdings reached 6,070,092 ETH following its latest disclosed purchase of 9,587 ETH. The position represents 4.97% of Ethereum’s circulating supply, bringing the company within touching distance of its ambitious 5% accumulation target.

🧵1/BitMine provided its latest holdings update for November 16, 2026$11.8 billion in total crypto + "moonshots":– 6,077,745 ETH at $1,823 per ETH (per @coinbase)– 216 Bitcoin (BTC)– $180 million stake in Beast Industries @MrBeast– $67 million stake in Eightco Holdings…

At recent prices around $1,820, those holdings are worth $11 billion. But BitMine has another advantage that Strategy cannot replicate with its Bitcoin treasury: staking income.

The company has already staked 5.23 million ETH, or more than 86% of its holdings. Tom Lee projected that fully staking its Ethereum treasury could generate approximately $359 million in annualized rewards.

That creates a potentially powerful combination. BitMine is accumulating a substantial share of Ethereum’s supply while putting most of its holdings to work.

Lee’s thesis extends beyond ETH price appreciation. He sees Ethereum benefiting from institutional tokenization, financial infrastructure moving onchain, and growing demand for blockchain-based settlement.

If those trends accelerate, BitMine could benefit from both Ethereum appreciation and recurring staking rewards.

This is where the competition gets interesting. Strategy has the larger dollar-denominated crypto treasury, but BitMine has a compelling argument for capital efficiency. Bitcoin offers a straightforward scarcity thesis, while Ethereum adds staking and exposure to expanding blockchain activity.

Strategy’s biggest advantage is its enormous Bitcoin position. With 850,849 BTC, even a substantial recovery in Bitcoin could translate into billions of dollars in additional treasury value.

BitMine, however, has built an Ethereum position approaching 5% of circulating supply. Its staking operation gives the company another potential source of returns while waiting for the next market expansion.

There is also a difference in what investors are buying. Strategy offers a concentrated Bitcoin treasury vehicle, while BitMine offers a leveraged corporate bet on Ethereum’s future financial infrastructure.

Our verdict? BitMine has the more productive treasury model, but Strategy remains the heavyweight in corporate crypto accumulation.

If Bitcoin leads the next recovery, Saylor could quickly reclaim the spotlight. If Ethereum outperforms and institutional adoption accelerates, Lee’s strategy could look considerably smarter.

Both companies are effectively making the same bet: today’s market weakness will look insignificant when the next major crypto cycle arrives.

The winner may ultimately depend on which asset leads that recovery. But neither Saylor nor Lee appears interested in waiting for confirmation before accumulating.

#5398. 1 Chase outage and 6 bank failures in 2026 reached customers' money differently

Free daily briefing on global business news.

A Nov. 16 Chase software bug disrupted banks and Zelle, and the FDIC listed 6 failures in 2026. Here is what each meant for customers' money.

When people say their bank is down, they can mean two very different things, and in 2026 Americans saw both. With the loud kind, customers could not reach their money, but none of it was lost. Customers trying to sign in during the November disruption met login errors. Chase said those customers still had access to their accounts and their money, according to TIME. The fear of loss and the reality did not match. The quiet kind is a bank closing for good. Such closures were rare going into this year, with just two bank failures in the U.S. in all of 2025, according to the Chicago Sun-Times. Closures picked up in 2026 but stayed uncommon. How much noise a banking problem makes and how much harm it does are two separate questions, and the answers often differ.

The November disruption felt bigger than it was partly because of when it came. It followed a Microsoft $MSFT outage on the Thursday before and an air traffic control outage on the Friday, then bank customers ran into trouble on Monday, according to The Associated Press. Nothing ties those three breakdowns to a common cause. What they share is timing. Still, a frozen login screen at the end of a week like that feels like a system in danger, while a small bank quietly changing hands on a Friday feels like nothing at all. People's instincts about which trouble is serious can easily run backward, and sorting the two kinds apart is the useful work.

USA TODAY set out to explain the Nov. 16 bank disruption that began at JPMorgan $JPM Chase and to list the year's bank failures, with entries ranging from Zelle to Nano Banc and Tioga-Franklin Savings Bank. The FDIC listed six bank failures in 2026, and none of them had any link to the November disruption. Each was a bank closed over its finances, not a technology breakdown. Read together, the two kinds of trouble show where the real cost of a banking problem falls. Sometimes it is a customer's lost afternoon. Sometimes it is a charge to the insurance fund that backs deposits. The question for any bank customer is which kind of trouble ever reaches their money, and why.

The November 16 bank disruption had a single source, JPMorgan $JPM Chase, and not a breakdown across the whole banking industry. The cause sat inside one institution's own systems, yet customers felt it at once and in large numbers. At the peak, nearly 4,800 to 5,000 reports of problems with Chase reached Downdetector, according to USA TODAY. That many people speaking up in the same stretch of time makes an outage feel like an assault, and the natural first guess is a hack.

The outage had no attacker behind it, which places it among the ordinary failures that have disrupted large banks before. Chase and DHS officials found no evidence of a cyberattack. Major banks have lost their systems to mundane faults in the past. At one large bank, smoke set off an automatic shutoff that cut power to a data center, and in 2016 Bank of New York could not send or receive SWIFT payment messages for 19 hours, according to a Federal Reserve analysis published in 2022. A fault with no villain behind it can still drag on for hours. Ruling out an attacker removes the villain from the story, but it does not remove the risk. A bank's own systems can fail for long stretches without anyone breaking in.

The fault began at one bank. Whether it stayed there is the next question.

On Nov. 16, customers of JPMorgan $JPM Chase were not the only ones who complained. TIME reports that people also flagged problems with Bank of America $BAC, Wells Fargo $WFC, Capital One $COF, Truist and Zelle that day. Bank of America, the next most reported, drew just over 2,000 reports on Downdetector, and Wells Fargo, Capital One, Truist and Zelle drew hundreds each. Those totals were far lighter than the flood of complaints at Chase, where the trouble began. A pattern that heavy at one bank and much lighter at the rest most likely reflects trouble spilling over from Chase, not six separate breakdowns at the same moment.

A bank can draw a flood of complaints while nothing inside it has broken. U.S. Bank customers filed 1,060 reports, according to TIME, yet the bank denied any fault of its own. "U.S. Bank systems are not directly impacted," a U.S. Bank spokesperson said. The likeliest explanation is that its customers were trying to send money to or through Chase that day. A reader who sees their own bank named in an outage report should expect that a payment might stall, not that the bank itself is in trouble.

Zelle was the most misunderstood name among the services customers reported. TIME reports that Zelle, according to its spokesperson, keeps no separate accounts for consumers and holds none of their money. A stalled Zelle payment is a stalled message between two banks, and the dollars stay at the bank on one end or the other. Zelle links many banks, so customers whose own banks were working could still find their transfers held up when Chase had trouble. When Zelle seems down, the banks on either end are the place to look. A delayed transfer could still leave someone waiting for money they needed that day, but the money itself stayed at a bank the whole time.

Customers made the November 16 disruption public through a flood of complaints. At the peak, nearly 4,800 to 5,000 people reported problems with Chase, according to Downdetector. That crowd was large enough to make the day feel like a national emergency, but it counts people who spoke up, not people who lost money. Reports about Zelle came in as well, though many people think of the payment app as separate from any one bank. Early Warning Services owns Zelle, The Associated Press reports, and that company's owners include financial institutions. Banks share that network, so customers who never opened Chase's app could still feel one bank's trouble. The people caught up in the outage were not only Chase customers. Anyone whose payment touched Chase that day could be caught up in it.

The disruption followed individual payments, not whole banks, and customers elsewhere slowed down only when Chase stood on the other side of a transfer. "This is not a systemic issue — other banks may have been impacted by slowness in transactions only to the extent that they were a party to a transaction with us," Joe Evangelisti, spokesman for JPMorgan $JPM Chase, told The Associated Press. That is the bank's own account of its own failure, and readers should weigh it as a claim, not a settled finding. It does fit the complaints about Zelle, whose job is moving money from one bank to another. For someone who banks elsewhere, the risk that day came from sending money to or through Chase, not from any fault at their own bank.

The complaints filled every board that Monday, yet people felt the outage only when their payments crossed the connections between banks, and those connections are the weak point worth watching.

JPMorgan $JPM Chase had its own systems working again on the same day the trouble began. Users had started flagging errors by 11:30 a.m. ET, according to CNBC. While complaints were still arriving, the bank promised a fix before the day was out. "We're working diligently to resolve this by the end of the day today," a JPMorgan spokesperson said. USA TODAY reports that Chase said its transactions were processing normally on Nov. 16, so by the bank's own account it kept that promise. Both the promise and the all-clear came from Chase, and the all-clear covered only its own transactions.

Customers dealt with the trouble for longer than the bank's timeline suggests. People kept reporting problems through Monday night, and the reports largely subsided only in the early hours of Tuesday, Nov. 17. No one has given a separate time when service returned to normal at other banks or at Zelle. For anyone outside Chase, the clearest sign that the trouble had ended was the drop in complaints overnight.

The outage gave no sign of a threat to the money in customers' accounts. Chase and officials at the Department of Homeland Security found no evidence of a cyberattack. By Chase's account, ending the outage meant fixing a fault inside its own systems, not driving out an intruder. For customers, the documented cost was the wait for logins and payments to work again.

A larger question remains: whether the banking system is built to absorb this kind of failure.

The bank where a disruption starts says little about whose payments end up stuck, because banks rely on the same few service providers and send payments to one another all day. The November 16 disruption began at JPMorgan $JPM Chase, according to USA TODAY, but the customers held up that day banked across the system. Federal Reserve Board analysts Chase Englund and Zach Modig report that in a scenario where one provider in their study, which they call Provider 2, was disrupted for an hour on a sample day, only one of the 23 firms most central to the payment network bought its service directly. Nearly all of the banks at the center of that scenario had no direct tie to the provider in trouble. A customer whose bank has no tie to Chase can still get caught in a Chase outage, and the more useful question is whether that bank sends payments along the same paths.

Community banks appear among the firms the payment network leans on most. In the hour the analysts studied, eight of those central firms belonged to a group of community bank holding companies, according to analysts at the Federal Reserve Board. Choosing a smaller bank does not, on its own, keep a customer away from the part of the network where trouble can spread.

The hour of an outage can matter as much as its length. Among the banks in the analysts' sample, about 26% of each day's Fedwire payment volume moved after 5 p.m., according to the Federal Reserve Board. An outage that runs into the evening therefore reaches a large share of those payments, all of which have to settle before the Fedwire settlement day closes at 7 p.m. Eastern. An outage fixed within hours can still be fixed too late, because payments that miss the close wait for the next settlement day even after customers can log in again.

For a household or a business, the real test of an outage is whether the rent, the payroll or the transfer due that day went through, not how long the login screen stayed frozen.

The year's string of bank closings began at a modest lender in Chicago. Metropolitan Capital Bank & Trust closed on Jan. 30, the first of the six bank failures the FDIC recorded in 2026, according to USA TODAY. The Chicago Sun-Times reports that the Illinois Department of Financial and Professional Regulation shut down the bank, which was based in the city's River North neighborhood. A state regulator closed it over its finances, and none of its systems had broken. It was also too small to signal trouble in banking as a whole, with about $261.1 million in assets as of Sept. 30, a modest sum by banking standards. Its customers kept their money because First Independence Bank of Detroit took over all of the deposits, and their accounts continued at the new bank.

The failure did cost money, but the bank's depositors did not pay it. Acting as receiver, the FDIC put the price of this closing for its Deposit Insurance Fund at about $19.7 million, according to the Chicago Sun-Times. The FDIC keeps that fund to cover losses of this kind. "We want to be clear that no depositor will lose any money as a result of this action," said Susana Soriano, acting director of the Division of Banking at the Illinois Department of Financial and Professional Regulation. A bank failure can carry a real price and still leave every customer's account whole, because the FDIC pays that price from its insurance fund.

A failed bank is not new to Chicago. The city has had 22 bank failures since 2000, according to the Chicago Sun-Times, and this closing adds one more to that long record. Soriano says the state closed this bank because it was operating in an unsafe way and did not have enough capital. That broad finding is the only reason on record, and no specific cause has been made public, so the failure points to no particular danger for other banks.

Nobody has explained in public what went wrong inside the bank, but its customers' deposits were already safe at a new bank.

Screenshot: Community Bank & Trust / Google Map

Community Bank and Trust - West Georgia closed so smoothly that its customers lost little more than a weekend. The bank became the second failure of 2026 on May 1, months after the year's first in January, according to the FDIC. That gap shows how rarely banks closed this year. The Georgia Department of Banking and Finance shut the LaGrange, Ga., community bank, and Anchor Bank of Palm Beach Gardens, Fla., took over its insured deposits. Customers ended up with a new bank rather than none, and the old branches reopened as Anchor Bank the following Monday, May 4. They saw none of the error screens that marked the November lockout.

The quiet weekend hid an expensive failure. Community Bank and Trust was a small lender that held $288 million in assets at the end of 2025, according to the FDIC. The modest size of the bank helps explain why its closing drew so little notice. Yet covering the failure is expected to take approximately $97 million out of the Deposit Insurance Fund, a sum that is large next to the bank's own size. Readers can't judge the price of a bank failure from the size of the bank alone. Regulators can close a small bank with little public notice and still draw heavily on the fund that stands behind every insured account.

The only depositors who faced real risk were those with balances above the insurance limit. Approximately $27 million in deposits went beyond that limit, a figure likely to change, according to the FDIC. That money sat in the bank's largest accounts, and it was the only depositor money without insurance behind it. The pattern here runs opposite to the November disruption. In November, nearly everyone was inconvenienced and no one's money was at stake. In LaGrange, almost no one was inconvenienced, and the only money without a guarantee was the part of the largest balances that went past the insurance limit.

A bank on the federal failure list can be one that few people outside a single small town have ever heard of. Kentland Federal Savings and Loan Association, a savings and loan in Kentland, Ind., failed on July 10, 2026, according to an FDIC list of the year's bank failures reported by USA TODAY. It was a very small bank, with about $3.65 million in deposits as of March 31, according to Financial Regulation News. A count of failures treats a bank of that size the same as a much larger one, and the number of closings alone says little about how much money was at stake.

Kentland did not close because of a hack or a system crash. Its own finances gave out. Financial Regulation News reports that the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency shut the association after finding it critically undercapitalized. In plain terms, the bank no longer had enough capital of its own to stay open. Customers cannot check a bank's capital on an app, and trouble of this kind never shows up as a frozen login screen. The problem that ends a bank can be the one its customers are least likely to see coming.

Kentland's depositors did not lose their money. Their deposits are now held at Kentland Bank and remain FDIC-insured, according to Financial Regulation News. Kentland Bank is a separate institution with no affiliation to the failed association. Customers' accounts changed hands, even though the name on their statements barely changed. The town's loss is practical rather than financial, because the association's only branch is closing for good. The FDIC expects to pay for the failure from its Deposit Insurance Fund, not from account holders, at an estimated cost of about $1.2 million, according to an FDIC estimate reported by Financial Regulation News.

A failure this quiet still costs real money, and Kentland's depositors were not the ones who paid it.

Bank failures came closer together in midsummer 2026. Small Business Bank, a lender in Lenexa, Kan., shut on July 17 and became the year's fourth failure only seven days after the Kentland savings and loan closed, according to USA TODAY. The Kansas Office of the State Bank Commissioner closed the bank, and the FDIC took charge as receiver, according to the FDIC. Whether a bank's collapse ever reaches its customers' money depends on that handoff to a federal insurer more than on the failure itself.

For depositors, the failure changed little beyond the name on the sign. Customers got no warning, and the FDIC reports that the public receives no advance notice when a bank is closed. The Farmers State Bank of Oakley, Kan., took on substantially all of the deposits along with certain assets, so savers' money moved to the new bank together with their accounts. The old locations reopened as Farmers State Bank branches, and customers walked through the same doors under a new name. The November outage kept people away from money that was never at risk. This failure ended a bank, and its customers went on banking.

Customers who already held accounts at Farmers State Bank have one detail to know. Their transferred deposits and their existing accounts at the bank are insured separately, according to the FDIC, so the two sets of balances do not fall under a single coverage limit. The rescue covered the depositors and stopped short of the bank's owner. Gardner Bancshares, Inc., the holding company that owned all of the bank's shares, was not included in the receivership.

The safety net carried the depositors through the failure and left the owner outside it.

Credit: Tioga Franklin Savings Bank / Google Reviews

State regulators kept closing banks through the summer, and Tioga-Franklin Savings Bank in Philadelphia became the fifth of the year's six FDIC-listed failures, according to USA TODAY. The FDIC reports that Pennsylvania's Department of Banking and Securities closed the bank on Friday, Aug. 21, 2026. The federal agency counts the closure among the year's failures, but a state agency made the decision. The FDIC stepped in only after the state acted, serving as receiver to take over and wind down what was left of the bank. Anyone tracking the national tally of bank failures is therefore, at least in this case, tracking a state regulator's decision about one local bank.

Depositors at Tioga-Franklin kept the basic services they depended on, even though the closure came without any advance public notice, according to the FDIC. The public learned of the failure only after the bank had already shut. Direct deposits continued as usual through the change of ownership, so paychecks and benefits kept arriving on schedule. The physical bank stayed in place too. Customers can keep using the same locations, which now operate under the name of Second Federal Savings and Loan Association of Philadelphia, a bank based in the same city. They could walk into the same buildings and deal with a local institution rather than a distant one.

A bank closed in Philadelphia that summer, yet its depositors kept both their direct deposits and their branches.

Nano Banc, a lender in Irvine, Calif., failed on Sept. 25, the latest of the six bank failures in 2026, according to FDIC figures reported by USA TODAY. It was a state-chartered member of the Federal Reserve, so the Fed oversaw it directly, according to the Federal Reserve. Regulators had been watching the bank for years before it closed. As early as February 2021, the bank had agreed in writing to corrective terms set by the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco. Nano Banc did not break overnight. Its trouble had been on the public record long before September.

The warnings grew more serious as regulators moved from a written agreement to legal orders. The state of California ordered the bank to cease and desist in December 2021, and the Fed followed the next month with a consent order that became binding on Jan. 18, 2022, according to the Federal Reserve. By the time of the 2022 order, examiners had found unsecured loans to shareholders of Nano Financial Holdings, the bank's parent company. When a bank lends to its owners without collateral, it puts their interests ahead of the safety of depositors' money. Nano Banc also had no permanent chief executive or chief financial officer in 2022, while it still had to carry out the corrective steps its 2021 agreement with the Fed required. The bank faced a large repair job with no one permanently in charge. That was a plausible warning sign, though not a forecast of failure.

The 2022 order reached past the bank to the companies that controlled it, binding both of its holding companies, Allegiant United Holdings and Nano Financial Holdings, according to the Federal Reserve. That fits a problem that involved the bank's owners. Still, a record of warnings does not establish a cause, and no reason for the September closing has been made public. The orders from 2021 and 2022 are evidence of long-running trouble, not an explanation of why the bank failed.

The warnings that mattered here never appeared as error screens. They were public orders from regulators, issued years before the failure, and for anyone worried about their own bank, those orders are a quieter and more telling place to look.

#5397. Amazon Reportedly Has an Ambitious Secret Plan to Ensure That You Never Shop Anywhere Else

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

A proposed initiative would give shoppers fewer reasons to leave Amazon.

Amazon’s secret plan goes beyond selling you everything. It also wants to be the place where you decide what to buy in the first place.

According to a recent Reuters report citing an internal document, Amazon is working on a secret initiative called World Product Graph to catalog products across the Internet, including items that it doesn’t currently sell. The project involves gathering data on essentially every item for sale on the web to keep shoppers from taking their research elsewhere.

World Product Graph could ensure that Amazon is the first place shoppers visit to figure out what they want to purchase. A detailed database could help customers compare product models, understand features and explore alternatives without jumping between search engines, manufacturers’ websites and competing stores.

That would give Amazon a stronger hold over the product research space, challenging Google while giving shoppers another reason to choose it over Walmart and other retailers.

“Amazon cannot be the go-destination for every shopping mission if customers must leave to research product relationships on Google, brand websites, and review sites,” the document read, according to Reuters. “These answers exist, ​but the only way to find them has been to leave Amazon for painstaking research on brand websites, third party review sites and tech forums.”

The project could also help Amazon navigate a shift in how people shop. Currently, some shoppers are using AI agents to research products and potentially make purchases. AI agents need reliable product information to make recommendations, which is something the World Product Graph could provide.

If the proposal becomes reality, it could offer Amazon an advantage that goes beyond competitive pricing. The site could offer information that makes other shopping sites feel less useful by comparison.

In a statement to Reuters, Amazon said it is “constantly working on new ideas and technologies.”

“Draft, outdated documents often paint an incomplete picture and the existence of a brainstorming document such as this one doesn’t necessarily reflect our current plans,” the company said in the statement.

The leaked document presents the proposal as a future press announcement, with October 1, 2027, as a target launch date. Reuters was not able to confirm a timeline or if Amazon would move forward with the plans.

Amazon currently has a stronger hold on shoppers who know what they want rather than those who are still deciding. A 2025 Morgan Stanley research report cited by Reuters found that 57% of online shoppers began product research on Google, compared with just 16% on Amazon.

Once shoppers have a specific product in mind, the rankings reverse. Amazon becomes the leading starting point, accounting for 41% of searches, compared with 23% for Google and 18% for Walmart.

Google currently leads in discovery, while Amazon has the advantage when customers arrive with a clearer purchase in mind.

A detailed database could help customers compare product models, understand features and explore alternatives without jumping between search engines, manufacturers’ websites and competing stores.
