#5387. Meet ‘Captain Keel,’ the 37-year-old steering a Bitcoin miner into the AI data center gold rush

In late 2023, Bitcoin miner Ben Gagnon concluded that his employer, Bitfarms of Quebec, was in the wrong business. For Gagnon, Bitfarms’ greatest value lay not in the giant racks of CPUs that generated Bitcoin, but the immense power supplies it controlled. The then 34-year-old chief mining officer who’d launched his career crafting makeshift crypto-minting rigs in Hong Kong and Taipei, reckoned that Bitfarms could make much more money by exiting the field full stop, demolishing the “mines,” selling the chips that filled them, and re-channeling its plentiful flow of megawatts to power-craving industrial users at plants newly built on the Bitfarms sites.

The big revelation came in March of 2024, when Core Scientific and CoreWeave unveiled a stunning new deal. Bitcoin titan Core Scientific would refashion a mining facility in Austin, Texas, as an AI data center, and rent the power and buildings to the neocloud. That Bitcoin-to-AI play struck Gagnon as a model that Bitfarms could follow on a grand scale, from Quebec to Washington state. “It was the big aha moment,” recalls Gagnon. “Suddenly, we saw who the right customer was.”

At the time, Bitfarms was mired in turmoil. In early 2024, the board was searching for its third leader in five years. The sitting chief agreed to depart when Bitfarms named a successor, but in May—believe it or not while still CEO—instead filed a $27 million suit for “wrongful termination and breach of contract,” plunging this Canadian exemplar of all-green, hydro-driven Bitcoin mining into legal warfare. Pounded by a sharp drop in the token’s prices, Bitfarms’ stock was languishing, and a rival pounced. Two days after the board fired the CEO, Riot Platforms unveiled a hostile $930 million takeover bid for Bitfarms at a lowly $2.30 a share, 75% below its peak in late 2021. After Bitfarms installed a “poison pill” defense, Riot launched a website dubbed “A Better Bitfarms” trashing allegedly poor corporate governance, and demanding the departure of the co-founder named as interim chief.

The board tapped Gagnon to both quell the war versus Riot, and pursue the strategy of total transformation he’d been advocating. In July of 2024, Gagnon took the helm, and over the next few months, helped broker an agreement where Riot named a director of its choice, and the co-founder left the board. Riot halted its attack and has since sold its shares.

While battling for Bitfarms’ independence, Gagnon kept his sights locked on engineering the Big Pivot. He describes the mission as “pursuing a strategy of steering the business away from Bitcoin mining, and taking it over to a pure energy infrastructure play in support of AI and high-performance computing. We’d shift our focus entirely to addressing the defining constraint of the most important technology of our lifetime.”

The venture needed a rebrand, so Gagnon picked “Keel” to evoke the structural backbone of a vessel that, as he says, “provides stability and converts energy into forward motion,” a reference to the stable long-term leases that he expects to provide a smooth and lucrative course versus the storms he encountered in Bitcoin. He’s now attempting to pull a hat trick seldom seen in the corporate world, the total reinvention of a large enterprise, including in product and nationality, on a crazy-rhythm beat. On April 1, 2026, the franchise was reborn as Keel Infrastructure and changed its domicile from Canada to the U.S. The photo on Gagnon’s X profile reprises the nautical theme, adding a whimsical accent. Gagnon grins from a porthole-sized frame, sporting his usual oversized rimless glasses, and a gold-braided yachtsman’s cap displaying his user name, “Captain Keel.”

Now 37, Gagnon is making by far his biggest wager yet in a career that careened from mining Bitcoin in remote oil patches by rescuing flared natural gas to rehabilitating some of the world’s dirtiest energy sites under the banner of AI.

Gagnon is the son of two American parents who settled in Hong Kong, where he attended international grammar and high schools that offered lots of, as he puts it, “Mandarin as a second language courses.” He gained a bachelor’s degree in business and economics (and a minor in Mandarin) at the Indiana University’s Kelley School of Business in 2011, on the Bloomington campus. “I got fascinated by Bitcoin, and could have bought it for 73 cents,” he recalls. “Instead, I did what every college kid does. I bought beer.” Over the next three-and-a-half years, he reflected on that choice while watching Bitcoin climb 1,400-fold to over $1,000.

Returning home, he attained a master’s in computer security and networking at the University of Hong Kong, where he took cryptography courses that renewed his interest in the science of generating cryptocurrencies. After graduating, Gagnon worked as a network technician at a company that offered mobile applications for investor conferences and other events. After less than two years, he quit his job and moved again, this time to Taiwan. His new venture: Building and running a jerry-rigged Ethereum mine at the home of his girlfriend’s (now his wife’s) parents in Taipei. “Everyone thought it was Bitcoin 2.0, so I figured, I’m not going to miss this opportunity like I missed Bitcoin as a college kid,” says Gagnon.

The business drew unwanted attention by using ten times the electricity of a typical home in Taipei—specifically, the phenomenon alerted the police. “They couldn’t figure out what we were doing,” he recalls. “They thought we were growing marijuana upstairs and kept raiding the house, like on a weekly basis. So we had to explain to the police every week that we weren’t doing anything illegal.” It took only a couple of intolerable months before Gagnon saw the necessity of uprooting his facility from his future in-laws’ home.

Gagnon then ran his operation in Guangzhou on China’s mainland, but shut down after two years due to a tough regulatory climate. “Let’s just say that the laws were somewhat selective for a young foreigner navigating a new industry,” he avows. In 2019, he joined Bitfarms, one of several Bitcoin miners, including HIVE, that sprouted in Quebec during the 2017 to 2018 boom, drawn by the province’s plentiful and relatively inexpensive hydroelectric power. As chief of development, his charge was expanding the business to the U.S. and other energy-rich areas of Canada.

Gagnon focused on the huge but remote Alberta oil patch. “I was always looking for the cheapest energy sources for mining, and that was Alberta,” he says. The producers were “flaring” the natural gas created from drilling, since no pipelines existed for sending it to population centers. Gagnon created the first containerized Bitcoin data center that incorporated a generator and offered 100% financing. His mobile units channeled natural gas right at the far-flung drilling sites for minting tokens. His rigs empowered the drillers to monetize energy they were burning into the atmosphere. The product proved a big winner for his new employer. “The drillers were using gas that cost 1.5 cents a MW versus 6 cents in the U.S.,” he recalls. “So we got great prices for our equipment because the payback period for the drillers was so short.”

When Gagnon started pushing the AI remake in 2023, he doubled-down on a possible acquisition that ideally fitted the new plotline. His target was Stronghold Digital, a startup using one of the most unusual models in all of Bitcoin mining. From the mid-19th century to the 1970s, mines in Pennsylvania routinely separated the low-quality coal—scraps mixed with rocks, often with high sulfur or ash content—from the good stuff. Children called “breaker boys” seated at conveyor belts or chutes would pick out the slate and rock by hand, no gloves permitted—brutal work that often left their fingers bleeding. The legacy: Black carbon mountains scarring the towns of Pennsylvania. For decades, the sites Stronghold owned had been performing a public service by scooping truckloads of waste coal and burning it in their boilers to supply electricity to the local grids, while pocketing big subsidies for the effort. The state government reasoned that the benefits of cleansing the countryside more than compensated for allowing just about the dirtiest form of electrical generation in America.

In 2021, a pair of entrepreneurs turned those locations into Bitcoin mining operations. But Stronghold way overinvested in chips and other equipment, and by 2023 it was foundering, hammered by crippling debt and legal disputes. Gagnon identified Stronghold’s sweet spots, one each in eastern and western Pennsylvania, as ideal locations for AI campuses. Stronghold already controlled significant amounts of power, but held the potential to obtain much more. Working with its owners, Gagnon applied to utilities and state authorities for big new batches of megawatts. Once assured the approvals were at hand, Gagnon, in August 2024, after a month as CEO, landed an agreement to purchase Stronghold for $175 million.

Increasingly, AI leaders are viewing power as the toughest chokepoint in the AI supply chain. As OpenAI co-founder and CEO Sam Altman characterizes the issue, “The bottleneck for AI isn’t code, it’s electrons.” Adds Elon Musk, “The limiting factor is fundamentally electrical power…[that’s leading to] producing more chips than the hyperscalers can plug in and turn on.” And Greg Abel, CEO of Berkshire Hathaway, a major energy provider to AI data centers via its sundry utilities, concurs, calling access to megawatts a “big constraint” for rapid buildouts.

The backlash against AI data centers gained fresh force on Election Day, when so many candidates seeking restraints or outright bans on their spread won congressional and statewide races. That result may actually strengthen the hand of the Bitcoin contingent, since they’ve already got a grip on the energy pipelines the hyperscalers and neoclouds need, and appear willing to pay up for. Put simply, the future “scarcity value” of the crucial asset these crypto producers control likely jumped on November 3. Gagnon calls Keel’s position “bird in the hand economics.”

Keel stands among the first and largest crypto operators to follow Core Scientific into AI. But today, more than ten major players are making the switch, in part or whole. Among those that have already secured big, long-term contracts are Riot, which clinched a $9.1 billion lease from Anthropic for the AI campus at its Bitcoin mine in Milam County, Texas; Hut 8, partnering on a $7 billion contract with Google and Anthropic at its River Bend complex in Louisiana; and Applied Digital, which will serve CoreWeave under an $11 billion agreement at its forthcoming campus in Ellendale, North Dakota.

All of these converts are essentially re-purposing the same land and power, or sometimes more of the latter, that they deployed to produce Bitcoin for the AI buildout. But they’re taking different approaches. The crypto-to-AI crowd falls into two categories, both in how completely they’re shifting, and the templates they embrace. On the first score, several participants are taking the Keel route by totally exiting Bitcoin for AI, including Core Scientific, Cipher Mining and Genesis Digital. Another group that encompasses Riot, Hut 8, HIVE Digital Technologies, and TeraWulf are adopting a hybrid model where they both channel power to AI campuses and continue to mine Bitcoin.

On the second criterion, the two main business models are “compute provider” and “developer” or co-location (co-lo) purveyor. As a compute provider, the former or hybrid Bitcoin outfit delivers a turnkey project. It commissions a contractor, often a REIT, to erect the buildings, and typically rents the structures long-term from the builder-partner. It then packs the cavernous boxes with GPUs and other gear that constitute by far the most expensive part of the project. The owner’s product is the full computing package that it then leases to the hyperscalers or neoclouds for running the likes of Google’s Gemini and Anthropic’s Claude.

The developer or co-lo arrangement works much the same way, except that the site’s owner doesn’t supply the hardware, and hence shoulders much lower up-front costs. Instead, it’s the hyperscaler or neocloud, a Microsoft or Crusoe, that brings the GPUs and other equipment. The company branching out from Bitcoin mining both supplies the structures that it leases from the REIT or other contractor, and the power that runs it––MW secured on long-term utility contracts form its essential business. The still-active or former Bitcoin miner rents the “powered shells” to the compute providers, for operating, say OpenAI’s ChatGPT or Microsoft’s Copilot. In today’s market, the developer garners a big markup on the scarcest item in AI.

The reasons so many are crossing from Bitcoin to follow either one or both of these strategies: Each megawatt of power at work generates far more cash flow at an AI campus than at plants churning codes to win the signature crypto coin. In a recent interview on the Schwab Network, Christian Lopez, head of blockchain and digital assets at broker-dealer Cohen & Co., estimates the numbers, over five years, at $1.7 million per KW for Bitcoin and almost five times as much, $7.9 million, for an AI campus. What about revenues? Sarah Friar, CFO of OpenAI, posits that each 1 GW (1,000 MW) fueling an AI data center garners $10 billion in revenues. Once again, the number can be one-fifth that amount for a Bitcoin mine.

Data center pioneers divide into two camps. The “compute” competitors (Bitdeer of Singapore, IREN of Australia and Canada’s HIVE Digital, Hut 8 to some degree) spend massively to buy the chips and rent them out, in exchange for higher rents, shorter leases, and more risk. For example, HIVE has a $350 million, 5-year deal with an as yet unnamed AI stalwart for campuses on Bell Canada sites where it’s supplying the hardware. “The cost of the GPUs is $190 million off the bat,” says HIVE CEO Aydin Kilic, who predicts the project will be multiple times as profitable per KW as Bitcoin mining.

By contrast, Keel is a pure-play developer. It doesn’t buy and install the GPUs and other gear that constitute as much as 70% of data centers that cost roughly $50 billion a GW to create (the other 30% covers land, the buildings and costs of connecting or providing onsite power). “We’re strictly in the power business, and make money on the difference between what we pay the utilities, and what the compute providers pay us on their leases,” says Gagnon.

Keel’s edge: It sits on an enormous amount of power. It has 2.2 GWs that are either approved for use, or in the last stages of the approval process. That’s more than the 1.9 GW that OpenAI was reportedly marshaling at the close of 2025. Gagnon acknowledges that Keel as a developer won’t collect revenues nearly as large as the miners turned compute providers, but insists that his cash flows will be more secure, and that the relatively low cost of the power and physical centers as a share of the whole makes customers willing to pay big premiums to get MW in a hurry.

In part, that’s because as of now, those AI campuses are sumptuously profitable. “The gross margins for data centers are 85%, and of the 15% in costs, only a max of 2% to 4% goes to leasing the power and buildings,” Gagnon explains. “So if a customer spends twice as much, their margins may ease to 81% or 83%. The GPUs in their warehouses are depreciating fast. So they’re saying, I’d rather take a hit to 83% in gross margin and start generating revenue in 6 months than wait 12 months for a margin that’s 2 points higher. And that’s what we’re seeing.”

Keel is shepherding three “priority projects” closest to clearing all hurdles and to signing leases. One of them is a former Stronghold facility: Panther Creek, 85 miles north of Philadelphia. Keel acquired another Pennsylvania site in a separate transaction. It’s located at the opposite end of the state in Sharon, near Youngstown, Ohio. On the two sites combined, Keel’s in the process of securing over 450 MW from the local grids. The third “priority” is a hydro project in Moses Lake, Washington, ringed by Seattle, Spokane and Portland. Gagnon marvels at the sight of the famous Boeing repair field almost adjoining the Keel site. “You’re driving to our facility and you’ll see 100 different 737 MAX, all painted different colors, what a fun sight!”

Gagnon points out that approvals fall into three categories: zoning, environmental, and development. At Moses Lake, Keel’s scored all three, and the site’s now under construction. At Sharon and Panther Creek, it has secured both zoning and development, and is working through the environmental permits, the final step. The most difficult requirement, he states, is zoning. “It’s the one that’s most political, most community-centric, and most emotional,” he says. “Projects can get shut down if you don’t behave the right way with community leaders. We got really good at advocating for Bitcoin mines that are a much harder sell than AI campuses.”

The second ex-Stronghold site is the biggest of them all, the 700-acre Scrubgrass facility near Sharon, and roughly an hour north of Pittsburgh. There, Keel’s applied for a massive 1 GW of power, 45% of the total capacity it’s seeking. At Scrubgrass, Keel is still working through all the initial permitting stages for securing power.

Gagnon says the biggest challenge isn’t attracting customers, it’s getting the final environmental permits in place. But he’s already encountered delays. In May, Gagnon guided to obtaining leases at all three priority projects by the end of 2026. But on the Q3 earnings call, he said that no deals will be signed this year, and declined to give dates for signing customers on those projects.

The rub: Keel’s now generating puny revenues since it’s now left Bitcoin mining and isn’t yet making money from AI. Gagnon’s sitting on a big cushion, having raised almost $600 million in convertible debt last year, and another almost $300 million by emptying its Bitcoin trove. Still, Keel’s burning cash fast. Will its trove prove big enough to fund crossing the span to AI on time? Investors are cautious about Keel’s prospects, to put it mildly. Keel’s stock dropped around 20% on Gagnon’s announcement of no deals this year, and currently has a paltry market cap of around $1.3 billion, about the same as when Riot bid back in 2024.

On the plus side, Gagnon’s collected a portfolio that potentially features some of the best AI sites in America and Canada. He notes that the big customers are now showing a strong preference for facilities near big population centers, just where he’s concentrating. “The difference is that until now, there’s been so much AI model training that wasn’t for customers, so it didn’t matter where the campus was located. The normal things that would have guided a developer to find a project and select a piece of land were thrown out the window in the interest of scale and time.”

Now, he says, the business is moving strongly towards “inference” where the compute providers sell to banks, research labs, call centers and other customers. “That’s where most of the money will be made, not on the retail side,” he says. “As the market moves to inference, more and more of the traditional data center qualities will come into play.” He notes that compute works much more efficiently when it’s near the customer than hundreds or thousands of miles away in a remote rural area. “It’s so important to get the fiber close to where people live and businesses are located, and in the frenzy, that’s been forgotten,” says Gagnon. The big distances cause sluggish responses that lead to poor user experiences in fields such as autonomous driving and interactive chatbots. Plus, he says, in the weeks leading up to and following the midterms, “we’ve seen a big uptick in level of demand and prioritization of our sites in Pennsylvania, driven that the support of data center had changed in many states. The Democratic candidates who won in Pennsylvania ran on platform favoring responsible data center development, the opposite the scenario in most other states.”

“The differentiator will be location, location and location,” says Gagnon. “This is a real estate industry and location is hugely important in real estate. That’s why you have so many cloud data centers in Loudoun County, Va. near D.C. and Quincy near Seattle. We’re near New York, Philly, and Pittsburgh, and have a great position in the Pacific Northwest, where there’s a big shortage of AI campuses. If you’re close to where the demand comes from, that should justify a premium going forward, just as it has in the past for data centers.”

Gagnon is especially bullish on the union of AI and the Keystone State. “Pennsylvania built this country, it had all the resources needed to launch the industrial revolution, steel, coal, railroads, natural gas. Texas was the first mover in AI data centers, and now Pennsylvania is the second mover. And we’ll be number one in Pennsylvania.”

It’s a long way from waste coal to GPUs. And Gagnon’s got a plausible story: The big guys have the GPUs, in fact too many of them. But he and his Bitcoin brethren have a lot of what the giants now need most, the power. The question for Keel is how fast Gagnon can turn it on.

Shawn Tully is a senior editor-at-large at Fortune, covering the biggest trends in business, aviation, politics, and leadership.

#5386. Nvidia’s interim CEO spent 13 years behind the scenes at Microsoft

by Todd Bishop on Nov 12, 2026 at 10:45 amNovember 14, 2026 at 11:15 am

Colette Kress, named Nvidia’s interim CEO on Thursday after Jensen Huang’s abrupt resignation, spent 13 years at Microsoft earlier in her career, including four as chief financial officer of the Redmond company’s Server and Tools business.

But to say she was under the radar would be an understatement: a search of Seattle-area news archives turns up a single mention of her name from her Microsoft years, in a 2007 press release listing her as a presenter at a Hotel 1000 seminar on Microsoft’s budgeting software.

Of course, that’s to be expected. Divisional finance execs aren’t typically public faces at Microsoft or anywhere else. But now she finds herself in the global spotlight, running the chipmaker at the center of the AI boom — at least for the time being.

Nvidia announced Thursday that Huang resigned as president, CEO and a member of the board, effective immediately, following reports of an extramarital affair with a woman U.S. intelligence officials reportedly concluded was a Chinese spy, and a second affair with a direct report.

Kress will remain CFO while the board searches for a permanent CEO, considering internal and external candidates. Director Harvey Jones, the former Synopsys CEO, becomes Nvidia’s first board chair. Nvidia shares fell more than 13% in early trading.

Wall Street analyst Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives & Co. wrote in a note Thursday morning that Kress has built “enormous credibility” inside and outside Nvidia. “We always believed she would eventually be CEO of a major public tech company, but she would have to leave Nvidia after many years there,” he wrote.

Kress joined Microsoft in 1997 after finance roles at Texas Instruments, and held senior positions in corporate planning and finance before becoming chief financial officer of the Server and Tools business, which sold Windows Server, SQL Server and Visual Studio. Her LinkedIn profile lists her as a Microsoft corporate vice president from April 2006 to November 2010.

Server and Tools was also a training ground for Microsoft’s current leadership. Satya Nadella took over the business in 2011, after Kress left, and used it as a springboard to the CEO job three years later. Amy Hood, now Microsoft’s CFO, served as its chief of staff earlier in her career.

From Microsoft, Kress went to Cisco as senior vice president and CFO of its Business Technology and Operations Finance organization. Nvidia hired her as CFO in September 2013, ending a search of more than two years.

Now as Nvidia’s interim CEO, her first major test comes quickly. Nvidia reports fiscal third-quarter results Tuesday, Nov. 17, with an earnings call scheduled for 2 p.m. Pacific.

#5385. Why Growing Brands Have an Edge Over Established Competitors in the AI Search Race

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Here’s why — and how — high-growth brands can leverage AEO to make gains against bigger competitors.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

My agency’s clients are heavily indexed in SMB B2B tech brands looking to raise money. Since we were founded in 2017, our clients have raised more than $2.5 billion in funding. Aside from having differentiated products, our most successful clients have had one thing in common: the ability to move swiftly and with agility to navigate shifts in micro and macro markets.

The same pattern is holding true with clients gaining market share through AEO (answer engine optimization). Brands are finding an edge by moving quickly to tackle the growth opportunity of a highly dynamic search landscape — one in which user behavior is changing by the day.

Here’s why — and how — they’re able to leverage AEO to make gains against bigger competitors.

Legacy content matters less than you’d think. Large language models (LLMs) carry a measurable recency bias. A decade’s worth of archived content doesn’t provide established companies with the head start many executives assume it does.

Speed wins in a market that changes monthly. AEO is one of the most dynamic disciplines in marketing today; what works this quarter may be obsolete next quarter. Large organizations rarely move with the agility this demands. Meanwhile, more and more less mature companies are hiring for fluency in LLMs and the content that feeds them.

Legacy assets can become liabilities. Structuring new content for AEO is far easier than retrofitting thousands of existing pages. Newer brands can build clean site architecture and easily retrievable content, all free of accumulated technical debt, from day one. They can also borrow credibility through comparison content, which performs exceptionally well in AEO and traditional SEO. Positioning yourself directly against an established competitor also puts your brand in the same conversation.

Paired with disciplined execution, those structural advantages can translate quickly into results and growth.

Dense paragraphs serve neither readers nor LLMs. “TL;DR” summaries, key takeaways, numbered lists and FAQs with concise answers are easy for both humans and machines to digest. When your content answers a likely prompt clearly and succinctly, it becomes a likely candidate for citation.

The most common obstacle I see among business leaders is time. Producing content for owned channels (your blog, LinkedIn, YouTube) and earned media (bylines and features on third-party platforms) is essential for building AEO momentum, but leaders rarely have time to take over those responsibilities on their own.

Work with your marketing leader to identify team members who can contribute insights on relevant topics, and commit to a sustainable cadence. Twice a week across your properties is a reasonable benchmark.

When I say “consistent,” I mean both in cadence and message; every piece must reinforce your positioning. If you sell the leading SaaS bookkeeping platform for local retailers, don’t publish content aimed at big-box chains. Inconsistency scrambles the signal LLMs use to understand who you are.

Through networking events, discovery calls and pitch meetings, I hear common questions, especially around emerging channels like AEO. Our client services leaders see the same thing: As trends develop, identical questions emerge across verticals and growth stages.

When your customers and prospects keep asking the same question, that’s a signal for you (or your team) to address that question publicly. Create a system for capturing these questions and feeding them directly into your content calendar. It’s the most reliable way to stay relevant and remain part of the conversation.

LLMs need an unambiguous picture of who you are and what you do. Audit your company address and contact details across your website and social profiles, update your Google Business Profile, and confirm that every online directory listing is accurate and current. This is basic hygiene, but it’s frequently overlooked.

Attributing revenue to AI search with precision remains difficult, largely because much of today’s buyer journey happens without a click to your website. We rely on a three-part framework that delivers reliable directional data:

Visibility and share of voice: Use an AI visibility tracking tool (we use Profound) to monitor how often your brand appears relative to competitors on high-priority industry prompts.

Citations and traffic: Use web analytics (we use Google Analytics) to measure traffic arriving from LLM citations.

Conversions and revenue: Track conversions in your analytics platform, including LLM referral traffic, which in my experience does account for a small share of total conversions. Supplement this with post-conversion surveys asking customers where they first discovered your brand. The data is directional rather than exact, but it provides a decent idea of impact.

None of these strategies is especially complex. What they require is resources, budget and prioritization from leadership. Especially for the B2B tech sector, where LLMs use is proliferating at all points of the purchase journey, leveraging inherent advantages in AEO is one of the most effective paths to the growth that piques investors’ interest.

My agency’s clients are heavily indexed in SMB B2B tech brands looking to raise money. Since we were founded in 2017, our clients have raised more than $2.5 billion in funding. Aside from having differentiated products, our most successful clients have had one thing in common: the ability to move swiftly and with agility to navigate shifts in micro and macro markets.

The same pattern is holding true with clients gaining market share through AEO (answer engine optimization). Brands are finding an edge by moving quickly to tackle the growth opportunity of a highly dynamic search landscape — one in which user behavior is changing by the day.

Here’s why — and how — they’re able to leverage AEO to make gains against bigger competitors.

#5384. XML pioneer Jean Paoli’s startup Docugami acquired by Inveniam after open-source partnership

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Todd Bishop on Nov 12, 2026 at 12:15 pmNovember 12, 2026 at 12:15 pm

Docugami, the Seattle-area startup led by XML co-creator Jean Paoli, has been acquired by Inveniam, a Detroit-area company that uses blockchain to help investors verify the data behind assets such as commercial real estate and private loans.

The deal follows a partnership this summer in which the companies released DGML, Docugami’s open-source format for turning business documents into data that AI agents can use and check.

Financial terms of the acquisition weren’t disclosed. All of Docugami’s employees are joining Inveniam, a Docugami spokesperson said. The team numbers about 50 including contractors. Paoli becomes Inveniam’s chief product and technology officer, and Docugami will keep operating from Kirkland, according to the announcement.

Paoli co-founded Docugami in 2018 after more than 20 years at Microsoft, where he helped create XML and the Office file formats.

The startup, based in Kirkland, Wash., raised a $10 million seed round in 2020 led by SignalFire, with backing from Bob Muglia, the former Microsoft executive and Snowflake CEO. Grammarly, the writing-assistant company now known as Superhuman, later disclosed that it had taken part in the round, its first investment in another company.

Prior to the acquisition, Docugami ranked No. 155 on the GeekWire 200, our list of the Pacific Northwest’s top independent, privately held startups.

DGML labels each piece of a document by what it is — a base rent, a loan payment, a liability cap — so a single figure can be traced back to the page it came from. Inveniam records a digital fingerprint of each of those data points on its blockchain, called NVNM Chain, so any later change shows up.

Inveniam executives said Thursday morning on a livestream with Paoli that DGML solves a problem they’ve had in bringing on new clients: every client’s documents are different, which required templates and standard formats before the data could be used.

“One promise I want to make personally: DGML stays open and its openness is strategic to Inveniam,” Paoli wrote in a LinkedIn post.

Inveniam, led by CEO Patrick O’Meara, also acquired Mantra, a crypto company that provided the original technology for NVNM Chain, earlier this year. Mantra co-founder John Patrick Mullin said on the livestream that NVNM Chain will move to its own independent blockchain, with the main network expected to launch in the next few weeks.

Fees on that network will help fund buybacks of an NVNM cryptocurrency token, Mullin said. O’Meara proposed a separate session on when that token will launch.

#5383. Circle Begins CCTP V1 Wind-Down Amid Doc Mismatch

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Burn limits on Circle's legacy USDC bridge began falling on October 31, and the V1 contracts pause on December 1.

On the same migration page, a block of instructions written for AI coding assistants still says Noble, Sui and Aptos "still require V1." Circle's own release notes say two of those three chains moved to V2 weeks ago.

Circle's legacy cross-chain transfer protocol entered its final month today. From October 31, burn limits on CCTP V1 start falling toward zero, and on December 1 the V1 contracts pause. Any app still using them will stop moving USDC between chains.

Most coverage has focused on those two dates. But the guide developers are told to follow, Circle's V1-to-V2 migration page, contains a mistake in the section written for AI tools.

Embedded in the page is an "Agent Instructions" block, guidance meant for AI coding assistants that read the documentation for developers. It says: "Noble, Sui, and Aptos still require V1." For two of those three chains, Circle's other published records say the opposite.

The schedule is fixed. Circle announced in an August 27 blog post that "CCTP V1 (Legacy) deprecation begins October 31, 2026 and completes on December 1, 2026."

From today, V1 burn limits fall, and the migration guide says "message limits will tighten over time until no new burns can be initiated." On December 1 the V1 contracts pause, and any integration still pointing at them can no longer transfer USDC between chains.

Circle has been firm about this. "Migration from CCTP V1 (Legacy) to CCTP V2 is required, not just recommended," the company wrote, adding that V2 "uses separate contracts and APIs and is not backward compatible."

Funds already in transit are protected. The guide says "all pending redemptions will remain available" during the phase-out, and that Circle "will maintain minter allowances greater than the total of pending attestations."

The migration page has two audiences. Human readers see the main guide. AI coding assistants also parse a separate instruction block, which tells them how to answer developer questions.

In that block, the guidance is clear: "Noble, Sui, and Aptos still require V1."

The main text above it says something different. According to the human-facing guide, "CCTP V2 contracts are available on all CCTP V1 chains except for Noble and Sui," and "Sui will be supported by V2 before the deprecation begins." Aptos isn't listed as an exception there at all.

So one page gives two different answers about the same chains, and the out-of-date answer is the one written for AI tools.

Circle's 2026 CCTP release notes show how out of date the instruction is:

Circle's supported chains and domains page now lists both Sui and Aptos in its CCTP table, with Standard Transfer support. The page's V1-only section names one chain: Noble.

As of today, Aptos has had V2 for more than two months and Sui for more than three weeks. The instruction telling AI tools that both "still require V1" was overtaken by Circle's own updates before the shutdown began.

Noble is the one chain in that line where the instruction is still accurate, and it is leaving CCTP entirely.

In a September 10 announcement, Circle said "Noble will not receive CCTP V2" and set out its exit:

For Noble, V1 is the only route available, and it is being closed.

A wrong line in documentation would normally be a small issue, but the timing makes this one more serious.

Many developers now ask AI assistants to write or update integration code, and those assistants read documentation like this page. A developer asking how to bridge USDC to Sui or Aptos could be told, based on Circle's own instruction block, to use V1. That is the route whose burn limits started falling today and which pauses in a month.

The fix in the code is not small either. Moving to V2 means:

An integration built on V1 now would have to be rebuilt within weeks.

For teams working with Sui and Aptos, the published records point one way: build on V2, using the contract addresses for domains 8 and 9. Don't follow the V1 guidance from the agent-instruction block.

For Noble, the deadline is January 12, 2027. Before then, integrators need to remove Noble as a CCTP route, and holders need to move or redeem their USDC.

For everyone else, the burn-limit reductions have started. December 1 is the last day V1 integrations work, and any app still on V1 after that will stop moving USDC between chains.

#5382. Current price of oil as of November 17, 2026

As of 8:15 a.m. Eastern Time today, oil is trading at $94.94 per barrel, based on the Brent benchmark we’ll explain in a bit. That’s $1.74 below yesterday morning’s level and about $30.70 higher than where it stood a year ago.

No one can say for sure where oil prices will go next. Many forces shape the market—but at the core, it’s still about supply and demand. When risks like a potential recession or war ramp up, oil prices can change direction quickly.

When you buy gas at the pump, you’re covering more than the cost of crude oil. You’re also paying for every step in the process, including refineries, wholesalers, taxes, and the markup your local gas station adds.

Even so, crude oil has the biggest influence on what you pay, often making up more than half the cost per gallon. When oil prices jump, gas prices usually climb right along with them. But when oil falls, gas prices often slip much more slowly—a pattern sometimes called “rockets and feathers.”

If an emergency hits, the U.S. keeps a backup supply of crude oil called the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. It’s mainly there to protect energy security during crises, such as sanctions, catastrophic storm damage, even war. It can also help cushion the blow when supply shocks send prices soaring.

It’s not meant to solve long-term problems. Instead, it provides quick relief for consumers and helps keep vital parts of the economy moving, like essential industries, emergency services, and public transit.

Oil and natural gas are two of the world’s primary energy sources. A big change in oil prices can affect natural gas by extension. For example, if oil prices increase, some industries may swap natural gas for some segments of their operations where possible, which which increases demand for natural gas.

When looking at how oil performs, two main benchmarks stand out:

Of the two, Brent gives a better picture of global oil performance because it prices a large share of the world’s traded crude. It’s also the go-to for tracking oil’s historical trends. In fact, even the U.S. Energy Information Administration now relies on Brent as its primary reference in its Annual Energy Outlook.

If you look at the Brent benchmark over several decades, oil has been far from stable. It has experienced sharp rises tied to wars and supply cuts, along with steep drops linked to global recessions and oversupply (called a “glut”). For example:

To sum up, oil’s historical performance has been anything but smooth. Again, it’s heavily influenced by wars, recessions, OPEC whims, shifting energy policies, and much more.

Looking to stay up-to-date regarding the latest energy developments? Check out our recent coverage:

The current price of oil per barrel depends largely on supply and demand, including news about potential future supply and demand (geopolitics, decisions made by OPEC+, etc.). In the U.S., prices also move based on how friendly an administration is to drilling, as it can affect future supply. For example, 2025 saw the Trump administration move to reopen more than 1.5 million acres in the Coastal Plain of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge for oil and gas leasing, reversing the Biden administration’s policy of limiting oil drilling in the Arctic.

The price of oil updates constantly when the “futures” markets are open. A futures market is effectively an auction where people agree to buy or sell oil in the future. As long as people and companies are trading contracts, the oil price is changing.

In short, shale is rock that contains oil and natural gas. Think of shale as energy yet to be tapped. The more shale the U.S. accesses, the more energy we’ll have—and the more easily oil prices can keep from spiking as much thanks to a greater supply.

When oil is expensive, it tends to make everyday items cost more. This can be related to energy (your heating, gas utilities, etc.), but it’s also due to the logistics involved with making those items accessible to you. Shipping, for example, can affect the price of things at the grocery store, as it’s more expensive to get those products from warehouses and farms onto the shelf.

#5380. The AI-Driven Agency Apocalypse Has Arrived. Here’s How to Survive It.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

As AI disrupts every industry and generating new business becomes tougher, the agencies that retain their clients will be the agencies that survive.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

If you’ve been feeling like the future of your agency is bleak, you are not alone. Every agency owner I’ve spoken to in the past year has been experiencing the same reality. New business is shrinking as our model, which relies on providing external expertise to bring business value, is heavily under attack by AI. This is a situation we must accept as fact if we are to properly navigate it.

Even though this is the worst year on record for net-new business in the seven years of running my agency, we’ve managed to retain our existing clients and have not seen a significant drop in monthly revenues or had to let staff go. We have not grown, but we have not shrunk either. And in 2026, that’s a big win.

I believe the reason we have managed to sustain our base, and why I am ultimately not feeling as stressed as some of my peers, is that we have been doing two things right since well before the recent AI impacts affected our industry:

Let’s dive into both of those in more detail so you can audit and adjust your delivery model as needed to ensure you survive this AI-caused agency apocalypse.

Before we review the contractual changes you need to institute, it is imperative that your team is doing top-notch work. Without that, nothing you do will help you survive. You need to be the best in class in your niche to even have a chance. B-grade delivery (or worse) no longer has a fighting chance.

It’s time for an audit! Review how many clients you have on locked-in, long-term managed service or support agreements. If you are used to selling your services on a fixed-fee and fixed-term model, where you are charging the same amount per month even if you don’t lift a finger and those contracts last for many months or years, your days are numbered.

Your clients will jump ship the moment that contract ends. This means you are on the clock to make things right. Our first client is still our client to this day, over six years later, and I believe it’s because they’ve never been forced to sign a contract of that nature. None of our clients ever have.

What do we do instead? We sign indefinite monthly agreements that have a straightforward adjustment, pause or cancellation clause. If you want to see the exact terminology of that clause, you can find a sample statement of work in my free book, How Do I Find Clients?

But the spirit of that clause is quite simple: value creation. Alongside each client, we agree what value we will bring for them each month and set our monthly compensation based on that value creation. If, at any point, the client feels that there’s a need to adjust that equation, take a short pause or cancel, they have the right to do so.

This clause has ensured our clients have always felt comfortable proceeding with us and staying on those agreements well beyond any fixed term we could have locked them in for. So, if you have any contracts that are locking clients in long-term, perhaps it’s time to adjust those contracts and ensure that your clients feel you are really there to support them.

Locked-in terms are only one part of the equation. Your other, and perhaps biggest, enemy is locked-in pricing. I always tell my students: Every single time a client receives an invoice from you, they are doing a mathematical equation in their head that has two possible outcomes: “worth it” or “not worth it.”

To fight resentment, you need to make sure that every single time they do that equation, the result is unequivocally “worth it!” The way you do that is by putting yourself in the shoes of your clients before you send that invoice. If you believe that there’s any reason they might feel a reduction in the monthly invoice is warranted, you need to apply it preemptively and communicate it openly. That conversation, believe me, goes very well every time.

It sounds very simple because it is. When you send the invoice, communicate the situation clearly. Take this as an example: “You were away on vacation for a week, and then I was sick the last few days of the month, so I’ve reduced the invoice by $1,000. Hope you don’t mind.” And guess what? Of course they don’t mind! But they certainly appreciate it, and they remember it. This type of decision builds stronger relationships.

Before you dismiss this, think about how you would feel if you got the full invoice in that situation. Your thought process would sound more like: “Man, I was away for a week, and nothing got done, and then they were sick and missed the call at the end of the month, and they’re still charging me the full price. That’s absurd!” Of course, that builds resentment. Fight against it!

Some of you may feel challenged by the two ideas I’ve just shared, but I’m going to challenge you even more. The reality is, if you feel that these are difficult changes for your business or a risk to your success, what you’re actually feeling is a fear of losing control and a scarcity mindset. Both of these are feelings you need to fight and resist. Your survival is at stake.

If you’ve been feeling like the future of your agency is bleak, you are not alone. Every agency owner I’ve spoken to in the past year has been experiencing the same reality. #5379. Amazon tops Forbes’ list of America’s best companies, edging out Apple for No. 1

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 12, 2026 at 1:16 pmNovember 12, 2026 at 1:16 pm

Amazon is the best company in America, according to Forbes.

The Seattle tech giant took the No. 1 spot on the publication’s 2027 “America’s Best Companies” list, moving up from No. 2 last year and edging out Apple.

Three other Washington state companies landed in the top 50: Microsoft at No. 6, Costco at No. 13 and Alaska Air Group at No. 39.

Last year’s No. 1, Berkshire Hathaway, slipped to No. 4. Nvidia ranked No. 3 on the same day CEO Jensen Huang resigned, following his admission of an extramarital affair. JPMorganChase, Alphabet, Royal Caribbean Group, Walmart and Marriott International round out the top 10.

Now in its third year, the ranking scores thousands of the largest public and private U.S. companies on factors including customer and employee sentiment, financial performance, creditworthiness, cybersecurity and innovation. Forbes said it worked with 12 data organizations to build the index.

Forbes said Amazon’s financial strength and size, its standing in news and social media, and the range of voices across the company and its leadership lifted it to No. 1. Apple scored especially well on employee satisfaction, customer loyalty, financial strength and innovation.

Forbes also pointed to Amazon’s speed, citing a feature that lets customers shop by text message. An employee suggested it in October and it launched Nov. 6.

“Innovating for customers, doing it fast, working backwards from their needs, that’s really at our core,” Beth Galetti, Amazon’s senior vice president of people, experience and technology, told Forbes.

In its own blog post Thursday, Amazon highlighted everything from faster delivery and custom AI chips to warehouse robotics and higher pay for frontline workers.

The ranking comes after a year of workforce cuts at Amazon. The company eliminated about 30,000 corporate jobs in rounds announced in October 2025 and January 2026, including more than 4,500 in Washington state. Smaller cuts followed throughout the year, including layoffs of fewer than 1,000 corporate employees in October, mainly in its Stores unit.

#5378. Mars CFO: $1.4 billion U.S. manufacturing investment aims to deliver ‘durable growth’

Good morning. Mars Inc., maker of M&M’s, Snickers and Pedigree, plans to invest an estimated $1.4 billion in U.S. manufacturing and operations in 2027, its largest single-year investment.

“It is fundamentally a growth investment,” Mars Inc. CFO Claus Aagaard told me. “In the near term, we are putting capital behind high-demand, high-growth brands and businesses where additional capacity can unlock growth.”

Longer term, Mars is modernizing its network with automation, high-speed lines and standardized systems “so we can scale efficiently and build a stronger, more resilient supply chain,” Aagaard explained.

Following its combination with Kellanova, Mars is now a more than $65 billion family-owned business, based on combined 2025 net sales, according to the company. In the Q&A below, Aagaard discusses the rationale for the investment in manufacturing, how Mars will measure its return and what it means for the communities where it operates.

Why is 2027 the right time for Mars’s largest single-year investment?

We have invested more than $9 billion in U.S. manufacturing and operations over the last decade, and while this $1.4 billion commitment is the largest we’ve invested in a single year, it is part of our long-term approach. Demand across our business is high, and American manufacturing is very strong.

Advances in smart factory automation, energy-efficiency technology and digital tools mean that retrofitting or building facilities today can deliver a higher return than it did a decade ago. Right now, we’re seeing a compelling opportunity to not only invest in meeting growing demand, but to unlock capabilities and ensure operational excellence for generations to come.

How is the $1.4 billion divided, and how do you measure the return?

The $1.4 billion investment in 2027 and the $9 billion that has been committed over the past decade, supports manufacturing and operations across our snacking, food and pet businesses, with capital allocated where we see clear opportunities to expand capacity, modernize facilities and strengthen resilience.

For example, we’ll spend more than $34 million to open four new Mars Veterinary Health hospitals in 2027, expand access to emergency and specialty veterinary care, bring innovative medical capabilities to growing communities, and support the development of highly skilled veterinary professionals.

We have invested $60 million in Salt Lake City to add two Trü Frü production lines to our recently opened Nature’s Bakery facility, unlocking capacity for 17 million frozen products annually. And, we have spent $49 million in Columbus, Ohio, to bring Temptations Lickable Treats manufacturing to the U.S., with a target of 400 million pouches annually.We measure return across several dimensions, including our ability to meet consumer demand, improve efficiency and productivity, strengthen supply chain resilience, support profitable growth, and expand access to high-quality veterinary care.

Why does keeping 94% of U.S. products made domestically matter to Mars?

Mars has operated in the U.S. for 115 years—it’s our largest market, and we’re globally headquartered here. The U.S. is critical for Mars. Making 94% of the products we sell in the U.S. domestically gives us an important foundation for long-term growth. A strong local manufacturing footprint puts production closer to consumers, creates greater supply-chain resilience, and allows us to expand capacity as demand grows. It also means that when we invest in growth, those investments can translate directly into facilities, capabilities, and jobs in the communities where we operate.

What does this investment mean for the communities where Mars operates?

We have operated in many U.S. communities for generations, so these investments are about more than adding capacity. They modernize and strengthen facilities, support skilled jobs, and create additional economic activity locally.

This month, our facility in Waco, Texas is celebrating 50 years of operations. Mars has steadily expanded and modernized the Waco site, which produces Snickers, Starburst, and Skittles, to meet growing consumer demand while advancing environmental sustainability. Mars has invested $165 million in the facility since 2024, with recent capital projects heavily focused on enhancing energy efficiency and operational excellence.

Today, the site is powered by nearly 900 dedicated associates, but the milestone speaks to the dedication of generations of associates and longstanding partnerships we share with the Central Texas community.

What would success look like for this investment a few years from now?

Success means we have converted this capital into durable growth and a stronger operating network. We should be able to serve more consumers and pet owners, scale high-growth brands, operate more efficiently, and have greater resilience across our supply chain.

#5377. OfferUp co-founder sees ‘mini power plants’ in buildings full of EVs

Challenges, breakthroughs and big ideas in the race to protect our planet. SEE MORE

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 12, 2026 at 2:41 pmNovember 12, 2026 at 2:41 pm

Nick Huzar co-founded Juicer Energy in 2023 to make electric vehicle charging more widespread and reliable. Now the Seattle-area startup is pursuing a broader goal: helping buildings manage rising electricity demand and costs.

Juicer installs and operates EV charging systems at apartment buildings, hotels and other properties. It is also developing battery systems to store electricity on-site and help manage the power needed for charging and other building uses.

The push comes as data centers and the growing use of electricity for transportation, heating and other needs put more pressure on the grid. Batteries can help balance supply and demand by storing energy when electricity is plentiful and releasing it when demand peaks. In some cases, they can reduce the need for costly grid upgrades or new power plants built to meet peak demand.

“We think there’s a big opportunity there,” Huzar said. He spoke at an event this week hosted by GeekWire and Bank of America at the Bellevue showroom of Ferrari of Seattle.

Other companies are similarly pairing EV charging with battery storage. Fellow Seattle startup Electric Era has deployed battery-backed fast chargers at retailers including Costco and convenience stores. ADS-TEC Energy and XCharge also sell fast-charging systems with integrated batteries.

Huzar, OfferUp’s co-founder and former CEO, sees an opportunity to make buildings more self-sufficient by combining hardware and energy-management software. He said Juicer has a project scheduled to come online in 2027 with 70 chargers in one building.

His longer-term vision also includes tapping the energy stored in vehicles connected to those buildings.

“Imagine you’re an apartment owner and you have 20 EVs, 40 EVs plugged in,” Huzar said. “That is a huge amount of power. Like you’re a mini power plant at that point.”

He described feeding excess electricity back to the grid as a possibility that remains years away. He also predicted that most businesses, apartments and homes would have on-site batteries within the next decade, in part because battery costs continue to fall.

Juicer started with EV charging, Huzar said, “but the more we’ve gotten into this, the more we realize that we actually can build an asset for buildings versus relying on the grid.”

Seven years later, the community has grown to over 700 signatories across 62 industries and 49 countries and territories, reducing emissions, scaling emerging climate solutions, and addressing challenges across operations and value chains.

#5376. Americans worry capitalism won’t work for them in the AI era. Here are 3 ways for companies to show that it can

Martin Whittaker is the chief executive officer of Just Capital, an independent organization advancing responsible business leadership. Co-founded by Paul Tudor Jones, its current chairman of the board is Dan Schulman. Just Capital is an Impact Partner of the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum, and this piece draws on Just Capital’s own survey and corporate-tracking research.

According to Just Capital’s 2026 Americans’ Views on Business survey, three in four Americans believe the nation’s best days of innovation are happening now or are still to come. Yet only half say our current form of capitalism gives people like them a fair shot at getting ahead financially. The percentage of people who believe they will be financially worse off this time next year is at its highest since 1960. In other words, Americans believe that—in the age of AI and related innovation—our economic system is working for someone else, not them.

Bridging this divide is the defining leadership challenge of our time. And as the recent midterm elections showed, when people feel strongly enough about something they are apt to seek change.

Americans haven’t given up on business as a driver of solutions—78% say large companies have a role to play in solving important societal issues. The key is to show Americans they have a place in the AI-powered economy. Our assessment of the 500 largest American employers shows that so far approximately 180 companies have publicly reported AI-related actions affecting their own employees or the broader workforce since December 2025. 161 of those companies announced actions that specifically aim to support their workers and the American workforce at large.

These companies are primarily in industries with large frontline workforces like Personal Care, Drug, & Grocery; and Telecommunications. Companies in industries with close ties to the AI buildout such as Energy; Construction & Materials; and Utilities were less likely to have announced an action in our analysis. Of the twenty industries we examined, six had a higher percentage of companies taking action than the Technology industry, which sits at the center of the AI transition. However, the Tech companies that did announce an action took roughly twice as many as peers in other industries.

The first movers can offer lessons for leaders in every industry: redefine roles rather than eliminate them, open pathways into skilled trades, and equip the next generation of innovators.

Many experts now predict AI will reshape jobs rather than lead to a wholesale disruption of the workforce. Our data reflects the same trend. In the Fall 2026 edition of Just Capital’s quarterly survey of the American public, investors, and corporate leaders, 52% of corporate leaders say they have redefined or transitioned existing roles over the past 12 months compared to 15% who say they have conducted layoffs. Several companies show how this could work in practice.

At General Dynamics Information Technology (GDIT), 12,000 employees have moved into new roles inside the company since 2023, and more than 9,000 have earned certifications in AI, cyber and other technologies. Kimberly-Clark takes a similar approach to training. Its “IT Digital University” covers 17 skill areas, and employees are assessed before and after, with completers averaging 60% skill growth. ServiceNow put AI agents to work on its own operations, and they now resolve 90% of IT service desk tickets. Instead of laying off the service desk team, the company assessed everyone’s skills, provided role-based training and held one-on-one career conversations before moving anyone. As a result, 85% of the service desk moved into new roles in security, AI operations and executive briefing, and the other 15% now supervise the AI agents.

While the dominant narrative has focused on the negative impacts AI may have on the American workforce or on communities across the country, the real story may be a revolution of reskilling and internal mobility.

Our polling shows 47% of Americans aged 18 to 25 worry AI will make it harder to land an entry-level job in their field, yet only 20% of recent grads are considering a trade or licensed profession despite the U.S. facing a historic skilled trades labor shortage.

Several companies are tackling the issue head on. Caterpillar is investing $100 million over five years in manufacturing and industry technician jobs in Illinois and Indiana, building a pipeline in the communities where it operates. Lowe’s has gone further by convening the nation’s largest skilled trades coalition, with NVIDIA, AT&T, Bank of America, Carrier, General Motors, DEWALT and Duke Energy, and a goal of training 1 million people. Beyond the founding corporate partners, Lowe’s also brought on over 75 educators, businesses, workforce organizations, industry vendors and stakeholders, including the National Association of Home Builders (NAHB), The National Center for Construction Education and Research (NCCER), SkillsUSA and Carhartt.

The message here is that workforce readiness is not a problem to be owned by any one company, and the firms with the most to gain from solving it are well placed to lead.

24% of Americans in the Americans’ Views on Business survey say that individual entrepreneurs and innovators are the primary driver of American innovation, more than large companies R&D investments (23%), venture capital and private investment (14%), government funding (13%), and universities and academic research (13%).

Several companies stand out for cultivating entrepreneurial capacity. Boeing put $250,000 behind Technovation, pairing its engineers as mentors with 25,000 girls building AI-powered solutions worldwide. DoorDash offers a one-day Local Business Workshop that gives small business owners training, tools, local connections and advertising credits. Duke Energy sponsored the third annual high school AI design contest at the University of Florida, where student teams used AI tools to design a smart power grid for their own communities.

Investments like these, aimed at people early in their careers or businesses, can widen who gets to participate in what comes next. Investing early in entrepreneurs is also an investment in the customers, suppliers and talent pools companies will depend on later.

Just Capital’s monthly National AI Monitor asks 1,000 Americans how they are experiencing AI as workers, customers, community members, investors and stewards of the environment. Americans are net positive about AI today (+37 overall, +44 at work). But their outlook for the next few years falls to +13, with job loss among the main concerns for the future.

The examples of corporate action outlined here illustrate the path forward for leadership to address these concerns in a new era. By redefining roles, creating internal mobility, and fostering the skills of the future, including a focus on entrepreneurship, these companies are showing how to broaden access to opportunity rather than narrow it.

What’s needed next is to measure the success of these initiatives, scale those that work, and continue to explore other pathways. Leaders willing to make meaningful investments in and test new solutions for the American workforce will be repaid in the form of greater trust, goodwill, growth, and social license to operate; all crucial determinants of success in the AI-powered economy. They will also strengthen Americans’ faith in capitalism in the process.

#5375. Akash’s Solana Migration Clears November 2 Vote at 97%, With Four More On-Chain Decisions Ahead

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

AKT stakers are close to approving Akash's move from Cosmos to Solana, with Mintscan projecting a pass at 97.2% yes as voting enters its final hours.

But a yes on Proposal 346 opens a door rather than completing a move. Before a single AKT reaches Solana, two independent audits and at least two more on-chain votes still have to happen.

The summary going around is simple: Akash is leaving Cosmos for Solana. The proposal itself is narrower than that, and the details matter for anyone holding AKT.

Proposal 346 on akashnet-2, titled "Migrate the Akash Protocol to Solana," closes at 15:02 UTC on November 2. A yes vote approves the migration plan and authorises AKT to launch as an SPL token through a one-way portal that stays open for two years. It does not set a cutover date, it does not move a single lease, and on its own it does not open the portal.

The technical spec for that portal was published the day after voting opened. It shows how many further steps lie between this vote and a working SPL AKT.

The proposal text in Akash's AEP repository says a yes vote does two things:

It also says plainly what it doesn't do: "it does not set a cutover date and does not move the marketplace." Live leases, staking and governance on akashnet-2 continue as normal. The marketplace moves only after audits and rehearsals pass and "a separate cutover proposal passes on this chain."

A no vote would stop the whole plan. In the proposal's words: "Nothing moves; the token does not launch and the program returns to option analysis."

At 08:43 UTC on November 2, about six hours before voting closed, Mintscan's page for Proposal 346 showed an expected result of "Will PASS":

Turnout stood at 68.80% of bonded stake, against a quorum of 33.40%. The same figures can be read from Akash's own chain API, through the proposal object and its tally endpoint.

Mintscan's 97.2% is yes as a share of all votes cast. Akash's pass threshold leaves abstentions out, and on that basis yes stands at about 98.7%, far above the 50% needed. The veto share is negligible.

The tally has barely changed since early morning. A read of the chain at 07:29 UTC showed almost exactly the same totals, with only a handful of AKT added to the yes side. With turnout and margin that large, the outcome is not in doubt. The more useful question is what happens after it passes.

The portal's design is in AEP-95, "One-Way AKT Sink to Solana,", a draft published on October 27 by core developers Artur Troian and Joseph Chalabi. It describes a "deliberately one-way" bridge with no return path. The authors say this removes "the largest class of bridge attacks."

Why supply doesn't change: every SPL AKT is backed by AKT locked on Akash, and nothing is minted independently on Solana. The token is a legacy SPL mint with six decimals and no freeze authority.

The spec's own risk table names the biggest trust point. The upgrade authority over the Solana programs could "mint without limit." That power is meant to sit with a time-locked multisig appointed by Akash governance, with monitors set to alert on every admin action.

At launch, SPL AKT has no protocol role. It will support "transfers and DEX liquidity only, with no staking or governance rights." Inflation stays on Akash. To seed trading, Overclock Labs, Akash's core developer, will send 1 million AKT through the bridge to a Solana treasury vault. That deposit follows the same rules as everyone else's.

Proposal 346 requires "two independent audits of the token and portal code before launch," with reports published within 30 days. AEP-95's launch sequence shows what that requirement means on-chain.

So Proposal 346 is the first of at least five on-chain decisions. The "2 to 3 weeks" launch estimate depends on the audits finishing and the upgrade and parameter votes passing on schedule.

For now, nothing. The proposal's disclosures set out what changes later:

Discussion of the proposal continues in GitHub Discussion #1123.

The proposal lists four items as "still open, to be settled and published before the cutover proposal":

The second item matters most to holders. The portal closes two years after launch, and the proposal doesn't yet say what happens to AKT that hasn't crossed by then. The final tally will confirm whether the plan goes ahead, but that answer, and the decisions in the votes that follow, will matter more to most holders than today's margin.

#5374. He Rose From Call Center to CEO of a $61 Billion Company. Here’s How He Got Promoted Quickly.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

This CEO’s path offers a lesson for anyone looking to climb the corporate ladder.

Have you ever wondered why some employees rise through the ranks quickly while others seem stuck?

Antonio Neri, the CEO of Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE), had a meteoric rise at the company. He began his career at HPE as a call center employee in Amsterdam in the 1990s. He worked his way up, job after job, and became CEO of HPE in 2018. At the time of writing, HPE’s market capitalization is $61 billion, up from $31 billion at the end of 2025.

Now Neri is revealing how he got the top job. In a recent interview with Business Insider, Neri said that the key to unlocking opportunities at work begins with one principle: Carry out your promises. In other words, if you say you’re going to do something, make sure you do it. Follow through.

He added that you should be transparent about your career goals. Your manager should know where you see yourself in three to five years, and you should have an outline of the steps you need to take to get there.

“Hold the manager accountable, but most importantly, hold yourself accountable, too, because it’s a two-way street,” Neri said.

Another tip Neri offered was to ask managers and colleagues for developmental opportunities, or workplace programs, resources and experiences designed to help employees build new skills. These events could help advance your career.

Common types of development programs include online courses, coaching and one-on-one mentoring initiatives.

Neri said that getting ahead starts with finding assignments that help you grow and introduce you to more people across the company. Building relationships with colleagues and senior leaders can put you on their radar when new roles or opportunities become available.

However, visibility is only one aspect of the equation. Neri advised being deliberate about which opportunities you pursue when you are presented with multiple routes. Is the opportunity going to bring you closer to your five-year career goals?

“Don’t overdo it, but also don’t be quiet behind the scenes,” he said. “Speak when it’s necessary and then listen most of the time.”

Leaders at PwC and Chipotle say getting promoted takes more than doing your job well. They say employees can stand out by showing that they can be trusted with greater responsibility before receiving a bigger paycheck.

For example, Dallas Dolen, a PwC executive who oversees 7,500 employees, told Business Insider earlier this year that promotions start with responsiveness. Employees who answer urgent messages and help colleagues are more likely to get promoted.

“You have to be willing to, at midnight, jump on the plane,” Dolen said.

Meanwhile, Chipotle COO Jason Kidd looks for employees who support their teams, anticipate problems and offer solutions. He has weekly dinners with regional employees where he assesses how they think and if they are worthy of a promotion.

Kidd told Business Insider that Chipotle promoted 23,000 employees last year, and all of the company’s regional vice presidents were internal hires.

#5373. ‘A huge pain in the ass’: Microsoft 365 starts to recover after a day of global email turmoil

by Todd Bishop on Nov 13, 2026 at 7:24 amNovember 13, 2026 at 4:23 pm

Updated at 4 p.m. PT Nov. 13 with additional Microsoft statements.

If emails sent by Outlook users on Thursday are just now landing in your inbox, no, you haven’t gone back to the days of the Pony Express. Microsoft is still digging out from a nearly daylong outage that cut off email for businesses, schools and governments around the world.

As of early Friday, the company reported that email queues were “significantly reduced and approaching normal levels,” though some users could still have trouble getting in or see delayed messages.

In a post on X Friday morning, Microsoft said it was “deeply sorry” for the disruption to customers and partners. The company said the outage was a technical issue, not related to a cyberattack or AI agents.

The problem was introduced during an earlier network capacity upgrade and surfaced after a more recent network change, the company said, adding that it has addressed the underlying issue and is still restoring service to remaining customers and regions.

We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners. We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously. We are seeing broad recovery and stability across our services.This was a technical issue…

In an update on its status page at 5 a.m. Pacific, Microsoft said it was seeing “broader improvements now observed in North America and sustained improvements across much of Europe,” along with early signs of recovery in Asia Pacific.

The problems started Thursday morning with Exchange Online, the Microsoft service that runs Outlook email for businesses, and spread to other Microsoft 365 services that depend on it, including Teams calendars, Copilot and SharePoint.

Microsoft said servers were failing automated health checks and dropping out of service, which overloaded the ones that were left. The company paused all deployments while it worked on a fix, and some of its repairs Thursday evening were “not taking as expected.” Microsoft said it restored service gradually, checking stability at each stage, which took longer but helped ensure a stable restoration.

Earlier, The Verge’s Tom Warren reported on X that his sources linked the outage to configuration changes in Azure Virtual Network, Microsoft’s cloud networking service.

Australia’s Home Affairs Minister, Tony Burke, told reporters in Sydney that Microsoft believes it is dealing with something similar in some ways to the 2024 CrowdStrike outage, “where there is an update that has gone awry,” the Associated Press reported.

“We know our customers rely on our services to get important work done every day, and regret the impact these outages had on those who depend on us,” said Charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, Agents and Platform, in a statement provided to GeekWire. He said Microsoft’s teams are reviewing what happened and how to prevent similar problems.

In a post on X Friday afternoon, Lamanna said the investigation points to “cascading failures + thundering herds at our network perimeter,” which made recovery harder than normal. A thundering herd happens when large numbers of clients try to reconnect at the same time, overwhelming systems as they come back online.

He said Microsoft will publish a post-mortem “shortly” with a step-by-step timeline and the repairs it plans to make to avoid similar outages.

The outage reached well beyond email. Government offices in Japan, Singapore and the Philippines reported disruptions, according to the AP. Workhorse Group delayed its quarterly earnings call, and OpenAI and Anthropic both reported problems connecting with Microsoft 365 tools.

Credit rating agency Morningstar DBRS estimated insured losses of $300 million to $500 million, well below estimates for CrowdStrike, which ranged from $400 million to $1.5 billion. Some cyber insurance policies cover only malicious attacks, the firm noted, though it said the toll could grow if the outage drags on for several days.

The disruption hit close to Microsoft’s home. Ansel Herz, a spokesperson for the Seattle mayor’s office, told the Seattle Times that the outage didn’t bring city government to a halt but knocked out the systems that move documents and messages around City Hall.

The newspaper quoted Herz calling the outage “a huge pain.” In a post on X, he chided the paper for not using his whole quote, which we presume was “a huge pain in the ass.”

We’ve followed up with him to confirm this important detail. Here’s hoping he gets the email.

Update, 10 a.m.: Herz did receive GeekWire’s message and responded, confirming the quote and saying that, to his knowledge, nothing public-facing was affected at the city. Email appears to be back and working properly as of Friday morning, he said.
