#5372. Kevin Warsh has Fed staff building Wall Street-style contingencies for AI outcomes: From a growth boom to bad actors attacking critical infrastructure

The role of the Federal Reserve in the AI boom has, so far, been undefined: Will the central bank be reactive, sitting on the sidelines until data impacting its mandate demands action? Or will it seek to get ahead of economic shifts driven by transformative technology? The Fed’s new chairman, Kevin Warsh, doesn’t seem content to watch from the sidelines.Speaking yesterday in San Francisco at the Productivity and Jobs Task Force Conference, hosted by the Federal Reserve Board and the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco, Warsh said the Fed is conducting contingency planning.

“The Board’s staff has begun to evaluate various contingencies, applying stylized, model-based frameworks to generate scenarios,” Warsh said. “These are illustrative scenarios, not forecasts. Moreover, many other outcomes—probably including one that will prove most accurate—could be drawn.”

Of course, the Fed’s expertise and analysis of AI are nothing new: it already publishes datasets monitoring everything from AI adoption rates by firm size to the impact of AI-related investment on the economy.

But Warsh hinted at work that establishes what outcomes may look like, rather than observing current trends. He continued: “As policymakers, we have to be mindful that great opportunities rarely come risk-free. And the risks in this case, if overlooked, can be highly disruptive and economically costly. SI [Super intelligence] empowers all, including bad actors, so we are thinking especially of critical infrastructures and their potential vulnerabilities.”

Before his return to the central bank (Warsh was the Fed’s youngest governor in history, previously serving between 2006 and 2011), hawkish analysts had been somewhat alarmed by how bullish the incoming chairman had been about AI.

But since his nomination by President Trump this spring, Warsh has struck a more speculative tone. “Our aim today is a humble one,” he said yesterday, “to ask the right questions.”

Warsh outlined multiple risks, for instance the threat posed to critical infrastructure if the technology falls into the wrong hands. He also said that widespread automation could increase unemployment. AI could also “disappoint,” he said, if expected returns fall flat, leading to an economic slowdown.

There’s also opportunity, he said: “SI leads to an increase in productivity and economic gains that are shared broadly across labor and the owners of capital. In that event, real GDP growth rises persistently above its long-run average, and the U.S. stays close to full employment.”

If contingency planning across a spectrum of outcomes sounds familiar, that’s because it’s a staple Wall Street habit. Warsh is a former Morgan Stanley vice president and executive director.

You don’t have to look far for examples: JPMorgan pulled together a war room in January last year following the re-election of President Trump, analyzing and evaluating the policies Trump had espoused while out on the campaign trail.

Bank of America and Citigroup reportedly set up similar internal functions to support investors.

Later that year, David Garfield, the co-CEO of consulting firm AlixPartners, told Fortune that his team was working with major companies across every industry to build tariff war rooms: mechanisms for responding to the shifting policy landscape navigated over the past two years.

Warsh’s planning is not a response to an immediate policy question, rather an issue of preparedness. “While I’m not here to offer predictions, I’m not exactly impartial about American leadership in a time so filled with both challenge and possibility,” Warsh said. His ultimate goal is to create a dynamic economy for future generations, and promote “human flourishing.”

Eleanor Pringle is an award-winning senior reporter at Fortune covering news, the economy, and personal finance. Eleanor previously worked as a business correspondent and news editor in regional news in the U.K. She completed her journalism training with the Press Association after earning a degree from the University of East Anglia.

#5371. Uncommon Thinkers: Alexis Harroun aims for space with a new engine — and stays grounded

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 13, 2026 at 7:46 amNovember 16, 2026 at 7:19 am

Editor’s note: This series profiles five Seattle-area “Uncommon Thinkers,” who will be recognized Dec. 10 at the GeekWire Gala in partnership with Greater Seattle Partners.

A few weeks after learning that her tiny startup had won a NASA prize to fly its engine in space, Alexis Harroun was camping in Yellowstone, sitting around a fire and looking up at the stars. Satellites kept drifting past overhead — and the news finally sank in.

“I’m like, oh, we’re going to be sending something up and we’re going to be able to see it,” she said. “That was very humbling in a lot of ways and very exciting.”

Harroun is co-founder and CEO of Juno Propulsion, a Tukwila, Wash.-based startup building a new kind of rocket engine. Instead of burning fuel in a steady flame, Juno’s engines use detonation, a supersonic combustion wave that releases more energy from the same amount of propellant.

“It’s essentially like a higher MPG rocket engine,” Harroun said.

The technology has been studied for decades but has never flown in orbit. Juno aims to change that next year, when its engine is set to fly aboard a Momentus satellite in a mission called Project Iris.

That’s a big goal for a company that, when the July 2025 NASA call came, was just Harroun, co-founder and CTO Ari Martinez and a summer intern working out of a one-room office.

If Iris succeeds, Juno’s engines could let satellites run on non-toxic fuel and maneuver far more freely in orbit, something both commercial and defense customers increasingly want. For Harroun, who earned her Ph.D. studying these engines, it would be the payoff of years of work.

Harroun sees the technology as a long-overdue leap. The basic physics behind today’s rocket engines dates to the 1930s and has been refined about as far as it can go, she said, calling it a constraint that’s “been a glass ceiling for too long, in my opinion.”

Harroun grew up south of Seattle in Federal Way. She didn’t come from an aerospace family or spend her childhood dreaming about space. Her dad was a physician and her mom a flight attendant and flight instructor.

What she did pick up at home was an entrepreneurial streak. Her dad ran his own practice for about 20 years, and her mom is now a real estate agent. Harroun said watching them make “something out of completely nothing” has shaped her own path, especially in building Juno.

She calls herself a “late bloomer” who fell for engineering as she was finishing high school and heading to the University of Washington. Sci-fi became an inspiration along the way, and it’s now one of her favorite genres.

She spent all four years at UW working with professor Carl Knowlen, who leads the Aeronautics & Astronautics Department’s Detonation Engines Lab, and she joined the student rocketry team, eventually leading its propulsion group.

Knowlen “sees the potential in everyone,” Harroun said, and the two built a strong relationship that’s still going. Juno’s $1.2 million National Science Foundation grant, awarded this summer, is a partnership with his research group.

Knowlen was also the faculty adviser for the student rocketry team, where he spent “many hot, and sometimes rainy, days” with Harroun and her teammates, test-firing motors and launching high-powered rockets.

“She always was level-headed and led by example,” Knowlen said. “No one worked harder than her to see these tests and launches go off as planned.”

He called her “an exceptional student, natural leader, creative thinker, and very independent,” and said it’s been a great satisfaction to see the engineer she has become.

During college, Harroun interned at NASA, Boeing and Blue Origin. That first stint at Blue Origin, in 2016, set her next move.

“I realized that everyone who had the job that I wanted had gone to Purdue,” she said.

She spent the next six years at Purdue University in West Lafayette, Ind., earning a master’s degree and a Ph.D. Her doctoral research was on the technology Juno is now building. She also met Martinez there. The two shared an office for years.

Harroun never planned to stay in academia.

“That just didn’t feel like my calling,” she said. “I wanted to use that very unique experience to get the technical chops to do the type of engineering that I wanted to do.”

Her doctoral advisor, Purdue professor Stephen Heister, still advises her and the company.

“He was one of the people who really pushed me to think about starting this company,” Harroun said. “I think he saw the potential that I had as a founder, both from a technical and a leadership perspective.”

Heister recalled their first technical discussion, when Harroun arrived as a new master’s student. He went deep on nozzle flows, her thesis topic, and the complications of building a nozzle for a detonation engine.

“At the end of my diatribe, she sat quietly and said, ‘You’ve given me a lot to think about,’” Heister said. “I can’t think of any other 22-year-old student with such a response but I knew she was indeed a special talent.”

He described Harroun as having “the unique ability to think deeply and at length,” and said it’s “terribly gratifying” to watch her commercialize the technology she worked on as a grad student.

After finishing her Ph.D. in 2023, Harroun came back to the Seattle region and started Juno. She knew the territory: her UW lab work and the rocketry team had put her in touch with local industry, and Juno now works with some of the same companies she did as a student.

Interning at Blue Origin was the first time she could say “there’s literally a rocket company in our backyard,” Harroun said. Its presence helped build a regional talent pool, which she described as “a contingent of rocket scientists that just live here.”

Starting a company comes with many unknowns, and coming home crossed one off the list.

“I knew how to go start doing stuff immediately,” she said. “So it made that calculus really easy.”

Harroun’s ambitions reach well beyond one demo flight.

“Our mission is to be the rocket engine provider for the U.S.,” she said. “Think of a Rocketdyne.”

That company built engines for the Saturn V and the space shuttle, and it’s now part of L3Harris. Juno wants to play a similar role with a new technology. It’s starting with in-space propulsion for satellites and plans to expand into engines for upper stages, orbital transfer vehicles and, eventually, the boosters that lift rockets off the pad.

The first step is Project Iris. NASA paid Juno about $500,000 through its TechLeap program to build the payload, and it’s also covering the Momentus spacecraft and the flight. There’s no paying customer yet, but the mission is designed to mimic the maneuvers a real satellite would make.

Japan’s space agency has flown rotating detonation engines on suborbital research rockets, but going to orbit is “a whole ‘nother game,” Harroun said. “Going to space is hard. I can attest to that.”

Building a company has taught Harroun things her Ph.D. didn’t. Handling toxic propellants is so complicated, she learned, that operators can spend more fueling a satellite than on “the propulsion system itself, which is kind of crazy.”

The bigger draw is mobility. For decades, satellites have mostly stayed in the orbit a rocket left them in, she said, and “that’s not really acceptable anymore in today’s world.”

To get there, Juno has raised a $1.4 million pre-seed round led by SOSV, on top of its NASA and NSF awards.

As for going to space herself, Harroun admits it would be hard to say no if she got the opportunity.

But the avid hiker and backpacker is partial to terra firma. Her best-case future is one where Earth is the place humanity gets to enjoy and space is what makes that possible.

“I don’t know that I would be the traveler,” Harroun said, “but I’d definitely like to be the enabler.”

#5370. Current price of oil as of November 16, 2026

As of 7:30 a.m. Eastern Time on November 16, 2026, oil sold for $96.68 per barrel (using Brent as the benchmark, which we’ll get into momentarily). That’s 42 cents lower than yesterday morning and approximately a $32.60 rise over the past year.

It’s impossible to predict the future of oil prices. Several factors determine the movement of oil, but it ultimately boils down to supply and demand. Again, when threats of economic downturn, war, etc. are high, the oil trajectory can turn rapidly.

When you pay for gas at the pump, you’re paying for more than just the crude oil itself; you’re also springing for links along the chain, such as the refineries and wholesalers—not to mention taxes and local gas station markups.

Still, the crude oil aspect affects the final price most dramatically, as it typically accounts for more than half the price per gallon. When oil prices spike, so do gas prices. And frustratingly, when oil prices drop, gas prices tend to take their time drifting down to the lower price (sometimes referred to as “rockets and feathers”).

In case of emergency, the U.S. has a store of crude oil known as the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. Its primary purpose is energy security in case of disaster (think sanctions, severe storm damage, even war). But it can also go a long way toward softening crippling price hikes during supply shocks.

It’s not a long-term answer—more of an immediate relief to assist the consumer and keep critical parts of the economy running, like key industries, emergency services, public transportation, etc.

Oil and natural gas are both major energy fuels. A big change in oil prices can affect natural gas by extension. For example, if oil prices increase, some industries may swap natural gas for some segments of their operations where possible—which increases demand for natural gas.

When examining oil’s performance, there are generally two major benchmarks:

Between the two, Brent better represents global oil performance because it prices much of the world’s traded crude. And, it’s often the best way to track historical oil performance. In fact, even the U.S. Energy Information Administration now uses Brent as its primary reference in its Annual Energy Outlook.

Looking at the Brent benchmark across several decades, oil has been anything but steady. It’s seen spikes due to factors such as wars and supply cuts, and it’s also seen crashes from global recessions and an oversupply (called a “glut”). For example:

All to say, oil’s historical performance has been anything but smooth. Again, it’s hugely affected by wars, recessions, OPEC whims, evolving energy initiatives and policies, and much more.

Looking to stay up-to-date regarding the latest energy developments? Check out our recent coverage:

The current price of oil per barrel depends largely on supply and demand, including news about potential future supply and demand (geopolitics, decisions made by OPEC+, etc.). In the U.S., prices also move based on how friendly an administration is to drilling, as it can affect future supply. For example, 2025 saw the Trump administration move to reopen more than 1.5 million acres in the Coastal Plain of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge for oil and gas leasing, reversing the Biden administration’s policy of limiting oil drilling in the Arctic.

The price of oil updates constantly when the “futures” markets are open. A futures market is effectively an auction where people agree to buy or sell oil in the future. As long as people and companies are trading contracts, the oil price is changing.

In short, shale is rock that contains oil and natural gas. Think of shale as energy yet to be tapped. The more shale the U.S. accesses, the more energy we’ll have—and the more easily oil prices can keep from spiking as much thanks to a greater supply.

When oil is expensive, it tends to make everyday items cost more. This can be related to energy (your heating, gas utilities, etc.), but it’s also due to the logistics involved with making those items accessible to you. Shipping, for example, can affect the price of things at the grocery store, as it’s more expensive to get those products from warehouses and farms onto the shelf.

#5369. Pepsi Is Quietly Testing a Dirty Soda Startup. Here’s What They’re Learning Gen Z Is Really Thirsty For.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Pepsi’s dirty soda line started as a pop-up. Now it’s testing new syrups, a delivery kitchen and stores of its own.

If you find yourself walking around the Formula 1 track in Las Vegas this week, you’re likely to spot a mirror-chrome Airstream gleaming under the desert sun. Like an oasis, it’s serving Instagram-worthy drinks you won’t find anywhere else.

The drinks are called DRIPS by Pepsi, and it’s the company’s answer to the dirty soda craze: classic sodas loaded with syrups, cold foam and popping boba. The trailer is how PepsiCo tests and markets them.

Even though PepsiCo is a nearly a $100 billion company, the DRIPS team runs like a startup.

“We actually work as almost an intrapreneur within the company,” says Scott Finlow, chief marketing officer of PepsiCo Away From Home.

Here’s how it built a dirty soda brand from scratch, and what it’s learned along the way.

Pepsi has been courting young drinkers for decades. In 1963, it invited them to “Come alive! You’re in the Pepsi Generation.” That pitch later became “The Choice of a New Generation.” DRIPS is a continuation of that playbook.

This time, PepsiCo took its cue from Gen Z, who wanted drinks they could personalize with “a little bit of flair, a little bit of fun,” Finlow says. As Gen Z sees it, why should the root beer float be the only soda with personality?

That craving fueled the rise of dirty soda, popularized by Swig, a Utah drive-thru chain that coined the term. So PepsiCo built its own version. It developed a menu and a brand, then took DRIPS on the road in a converted Airstream. DRIPS has since popped up at festivals like Austin City Limits and landed on menus at Saucy, KFC’s chicken-tender chain, and Vail Resorts.

PepsiCo’s chefs are “the magicians behind these drinks,” Finlow says. They start with a popular flavor trend, pair it with a cultural moment and build the drink on a PepsiCo brand, adding texture like boba or layers of cold foam.

For example, bananas are big this season (who knew?). For F1, the team created a banana float made with Mug root beer. “Very rapidly, we can take a flavor trend and then a big moment in culture like F1,” Finlow says, “and we can then get in the kitchen with those chefs.”

The menu spans what the team calls “vibe states,” from indulgent to refreshing. Buzzy brands like poppi and Celsius are now in the mix. Energy in particular is becoming “an increasingly important base for crafted drinks as Gen Z shifts toward cold caffeinated drinks,” Finlow says.

Every recipe is also designed for the restaurants that serve DRIPS, down to the hand movements and the time it takes to make each drink. PepsiCo supplies operators with recipe kits, ingredients, marketing and help adding the drinks to their point-of-sale systems.

Now PepsiCo is packaging what it has learned for operators. Just today, it launched DRIPS by Pepsi Signature Mixes, its first standalone syrups, built on data from DRIPS pop-ups and customer feedback. Each of the five no-added-sugar syrups has several flavors in one pump, from Island Escape (mango, pineapple and coconut) to Mocha Mood (chocolate, caramel and warm spice). A new Lipton Green Tea concentrate mixes with still or sparkling water, so restaurants can make refreshers without new equipment

PepsiCo is also exploring standalone DRIPS stores in Austin and New York City. Finlow calls them “lab stores,” where the team can test prices, flavors and how fast staff can make each drink. Meanwhile, PepsiCo is piloting a DRIPS test kitchen in Manhattan that delivers six flavors.

Like any startup, the team is learning as they go and pivoting accordingly. Making sure the drinks work in busy restaurant kitchens is “the single biggest ongoing challenge,” Finlow says. There’s also pressure to grow fast, what he calls “a healthy tension” familiar to any founder going from early stage to scale.

So far, DRIPS is more of a pour. Last month at the U.S. Grand Prix in Austin, there was a line of mostly Gen Zers waiting to get their dulche de leche and gochujang on. The trailer did close to $10,000 a day in sales and served up to 130 drinks an hour at peak, Finlow says. The top seller was a Pepsi mixed with peach, lime and lychee jelly called Pole Position.

#5368. Araceli raises $4.5M for drug discovery tools aimed at reducing animal testing

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 13, 2026 at 12:51 pmNovember 13, 2026 at 4:38 pm

Araceli Biosciences, a Portland-area biotech company, has secured $4.5 million in funding to help commercialize technology and develop new products that support using human cells instead of animal studies to test new drugs.

The Tigard, Ore., startup offers instruments and software for creating images of cells and automating analysis. Its technologies fall under the umbrella term “New Approach Methodologies,” which includes human-tissue models, computer simulations and AI-based approaches that reduce or avoid experimentation on animals such as mice, rats and monkeys.

Supporters of the methods, known as NAMs, argue that they can yield better outcomes because animals are not a perfect substitute for humans and can generate irrelevant findings. That can lead to costly, time-intensive development of drugs that fail to perform in people. Advocates also promote the alternatives as more humane.

The National Institutes of Health announced $84 million in September to build infrastructure for NAMs research at 10 sites nationwide.

“[T]he efforts signal a significant investment into human-based technologies as the future of preclinical science, aiming to make research faster, more predictive, and more directly relevant to human health,” the NIH said in a release.

Araceli said it has raised a total of $22.7 million from investors. The new round was led by William Cortelyou and included Fluke Venture Partners, according to PitchBook. The company disclosed Thursday that businessman and animal welfare advocate Jeff Swickard was also an investor.

Swickard owns 54 auto dealerships across Western states and is a commercial real estate investor with $250 million invested in Portland properties.

Shawn MacDonald, chief financial officer for Araceli, said Swickard’s “support reflects a belief that we share, which is that better science and more humane science go hand-in-hand.”

Araceli launched in 2023 as a spinoff from Phoseon Technology, which makes UV LED units for industrial curing and life sciences applications.

The company said that companies and institutions using Araceli technology include the Max Planck Institute and Evotec in Germany, the Wertheim UF Scripps Institute in Florida, VALID Therapeutics in Boston, and Ginkgo Bioworks, as well as large pharmaceutical companies. It has 30 employees.

#5367. Pantera-backed Codex raises $30 million to link Asia to global markets with stablecoins

Money might make the world go round—but that doesn’t mean getting it around the world is easy. And while stablecoins, or cryptocurrencies pegged to fiat money, can simplify the process considerably, many businesses still lack the infrastructure to use them for cross-border payments. That’s where Codex sees an opportunity.

The Delaware-based startup announced Tuesday it raised $30 million in a Series A round to help businesses send money across borders and exchange currencies, without the need to deposit money in advance to use the service. Codex aims to carve out a niche in Asia and connect the region to markets in Latin America and sub-Saharan Africa.

“We help people convert money into whatever form they want and give it to whoever they want, wherever they want,” Haonan Li, cofounder and CEO of Codex, told Fortune. “Turns out, in lots of parts of the world, this is actually super hard to do.”

The 35-person company plans to use part of the capital to further automate its foreign-exchange platform, with AI agents central to its vision for how the business will operate, and keep costs down as transaction volumes grow.

Pantera Capital led the round, with participation from Dragonfly and Coinbase Ventures, at a $130 million post-money valuation. Both participated in Codex’s earlier seed round, which Dragonfly led alongside backers Circle Ventures, Cumberland, and Wintermute.

Stablecoins have been one of cryptocurrency’s longest-lasting trends, gaining traction as a lifeline in countries with high inflation or capital controls, and as a low-cost payment tool for businesses. Payments made with stablecoins reached at least $401 billion in the first eight months of 2026, up 42% year over year, with businesses on the receiving end of an estimated 58% to 64% of that volume, according to a September report by global consulting firm Alvarez & Marsal.

“[The team] is building Codex to meet the challenge of what happens after this massive explosion of stablecoin issuance, which is… a really fragmented system,” Franklin Bi general partner at Pantera Capital, said.

An economist by training, Li began his career in geopolitical forecasting research for political psychologist and writer Philip Tetlock, followed by a stint in quantitative finance. He later caught the “crypto bug” and became an early employee at Optimism, where he worked on Ethereum scaling and protocol economics.

There, he began to explore crypto’s most practical applications and landed on stablecoins, which some in Ethereum circles dismissed as boring. Li saw a way to help people excluded from traditional financial networks save, transfer, and exchange money.

To build that business, he teamed up with an old friend from his military days. Li had met Victor Yaw, now a Codex cofounder, about a decade earlier in infantry officer candidate school in Singapore’s military. Fellow cofounder Momo Ong, whom Li met through San Francisco’s founder community, initially advised the team before he joined full time. Together, they founded Codex in 2024.

After a few iterations, the company settled on its current product about a year ago. It now has offices in Singapore, Hong Kong and London, as well as New York and San Francisco. As Li put it: “the journey stretched from the jungles of Brunei to the skyscrapers of New York.”

#5366. Blue Origin puts its space station plans on hold to concentrate on moon missions instead

by Alan Boyle on Nov 13, 2026 at 2:35 pmNovember 13, 2026 at 2:35 pm

Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin space venture has decided not to seek further NASA funding for its Orbital Reef space station project in order to tighten its focus on lunar missions.

For the past five years, Blue Origin has played a lead role in Orbital Reef, alongside partners including Sierra Space and Boeing. In late 2021, Blue Origin won a $130 million contract from NASA in the first phase of the space agency’s Commercial Low Earth Orbit Destinations program, or CLD.

Now NASA is seeking proposals for the next phase of the program, which will fund the development of orbital outposts to replace International Space Station in the 2030s. Proposals are due on Dec. 8, with contracts expected to be awarded next spring.

Blue Origin indicated that it will not submit a bid.

“Blue Origin’s mission is to build a road to space for the benefit of Earth so that millions of people can live and work in space. Establishing a sustained human presence on the moon is a critical step toward that future,” the company said in an emailed statement.

“As our role supporting NASA’s Artemis and Moon Base missions continues to grow, we’re focusing resources on capabilities that directly advance our lunar projects,” Blue Origin said. “By sharpening that focus, we can move faster on the technologies and infrastructure needed to make lunar permanence a reality.”

Orbital Reef was once touted as a “mixed-use business park” in space — and was even slated to star in a sci-fi thriller titled “Helios.” But much like that delayed film project, the space station is now on the back burner.

Orbital Reef isn’t the only initiative Blue Origin has put on hold to prioritize moon missions. In January, the company suspended its suborbital New Shepard program for at least two years for similar reasons.

Blue Origin is building landers for delivering cargo and crews to the lunar surface for NASA. An uncrewed Blue Moon Mark 1 lunar lander is scheduled for launch early next year, and a crew-capable Mark 2 version is scheduled for testing in low Earth orbit next year during NASA’s Artemis 3 mission.

Last week, NASA awarded Blue Origin a $94 million base contract, plus a $140 million option, to deliver a nuclear-powered rover to the lunar south pole. Blue Origin also won a spot in NASA’s broader lunar cargo delivery program. In addition, Honeybee Robotics, a Blue Origin subsidiary, will contribute to a lunar power-generating project known as miniCAST.

Blue Origin is pursuing several other moon development initiatives, including a program called Blue Alchemist that aims to use lunar materials to manufacture solar cells and electrical wire.

Several competitors are still working on commercial space stations. Voyager Technologies, Airbus and Northrop Grumman lead the Starlab consortium, which received CLD Phase 1 funding from NASA and is expected to put in a proposal for Phase 2.

Axiom Space and Vast are also developing outposts that could take the place of the ISS. Meanwhile, Marysville, Wash.-based Gravitics is building space station hardware for Axiom and an orbital carrier for the U.S. Space Force.

#5365. The 1 Skill AI Will Never Master — No Matter How Advanced It Gets

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

As AI does more, we need to know its limits.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Everywhere we look, we’re confronted with new things AI is doing, from making full-length movies to solving seemingly unsolvable math problems. That makes automating marketing, sales and communications, among other things, seem all but certain. AI is truly everywhere, and it seems to be capable of just about anything — if not today, then tomorrow.

As AI reaches deeper into new corners of our personal and professional lives, there’s at least one thing it will never be able to do by itself: persuade. Persuasion — understood properly as “shared action” — will always require a uniquely human touch.

Despite — or, indeed, because of AI’s many remarkable strengths — it will only ever be a supplemental tool for all of your persuasive endeavors, especially in business and leadership. Understanding AI’s limitations when it comes to persuasion will help you excel whenever you need to use it to engage others professionally and personally, whether you’re making the sale to a potential client or your spouse.

AI assistants like ChatGPT and Google’s Gemini have enormous strengths when it comes to communicating more persuasively.

Their ability to capture, analyze and synthesize massive amounts of information is unparalleled. AI can quickly provide data on just about any subject. More than that, it can sort through the data, looking for trends and differences among viewpoints. AI’s ability to research exceeds the skills not just of interns, but of entry-level employees like Research Assistants and consultants, and even mid-level knowledge workers. Even teams of knowledge workers. That’s why many of these positions are being partially or entirely automated across many sectors, including at companies like McKinsey.

AI doesn’t stop at simply collecting information. It can make arguments for and against positions, too. It will structure those arguments logically and support them with facts. It can identify and respond to counterarguments to your position.

It will even make arguments against using AI itself. I asked ChatGPT if AI should be eliminated, and it quickly answered, “Probably not.” Then it responded with many paragraphs nuancing the answer. Gemini responded, “Eliminating artificial intelligence entirely would mean losing transformative advancements.”

AI can frame arguments for diverse audiences. I asked ChatGPT how it would frame advocating for zoning reform to progressives and conservatives (housing policy is one of my areas of expertise). It identified seven issues like equity and property rights and suggested thoughtful ways to navigate them with both groups.

AI can even craft stories. I asked it for compelling stories to advance housing reform, and it offered 10. The first was about “The young couple who can afford the mortgage — but can’t afford the house.” Good place to start.

So, what’s missing from AI’s approach to persuasion? There are three areas where AI will continue to fall short.

First, getting what we want begins by adopting what I call “the persuader’s mindset”: It’s about them, not you. Which means you have to put them first. Only when you truly understand your counterpart, put their needs front and center, and show them how you can meet them (while also meeting yours), will they be eager to work with you not once but repeatedly.

Adopting this mindset requires you to be fully in tune with your audience. AI can offer general understandings of an audience. It cannot, however, do a few critical things. It cannot relate to someone interpersonally since, well, it’s not a person. Groups are comprised of individuals with nuanced views. Humans can poke, probe, dig and explore in ways AI can’t — with emotional intelligence.

Second, AI’s approach to persuasion is, unsurprisingly, logic-first. This is, in many ways, a virtue: AI can quickly bring an abundance of data to bear on any issue.

The trouble with this logic-first approach is that it’s not in accordance with how our brains work. All the neuroscience and all the psychology show that humans are wired to feel first, then reason. This means that you need to start with feelings before turning to logic.

Indeed, AI recognizes this limitation. When I asked Gemini what areas it would struggle with in persuading, it replied: “Gemini faces distinct limitations in persuasion whenever success relies entirely on deeply human emotional intelligence, physical presence or lived experience.” ChatGPT emphasized that it cannot experience any emotions it’d be responding to.

AI’s logic-first approach will fall flat if it isn’t coupled with sufficient emotional intelligence. That’s where only humans can come in.

Third, AI can’t bring the human elements to interacting with others.

Humans listen not just to what others say, but how they say something. Were they excited or anxious? We watch for body language. She grimaced when I said that — uh oh! Maybe I shouldn’t have said it.

Humans can bring dynamism to how they share their ideas. They can be charismatic, warm and exciting. AI? Not so much.

Ultimately, the best way to leverage AI for all of your persuasive endeavors is to lean on its strengths — research, data, logic, arguments and the like — and then build a human-centered, emotionally intelligent edifice on top of it.

Everywhere we look, we’re confronted with new things AI is doing, from making full-length movies to solving seemingly unsolvable math problems. That makes automating marketing, sales and communications, among other things, seem all but certain. AI is truly everywhere, and it seems to be capable of just about anything — if not today, then tomorrow.

As AI reaches deeper into new corners of our personal and professional lives, there’s at least one thing it will never be able to do by itself: persuade. Persuasion — understood properly as “shared action” — will always require a uniquely human touch.

Despite — or, indeed, because of AI’s many remarkable strengths — it will only ever be a supplemental tool for all of your persuasive endeavors, especially in business and leadership. Understanding AI’s limitations when it comes to persuasion will help you excel whenever you need to use it to engage others professionally and personally, whether you’re making the sale to a potential client or your spouse.

#5364. Officials blame aging FAA telecom gear as U.S. airspace reopens, see no link to Microsoft or AI

by Todd Bishop on Nov 13, 2026 at 3:04 pmNovember 13, 2026 at 7:58 pm

Updated with officials’ explanation of the cause and the reopening of U.S. airspace.

The nationwide ground stop that halted U.S. commercial air travel Friday was not caused by the Microsoft 365 outage that began a day earlier, federal officials said at an evening news conference, blaming aging FAA telecom equipment that was overloaded with data.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin opened the news conference by raising the Microsoft outage himself. “I want to make sure everybody understands that there is no connection between this and Microsoft,” he said. “I know a lot of people are making that jump.”

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy likewise ruled out a role for SMART, the FAA’s new AI traffic-planning tool, saying it isn’t connected to the core systems controllers use to track flights.

“There was no possible way SMART would have impacted what happened today,” he said.

The FAA reopened U.S. airspace at 5:15 p.m. Pacific, more than four hours after the problems began, Duffy said. He said flights would resume slowly, depending on whether airlines had crews available, and some may not depart until Saturday morning.

Microsoft confirmed in a statement that it had no indication the FAA ground stop was related to its service disruption.

Asked whether a cyberattack or “rogue AI” could be ruled out, Mullin said there was “nothing completely certain right now,” but “it appears that this was mechanically driven.” He said he could not rule out the possibility of a cyberattack but said there was “zero evidence” of one so far.

What happened: Duffy said the FAA began seeing unstable radar and communications data at air traffic control facilities across the country at 12:36 p.m. Pacific. Aging switches and routers in the agency’s telecom network “got overloaded with data” and began producing inconsistent information, he said, adding that the FAA still relies on “1980s little copper lines.”

“Our new IP switches did not go down. It’s the old hardware that went down,” he said. The FAA restored service after deploying fixes to reduce the overloading on its switches, he said.

Mullin said the overload appeared to have been triggered by new equipment the FAA was installing. As the agency put “patches into the system” and added “new equipment and new technology,” he said, it “was overwhelming the older system.” Neither official said exactly what that equipment was.

The FAA is in the middle of replacing its legacy telecom network with a modern internet-protocol network. AT&T took over the lead role on that project in August with an initial $74.3 million award, as the FAA works toward a goal of finishing by the end of 2028.

Duffy and Mullin used the briefing to press Congress for money to finish rebuilding the air traffic control system. Mullin said President Trump has declared the situation a national emergency.

The administration has asked Congress for an additional $30.1 billion for aviation infrastructure, AeroTime reported. Duffy said at the evening news conference that he wants $50 billion.

Earlier in the day, Mullin had said officials were looking into a possible link to SMART, including through DHS’s Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA). The FAA said Tuesday it was expanding the system to the airspace managed by all 22 of its en route air traffic control centers.

The agency describes SMART as a cloud-based system that pulls in about 200 data streams, including weather, flight paths and controller staffing, to recommend flight schedules and routes. FAA specialists review its recommendations, and local facilities decide whether to act on them.

SMART is part of a 12-year, $875 million FAA contract with Boston-based Air Space Intelligence, which denied any connection to the issue. “The current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC,” the company said.

The FAA halted departures nationwide shortly before 1 p.m. Pacific. More than 3,500 planes were in the air at the time, Duffy said. It’s the second nationwide ground stop since the Sept. 11 attacks, after a January 2023 failure of the FAA’s Notice to Air Missions system.

FlightAware counted nearly 7,000 flights delayed or canceled as of Friday afternoon.

#5363. The death of the internet ‘built for human eyeballs’ is still ‘underappreciated’ by financial markets, UBS warns

The internet was built on a simple bet: a person is looking at the screen. UBS says AI agents are starting to break that bargain.

“Since its inception, the internet has been built for human eyeballs,” Ulrike Hoffmann-Burchardi, chief investment officer for the Americas at UBS Wealth Management, said in a note and podcast released Monday. “Every website, every checkout button, and every software dashboard assumes a person is sitting behind the screen, clicking through tabs.” AI agents that shop, compare and click on a person’s behalf break that assumption, she argued, and with it two of tech’s most profitable business models: digital advertising and enterprise software sold as a service.

Her name for the shift: “We are moving from B2C (business to consumer) to B2A (business to agent).” And her warning to investors: “We believe the speed of AI disruption is still underappreciated by the markets.”

The stakes are plain for any company whose revenue depends on a customer’s attention, or lack of it. On the same day, BofA Global Research put numbers on what that could look like for one company whose model leans on the second kind.

Hoffmann-Burchardi’s example seems banal on its face. A shopper tells an agent to find waterproof trail-running shoes under $150 that arrive by Thursday, and the agent checks inventory, compares specs and buys.

“AI agents do not have emotions,” she said. “They don’t care about a clever Super Bowl spot or a brightly colored retargeting banner.” Brands that want to be found, UBS argues, will need to expose machine-readable product data and real-time inventory, because search-engine optimization alone is no longer enough.

The same logic hits enterprise software. If one AI-augmented employee or an automated workflow can work at the speed of five to 10 people, Hoffmann-Burchardi said, companies don’t need to buy more software seats, and if agents talk straight to a database, the dashboard becomes obsolete.

The consumer side is already moving. Meta’s Muse agent app passed an estimated 10 million U.S. downloads in its first 40 days, according to Sensor Tower estimates reported in October, and Instinct, a personal-agent app, reported that 40% of users connected their credit cards to its assistant by week three, according to UBS.

Bending Spoons, the Milan-based company that has bought more than 50 businesses, including AOL, Vimeo, Eventbrite, Evernote and WeTransfer, is close to a pure test of that idea. Its model, as BofA describes it, is to buy durable but under-optimized subscription businesses, cut costs, raise prices and use the cash to buy more.

BofA’s analysts, Omar Dessouky and Ethan Liu, built their Nov. 16 report around one line: “Inconvenience is the main moat against AI.” People keep paying because finding the subscription they forgot, researching alternatives or moving years of notes is a chore. An agent does chores.

BofA rates about 29% of Bending Spoons’ projected 2027 revenue as high risk from AI agents. That’s AOL ($778.8 million in BofA’s 2027 estimate), where AI can compare the bundled security add-ons it sells on convenience and AI assistants can replace its tech-help subscriptions; Eventbrite ($403.1 million); and Evernote ($125.5 million), where “AI assistants become a new ‘second brain.’” WeTransfer is medium risk. Vimeo is low, because big video libraries are hard to move and AI may get more people making video. BofA hasn’t rated the other 53%.

Bending Spoons says it hasn’t seen this happening. “We closely monitor our businesses’ KPIs and haven’t seen any signs that AI agents are driving cancellations or switching to alternative products,” a company spokesperson told Fortune.

BofA analysts largely concur, saying they “have yet to track data to test our hypotheses,” and they “have not yet seen data to suggest that is currently happening at large scale.” The savings from cancelling AOL, WeTransfer, Evernote, Eventbrite or Vimeo, they wrote, run from about $228 to $728 a year, “equivalent to a weekly cup of coffee.” Their preliminary conclusion: “the value gained from switching to cheaper or better solutions rarely exceeds the cost of staying put.”

They also see third-quarter organic growth risks “skewed mildly to the upside.” BofA rates the stock Underperform, with a $38 price objective against a $41.08 share price, mostly on valuation and on whether Bending Spoons can keep buying companies at its target returns. It carried net debt of 205% of equity at the end of 2025, by BofA’s count, and its recent deals include Airtable for $1.285 billion and Miro for $1.355 billion.

Economists have measured the moat BofA is describing. In a 2006 study of 7,752 health-club members, Stefano DellaVigna and Ulrike Malmendier found people on monthly contracts paid more than $17 per expected visit when a 10-visit pass would have cost them $10 a visit, and that an average of 2.31 months passed between a member’s last workout and the cancellation.

Regulators have tried to shrink it. The Federal Trade Commission’s “click-to-cancel” rule was vacated by the Eighth Circuit in 2025 on procedural grounds; the agency reopened the rulemaking in March, according to law firm Jones Day.

In February 2000, Fortune asked, “How Much Are Your Eyeballs Worth?” Analysts then were valuing internet companies by “market capitalization per pair of eyeballs.” Lycos came out at $244 a pair. “Eyeballs aren’t earnings,” the story argued.

UBS cited that story Monday to make the opposite point: the next visitor may not have eyeballs at all. Bending Spoons reports third-quarter results Nov. 20, the first test since BofA’s report of whether its customers are still staying put.

Nick Lichtenberg is business editor and was formerly Fortune's executive editor of global news.

#5362. Binance’s $6.3B Hack Fix Is Coming Tomorrow: Why the ZK Math Doesn't Tell the Whole Story

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

On-chain data shows the attacker behind the $6.3 billion Binance theft depositing about $4 million into three Binance deposit addresses.

At the same time, Binance's first post-hack reserve snapshot shows its biggest assets covered with buffers as small as 2.7 ETH and $6 of USDT. Binance's full zero-knowledge proof of those figures is due by Tuesday.

Some of the money stolen from Binance has started going back to Binance.

Blockchain intelligence firm Arkham has flagged the entity it tracks as "Binance Hacker" depositing about $4 million into three Binance deposit addresses. Arkham says those addresses "likely represent nested service(s)." These are third-party exchanges that use Binance for liquidity and custody, giving their own customers deposit addresses that sit on Binance's infrastructure.

If Arkham is right, the hacker isn't depositing into an ordinary Binance account. The money would be going to smaller platforms that operate through Binance. Exchanges have long known this is a weak point for stolen funds moving into normal trading. Either way, Binance is now receiving stolen funds at its own deposit addresses while it works to show customers it has replaced what was taken.

The FBI has attributed the October 29 theft to North Korea. The deposits come at a sensitive moment. Binance has just published its first reserve snapshot since the hack and has promised a full cryptographic proof of it by Tuesday.

$4 million is a small slice of a theft worth about $6.3 billion, but it matters for two reasons.

It shows how the laundering works. Nested services are a common way into the regulated financial system. A third-party platform that relies on Binance for custody may run weaker identity checks on its own users. Funds deposited there can be swapped and withdrawn without the hacker ever opening a Binance account.

Binance can act on it. Binance can't freeze bitcoin and ether sitting in wallets nobody controls, and it doesn't control the stablecoins that issuers like Tether and Circle have frozen. Deposits that land at its own addresses are different: they are on Binance's platform, so Binance can freeze them itself. One of the first tests of how Binance handles the money still in the hacker's hands is whether it freezes these funds and identifies the services that own the addresses.

While the hacker's funds move, Binance has been rebuilding its reserves. Its proof-of-reserves page now shows:

The first page covers Binance's six largest assets. Customer balances are what users hold. Reserves are on-chain wallet balances, including assets held with outside custodians.

The second page has four more assets, and two of them stand out:

Why USD1 and RLUSD matter: these are two of the stablecoins whose issuers froze stolen funds after the attack. World Liberty Financial froze $27 million of USD1, and Ripple began freezing RLUSD the same night. Both now show reserves above what Binance owes customers.

Assets with outside custodians: part of several reserves sits with outside custodians rather than in Binance's own exchange wallets:

The striking part isn't that the ratios reach 100%. It's how closely they stop there.

Compared with October's report: Binance's previous monthly report, published in early October before the hack, showed BTC at 100.35% and USDT at 103.88%. ETH was already at exactly 100.00%. After the theft:

Not every asset is that tight. USDC, ZEC and BNB carry buffers of 1.3% to 6%. The thinnest buffers are in BTC, ETH, USDT and SOL, which are among the assets the attacker took in the largest amounts.

How Binance says it got here: the pattern fits Binance's account of replacing the stolen assets in stages. It reported 80% replaced on Friday, 90% on Saturday and 95% on Sunday. The remaining 5% is in less-liquid tokens it is still buying. The money came from:

Binance confirmed taking 7,499 BTC from SAFU and has pledged to refill the fund to about $1 billion.

What the snapshot can't show: it was taken a little over a day after the theft, once the rebuild was under way. It shows the balance sheet after the replacement, not how large the gap was on October 29.

Binance says the full proof takes 40 to 50 hours to compute. Its latest update says it will be ready "by Tuesday, 2026-11-03 (UTC)." The system is open source, in Binance's zkmerkle-proof-of-solvency repository.

What the proof guarantees, according to the project's circuit design document:

The design also guards against a "dummy user attack" identified by Ethereum Foundation researcher Enrico Bottazzi. In that attack, fake accounts holding cheap tokens are used to offset debts in major assets.

What it doesn't prove: the reserve side. The project's verifier config describes the totals as information "published by CEX, it represents CEX's liability." The reserve figures are checked a different way, against the wallet addresses Binance publishes through the page's "Download All Address" option.

What customers can do: each user can get a Merkle proof for their account and check it against the published root. They can use the verifier code in Binance's repository rather than Binance's own interface. That doesn't prove Binance is solvent, but it confirms the user's balance was counted.

Binance has rebuilt its reserves to 100% across its ten largest assets, but on several of them the buffer is only a few coins. Meanwhile, stolen funds are reaching its deposit addresses through platforms that run on its infrastructure. Tuesday's proof can confirm customer balances. It can't show how Binance handles the stolen money arriving at its own door.

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

XRP is struggling to reclaim $1, but its derivatives market is showing an increasingly unusual setup. Traders betting against the token are now paying funding fees to maintain their positions. This creates an interesting possibility for the XRP price prediction. If buying pressure returns, bearish traders could face mounting losses and forced liquidations.

However, the market is not quite ready for a bullish victory lap. Open interest is falling, long positions have already suffered heavy liquidations, and XRP still needs to reclaim important resistance levels.

XRP traded around $0.95, following another difficult session for the crypto market. Meanwhile, its futures market is flashing a rate that dropped in aggregated funding to -0.0068% every eight hours, equivalent to roughly -7.4% annually.

Negative funding means short sellers pay long traders to maintain their perpetual futures positions. In other words, bears are effectively paying a premium to maintain their bearish exposure.

Hyperliquid showed an even more pronounced imbalance, with XRP funding reaching approximately -10.2% annually. The figures suggest bearish positioning has become increasingly expensive across several derivatives markets.

However, there is another side to this trade. XRP open interest declined 5.74% over 24 hours to approximately $1.97 billion, so traders are reducing leverage rather than aggressively opening fresh positions.

While XRP traders debate whether another recovery is coming, Bitcoin Hyper ($HYPER) is approaching an important milestone of its own. The Bitcoin Layer 2 project has raised more than $33.2 million during its presale, with its token currently priced at just $0.0136.

The presale is scheduled to conclude on November 26, leaving a narrowing window before its anticipated token launch. Buyers choosing the staking option are also being offered an advertised 35% APY during the presale period.

The project has already introduced testnet components, including its explorer, wallet, faucet, and bridge. With the presale approaching its scheduled conclusion, the remaining allocation and upcoming launch milestone could attract additional attention from traders looking beyond established crypto networks.

The immediate question is whether bearish positioning has become sufficiently expensive to trigger an unexpected reversal. A negative funding rate alone cannot confirm a short squeeze. XRP needs to attract fresh spot buyers, recover momentum, and force short sellers to close their positions.

The first important hurdle remains $1.00. Reclaiming this psychological level could encourage sidelined buyers to return and create additional pressure on leveraged shorts.

A sustained move above $1.00 would put $1.10 within reach, followed by a potential test of $1.20 if short liquidations accelerate.

However, the bearish scenario remains firmly in play. Losing the recent $0.89 low could expose XRP to another decline toward $0.80, particularly if Bitcoin continues weakening.

For now, the XRP price prediction hinges on whether negative funding translates into actual buying pressure. Bears are paying longs, but bulls still need to deliver the rally. If they do, the same traders betting against XRP could become the fuel behind its next recovery.

#5360. I Eliminated Busywork From My Schedule. So Why Was I Still Running Out of Time?

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Sometimes, no matter how organized you are, life happens and you find yourself with way too much to do. Here’s how to handle it.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

On a recent Tuesday, I sat down at my desk. The sun was just coming up, the air was crisp, my coffee was full. I blinked, and then, suddenly, it was night. I didn’t understand. Nearly 12 hours flew by, and I still had so much to do.

To be clear, it’s not because I’m inefficient. My schedule is largely empty of busywork; I pride myself on a streamlined schedule and my ability to banish time-sucking tasks. I love testing out apps and finding new ways to clear my calendar for what matters most.

But some days, no matter how many items I take off my plate or how little time I waste, the fact remains: I just have too much to do. A deadline gets pushed, a kid gets sick, a task takes longer than I thought it would. Life is like that sometimes. And when that happens, here’s what I do.

Perfectionism sounds good on paper. Who doesn’t want things to be perfect? But when you’ve got too much to do, it can be like quicksand, trapping you under work that could have been completed in a fraction of the time.

There’s a reason why entrepreneurs should always build MVPs — minimum viable products — before getting too deep into an idea. You want to be agile enough to fix what’s broken and respond to user testing before wasting time creating something polished. When you have too much on your plate, embracing “good enough” as a mindset can make the difference between successfully doing what needs to be done, and not.

There’s one surefire way to knock more items off your to-do list: Work more. As an entrepreneur, there will be some inevitable late nights, early mornings and weekends in front of your laptop. But you have to be careful to keep it from becoming the norm.

Despite all the science advising against it, the fact is that grinding is still very much embraced in startup culture. But it’s not worth it. Overwork causes high blood pressure, increasing your risk for stroke and heart disease. It also weakens your immune system — if you thought you had too much to do now, imagine trying to fight through your to-do list while battling the brain fog brought on by a virus.

You’re also risking burnout, which kills productivity — exactly what you don’t want. You might think it doesn’t apply to you, which is what The 5 Resets author and Harvard researcher Dr. Aditi Nerurkar thought, too — wrongly. “I thought: ‘Stress doesn’t happen to people like me; I’m resilient,’” she told The Guardian. “Now we know that that’s scientifically untrue — resilience, while protective, is by no means preventive for burnout.”

Instead, go for a walk. Even a few minutes outside, away from your screen, can be enough to help your brain reset. Get enough sleep and eat well. These are the best protections you have against keeping your body and mind working at capacity — which, when you have too much to do, is critical.

I hate flaking. It’s satisfying to be reliable and follow through on what I say I am going to do. Sometimes, though, there’s no other option.

When I really have too much to do, I take a hard look at my calendar and ask which commitments genuinely make sense. What items on there are “shoulds” rather than “musts”? What can be reshuffled to a less stressful time? What will happen if you ask to reschedule a podcast interview, or pass on a networking dinner? Will the world end if you miss a recurring weekly meeting, just this once? If the repercussions for canceling are minor, do it.

To avoid stepping on toes, it pays to be both honest and prompt. When you realize you’re in over your head, a short note that explains that you’re overcommitted and need to reschedule usually does the trick. People understand; they’ve been there, too. There’s no need to go into excessive detail — the most important thing is letting them know as soon as possible so they can adjust their plans accordingly.

Life gets hectic, and so much is outside of our control. Your schedule could be perfectly calibrated, and then your car breaks down. You’re preparing for a launch, and then a pipe bursts. You get called for jury duty, sending your week into chaos.

When things happen, take a deep breath. Getting stressed won’t fix the situation, but it will make it worse. I try to remind myself that a derailed day isn’t a reflection of my discipline or capability. It’s just a day.

Being kind to yourself also has practical benefits. Researchers have found that self-compassion helps people recover from setbacks faster and stay motivated longer than self-criticism does. The energy you would expend replaying what went wrong can be used to make it go right tomorrow.

On a recent Tuesday, I sat down at my desk. The sun was just coming up, the air was crisp, my coffee was full. I blinked, and then, suddenly, it was night. I didn’t understand. Nearly 12 hours flew by, and I still had so much to do.

To be clear, it’s not because I’m inefficient. My schedule is largely empty of busywork; I pride myself on a streamlined schedule and my ability to banish time-sucking tasks. I love testing out apps and finding new ways to clear my calendar for what matters most.

But some days, no matter how many items I take off my plate or how little time I waste, the fact remains: I just have too much to do. A deadline gets pushed, a kid gets sick, a task takes longer than I thought it would. Life is like that sometimes. And when that happens, here’s what I do.

#5359. Gov. Ferguson seeks $10M to help develop Eastern Wash. clean-energy hub

Challenges, breakthroughs and big ideas in the race to protect our planet. SEE MORE

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 13, 2026 at 4:32 pmNovember 16, 2026 at 10:09 am

Gov. Bob Ferguson is proposing $10 million to fund basic infrastructure needed for the Northwest Advanced Clean Energy Park, a master-planned industrial area in Eastern Washington that will foster development of large-scale clean energy, advanced manufacturing and supply chains. The proposal will be included in his 2027–29 capital budget.

If approved by lawmakers, the funding would support sewer, water, electrical and road infrastructure at the park.

“This investment will support thousands of good-paying jobs in the trades and advanced industries, and unlock billions in private investment,” Ferguson said in a statement.

The 1,641-acre site was formerly part of the Hanford Nuclear Reservation, a sprawling federal property along the Columbia River near the Tri-Cities that is undergoing a massive environmental cleanup. Hanford was established during World War II to produce plutonium for the Manhattan Project.

Mel Clark, president and CEO of the CleanTech Alliance, an industry trade group, welcomed the news as the state struggles to get clean power plugged into the grid.

“Washington needs more energy generation, more clean energy, and more manufacturing,” Clark told GeekWire via email. “We’re excited to see the Governor take action to change our last-place ranking in building new clean energy projects.”

According to the governor’s office, two projects have committed to locating at the park once infrastructure construction is complete: Atlas Agro’s low-carbon fertilizer production plant and the utility-scale Ruby Flats Solar Farm.

State officials said General Matter is also considering the location for producing advanced nuclear fuel for small reactors. That siting could potentially be beneficial for another project planned for the same area: Amazon, X-energy and Energy Northwest are developing plans for the Cascade Advanced Energy Facility, a nuclear plant comprised of clustered, small reactors.

In 2024, the Norwegian company Cenate expressed interest in building a factory at the park to produce lithium-ion battery components, according to the Tri-Cities Area Journal of Business, ultimately withdrew its plans.

The Tri-Cities is also attracting fusion-energy investment. Last year, Seattle startup Avalanche Energy landed a $10 million grant from the Washington State Department of Commerce’s Green Jobs Grant Program to develop FusionWERX, a commercial-scale testing facility for fusion technologies. The project is being developed in an existing Port of Benton building in Richland.

Washington is heading into its 2027–29 biennial budget with a multibillion-dollar shortfall, but officials have not yet settled on a definitive public estimate.

Ferguson has acknowledged the scale of the gap but has not publicly specified an amount. The shortfall concerns the state’s operating budget, which is separate from the capital budget funding proposed for the energy park.

Editor’s note: Comment from CleanTech Alliance President and CEO Mel Clark added 11/16.

The Climate Pledge is a commitment to reach net-zero carbon emissions by 2040, co-founded by Amazon and Global Optimism in 2019.

Seven years later, the community has grown to over 700 signatories across 62 industries and 49 countries and territories, reducing emissions, scaling emerging climate solutions, and addressing challenges across operations and value chains.

#5357. I’ve Spent the Past Year Analyzing Why AI Recommends Some Products Over Others. Here’s How to Win the Holiday Shopping Game.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Courtney Sandora, founder of Go Social, helps brands compete across AI search.

This as-told-to story is based on a conversation with Courtney Sandora, founder of digital marketing agency Go Social, which focuses on the spirits industry. With a journalism and PR background, Sandora enjoys getting people to discover and talk about brands. Read on to see her top tips for brands that want to compete in the AEO (answer engine optimization) era and win customers this holiday shopping season and beyond. The piece has been edited for length and clarity.

I started my own business about 16 years ago. I wanted more flexibility and to do my own thing. I’ve always been interested in when something new comes on the scene. How does that impact how people discover brands and how our brands are recommended? Post-influencer marketing, AI visibility is what I’ve been super excited about.

About a year and a half ago, I began looking for our clients on ChatGPT. We do a lot in the wine and whiskey space. I was like, “Wow, ChatGPT is citing the publication Whiskey Wash” and some of these trade publications that quite honestly when you tell clients, “Oh, I got you in that,” they’re like, “Meh, it’s okay.” It’s not the Men’s Journal of the world. But I realized it was being cited because AI sees it as an authority and niche publication.

But when I talk to clients, a lot of people don’t understand that there’s now an AI brand shortlist, and brands that aren’t optimized for AI will become invisible really fast. I’m not saying SEO is totally going away, but there’s a reason I never went into SEO. It’s a different side of the brain. I’m interested in storytelling and brand positioning. Historically, SEO has been more technical — site links, keywords, etc. This new AI world is really about understanding, Where are you relevant in consumers’ lives? What are the questions they’re going to ask that you’re going to answer?

A McKinsey study showed that when you look at the referrals on ChatGPT, where it’s pulling sources from, only 5% to 10% were coming from websites. It makes a lot of sense. If you’re asking an LLM a specific product question, about an ingredient or comparing two brands within the same portfolio, it’s more likely to go to a website. But that’s not really a lot of the questions people are asking. They’re like, “I’m going to San Francisco. What’s a great bar downtown?”

AI is not going to pull its response from a brand’s website; it’s smart enough not to do that. So knowing how to tell a story and seeding the right message with third-party authorities like journalists and creators becomes critical. We do a lot of social media for our clients, and for B2B, LinkedIn matters, but we’re not seeing platforms like Instagram drive a lot of results on the LLMs. At one point, AI was pulling a ton from Reddit, but recently it’s been less. Even with things like press releases, AI is savvy enough to say, “This is a press release. This isn’t an article,” and not give it the same weight.

Now, the approach has to start with the consumer. The first thing we do is we look at the category as a whole. What are people asking about bourbon in the category? You have to understand that landscape. Usually, you can’t see every question that people are asking, but they start to group into certain categories. So you can see what kinds of questions people are asking ChatGPT about bourbon. You need to determine if your brand is showing up when you ask those questions. If it’s not — and that’s very possible, especially if it’s a newer brand — you have to consider which questions you could credibly own.

You don’t want to go out there and say, “I want to be the best bourbon.” Good luck. But what are your strengths as a brand? And also, do people care? We had a client who’s trying to own a certain cocktail that no one was asking about. So we had to ask if that’s really where we should put forth our effort. Because if no one’s asking about that specific cocktail, does it matter?

Once you understand the landscape, what you could credibly own and where you can fit in, the next step is seeding stories. That storytelling extends across everything from PR to creators, even how you appear on a retailer website. Typically, on retailer websites, there’s a short description. Is the message you want to tell in that retailer website description? Consistency matters too.

To use the example of bourbon again — there are some bourbons that own the gifting category. It’s an important category that people ask about. If that’s your brand’s strength, and then it stops appearing in gift guides, you make room for a competitor to slide in. It is all about patterns. The more AI sees a third party recommending you, the more likely you’ll appear in AI searches. But you also have to have retail availability. If people can’t purchase, that’s going to be a problem.

Early on, as I researched AEO on Reddit, people didn’t think it was a real thing that would actually compete with SEO. Even now, sometimes when I’m talking to clients, they’re like, “Well, my SEO contact said all I need to do is put up an FAQ page and tweak my website.” That doesn’t hurt, but it’s not going to move the needle. AEO is a different beast.

Just like we witnessed in the social media world, where all of a sudden you could schedule within a platform and the businesses offering that service shuttered overnight, I think a lot of the early movers helping people navigate LLMs will be pushed aside as tools become more sophisticated and integrated into the various platforms. But I’m banking on the idea that people are still going to need help figuring out the story they want to own and how to tell it.

#5356. ‘I hope this email finds you’: Microsoft declares outage over as the world digs out of its inbox

by Todd Bishop on Nov 14, 2026 at 10:35 amNovember 16, 2026 at 7:28 am

Steven Sinofsky was relieved this week to finally give up a title he never wanted.

“Somewhat happy to say I am no longer responsible for the worst Outlook outage,” the former Microsoft executive posted on X Friday, sharing a May 2000 news story about the “I Love You” worm, which overwhelmed corporate email systems when he ran the Office group.

Later in the day, he aired a pet peeve. After a plumber emailed to say he’d missed an appointment because of the “Outlook outage,” Sinofsky noted that this one wasn’t really the application’s fault. “This time it is the data center layer,” he wrote.

Microsoft’s explanation backs him up. The company says the failure, which cut off email for people and organizations in more than 70 countries this week, was introduced during an earlier network capacity upgrade in its Microsoft 365 cloud and surfaced after a more recent network change. It hasn’t given more details.

The company said late Friday it had restored service to the remaining customers and regions. The disruption lasted about 30 hours, according to Microsoft’s incident log. Microsoft offered a public apology and promised a detailed post-mortem explaining what went wrong and next steps.

Charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, Agents and Platform, said on X Friday afternoon that “cascading failures + thundering herds at our network perimeter” made recovery more difficult than normal.

A “thundering herd” isn’t a stampede of frustrated IT admins descending on Redmond, as fitting as that might have been. It happens when huge numbers of devices try to reconnect at the same time, overwhelming systems as they come back online.

He said the post-mortem would come “shortly,” with a “step-by-step timeline and our many repair items to avoid similar outages in the future.” In a reply to another user, he said Microsoft “will be very specific on what happened.” In its notice to customers, Microsoft said it would provide a preliminary post-incident report within two business days and a final report within five.

In the meantime, like prior incidents involving AWS and others, the “Outlook outage” became the latest example of how much depends on one company’s cloud.

Microsoft reported in January that it had more than 450 million paid commercial Microsoft 365 seats, roughly one for every 18 people on Earth.

Among those affected this week were Unity Health Toronto, a hospital network that had to declare a Code Grey, the alert for a systems failure; a Colorado jail that couldn’t take online bond payments; and Pennsylvania lawmakers who went about 18 hours without email. Unity Health said patient care continued without disruption.

In Japan, securities firms and asset managers fell back on fax machines when trade-confirmation emails stopped coming through, Business Upturn reported, citing Nikkei.

In New York, the city’s Emergency Management office warned of delays reaching city agencies. In Singapore, the outage disrupted some government systems, including email, and in London, the UK Supreme Court wasn’t receiving email.

About the only thing that wasn’t Microsoft’s fault was Friday’s nationwide FAA ground stop. Federal officials blamed aging FAA telecom gear. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin opened an evening news conference — before even getting to the news that U.S. airspace had reopened — by saying there was “no connection between this and Microsoft,” adding, “I know a lot of people are making that jump.”

Microsoft itself looked to preempt the speculation a few hours earlier, posting on X that it had “no indication that the FAA’s nationwide ground stop is related to any Microsoft services.”

The Microsoft 365 outage was at least the fourth significant one this year. A January outage lasted nearly 10 hours, and in July a bug in Microsoft’s automated network maintenance system disrupted Azure and Microsoft 365 services for hours. On Aug. 31, an Exchange Online outage also hit Teams, OneDrive and SharePoint.

Instead of “I hope this email finds you well,” many people joked, it should just be “I hope this email finds you.” (Consider this our nomination for the “Overworked Twitter Joke of the Week” on The Ringer’s Press Box podcast.)

Microsoft said Friday afternoon that it was watching the backlog of delayed email “to ensure all process successfully before considering the issue resolved.” The University of Washington’s IT department told its users that email delayed during the outage would be delivered as mail queues continued to be processed.

Many people coped with the flood of returning email with a bit of levity.

As the mail started flowing again, CNN chief media analyst Brian Stelter said he was getting “a deluge of emails from PR people pitching their clients to talk about the Outlook outage.” Most were sent during the outage, he noted, “which, fittingly, prevented the pitches from reaching me.”

The security company Malwarebytes captured the paradox in a message to its followers: “We regret to inform you that Teams and Outlook are coming back online after a global outage.”
