#5355. Yield-Bearing eZAR Blurs the Line Between Stablecoin and Investment Product

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

eZAR opened its rand-pegged token to the public on November 2 with R303 million in circulation. Its reserve yield is the feature that puts the stablecoin label to the test.

Most stablecoin launches promise a token that never moves. eZAR's disclosures say its holders can make money or lose it. The rand-pegged token went live to the public on November 2, and its fine print reads more like an investment product than a payments coin.

According to launch reports, eZAR is now open to the public and to new institutional partners after almost a year of pilot operations. The company says R303 million worth of tokens had been issued and were in circulation as of October 30.

The project is a partnership between eZAR Ltd, asset manager Ninety One and AVBOB Financial Services, with AVBOB acting as lead institution and liquidity partner. CEO Sean Emery said the team put "getting it right" ahead of "getting it big" during the pilot. The message now is that eZAR is ready to scale.

The model also departs from the typical single-issuer coin. Neobanks, retailers, insurers and payment firms can plug the token into their own branded wallets and share in the economics. Transfers between participating wallets settle within seconds at any hour and, according to the company, cost nothing.

The reserves backing eZAR are invested through a money market strategy run by Ninety One, mainly in the Ninety One Money Market Fund. Returns are distributed daily to partners after partnership fees, and each partner then decides on what terms its own customers receive a share.

Ninety One's head of digital assets, Adam Duxbury, described it as new rails under an old discipline. His firm has run money market strategies for 25 years, he said, and South Africa should build its own digital rand rather than import a dollar coin.

The framing is clever, since it presents the yield as a feature of "digital cash that can grow." Yet that same feature makes the classification question hard to avoid.

The risk language is the most revealing part of the launch. eZAR describes itself as a crypto asset issued by the eZAR En Commandite Partnership. It states that the token is not legal tender, not a bank deposit and not a banking product, and that it carries no guarantee.

The details that follow set it further apart. The R1 redemption value depends on available liquidity. Money market returns can be positive or negative, so capital is at risk. Holders also own no units in the underlying fund and have no direct claim on it.

"Capital at risk" rarely appears in stablecoin terms. A payments token is meant to hold its value and let users redeem at par, yet eZAR's own documents hedge on both counts. Back in March, a market survey from Blockhouse had already noted that eZAR doesn't qualify as a stablecoin under most regulations. The live launch now tests that observation against a real product.

In the major rulebooks, the yield is the sticking point. The US GENIUS Act bars permitted payment stablecoin issuers from paying holders any form of interest or yield solely for holding, using or retaining the token. The EU's MiCA framework takes a similar line on interest. The logic is that a payment token paying a return starts to function like an unregulated deposit.

The OCC issued its final GENIUS Act rules on October 21, and they confirmed that ban for covered issuers. The contested ground lies elsewhere, in who sits between the issuer and the holder. Earlier OCC proposals set a rebuttable presumption against yield arrangements run through affiliates and related third parties, whereas the statute itself names only issuers.

eZAR's design lands squarely in that gray zone. Returns flow to partners, and the partners decide how customers share in them. Whether that amounts to an issuer paying yield or a partner passing on profit is precisely the kind of question US regulators are now wrestling with, and it would be a difficult one to argue before the OCC.

eZAR doesn't operate under the US or EU regimes, so none of those rules apply to it directly. eZAR Ltd is described as an authorised financial services provider responsible for the main technology and services behind the partnership. That technology also draws on the South African Reserve Bank's Project Khokha 2, where eZAR's parent company, Block Markets Africa, was a technical contributor.

This background signals a serious, institution-backed build rather than a speculative launch. Even so, the rand stablecoin field is getting crowded. ZARU launched earlier this year as an institutional-grade rand coin, and a pattern is emerging of different models competing for the same local payments niche.

The bigger question is whether South Africa will define stablecoins narrowly, as the US and EU do, or leave room for hybrid products like this one. Because the network is permissioned, the reported circulation figure also rests on company disclosure rather than a public ledger, which makes the regulatory and disclosure framework matter even more.

For everyday users, the appeal is easy to see. A rand token that moves in seconds, costs nothing to send and might earn a daily return makes an attractive pitch. For partners, shared infrastructure with a revenue share offers a way into digital payments without building a coin from scratch.

The trade-off sits in the disclaimers. A holder who treats eZAR like a bank balance could be caught off guard by liquidity-dependent redemption, or by a money market return that dips below zero. That gap between how the product feels and how it is legally defined is where regulators tend to step in.

eZAR is best understood as a hybrid: a payments token with an investment return attached. It may well succeed on those terms. Still, as more jurisdictions tighten the stablecoin definition around no-yield, par-redemption tokens, products like this will increasingly be judged on what they are rather than what they are called. How South African regulators treat eZAR in the coming months will show which way that debate is heading.

#5354. Who should run Nvidia? Our picks for Jensen Huang’s successor, whether the board likes it or not

by Todd Bishop & John Cook on Nov 14, 2026 at 2:10 pmNovember 14, 2026 at 2:10 pm

Nvidia’s board says it’s too early to speculate about who will succeed Jensen Huang. Sorry, we’re having too much fun coming up with names.

The board said in a statement Friday that it’s still choosing a search firm and hasn’t formally engaged any candidates. That came after the Financial Times reported that the board had approached Arm CEO Rene Haas — a name John had presciently floated when we recorded this week’s GeekWire Podcast on Thursday.

Nvidia announced Huang’s resignation Thursday, a day after the New York Times reported that he’d had an affair with an Nvidia executive who reported to him. Days earlier, he admitted to an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence officials reportedly suspected of being a Chinese spy.

Colette Kress, the company’s longtime CFO, is serving as interim CEO. She spent 13 years at Microsoft earlier in her career.

Two major Nvidia investors, Altimeter Capital’s Brad Gerstner and Atreides Management’s Gavin Baker, asked the board to run a deliberate search that leaves open “the potential return of Jensen Huang.” Elon Musk said on X that he was signing a petition to reinstate Huang.

The organizers of one, called “Stand with Jensen,” say it has more than 108,000 names, including more than 5,600 people who identify themselves as current Nvidia employees.

The case for Haas: The Arm CEO spent about seven years at Nvidia, rising to vice president and general manager of its computing products business, before joining Arm in 2013. He became Arm’s CEO in February 2022, when Nvidia’s $40 billion deal to acquire Arm collapsed amid regulatory opposition. SoftBank, Arm’s majority owner, kept Nvidia’s $1.25 billion prepayment.

Arm, based in Cambridge, England, designs processor technology that’s ubiquitous in smartphones, and licenses it to other chipmakers. That includes Nvidia, whose Grace data center CPU, paired with its GPUs in AI systems, is built on Arm cores. Amazon’s Graviton and Microsoft’s Cobalt server chips also use Arm designs.

Haas is one of several candidates, and there’s no guarantee he’ll be offered the job or take it, the FT reported.

He also has a link to Harvey Jones, the longtime Nvidia director named the company’s first board chair this week. Haas was vice president of sales at Tensilica, a chip-design company, from 1999 to 2004, according to his LinkedIn profile. Jones co-founded Tensilica and chaired its board until chip-design software maker Cadence acquired it in 2013.

Haas has also seen Huang’s resistance to succession planning firsthand. “He didn’t like the idea,” Haas said in a 2024 interview, as quoted by the New York Times this week. “He felt it would create competition among executives and be divisive.”

One complication: SoftBank named Haas CEO of SoftBank Group International in April, helping coordinate chip and AI companies in its international portfolio while he continues to run Arm. The FT reported that the appointment was aimed at pushing forward Project Izanagi, SoftBank’s AI chip effort launched to compete with Nvidia.

He knows Nvidia from the inside, but he also knows what it’s like to run a public company — which matters for a board searching in the middle of a crisis.

John’s argument on the podcast: Nvidia needs someone who can shepherd a company through turmoil, not just a great technologist. Think Alan Mulally going from Boeing to Ford, or Dara Khosrowshahi moving from Expedia to Uber after Travis Kalanick’s ouster.

What the betting markets say: On Kalshi, Ian Buck, the Nvidia vice president who created the CUDA software platform, was the favorite at midday Friday. By midday Saturday, Haas had overtaken him, at 25% to Buck’s 18%. Kress was at 10%.

The Axios list of 11 names also includes Apple Executive Chair Tim Cook, for whom President Trump lobbied on Truth Social (“A Legend replaces a Legend!”), along with AMD CEO Lisa Su and Google Cloud CEO Thomas Kurian.

A Northwest wildcard: Analysts have also floated Sanjay Mehrotra, CEO of Boise, Idaho-based Micron Technology, whose memory chips power Nvidia’s AI servers. Mehrotra co-founded SanDisk in 1988 and has run Micron since 2017.

The AWS chief: Matt Garman has run Amazon Web Services since June 2024, overseeing a business with a $142 billion annual revenue run rate at the end of last year. He started at Amazon as an MBA intern in 2005, joined AWS full time in 2006 as one of its first product managers, and later led its compute business and then its sales and marketing organization.

Another Amazon pick: We’d also look at Peter DeSantis, who now leads a new organization that includes Amazon’s AI models, custom chips and quantum computing, reporting directly to CEO Andy Jassy.

DeSantis joined Amazon as a software developer in 1998. He led the EC2 team from Cape Town, South Africa, through its 2006 launch, and spearheaded Amazon’s 2015 acquisition of Annapurna Labs, the Israeli chip designer behind its custom silicon.

In 2018, DeSantis unveiled Graviton. In June, he told Bloomberg that AWS was in talks to sell its Trainium AI chips to other companies for their own data centers.

He knows chips, data centers and AI infrastructure at enormous scale. The catch, as John noted: he’s never been a CEO, and the board may want that experience given the circumstances.

The other Amazon name: Dave Treadwell took over AWS compute and machine learning services in August. Treadwell spent 27 years at Microsoft, where he worked on Windows NT, .NET and Xbox and rose to corporate vice president, before joining Amazon in 2016.

The Microsoft bench: On the podcast, Todd ran through a few Microsoft executives who would bring relevant experience:

The insider with Microsoft roots: Nick Parker, a 26-year Microsoft sales veteran, joined Nvidia in August as executive vice president of worldwide field operations, with a pay package worth more than $40 million. He’s new, but he already runs the team that sells Nvidia’s chips to the world’s largest companies.

One more angle: Whoever gets the job will face a growing list of customers trying to reduce their reliance on Nvidia, including Amazon. In his annual shareholder letter in April, Jassy wrote that Amazon’s chips business would have an annual run rate of about $50 billion if it sold chips to AWS and other third parties the way other chipmakers do.

Jassy said it’s “quite possible” Amazon will sell racks of them to third parties in the future.

In a Bloomberg interview recorded Oct. 14, Huang said he hoped his successor was already inside the company. The board has said it will consider both internal and external candidates.

Listen to our full discussion on this week’s GeekWire Podcast.

MediaTek powers more than two billion devices every year, from the most advanced AI infrastructure on the planet to the everyday devices that make life smarter, faster, and more connected. For everyone. MediaTek silicon is the common thread running through all of it. Yeah, MediaTek does that.

#5352. Etzioni on AI: Startup speed is not a strategy

by Oren Etzioni on Nov 15, 2026 at 8:13 amNovember 15, 2026 at 8:14 am

The world of AI startups has fetishized “speed” and whipped itself into a frenzy. Sure, the feature that took a quarter to build back in 2023 takes a mere AI-fueled weekend in 2026, but many AI startups are running on FOMO, caffeine and tokens without a clear strategy.

A startup is a marathon, and a team that attempts to sprint the whole way will burn out before the finish line.

Sam Altman’s Startup Playbook puts the speed creed in one line: “I have never, not once, seen a slow-moving founder be really successful.” I was singing from the same hymnbook earlier this year. In my column on ten commandments for AI startups I wrote that “velocity is the new moat.” Then everyone got fast, and I stopped singing.

Here are the five arguments usually made for that creed.

The window is closing. Each model release opens a gap that the frontier labs close within a release cycle or so. But if the labs will close it anyway, speed merely buys you a nicer funeral. The argument supports picking a different direction, not running faster in this one.

Competitors are everywhere. AI makes building cheap, so clones show up in weeks. True, and that’s the reason velocity isn’t a moat. When building is cheap, defensibility matters more than being first. Peter Thiel’s last-mover argument from Zero to One is stronger today than when he wrote it. In his words: “It’s much better to be the last mover—that is, to make the last great development in a specific market and enjoy years or even decades of monopoly profits.”

The data flywheel. Early users generate data that improves the product, so get there first. Except that each new model generation resets the flywheel, and data that taught a fine-tuned model something in 2024 is worth little once a frontier model does the task out of the box.

The data that matters is data the labs can’t easily get: clinical records, industrial sensor readings, proprietary transactions. Access to proprietary data often comes through trust and partnerships, which take time, and moving too fast can cost you the trust required to obtain that precious data.

Momentum attracts capital and talent. That’s true. However, capital raised on growth hype may be planting the seeds of its own demise. A high valuation can box you into the growth story that justified it. Startups that raise at a saner pace retain the option to change direction.

Learning speed. Fast iteration finds product-market fit sooner. This one holds, but there are two kinds of speed.

Fast iteration means cheap experiments: a prototype, a pilot, a feature shipped to 20 users and pulled if it flops. Fast scaling means hiring ahead of revenue, signing multi-year contracts, buying compute and raising at a valuation you then have to grow into.

Iteration should be as fast as you can make it, because each cycle is cheap to undo. Scaling should come more slowly, because each step is a major commitment that’s hard to unwind, and scaling too early is one of the most expensive mistakes a startup can make: a 2011 study of more than 3,200 high-growth technology startups blamed premature scaling for about 74% of internet startup failures.

Jeff Bezos drew a similar distinction in his 2015 letter to Amazon shareholders. A few decisions are one-way doors, irreversible once you walk through, and deserve deliberation. Most decisions are two-way doors, and those should be made fast by a small group. A startup’s experiments are two-way doors. Its big commitments, a large raise, a long contract, a hiring spree, are not.

At AI House, Sri Chandrasekar, one of our managing directors, puts it this way: “We don’t hand founders a thesis. We expect them to find the right problem, and that takes judgment, not speed. Building is nearly free now, so run every experiment fast and manually, and only build the machine once something works.”

Finding the right problem takes iteration, acumen and judgment. Speed helps with the first and does little for the other two. A hamster on a wheel at 200 mph has plenty of speed and no chance of progress. Even Altman’s playbook says Y Combinator looks for “businesses that get more powerful with scale and that are difficult to copy.”

Prof. Herbert Simon, the Nobel laureate who helped invent AI at Carnegie Mellon, advised his graduate students to pick important problems for which they had a secret weapon, because they would win only “by having access to some knowledge or research methods the others do not have.”

Swap students for founders and research methods for data and relationships, and the advice holds. A startup’s secret weapon is an asset you hold that a competitor can’t acquire by moving faster: a dataset nobody else can assemble, a relationship that took years to nurture.

Farecast, the airfare prediction company I founded in 2003, developed a secret weapon by gathering a massive amount of labeled data. By 2007 we were mining more than 175 billion airfares, and every prediction we made was later scored against what the fare actually did, so the labeled set grew every day, and it grew only by waiting for fares to play out.

A startup that signs a data agreement with a hospital network has the same kind of weapon. So does a payments company whose fraud labels come from its own transaction stream. In each case the data is the asset a faster rival can’t copy.

Laurence Peter, of Peter Principle fame, said it decades ago: “If you don’t know where you are going, you will probably end up somewhere else.”

So pick a direction where frontier labs won’t go and clearly articulate why. Run experiments fast but make commitments slowly. Jim Collins, the Good to Great author, called it firing bullets before cannonballs: cheap shots to find the range, then the one big shot once you have it.

Chase the data and the relationships the labs can’t buy and accept that trust is the slow road to both. Raise at a pace that leaves you the option to pivot when the next model lands. And name your secret weapon in one sentence.

To repurpose an old joke: two bulls stand on a hill above a herd. The young one says, let’s charge down there. The old one retorts: charge and they scatter. Walk, and they’ll be waiting when we arrive.

In AI right now, everyone is charging. The founders who end up with the prize will be the ones who are more judicious.

#5350. Amazon loses 40 Leo satellites in ULA Vulcan launch failure — a new setback for its Starlink rival

by Todd Bishop on Nov 15, 2026 at 1:41 pmNovember 15, 2026 at 2:16 pm

A United Launch Alliance Vulcan rocket malfunctioned about 10 minutes after liftoff Sunday and failed to reach orbit, losing 40 satellites for Amazon Leo, the Seattle company’s planned challenger to SpaceX’s Starlink internet service.

It was ULA’s first total mission failure since the Boeing–Lockheed Martin joint venture was formed in 2006, Spaceflight Now reported. The flight was Vulcan’s first in nine months, and the first of 38 Vulcan launches that Amazon has purchased.

ULA said it doesn’t yet have specific data on what went wrong, and that it will work with Amazon and others to find the cause and return to flight as quickly as possible.

Amazon Leo said in a post on X that “there is risk with any launch, and that’s especially true for inaugural missions like LV-01.” It added, “ULA has been a trusted partner for Amazon, and we believe they’ll learn from this mission and deliver on their long-term plans for Vulcan.”

The rocket lifted off from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station at 12:40 p.m. ET (9:40 a.m. PT), after two days of delays and a countdown hold with 20 seconds left on the clock to resolve a technical issue. It isn’t known whether that issue played any role.

The rocket’s six solid rocket boosters, made by Northrop Grumman and the source of problems on two earlier Vulcan flights, appeared to perform normally and burned out less than two minutes after liftoff, according to Space.com and Spaceflight Now.

The first stage, powered by two BE-4 engines from Jeff Bezos’ Kent, Wash.-based Blue Origin, fired from liftoff before separating from the Centaur upper stage, which carries the payload the rest of the way to orbit.

The anomaly came about 10 minutes into the flight, during the Centaur’s burn, according to Spaceflight Now. The Centaur is powered by two RL10 engines made by L3Harris.

Spaceflight Now also reported that the first stage appeared to burn longer than planned, and that a telemetry-driven animation showed the Centaur making unusual orientation adjustments early in its burn. ULA hasn’t identified the cause.

Impact on Amazon Leo: Before Sunday, Amazon had launched 396 satellites for its Redmond-based satellite internet network, formerly known as Project Kuiper, on 14 missions since April 2025. Its last successful launch was in July, when ULA flew the last of eight Leo missions on its Atlas 5, the older rocket that Vulcan is replacing.

The larger Vulcan carried 40 satellites on Sunday, compared with 29 on the last Atlas 5 launch, and is slated to carry more than 1,500 of Amazon’s first-generation satellites, more than any other rocket in the program.

Melissa Wuerl, Amazon Leo’s director of launch systems, called it the program’s “primary workhorse over the next several years” in a preview of the mission. Amazon had said the second Vulcan mission could fly within weeks of the first. That flight now has to wait for ULA’s investigation.

Amazon also has 24 launches reserved on Blue Origin’s New Glenn, which has been grounded since a May ground-test explosion, and has booked others on Arianespace’s Ariane 6 and SpaceX’s Falcon 9.

In June, the Federal Communications Commission gave Amazon permission to keep deploying satellites even if it missed its July 30 deadline to put 1,616 into service. Satellites that weren’t operational by then temporarily lose priority in key spectrum bands.

Amazon still has until July 30, 2029, to deploy and operate all 3,232 first-generation satellites. Amazon has said it plans an initial rollout of commercial internet service this year.

Vulcan’s track record: Sunday’s mission was the fifth for Vulcan, which debuted in January 2024, and the first with six solid boosters. Boosters suffered nozzle failures on the second flight in October 2024 and on a national security mission in February. Both reached orbit, but the Space Force paused Vulcan national security launches after February.

ULA flew Sunday’s mission with an improved nozzle design. The rocket’s BE-4 engines had also been retrofitted to fix the oxygen valve problem behind the New Glenn explosion in May, ULA CEO Mark Peller said before the flight, CBS News reported.

ULA is also under new leadership. Longtime CEO Tory Bruno left last December for Blue Origin, and Peller, who led Vulcan’s development, was named CEO in August.

Amazon’s next scheduled Leo launch is an Ariane 6 mission carrying 36 satellites, targeted for Nov. 23 at the earliest.

#5349. Ripple’s Bank-Style Lending on XRPL Nears Launch: What XRP Holders Actually Get

Disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. We believe that all content is accurate as of the date of publication, but certain offers mentioned may no longer be available.

The LendingProtocolV1_1 amendment on the XRP Ledger (XRPL) has collected 22 of 35 votes (62.86%).

Three more validators have signed on over the past three weeks. Ripple's own nodes have already voted yes, along with the University of Waterloo and UC Berkeley.

To go live, the amendment has to clear the 80% bar (29 votes) and hold it for two straight weeks.

The related SingleAssetVault amendment (XLS-65) has 23 votes (65.7%) and needs six more.

The XLS-65 and XLS-66 standards drop overcollateralization and instant liquidations and let companies take out fixed-term, uncollateralized loans directly on XRPL. The loans work similarly to traditional bank credit, with a fixed term and pre-set interest terms.

Ripple has already tested the protocol on a private XRPL network with nine nodes that matched the hardware of its mainnet nodes.

Holders deposit XRP or stablecoins such as RLUSD into Single Asset Vaults and receive shares. Interest is paid on a cash basis. Depositors receive it only after the borrower has sent the money. Withdrawals from a vault are processed on a first-come, first-served basis.

Borrowers are vetted off-chain by Loan Brokers, who record each disbursement on the ledger. According to the XRPL documentation, the protocol "relies on off-chain underwriting and risk management to assess the creditworthiness of borrowers."

The broker's own "first-loss capital" covers losses first when a client stops paying.

Issuers can also freeze assets or claw them back. According to Ripple, all operations in a vault and in the connected lending protocol stop when an asset issuer freezes the vault.

Until now, XRP holders who wanted passive income had to use third-party bridges and wrapped tokens. After the amendment activates, holders can deposit XRP in a pool on XRPL, with its fraction-of-a-cent fees, and collect part of the interest paid by borrowers. Their income will depend on the terms set by the loan broker and on borrowers' repayments.

If a major borrower defaults and the broker's first-loss capital runs out, depositors bear the losses and their shares drop in value.

#5348. Why Microsoft is aiming to make Copilot the ‘OS for work’

by Mary Jo Foley on Nov 16, 2026 at 5:44 amNovember 16, 2026 at 5:44 am

It’s been quite a while since Microsoft was “the Windows company,” meaning it derived the bulk of its revenues from Windows. However, Windows — along with Office — has helped Microsoft build a moat that has largely shielded it from forces that have battered some of its competitors as AI has risen to prominence.

These days, Microsoft executives have likened Copilot to an operating system, or as CEO Satya Nadella called it, “a new OS for work.” This doesn’t mean Microsoft is replacing Windows with Copilot (even though there was a Microsoft incubation project, codenamed “Project Aion,” that focused on the idea of a “Copilot OS”).

Plus, as the head of Windows discovered the hard way, many Windows users are dead set against Windows morphing into an “agentic OS.”

Instead, the Copilot as “a new OS for work” descriptor is a metaphor, but one with considerable history and significance.

Microsoft is betting that the race to bring AI into the workplace will be won by whoever controls the layer underneath the models — the data, permissions, security and management tools that businesses already run on Microsoft software. That’s the job Windows has done for decades, and it’s the part of the AI business where Microsoft starts out ahead.

Many of the components behind the OS metaphor are likely to be on display at the company’s annual Ignite conference in San Francisco this week. According to the session list for the weeklong event for customers and partners, Microsoft will highlight how Copilot acts as a platform for building, hosting and managing AI solutions.

The high-level pitch: Copilot can do it all. It can be the foundational layer for your agents, applications, and business processes.

Operating systems like Windows provide users with a way to interact with their applications and resources via a common interface across software and data. They orchestrate under the covers what’s happening when users perform specific tasks.

Taking the metaphor to the extreme, if Copilot can be seen as the new Windows, agents are the new apps; skills are the Win32 programming interfaces; and the Graph and IQ layers are like File Explorer.

The New OS Metaphor: Why Now? For the past year-plus, Microsoft has been working to get customers to think about Copilot as not so much a chatbot, but more a full-stack platform. Its recently introduced Copilot “super app” is meant to be the unifying interface across this platform.

Currently, the new Copilot app provides customers with Code, Cowork and Autopilot access. But beneath that top layer, Microsoft is adding other integrations to its core Microsoft Office experiences, Microsoft IQ intelligence backends, its CRM and ERP Dynamics capabilities, and agents and applications from other vendors and customers, as well.

Microsoft’s inclusion of its core Office capabilities in the new Copilot comes none too soon, as Anthropic last week introduced new Claude-based tools for spreadsheets and whiteboards, and previewed one for meetings, that compete more directly with Microsoft’s Office apps.

The “Copilot as New OS” metaphor also works when you consider that Microsoft is looking to the new Copilot app to raise the level of abstraction, or hide the underlying complexities, of how agentic computing works.

If you believe the AI story lines, we’re moving to a world where many customers expect to be able to ask a system to turn a bunch of slides into a business plan and then share that plan with a group of coworkers. In this scenario, users don’t have to think about which apps and data sources they need to pull together to achieve this; they will count on their AI system to figure it out and just do it on their behalf.

“We increasingly think of all our apps together as a new operating system for work that transcends traditional software categories to understand user intent and act on it,” said Nadella in his letter to shareholders, published as part of Microsoft’s annual report on Oct. 21.

The end goal? “As our apps move toward agent-first capabilities that can be called and orchestrated in the flow of work, the system becomes more valuable and more deeply embedded,” Nadella said.

The Slow and Unsexy Enterprise Race: In the enterprise space, being first and fastest doesn’t always win the race. While AI companies like OpenAI and Anthropic vie to be the AI model kingmakers, Microsoft is content to focus on the less sexy but more difficult-to-deliver elements like context, permissions, skills, orchestration, governance and security, all hallmarks of operating systems like Windows.

Microsoft will try to pull all these OS-like pieces together at this week’s Ignite and show customers that it’s got what it takes with Copilot to make AI promises more than just demoware.

#5347. Canton Coin Gets SEC "Digital Commodity" Label: Here's What the Two Prongs Actually Mean

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

The SEC's Division of Corporation Finance called Canton Coin a digital commodity on November 3. The ruling rests on two representations, including the absence of a "central party."

The most important words in the SEC's Canton Coin letter aren't "digital commodity." They are the ones the staff put in front of that label: the conclusion holds "in reliance on the representations" Canton's lawyers made. The SEC didn't independently prove the network has no central party. It accepted a description and attached a conclusion to it.

On November 3, the Division of Corporation Finance's Office of Chief Counsel answered Canton Network's October 30 request. The response came from Deputy Chief Counsel Jonathan A. Ingram and was addressed to the staff team of Ted Yu, Andrew Schoeffler and Mark Vilardo. The Division said it views Canton Coin as a "digital commodity" as the term is described in the SEC's March interpretation.

It also said it will not recommend enforcement action if Canton Coin is minted programmatically by Super Validators, Validators and application providers, as described in the request. That holds without registration under Section 5 of the Securities Act or Section 12(g) of the Exchange Act, and it applies if the issuer relies on an opinion of counsel. The facts the staff relied on are laid out in the Canton Network's incoming letter.

Early coverage focused on the classification label. The more useful story, though, is how the staff got there.

The staff pointed to two representations. The first is that Canton Coin is intrinsically linked to, and derives its value from, the programmatic operation of the Canton Network, along with supply and demand dynamics. Its value does not come from an expectation of profits from the essential managerial efforts of others.

That phrase echoes the Howey test, the long-standing U.S. framework for investment contracts. The prong asks a simple question: when someone holds this token, are they betting on a team's work, or on a network that runs by itself? On the facts presented, the staff's answer was the network.

This is the more familiar half of the analysis, and most token projects argue some version of it. Because almost every issuer makes the same claim, the first prong carries less weight on its own, which is why the second one deserves a closer look.

The second representation is that the Canton Network has no "central party," as the March interpretation defines that term. In the SEC and CFTC's framework, a digital commodity belongs to a functional crypto system that has no central party overseeing participation or distributing rewards to users.

This prong is the one to watch, because Canton Coin is minted by Super Validators, Validators and application providers. Those are named roles in a structured network, so a skeptic could fairly ask whether the Super Validator tier looks like a central party in practice. The letter's answer rests on the word "programmatically": the minting follows protocol rules rather than anyone's discretion.

Legal commentators reading the March interpretation have also pointed out that it doesn't fully explain how the "central party" concept relates to its separate definition of decentralization. The Canton letter doesn't settle that either. It applies the term to one set of facts and stops there.

A no-action letter is narrower than it sounds. The Division itself says the response states its position on enforcement action only and expresses no legal conclusion on the issues presented. It also says the positions rest on the representations in the request, and that different facts or conditions might lead to different conclusions.

In practice, that comes down to three points. First, the letter is staff-level guidance rather than a Commission vote. Second, it protects reliance on the specific arrangement described, not the token in every future circumstance. Third, if the representations change, the comfort can disappear.

For a company, the letter is still valuable, since a written statement that staff won't recommend enforcement is a strong signal. Even so, it shouldn't be mistaken for a permanent legal classification. It is a snapshot of staff views based on facts someone else supplied.

The framework behind the letter is the Commission's March 17 interpretation, which the CFTC joined. It sorts crypto assets into five categories: digital commodities, digital collectibles, digital tools, stablecoins and digital securities. Four of the five are generally treated as non-securities, and the securities analysis stays fact-specific for the rest.

The two documents do different jobs. The interpretation is a general map: it tells the market how the Commission thinks about categories and which features push an asset one way or the other. The Canton letter is an application. It takes a named token, tests it against the map's digital commodity category, and gives a case-specific enforcement answer.

That sequence matters. The interpretation says what a digital commodity looks like, and the letter says that, if the facts are as represented, Canton Coin looks like one.

The practical lesson is about preparation. Canton's request framed its facts to fit the two prongs, and the staff responded in those terms. Projects hoping for similar treatment will likely follow the same template: document how value arises from network operation, and document why no single party oversees participation or distributes rewards.

The harder test will come from tokens with more visible governance or a more active operating team. Those projects will have to explain why their structure doesn't amount to a central party, and the Canton letter doesn't say where that line sits.

For now, the letter works best as an early data point rather than a final answer. The classification label drew the attention, but the representations behind it are what other projects will study. How the staff handles the next request, especially one with a messier governance story, will show whether the "no central party" prong is a narrow gate or a wide one.

#5344. What went wrong with Outlook: Microsoft blames ‘thundering herds’ and a bug unnoticed for months

by Todd Bishop on Nov 16, 2026 at 7:31 amNovember 16, 2026 at 7:31 am

Microsoft’s own safety systems helped turn a dormant software flaw into last week’s global Outlook outage, rerouting traffic from failing servers onto healthy ones that had the same problem, until more than 80% of the servers in its Microsoft 365 networking gateway had stopped responding.

That phenomenon, known as a cascading failure, is one of the findings in Microsoft’s preliminary report on the outage, released overnight, dissecting the failure that cut off email for people and organizations in more than 70 countries.

According to the report, the attempts to recover were further complicated by a second problem: servers that engineers restarted were immediately overwhelmed by waiting traffic and stopped responding again, a phenomenon known as a “thundering herd.”

Microsoft says active service disruptions lasted nearly 24 hours. Delayed email continued to be delivered after service returned Friday morning, and the company posted its public all-clear on X late Friday night, nearly 38 hours after the outage began.

The underlying flaw dates to July, when Microsoft began rolling out a fix to the software that handles incoming connections on its networking gateway, the servers that sit in front of Outlook and many other Microsoft 365 services.

Microsoft hasn’t said what the fix was meant to address. It ran worldwide for more than three months without problems, according to the report.

Under heavy load, however, parts of that software could get stuck waiting on one another, using up the servers’ processing power and memory until they froze.

That’s what happened last week. About 15 hours before the outage, Microsoft’s systems automatically moved Teams traffic onto the same servers that handle Outlook email, adding to their load, according to the report. Microsoft called the switch part of normal operations but didn’t say what prompted it.

Complicating matters, nearly 14% of the gateway’s server capacity was already out of service because of an unrelated problem, which also isn’t detailed in the report.

When traffic peaked during the U.S. workday, that was enough to trigger the outage.

Two things stand out as likely areas of scrutiny:

Microsoft’s testing didn’t catch the bug. Its labs mostly used less powerful machines with fewer processing cores, running a different mix of traffic, while the problem was worst on the newer servers handling real customer load.

The fix also passed through Microsoft’s standard staged rollout, spreading worldwide over several weeks without any sign of trouble, according to the report.

The company certainly has the means to test on the hardware it actually runs. It spent $45.2 billion on capital expenditures in its most recent quarter, much of it on AI infrastructure.

The safeguards meant to contain the damage didn’t hold. Walls between regions failed because of what the report calls “a separate issue,” which it doesn’t explain, so the outage went global.

The gateway is made up of thousands of “capacity units” grouped into regions, with walls between them meant to keep a failure in one place. Microsoft also runs a second, independent gateway so services can switch over during a disruption.

Teams, OneDrive, SharePoint and Office apps made that switch, which is why Teams chats and meetings mostly kept working. Exchange couldn’t, “for scale reasons,” as the company put it, so email stayed down.

Microsoft’s own tools added to the problem. Its automated recovery “was not designed” for a fleet that was almost entirely unresponsive, according to the report, and its usual ways of rolling back a bad change couldn’t quickly undo one that was months old.

The company’s systems automatically shifted traffic from unresponsive servers to healthy ones, and the extra load triggered the same bug on those servers, too. About 10 hours in, engineers turned off some of that automatic rerouting.

Charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, Agents and Platform, posted an abridged version of the report on X late Sunday. “We are deeply sorry for the impact to all our customers and recognize the impact that this has on their normal business & operations,” he wrote.

Lamanna had previewed the findings Friday afternoon, blaming “cascading failures + thundering herds at our network perimeter” for the slow recovery, as GeekWire reported when Microsoft declared the outage over.

Microsoft says it has rolled back the defective code, added server capacity and monitoring, and put new limits on how traffic is redistributed to avoid another cascade. A final report with a full list of repairs is due Nov. 20.

It may also answer the biggest question the preliminary report leaves open: why the walls between regions didn’t stop the outage from spreading worldwide. Microsoft blames that on “a separate issue,” apart from the July bug, but hasn’t said what it was.

#5341. Amazon picks its Bond: Robert Pattinson to play 007, ending years of speculation over coveted role

Geek Life: Fun stories, memes, humor and other random items at the intersection of tech, science, business and culture.  SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 16, 2026 at 8:31 amNovember 16, 2026 at 8:32 am

Last year, Jeff Bezos asked social media, “Who’d you pick as the next Bond?” Amazon now has its own answer: Robert Pattinson.

The 40-year-old Pattinson — best known for “Twilight,” “The Batman” and this summer’s “The Odyssey” — becomes the seventh actor to play 007 in the official film series. He takes over from Daniel Craig, whose fifth and last Bond film, “No Time to Die,” came out in 2021.

Amazon got a 50% stake in the Bond films when it bought MGM for $8.5 billion in 2022, and it took creative control last year in a joint venture with longtime producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael G. Wilson. Fans and bookmakers had been guessing about Craig’s successor since he said in 2019 he was leaving the role.

Over the years, the rumored contenders included Idris Elba, Tom Hardy, Aaron Taylor-Johnson, Tom Holland and Henry Cavill. By the end, there were five finalists. Pattinson beat out Nicholas Hoult, Jack Lowden, Josh O’Connor and Callum Turner after screen tests in London in late October, according to The New York Times. Casting director Nina Gold ran the tests, which covered stunts, dialogue and camera presence.

Bond is one of the most valuable properties Amazon got in the MGM deal, its second-largest acquisition ever behind Whole Foods. The franchise has earned nearly $7 billion at the domestic box office, adjusted for inflation, since “Dr. No” in 1962. Now Amazon is running it without the Broccoli family, whose stewardship over six decades built it into one of Hollywood’s biggest moneymakers.

Pattinson’s casting is the most visible move yet in Amazon’s plans for Bond. As the Times noted, the 2025 deal followed years of behind-the-scenes friction over Amazon’s ambitions to expand the Bond universe beyond the films. The Times also pointed out that Amazon has to win over a generation of moviegoers who grew up during the franchise’s long hiatus and gravitated toward superheroes, horror movies and video game adaptations.

Amazon is already putting the back catalog to work. Alongside Monday’s announcement, it published a guide to streaming the 007 films on Prime Video.

Identity Confirmed pic.twitter.com/FCU5A9c1wk

To lead the next film, Amazon brought in producers Amy Pascal, the former Sony Pictures chairwoman, and David Heyman, who produced all eight “Harry Potter” movies. Denis Villeneuve (“Dune”) is directing from an original screenplay by “Peaky Blinders” creator Steven Knight. No release date has been set, and the Times reports that a theatrical release before 2028 is unlikely.

“Today marks a defining moment for our studio and a significant milestone in the history of James Bond,” Mike Hopkins, head of Prime Video and Amazon MGM Studios, said in a statement. Hopkins said Pattinson’s “remarkable range, magnetic screen presence, and quiet intensity make him an exceptional choice” to carry on the 007 legacy.

“James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honor of a lifetime,” Pattinson said. “To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement.”

Some longtime fans have worried that under Amazon, Bond will lose his distinctly British character and become more corporate and American, the Times reported. Pascal and Heyman, in a joint statement, called the English actor “the perfect Bond for our times.”

Bezos had yet to weigh back in on social media about Amazon’s pick, but Amazon CEO Andy Jassy did in a LinkedIn post, writing that he was “excited” to have Pattinson in the role, calling him “one of the most versatile actors of his generation, who consistently makes fearless choices, and keeps surprising people with his performances.”

Fans online were split. Some posted images of Elba or Cavill, calling Pattinson as 007 a “huge miss.” Others said the actor was on a “generational run” right now with the roles he’s landing. Others shared GIFs of Sean Connery, saying there will only ever be one Bond.

I checked in with my mom, a longtime Bond lover and the biggest movie fan I know. She quickly responded via text.

“No way … not sexy enough for me,” she wrote of Pattinson. “I really liked Daniel Craig, but Sean Connery has always been a favorite.”

#5340. XRP Risks Losing $1 Amid Aggressive $2.5 Billion Shift

As XRP continues to struggle amid the broad crypto market volatility while failing in multiple attempts to recover, key on-chain metrics are pointing to increased selling pressure among traders.

While momentum remains extremely weak, latest data from crypto analytics platform, Cryptoquant, shows that sellers have dominated both XRP’s spot and futures markets, putting it at risk of losing the long-held $1 mark.

Per the data, XRP’s cumulative volume delta (CVD) across major cryptocurrency exchanges shows that aggressive selling has dominated both its spot and futures market since September 23.

As of November 12, XRP’s Perpetual CVD on Binance has fallen from -$109 million to about -$1.1 billion. It is important to note that the CVD of an asset is a key metric that measures the difference between the volume of aggressive buy orders and aggressive sell orders over time.

While the metric turns negative when more traders are aggressively selling than buying, the -991 million negative balance in the Binance perpetual CVD signals stronger selling pressure.

With the negative balance on Binance exceeding its previous level by more than 10 times, this shows that traders have placed significantly more market sell orders than buy orders, either by opening short positions or closing existing long positions.

Apart from its futures market, further data shows that sellers have also dominated XRP’s spot activity across all major crypto exchanges, including Binance.

Notably, XRP’s All CEX Estimated Spot CVD moved from -$400 million to -$2.9 billion over the same period.

While this marks a $2.5 billion increase in the imbalance favoring sellers, it indicates that XRP spot traders have also been selling XRP more aggressively rather than buying, propelling the asset for further price declines.

#5339. Study: 403 U.S. hyperscale data centers rival Denmark’s emissions; Oregon ranked No. 2 in power use

Challenges, breakthroughs and big ideas in the race to protect our planet. SEE MORE

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 16, 2026 at 10:01 amNovember 16, 2026 at 10:14 am

A Harvard-led study estimates that electricity use at 403 U.S. hyperscale data centers was equal to roughly 25.7 million metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions — a volume roughly comparable to Denmark’s carbon footprint.

The research examined some of the nation’s largest and most powerful data center facilities operating between May 2024 and April 2025. Together, those facilities accounted for an estimated 1.8% of total U.S. electricity consumption.

“What we’re seeing is already striking, but it’s only a snapshot of a rapidly expanding industry,” Gianluca Guidi, the study’s lead author and a postdoctoral fellow in the Department of Biostatistics at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, said in a statement.

Guidi noted that the data center boom has continued since the study period ended. “That means the electricity use and carbon footprint we’re reporting could already be substantially larger now in 2026.”

The research, published in the journal Nature Sustainability, comes amid growing pushback and concerns about the facilities’ impacts on electric bills, water consumption, noise and carbon emissions. The authors also built a website about the report.

In the Pacific Northwest, government officials are enacting moratoriums and exploring legislation to regulate data center development. Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek in October directed a state agency to pause processing and issuing permits for new and expanding data centers until July 2027. In Washington, state Rep. Beth Doglio, D-Olympia, will propose data center rules in the legislative session that starts in January.

Hyperscale sites handle massive computing workloads and data storage, supporting operations including large language model training and AI deployment.

The researchers found that Oregon ranked second in electricity used by hyperscale data centers in the study, consuming about half as much as those in Virginia. Given Oregon’s access to clean hydropower, the state ranked sixth in carbon dioxide emissions attributed to the facilities’ electricity use. The publication highlighted data from the top 10 states for energy use, which does not include Washington.

Nationwide, roughly 54% of the electricity attributed to the facilities came from fossil fuels, primarily natural gas and coal. The estimates were based on regional power generation mixes, not individual operators’ clean energy purchases.

The study did not break out energy use by data center operator. Amazon, Microsoft and Google have the largest data center footprints worldwide and account for 57% of hyperscale data center capacity, according to Synergy Research Group.

All three have aggressive carbon reduction targets. While their emissions have all increased in recent years, the companies say they remain committed to their goals. Microsoft and Amazon point to their support for new clean power projects and investments in low-carbon building materials for the facilities as positive steps towards reductions.

“We continue to really be focused around carbon negativity by 2030,” Melanie Nakagawa, Microsoft’s chief sustainability officer, told GeekWire in July.

Kara Hurst, Amazon’s chief sustainability officer, acknowledged that it will be difficult for the company to reach its target of net-zero emissions by 2040.

“So that is a real challenge,” Hurst said in September, “and we’re here to meet the moment. I’m not saying that it’s going to be easy, and I’m not saying it’s going to be linear. But we’re going to put everything we have behind that.”

At the same time, both tech giants are pursuing projects involving fossil fuel energy in Texas. Microsoft in June signed a 20-year deal to purchase power from a natural gas facility slated to come online in 2028. Amazon has agreed to become the anchor tenant of a massive planned data center campus with proposed natural gas and nuclear power generation, according to the Financial Times.

“Assessing the Carbon Emissions and Energy Consumption of US Hyperscale Data Centers” published in Nature Sustainability and researchers from the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, University of Pisa, IMT School of Advanced Studies, Aurora Energy Research, Environmental Systems Research Institute, Baxtel and UCLA Fielding School of Public Health.

The Climate Pledge is a commitment to reach net-zero carbon emissions by 2040, co-founded by Amazon and Global Optimism in 2019.

Seven years later, the community has grown to over 700 signatories across 62 industries and 49 countries and territories, reducing emissions, scaling emerging climate solutions, and addressing challenges across operations and value chains.

The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. We believe that all content is accurate as of the date of publication, but certain offers mentioned may no longer be available.

F2Pool co-founder Chun Wang, known on X as Satofishi, bought 5,246 ETH worth $10.78 million over the past two days at an average price of $2,054, according to Lookonchain and Arkham data.

On Nov. 5, with ether trading near $2,400, Wang sold 6,200 wrapped staked ETH (wstETH) for $18.5 million in USDC. Wrapped staked ETH is a version of Lido's staked ether (stETH) that can be used in DeFi protocols.

This week, ether traded about 14% lower than on the day of the sale, and Wang started buying it back.

He withdrew 5,246 ETH from Binance hot wallets in two transfers of 3,996 ETH and 1,250 ETH. The purchase cost him $10.78 million, so about $7.7 million from the Nov. 5 sale is still left in USDC, according to Lookonchain.

Wang then sent 3,996 ETH ($8.23 million) to Lido. Lido is the largest liquid staking protocol on Ethereum. He deposited the wstETH he received into Spark, a lending protocol in the Sky ecosystem, which was previously known as MakerDAO. In Spark, wstETH can be used as collateral, while it continues to earn staking rewards.

He started out arbitraging Bitcoin between overseas exchanges and China's Taobao and later co-founded F2Pool. He launched the pool in 2013 together with Mao Shixing. At that time, F2Pool was one of the first Bitcoin mining pools in China.

In 2015, he bought a condo in Pattaya for 2,900 BTC. He later sold it for 7 BTC, as the price of Bitcoin had risen many times over.

In 2025, Wang also funded and commanded Fram2, the first crewed spaceflight over Earth's polar regions, on a SpaceX Crew Dragon.

F2Pool also mined ether until Ethereum moved to proof-of-stake in September 2022. Before that, Wang launched the non-custodial staking service stakefish. According to Wang, he decided to do it after a conversation with Vitalik Buterin in 2017. Stakefish was also one of the first node operators of Lido.

Ether is down more than 15% since the start of the month amid outflows from spot ETFs, according to SoSoValue. At press time, ETH is trading at $2,020.

#5337. Former UW AI researchers Yejin Choi and Carlos Guestrin raise $110M for AI startup Noeri

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Todd Bishop on Nov 16, 2026 at 10:37 amNovember 16, 2026 at 10:38 am

Yejin Choi and Carlos Guestrin, two prominent AI researchers who spent years at the University of Washington before moving to Stanford, have raised $110 million for Noeri, a startup building AI systems that keep improving on a company’s own work.

Menlo Ventures led the round, with participation from Seattle-based Madrona, Kindred Ventures, Wing Venture Capital and NEA. Cisco Investments, Nvidia and Snowflake also invested.

Bloomberg first reported the funding Monday; the valuation wasn’t disclosed.

Noeri’s software studies a company’s data and workflows, then proposes changes to the system around a specific task: the instructions, the tools, which model handles each step and, in some cases, the models themselves. Each change is explained and sent to a person for approval, much like a code review, the company said.

It works with closed and open-weight models. Customers keep ownership of the workflows and models they develop, subject to third-party model licenses, the company said.

The pitch is aimed at companies stuck choosing between paying for the most capable model and accepting weaker results from a cheaper one. The idea grew partly out of an effort to help a Stanford microbiology and immunology team use OpenAI’s models more cheaply, Bloomberg reported.

The small model they built learned to use older OpenAI models and, to the founders’ surprise, outperformed GPT-5 on that team’s research needs, Choi told Bloomberg.

The name Noeri means “intelligence, in the plural,” reflecting the founders’ argument against a future dominated by one powerful model. Guestrin said at Madrona’s IA40 Summit in late September that intelligence shouldn’t be controlled by one or two companies that own the models.

“Few companies would build their core operations on a single consultant who also advises every competitor, can change its terms at will, and can never be brought in-house,” Choi and Guestrin wrote in an essay posted with the launch. “A single, centralized AI offers exactly that arrangement.”

Noeri isn’t alone in helping businesses tailor models. In a July report on Noeri’s fundraising, The Information cited Thinking Machines Lab’s Tinker, fine-tuning software that developers use through an API, and Applied Compute, which embeds engineers with its customers.

Guestrin helped develop XGBoost, a widely used machine learning tool, and co-founded Turi, the Seattle startup formerly known as GraphLab and Dato, which Apple acquired in 2016. He went on to lead Apple’s central machine learning and AI organization.

Choi, a 2022 MacArthur Fellow, led common-sense reasoning research at the Allen Institute for AI (Ai2) before she left UW and Ai2 in 2024 to join Nvidia as a distinguished scientist, a role she held until starting Noeri in May. She joined Stanford’s faculty in early 2025. The two are co-CEOs.

Noeri is based in Palo Alto with an office in Zurich. Madrona and NEA have backed Guestrin before: the two firms led a $6.75 million round in GraphLab, the startup that became Turi, in 2013.

#5336. Portland startup Fairly raises $22M to pair local caretakers with AI for vacation rentals

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 17, 2026 at 3:00 amNovember 16, 2026 at 12:58 pm

Fairly, a Portland, Ore.-based vacation rental startup led by Vacasa founder Eric Breon, raised a $22.4 million Series A round, the company announced Tuesday.

Oregon Venture Fund led the round, with participation from Elevate Capital and Breon.

Fairly pairs vacation rental owners with local caretakers who look after the homes. Its software handles pricing, bookings and scheduling, and uses AI to draft routine guest messages and flag maintenance problems.

Guests booked more than $66 million in reservations through Fairly over the past year, up from about $5 million the year before, the company said. Nearly 900 caretakers now manage about 2,000 homes across 47 states, Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands.

Owners pay a single 20% fee, which Fairly splits with the caretaker, compared with the 25% to 40% the company says other managers typically charge. Fairly also says it doesn’t tack extra fees onto guest bills, so guests pay less overall.

“At Vacasa, I led a 7,000-person team, and delivering quality, individualized care at that scale is not an easy task,” Breon said in a statement. “At Fairly, we take a completely different approach: we empower dedicated, hyperlocal caretakers to care for homes, and our systems do the heavy lifting around them.”

Breon founded Vacasa in Portland in 2009 and spent more than a decade there. The company went public via a SPAC deal in 2021 and was acquired in May 2025 by Phoenix-based Casago, a vacation rental manager.

Fairly, founded in 2023, emerged from stealth in December 2024 with $10.1 million in pre-seed funding. The company has now raised $32.5 million in total.

Fairly now employs 106 people, up from 25 at its launch in 2024. Co-founder Subechya Person remains chief product officer; co-founder and former CTO Jeff Flitton left the company in February.

#5334. ZetaChain's 55M ZETA Burn Isn't a One-Time Event: What Proposal 2 Really Does

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

ZetaChain's Governance Proposal 2 would halt its L1 around Dec 9, mint ZETA 1:1 on Solana and burn about 55M ZETA in monthly installments. Voting closes Nov 7.

Headlines are calling it a 55 million ZETA burn. Read the proposal's own schedule, though, and nothing close to 55 million disappears on the day the chain halts. The figure is real, but it arrives in twelve installments over 2027.

ZetaChain published Governance Proposal 2 on November 4, and its announcement post lays out the mechanics. About 55 million ZETA of undistributed validator emissions will be burned monthly through 2027, following the schedule on which they would have been emitted. The roadmap in the same post puts the pace at twelve monthly burns of roughly 4.6 million ZETA each, from January to December 2027.

That detail changes how the number should be read. Most of the early flash coverage collapsed it into a single burn, which implies an immediate supply shock. The staged schedule tells a different story. These tokens were never going to circulate, because they are validator rewards for an L1 that is about to stop. Burning them on the original emission timetable keeps the published release schedule intact and introduces no new mechanism, as ZetaChain's FAQ puts it.

Governance Proposal 2 builds on Proposal 68, which approved the move to Solana in September with 99.4% in favor. Proposal 2 supplies the mechanics. Voting runs 72 hours and closes on November 7, and ZetaChain says nothing moves unless it passes.

If it does pass, every ZETA balance is recorded at snapshot block 20,755,000, expected around December 9. The ZetaChain L1 halts at that same height and isn't restarted. Claims open the same day through the ZetaHub migration portal, and ZetaChain's new private AI app, ZetaLabs, launches alongside it.

The proposal also pairs the migration with a new whitepaper, which ZetaChain calls the document of record for the token after the move.

The snapshot goes well beyond a simple wallet count. It records liquid, staked, unbonding and unclaimed-reward balances. Staked ZETA is credited automatically, so nobody has to unstake, and exchange balances convert without any action from holders. Staking rewards stop at the snapshot height.

Holders who want to claim directly face a short process. They connect the wallet that held ZETA, sign a message naming a Solana wallet, and receive the full balance shortly afterward. The claim costs no fee and requires no SOL. According to the post, the portal asks only for a signature, never for a transaction or a seed phrase. A minimum of 10 ZETA at the snapshot is needed to claim.

Two edge cases deserve attention. First, ZETA wrapped or sitting in pools and contracts can't be claimed by a key, so holders need to unwrap and exit before the snapshot. Second, assets still held as ZRC-20 tokens at the snapshot can be claimed back on their original chain through a separate bridged-assets page, with a $5 minimum per token. Both are the kind of detail that catches people out when a deadline arrives.

On Solana, ZETA becomes a native SPL token under the same ticker, with 9 decimals and no freeze authority. The full snapshot total is minted before the portal opens, and then the mint authority is revoked, so no one can ever mint more. No third-party bridge is involved.

That sequence is the strongest holder protection in the plan, and it is also the part that can be checked in public. The supply stays capped at 2.1 billion less whatever has been burned, and ZetaChain says it will publish the SPL mint address and the migration program address before December 9. Once those exist, anyone can compare the minted total against the snapshot and confirm that the authority was actually revoked. That confirmation deserves the most scrutiny.

Meanwhile, the portal and its program are under independent review by Hacken, and ZetaChain says the portal opens only after the review is complete and the report is published. The ERC-20 version of ZETA on Ethereum is unaffected by the proposal. Purchaser and core contributor vesting completes on January 1, 2027, and ZetaChain says no newly released ZETA will be sold in 2027.

The biggest practical risk is inattention. Most holders don't need to do anything until December 9, but exchange users depend on each exchange's own conversion window, and anyone holding ZETA through a contract or pool has homework to do beforehand.

Scams add another layer of risk. Any migration with a claim portal invites imitators, and ZetaChain tells holders to trust only its official domains and social accounts. A simple rule of thumb helps here: a site that asks for a seed phrase should be closed immediately, since the legitimate flow only needs a message signature.

On the technical side, claims are checked against the published snapshot rather than the live chain, so they continue to work after the halt. ZetaChain says it will announce any change to the process in advance.

The vote decides the terms, not the direction. If Proposal 2 fails, the direction approved in Proposal 68 stands and ZetaChain returns with a revised proposal. Nothing moves on these terms.

If it passes, the sequence is clear. The security report, mint address and migration program address arrive before December 9. The snapshot, halt, mint and portal opening follow on the day, and the monthly burns run through 2027. ZetaLabs then adds a Premium tier in the first quarter of 2027, with ZETA as the token for access and payment.

Taken together, this looks more like a retirement plan for an L1 than a dramatic supply event. The burn is gradual, the mint is capped, and the claim process is simple on paper. Execution is what will matter most: the audit report, the published addresses and the clean revocation of mint authority. Those are the items to watch between now and December 9.

WeWork co-founder Adam Neumann didn’t plan for his family’s control of WeWork to end at his death but instead expected to pass that control to future generations of Neumanns, too, says Business Insider.

The outlet reports that in a speech Neumann gave to employees in January of this year, footage of which it says it has viewed, Neumann is seen saying that WeWork isn’t “just controlled — we’re generationally controlled.” He reportedly goes on to say that while the five children he shares with wife Rebekah Neumann “don’t have to run the company,” they “do have to stay the moral compass of the company.”

According to BI, Neumann even invoked his future grandchildren, telling those gathered: “It’s important that one day, maybe in 100 years, maybe in 300 years, a great-great-granddaughter of mine will walk into that room and say, ‘Hey, you don’t know me; I actually control the place. These may sound like more outlandish proclamations from Neumann, who has a flair for the dramatic. (Talking to Fast Company earlier this year, he compared WeWork to a rare jewel, asking, “Do you know how long it takes a diamond to be created?”)

But before WeWork began coming apart at the seams, Neumann had every reason to believe that he could pass power down to his heirs.

#5332. Radian Aerospace plans to make its own composite materials for space plane (and for other companies, too)

by Alan Boyle on Nov 17, 2026 at 4:00 amNovember 17, 2026 at 4:00 am

On the way to building a space plane, Seattle-based Radian Aerospace is planning a factory to make the advanced materials it’ll need — and it plans to sell those materials to other companies as well.

Radian CEO Richard Humphrey said he envisions the factory, known as Foundry 1, as a state-of-the-art manufacturing facility with a footprint spanning “just under 100,000 square feet.” Six to 12 sites around the country — including sites in the Pacific Northwest — are currently under consideration, with late 2027 as the target for starting production, he said.

Foundry 1 is meant to produce ceramic matrix composites, or CMCs — not only for Radian’s space plane, but also for other applications ranging from gas-turbine components to high-performance braking systems.

“Each of these industries has a bottleneck that’s being driven by a lack of an industrial base to really build these next-gen materials,” Humphrey told GeekWire.

Humphrey and his teammates ran into that bottleneck while developing Radian One, a reusable rocket-powered plane that’s meant to transport cargo and crew to and from low Earth orbit. Securing a reliable supply chain for the required materials proved so challenging that Radian decided to produce its own.

“Defense and space programs need these materials at costs and production rates that today’s supply base cannot deliver,” Humphrey said today in a news release. “Foundry 1 unlocks a substantial commercial opportunity for Radian and a more direct path to revenue. It positions us to supply customers across these industries while advancing the technology that will make Radian One possible.”

Ceramic matrix composites embed reinforcing fibers, such as carbon or silicon carbide, within a lightweight ceramic material. The ceramic provides resistance to extreme heat, while the fibers help the material carry loads and resist damage from cracking.

Carbon-fiber composites have been around for decades, but turning them into products is typically labor-intensive and expensive. To drive down the cost while improving quality, Radian is developing an automated system for producing CMCs. The company says it’s targeting a 50% reduction in CMC manufacturing costs by cutting manual labor, shortening processing cycles and minimizing waste.

Artificial intelligence will play a role as well, Humphrey said. “We see an AI-native base where we can actually learn from each individual piece while digital-twinning them, so each piece ends up with a digital passport,” he said. “We know exactly where every fiber is, the angle of each fiber to the fiber next to it, and then we do in-process CT screening.”

Greg Scofield, an adviser to Radian and former director of the Purdue Hypersonics Laboratory, said Radian is taking an integrated approach to the challenges surrounding CMC production. “Designing fiber placement, thermal processing and inspection together creates an opportunity to improve cost and quality throughout the production line, with benefits for customers across defense and space,” he said.

The payoff could be huge: A report from Polaris Market Research suggests the global market for advanced composites could rise to $126 billion by 2034.

In partnership with NASA’s Glenn Research Center, Radian has already tested a patent-pending composite material called Dur-E-Therm at temperatures exceeding 2,700 degrees Fahrenheit (1,480 degrees Celsius) under conditions that simulate hypersonic flight.

Radian’s next steps are to select the site for Foundry 1 and begin construction while continuing CMC development at partner facilities. That’s a tall order for a small company.

Humphrey said the company currently has about 20 employees working at locations including the University of Washington’s Advanced Composites Center. Back in 2022, Radian announced a $27.5 million funding round that brought total investment to $32 million at the time. Humphrey said Radian has raised additional funding since then, but he wasn’t ready to share updated figures.

So, how much will Foundry 1 cost? “We’re not quite ready to put a pin in the number,” Humphrey said. “It’s fair to say it’s sub — not a lot less, but it’s sub $100 million in terms of total capital to stand this up for what we’re doing.”

He acknowledged that following through on the plan for Foundry 1 will require raising more capital. “It is part of what we do, and we have a really super group of investors that have been behind us for a long time,” he said.

Humphrey said the Radian One space plane remains the focus of the company’s long-term vision — but for now, the company is devoting all of its resources and capital to Foundry 1.

“It’s the bottleneck to Radian One being successful,” he said. “We think that by applying all of our attention to that, it serves the broader market but also serves advancing Radian One. Both of those are hard things, so we’re going to focus on one hard thing at a time.”

Is Radian becoming an advanced materials and aerospace company? Humphrey said that’s “a good way to think about it,” but he emphasized that aerospace still gets top billing.

“I’d rather be launching today than just be building CMCs,” he said. “But building CMCs is what gets us to flying tomorrow. By advancing materials, it’s our single best way to be ready for Space 3.0, if you want to call it that. … At times we have to be adaptable to really move the project forward, and sometimes it goes a little sideways before you go forward. It’s just the way I’ve come to accept it.”

#5331. Solana (SOL) to Connect With Wall Street’s $4.7 Quadrillion Clearing Giant

Disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. We believe that all content is accurate as of the date of publication, but certain offers mentioned may no longer be available.

The Depository Trust & Clearing Corporation (DTCC) will connect its tokenization service to Solana (SOL) in the second half of 2027, the company said on Nov. 12.

The integration will allow "digital twins" of Russell 1000 stocks, major ETFs and U.S. Treasuries to be issued on the Solana blockchain. In December 2025, the SEC issued a no-action letter that allowed DTC to tokenize these assets.

In 2025, DTCC processed $4.7 quadrillion in securities transactions. Its depository, DTC, holds and services $114 trillion in assets from more than 150 countries.

The DTCC Tokenization Service (DTS) will let large market participants convert conventional securities into tokens, move them across the Solana network and redeem them.

"DTC-tokenized assets made available on Solana – and all blockchain networks integrated with the service – will retain the same investor protections, ownership rights and regulatory safeguards that apply to traditionally held securities," said Brian Steele, president of DTCC Clearing & Securities Services.

According to DTCC CEO Frank La Salla, the integration will also free up securities for use as collateral.

DTS went live on Oct. 28, 2026. At launch, it worked with Canton Network and a private ledger. DTCC said that it adds new networks at clients' request.

"DTCC is committed to providing an open and connected platform that provides our users with access to mature distributed ledger technology networks like Solana that have established performance, security and governance features," said Nadine Chakar, global head of DTCC Digital Assets.

Nick Ducoff, general manager for institutional at the Solana Foundation, also commented on the news. "Institutions choose Solana because it already runs real financial activity at scale," he said.

According to Ducoff, the integration "connects one of the most trusted names in post-trade infrastructure with a network built for always-on markets."

As of Nov. 12, distributed real-world assets (RWA) in the Solana ecosystem reached $5.13 billion across more than 1.02 million holders, according to RWA.xyz. Transfers over the past 30 days totaled $16.48 billion.

The stablecoin market cap on Solana stands at $13.85 billion, with monthly turnover of $387.41 billion.
